CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
DEFINITION OF FOREST 
Recommendation/ Observation  
1.1 The Committee observes that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has 
provided the Committee with a working definition as provided by the Supreme Court.  The Committee 
agrees that any narrow and specific definition of forests may leave out certain types of forests and 
open up the possibility of loopholes being exploited by vested interests. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry must come out with a comprehensive, clear-cut and legally sustainable 
definition of Forest to dispel any kind of doubt in this regard.                                       (Para 3.6) 
Action Taken 
1.2 The Ministry has drafted a comprehensive amendment of Indian Fores t Act, 1927. In this 
draft, a definition of forest has been attempted. The concerns of the Committee have been taken up in 
the said amendment. 
ASSESSMENT OF FOREST COVER  
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.3 It is evident that the anthropogenic pressure endured  by nation's forest is enormous. With 
rapidly growing population, this pressure is set to rise in future. This will seriously affect the quality 
of forests and their sequestration potential. The Committee is of the view that in a developing nation, 
the demand for development imperatives and for creation of infrastructure will always be there. The 
need is, therefore, that our policies are geared to judicious use of forests so that this resource is not 
depleted and the pace of increase of forest cover in the country continues in future too. The 
Committee, accordingly, recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change 
should judiciously manage the forests in the country, if required through necessary policy 
interventions, and ensure that whatever  forest depletion is there or diversion of forest land is 
permitted, we are able to make up more than the area depleted/permitted for diversion so that the 
forest cover of the country remains intact. Environment and Development are supplementary and 
complementary as the two sustain each other.  The need, therefore, is to strike a fine balance between 
the two and to pay due attention on both, within sustainable development framework.         (Para 4.9)                                                                                                                                 
Action Taken 
1.4 The Ministry considers the proposals for diversion of forest land for non -forestry purpose 
under Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. For such diversions of forest lands for non -forestry purposes, 
following measures are taken up to mitigate the possible advers e effects of diversion of such vast 
areas of forests:  
(i)  Compensatory Afforestation (CA) on equivalent non -forest land (except exempted 
category)  
(ii)  Catchment Area Treatment Plan (CATP). 
(iii)  Wildlife Habitat improvement. 
(iv)  Implementation of Rehabilitation & Resettlement. 
(v)  Levy of Net Present Value (NPV) 
(vi)  Monitoring of above activities. 
 

3 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.5 The Committee is also concerned about the decline in the forest cover in the North -Eastern 
States, which is 65.34% of  its geographical area in comparison to the national forest cover of 
21.54%. The Committee recommends that the concerned State Governments and the Union Ministry 
of Environment, Forest & Climate Change must look into the factors responsible for the decline  in 
the forest cover and take all necessary steps to ensure that the trend of decline in forest cover in these 
States is arrested at the earliest.                       (Para 4.10) 
Action Taken 
1.6 As per India State of Forest Report (ISFR) -2017, a decline of 630 sq. km. of forest area has 
been observed in the North Eastern States/UTs. As per India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2017, 
shifting cultivation and development activities have been mentioned  as the reasons for decline in 
forest cover in North -Eastern States. 
1.7 The Ministry has implemented National Afforestation Programme (NAP) since 2000 -02, for 
regeneration of degraded forest area and due weightage is given for NE states in allocating the 
funds under the scheme. An amount of Rs. 828 crores have been released to NE states, since 
inception of the scheme in 2000 -02 till 2018 -19. The percentage relea se to NE States has been 
steadily increasing over 11th, 12th and beyond 12 th Plan Periods as 21%, 24% & 28% respectively.  
 1.8 Further, Green India Mission (GIM) activities were started in the FY 2015-16. So far, a sum of 
Rs. 237.067 crore has been released under GIM to twelve States for carrying out GIM activities. A sum 
of Rs. 79.723 crore has been released in three North -Eastern states namely Manipur, Mizoram and 
Sikkim. Proposals of other States will be considered based on fund availability and project norms.  
Progress reports indicate positive impacts in terms of increase in forest/plantation cover in the project areas 
under GIM.  
1.9 In addition to the above, steps are being taken by the State Forest Departments of North 
Eastern States to increase forest cover. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.10 The Committee notes that only 16 States/Union Territories have been able to provide details 
of digitized boundaries of Recorded Forest Area for incorporation in the India State of Forest Report, 
2017 and as such, it has not been possible to give forest cover inside and outside the recorded forest 
areas of such States. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and

FOREST FIRES  
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.32 The Committee notes with concern the loss of lives in forest fires besides the severe 
degradation of forests & irreparable losses to valuable flora & fauna, there is a crucial need for 
developing an integrated approach for firefighting. The Committee feels that there should be a proper 
co-ordination mechanism between the State Governments, Forest Departments, National Disaster 
Management Authority (NDMA), local Air force authorities and the Central Ministry for quelling 
forest fires. The Committee also feels that public awareness programmes sh ould be conducted 
periodically in the vulnerable forest fire areas about the safety measures. Further, all  State 
Governments should make the registration of the mobile numbers of the concerned areas mandatory 
and ensure that the data base of the registered  mobile numbers of the State Forest Departments is 
kept up-to-date so that any information/alert is passed on to the maximum number of persons. 
            (Para 7.6)
            
 

8 
 
Action Taken 
1.33 Most of the forest fires in the country are ground fire. Forest fires do cause damage to the 
flora and fauna in the forests. However, due to various preventive and management measures taken 
by the forest departments in this regard, the loss of forest wealth is reduced to a great extent.   The 
Ministry coordinates with NDMA, National Institute of Disaster Management, (NIDM), and the 
Ministry of Defence to take any exigent measure to effectively control and douse forest fires taking 
the shape of disaster which are beyond the capacity of State Forest Department.  
1.34 The Ministry has also constituted a Crisis Management Group under the chairmanship of 
Secretary (EF&CC), which has representatives of various Ministries as its members to deal with 
crises arising due to disaster caused by forest f ire. The Ministry recognizes the fact that publicity and 
awareness programme for general public is important to prevent forest fires in the country.   States 
Forest Department also carry out awareness campaigns to educate people regarding forest fires.  
1.35 The Ministry has prepared a National Action Plan on Forest Fire (NAPFF) and sent it to all 
State/UT Governments for taking appropriate action for effective prevention and management of 
forest fire. The NAPFF emphasizes the role of local communities in p revention and control of forest 
fire.  
1.36 The Forest Survey of India, monitors fire incidences in the country based on the data received 
from various sources including National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC). Based on analysis of data, 
it provides fire ale rts to various authorities and the public in the States/UTs on registered mobile 
numbers at an interval of 6 hours every day. Early Warning System for forest fire is functional at FSI 
since 2016. The Early warning alerts are generated every Friday during t he Fires season (January -
June) and are valid during the ensuing week. The Early Warning alerts are sent to the Nodal Officers 
of concerned States/UTs for taking requisite action in the alerted forest areas. These alerts are based 
on parameters like forest cover, forest type, climate variables like temperature and rainfall and recent 
fire incidences over the area. About 50,000 users have been registered to receive fire alerts.  
Recommendation/ Observation

respective Forest Departments and Central Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for

CAUSES OF WILDLIFE DESTRUCTION: MAN -ANIMAL CONFLICT,  POACHING, 
FRAGMENTATION OF HABITAT 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.41 The Committee notes with serious concern that wildlife is increasingly coming under pressure 
in all parts of the country. Reports of man - animal conflict threaten to tear apart the respec t for 
wildlife that has traditionally been the hallmark of conservation in India. The Committee feels that 
community led solutions must be explored in order to prevent fragmentation of habitats of wild lives 
besides policy interventions of the Ministry.          (Para 9.6) 
Action Taken 
1.42   Human-animal conflict has become a serious issue in several parts of the country during the 
recent times. Incidences of crop damage by straying wild animals are also reported from time to time. 
Management of such conflict situations is the primary responsibility of the respective State Governments. 
Central Government provides some financial and technical assistance to the State/UT Governments 
under the various Centrally Sponsored Schemes for management of wildlife including conflict situations.  
1.43 Under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 there are provisions to deal with problematic wild 
animals, Section 11& 12 of the Act, inter-alia, empowers the Chief Wildlife Warden and authorized 
officers to take necessary steps to handle problematic wild animals and population management of wild 
animals responsible for damage and destruction of crops. 
1.44 This Ministry vide O.M. No. 1 -5212014-VVL-1 dated 24 th December, 2014 had issued an 
Advisory in the context of human-wildlife conflict wherein the States have been requested to take pro-
active steps including exercise of powers under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 for mitigation of 
human-wildlife confli ct. Ministry has also issued a detailed advisory on 1 st June, 2015 to the 
State/Union Territory Governments on the priority actions for management of human wildlife conflict. 
1.45 Further, the Ministry has approved a pilot project on the immuno-contraception for controlling the 
population of wild animals responsible for damage and destruction of crops, namely; elephant, wild boar, 
monkey, and nilgai. 
1.46 Ministry has increased the ex-gratia rates for loss of life and damage to crops/property 
by wild animals vide letter No. 14 -2/2011 WL -1 (part) dated  9th February, 2018. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.47 The Committee is also of the view that wildlife protection requires concerted efforts and that 
growing incidents of poaching, encroachment and habitat destruction should be tackled in an 
effective manner and it also requires implementation of various Acts such as Wildlife Protection Act, 
1972 etc. and statutes in letter and spirit.                                                                                (Para 9.7)           
Action Taken 
1.48 Forest and Wildlife areas are managed by the State Governments. Forest and Wildlife areas 
are notified as per provisions of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 or the State 
Forest Act. State Forest and Wildlife Departments are mandated for management in accordance with the 
Working/Management Plans prepared for this purpose.  
1.49 Both the Central and State Governments are taking steps for effective management of wildlife. 
The provisions contained in the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, enable the concerned authorities for 
taking steps for wildlife conservation. The important provisions in this regard are as given below: 

10 
 
i. Designation of Officers: The Act provides for designation of Officers by the State 
Government (e.g., the Chief Wildlife Warden, Honorary Wildlife warden, etc.) for implementation of 
the provisions of the Act. The Chief Wildlife Wardens are assisted by the respective Park Managers/ 
Field Directors and Range Forest Officers in management of Wildlife areas including pro tection and 
conservation of wild species,  their habitats, enforcement aspects for control of poaching and illegal 
trade in wildlife and their parts and products, regulation in entry in Protected Areas, scientific 
research, photography, etc. on wildlife and  their habitats; control of introduction of exotic and 
invasive alien species; protection of captive wild animals, including those in the zoo, rescue centres 
etc. 
ii. Measures for protection of National Parks and Sanctuaries: As a general practice, 
National Parks and Sanctuaries are declared by the respective State Governments. Section 33 of the Wild 
Life (Protection) Act, 1972 places responsibility on the respective State Chief Wildlife Wardens to take 
such measures, in the interest of wildlife and take such steps to ensure the security of wild animals in 
the Sanctuary and for the preservation of the Sanctuary and wild animals therein. 
iii. Regulating Hunting of wild animals: Hunting of wild animals is prohibited except under 
certain special circumstances wherein the State Chief Wildlife Wardens are empowered to grant permit. 
In case of a Schedule-I animal becoming dangerous to human life or is so disabled or diseased beyond 
recovery and that that such animal cannot be ca ptured, tranquilized or translocated, then the Chief 
Wildlife Warden maypermit any person to hunt such animal. In case the animal can be captured, then 
it should not be kept in captivity unless the animal cannot be rehabilitated in the wild. In case of any  
wild animal listed in Schedule -II, Schedule-III or Schedule -IV has become dangerous to human life 
or to property (including standing crops on any land) or is disabled or diseased beyond recovery, the 
Chief Wildlife Warden may permit any person to hunt suc h animal or group of animals in a specified 
area. 
iv. Regulation in entry to Protected Areas : Entry into a Sanctuary and National Park is 
regulated and a permission to enter a Sanctuary can be granted by the State Chief Wildlife Warden. 
The Wild life (Protecti on) Act, 1972 also empowers an officer, not below the rank of Assistant 
Conservator of Forests to evict any person from a Sanctuary/National Park, who unauthorisedly 
occupies Government land in contravention of the provisions of the Act. 
1.50 In addition, at the Central Government level, MoEFCC has adopted a National Wildlife 
Action Plan. The Action Plan was first adopted in 1983 and was revised in 2002 for a period till 2016. 
The Action Plan has been further revised for the period 2017 -2031 and envisages m anagement of 
wildlife on a Landscape level.  
1.51 Besides, the National Environment Policy adopted by the Ministry in 2006 also has actionable 
points for management of wildlife and its habitat, including Protected Areas. 
1.52 The Ministry, through its policies and programmes have also been concentrating in a more 
collective and coordinated governance approach wherein the Government, Non Government 
Organizations, communities, local bodies, Gram Sabhas facilitate decision making process. People 
are being made important actors in preserving the natural resources for their own future. The local 
and traditional knowledge base of the indigenous and local communities offers an excellent 
opportunity for enhancing the management interventions. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1. 53 The Committee notes that there exists a manual prepared by Wildlife Institute of India, 
Dehradun for making roads or any linear infrastructure and what care should be taken for wildlife 
and National Board of Wildlife has also made it mand atory that any linear projects whether it is a 
rail tracks, roads or canals or transmission lines, they have to follow the guidelines when the 
clearance is given particularly in the eco -fragile and wildlife areas. However, the Committee feels 

11 
 
that this is not being followed in right earnest and even some national parks/sanctuaries have 
roads/highways within its periphery. Therefore, the Committee recommends that prior to approval of 
any infrastructural/ development projects, this aspect must be looked into by the competent 
authorities or the concerned agencies. Further, the Committee hopes that Ministry shall sensitize the 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways while considering the highway projects, and persuade 
them to spare the natural resources as well as wildlife sanctuaries/national parks/animal corridors 
etc. at the planning stage itself and wherever possible take a detour and completely leave it.                                                      
                       (Para 9.11) 
Action Taken 
1.54 This recommendation has been noted and the matter has been sent to Ministry of Road

1.56 The Standing Committee of National Board for Wild Life considers and recommends the linear

DRAFT NATIONAL FOREST POLICY, 2018 AND RELATED ASPECTS 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.78 The Committee also observed that the general perception of the public is that the Draft Policy 
emphasizes the commercialization of forests,  particularly refer to as the degraded forests, so as to 
serve the interests of industry and to bring the private sector in for the management of forests through 
the means of Public Private Partnersh ip Model. Similarly, apprehensions have been conveyed by 
various stakeholders that the Draft Policy envisages curtailing of rights of tribals, and tribal 
communities and Traditional Forest-Dwellers in ownership and control of non timber forest produce 
as also in community resources. Concerns are also being expressed that the Draft Policy aims to take 
away the rights of Gram Sabhas for management of forests and instead hands it over to the proposed 
centrally-controlled Corporations. The Committee feels that if too much emphasis given to Private 
Partnership Model in management of forests in the proposed DNFP, we might end up with losing the 
forest lands whether it is degraded or otherwise. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
adequate safeguards be taken after due consultations with the stakeholders in order to protect the 
forests from over exploitation by private parties alongwith the legitimate rights of tribals and Gram 
Sabhas.                                                         (Para 10.7)  
Action Taken 
1.79 The basic objectives, principles and goals of previous policy have been retained in the Draft 
New Policy. A massive need based programme of afforestation and tree planting on all degraded land 
for enhancing the forest cover in the country and meeting national needs while safeguarding rights of 
local people and tribal was also highlighted in the previous Policy of 1988. The present policy has 
only further emphasized the need to increase productivity of plantations for growing more wood, 
which is a carbon neutral renewable resource.  Role and responsibility of Gram Sabha, tribals and 
other traditional forest dwellers have been duly reflected at all relevant section of the present policy 
including in the preamble of proposed Policy. 
1.80 The policy  promotes afforestation in Public Private Partnership (PPP) mode only in scrub/ 
degraded forest areas which are not wildlife habitats or of any substantial ecological importance and 
also in areas outside forests. Further promotion of trees plantation in de graded areas will help in 
reducing the dependency on import of timber and its products by the country. Afforestation in PPP 
mode emphasizes that the communities, Van Sanrakshan  Samiti (VSS), Joint Forest Management 
Committees (JFMCs) will be equal partners  in the process and will get their due share from the 
harvest.  All the forestry operations in forests will take place as per approved working plans.  
1.81 It has been highlighted in the present Draft policy that management of forests will be done 
only as per the Central Government approved Working /Management Plans. It will be ensured that 
there is no violation of FRA, PESA and other Acts regarding rights of tribals and other forest 
dwellers.

TADOBA-ANDHARI TIGER RESERVE 
Recommendation/ Observation 
4.1 The Committee observes that Tadoba -Andhari Tiger Reserve has emerged as one the most 
important tourist destinations for wildlife lovers and enthusiasts  as a result of which the revenue 
generation by the tiger reserve has seen a consistent increase during the last few years. The tiger 
reserve has also become an important source of livelihood for a large number of people in the area. 
In this backdrop, the Committee is constrained to note the environmental issues pertaining to the 
Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve brought to the notice of the Committee and is of the view that these 
issues deserve a serious consideration. The Committee, accordingly, recommends tha t while 
establishing the irrigation project on the Human River, it should be ensured that the tiger corridor 
between Tadoba -Andhari Tiger Reserve and Bramhapuri Forest  Division that connects Satpuda -
Maikal Landscape is not cut -off. Similarly, it should be ensured that movement of animals across the 
corridors is not the least restricted while four -laning the Chandrapur -Mul-Gadchiroli road and 
Nagpur-Umred-Nagbhid-Bramhapuri road. The Committee also recommends that the environmental 
assessment of the coal min es of Western Coalfields Limited and the thermal power plant of 
Chandrapura Thermal Power Station located along the southern border of the tiger reserve on the 
activities of the wildlife needs to be carried out at the earliest and remedial measures in resp ect of 
adverse impact of the same be taken on priority.  The Ministry should also consider carrying out 
environmental assessment of other wildlife  sanctuaries/parks affected by such industries/power 
plants.                                                    (Para 9.28)  
Action Taken 
4.2  A team was constituted to suggest options for retaining vital tiger corridors vis -à-vis the 
proposed Hooman dam, which submitted its report in 2015 and suggested the following options:  
Option A : Shifting the location of the  human river project upstream by a distance of 5 Km, this 
will make sure that the structural corridor of 5 -6 km will be safeguard downstream and will also 
reduce human -wildlife interface on the northern side of the Tadoba and will help in reducing 
human-wildlife conflict in the area.  
Option B: Restore the structural corridor of 3 -4 km downstream by purchasing the private land and 
converting the purchased land into forest by planting native trees. The construction work will only 
start once the land is purcha sed and first phase of plantation work on the purchased land is

24. As regards the Antarctica Research Programme, the Department has originally 
sought Rs. 23 crores . The Planning Commission had first agreed to provide Rs. 20.20 crores 
but it finally approved an outlay of Rs. 20 crores. India's foray in the Antarctica commenced 
with the launching of the first expedition in 1981. Thereafter a number of multi-disciplinary 
and multi-institutional scientific expenditions have beeri sent to the Antarctica regularly on 
annual basis. The first research station in the Antarctica, "Dakshin Gangotri" was 
commissioned in 1983 and was functional until 1987. In 1988 the settting of Indian permanent 
station "Maitri", with modern infrastructural facilities for conducting temporary scientific 
research was established in the Schirmachar Oasis. Dakshin Gangotri Station is being 
maintained as a supply base. Sdentists from diverse fields drawn from national laboratories, 
institutions and universities are P.rovided with adequate opportunities to carry out experi­
ments in all major branches of polar science. The ·logistic support is extended by various 
wings of the Defence Services and Laboratories of the Defence Research and Development 
Organisation. The programme has thus become one of international Prestige and is therefore 
necessary that the programme is allowed to continue with adequate budgetary support. 
25. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should get what it had 
originally projected i.e. a sum of Rs. 23 crores. Besides, the Department should endeavour for 
commercial exploitation of the Krill ftshery and other such resources in the Antarctic waters 
because of its demand in the overseas markets.

programme is reviewed and guided by the PMN Board of Management. Considering the 
potential of the benefits that could accrue for future industrial programmes, the Committee 
feels that in view of the need for India to be among the developed nations in the high 
technology in the Ocean sector and from the long-term strategy and geo-political considera-

tions, it is essential to continue technology development efforts for exploration and exploitation 
of the polymetallic nodules so that we do not lag behind other pioneer investors and enable 
' the country to begin commercial exploitation when economic feasibility is established. Here 
also the Committee is of the view that the Department's original demand of Rs. 11 crores 
should be met in full whereas the Planning Commission has sanctioned only a sum of Rs. 9 
crores.

new ship may cost Rs. 100 crores keeping in view our requirements in respect of the design of 
construction and it may take 3 to 4 years to time to get the same. Therefore, the ready 
availability of the suitable second-hand ship may be explored for the purpose. The Committee 
has now been given to understand that the offers made by South Africa, Germany, Ukraine, 
Finland, Norway and Denmark in response to the global enquiry did not conform to our 
detailed specifications, the Department has evaluated in the meantime, the option of 
chartering a vessel for a period of 3 years instead of annual charter which could result in 
reduction of charter cost. Accordingly, Department has entered ;-into a contract with M/s. 
Reiber Shipping Company, Norway for a three year charter. They have stated that an official 
delegation which visited Russia for a on-the-spot market survey in January, 1995 could not 
identify a suitable second-hand vessel meeting our requirements. 
28. The Committee feels that the Department should work out the economics for all the 
alternatives to acquire including the purchase of a new vessel and plan its strategy 
accordingly. The Committee should be apprised of economic of all the proposals. 
29. The marine instrumentation has received an allocation of Rs. 2 crores· in the budget 
estimates for 1996-97 against the budgetary support of Rs. 1 crore last year. The allocation 
covers shore to fishing vessel communication which is a reliable means of passing messages. 
SOS signals and data with the help of a fixed shore station and a hand held VHF radio 
telephone on board the fishing craft. The system would help the traditional and small-scale 
fishermen who are venturing for fishing for a range of about 40 kms. from the shore and had 
no means to communication from the fishing craft and vice-a-versa. With the advancement in 
the communication technology it has become possible to provide such facilities to the 
fishermen for ensuring their safety at sea. 
30. The Committee therefore recommends that expeditious steps be taken to select a 
suitable model of walkie-talkie set and the other technology to cover maximum number of 
fishermen within a short span of time across the country. 
31. The Committee is of the view that the extraction of drugs from the ~ea has immense 
potential. By now more than 100 pure compounds have been isolated and characterised 
some of which posses interesting biological activities while others even though biologically 
not promising possess interesting structures. The Department has taken up standardisation 
and introduction of new bioassay methods for violating anti-viral activity both IN VITRO 
and IN VIVO, casting hepatoprotective agents, anti-diabetic agents, anti-filarial agents, anti­
fungal agents using multi-fungal infection models. 
32. The Committee recommends that the Department should put in sustained effort in 
tapping this potential by involving universities/institutes. The Committee is happy to note that 

the number of active/modern organisms have been screened. The Committee hopes that in the 
near future it will be possible to commercially exploit the area for development of drugs from 
medical substances obtained from sea.

REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Committee deals with the action taken 
by the Government on the recommendations/observations contained in Three Hundred 
Twenty Fifth Report of the Committee on 'An Expanded Role for the Department of 
Atomic Energy (DAE) in Cancer Treatment in India through An Enlarged Network of 
the Tata Memorial Centre  (TMC)'.  The Report was presented to Hon'ble Chairman, 
Rajya Sabha and forwarded to Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha on 11 th November, 2019 
and thereafter presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 19th 
November, 2019. 
2.  Action Taken Note (ATN) was received from the Department of Atomic Energy 
on the  recommendations/observations contained in the Three Hundred Twenty F ifth 
Report.  This has been categorized as follows:- 
Chapter I:  Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
Government:  
Para:- 5.2, 5.4, 5.5, 5.7, 5.8, 5.9, 5.10, 5.11, 5.12, 5.13, 5.14 and 5.15   
Total recommendations – 12.  Accepted. 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Department has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in Chapter-1 of the Report. 
Chapter II: Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire 
to    pursue in   view of the Government’s replies:  
                      Para:-. 5.6 
                      Total recommendations  – 01.  Not to be pursued further. 
The Committee is convinced with the replies furnished by the Department 
and, therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendation further. 
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee:  
                       Para:-    5.3  
       Total recommendation  – 01.  Not convincing reply. 
The Committee expresses its concern over the non -implementation of its 
recommendation contained in Chapter-III and desires that the Department 
should furnish convincing action taken steps in respect of th se 
recommendation.

the Government are still awaited:   

2 
 
 
 
 
  Para:- 6.2 
Total recommendation - 01. To be pursued further.  
The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and 
detailed Action Taken Notes in respect of the further 
Recommendations/Observations made by the Committee in Chapter I and 
III of the Report.   The Department should also furnish the updated 
information regarding the paragraph men tioned in Chapter IV of the 
Report.  
3. The details of the ATR have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters. 
  

3 
 
 
 
 
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED 
BY THE GOVERNMENT 
 
HUB AND SPOKE MODEL – A PROPOSAL 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.1 The Committee acknowledges the fact that DAE , through the Tata Memorial 
Centre, has significant experience in setting up cancer centres in different parts of the 
country as well as the Hub and Spoke model of care delivery. The close link between 
radiation and radionuclide based diagnosis and treatment for cancer, and their 
experience with setting up and running the National Cancer Grid. This makes TMC 
under DAE an uniquely, ideal organization to take up the responsibility of a 
nationwide government funded Hub and Spoke network which will take high quality 
cancer care closer to the district and region of patients across the country.   (Para 5.2) 
Action Taken  
1.2 Noted a separate budgetary head for TMC (through DAE) would be necessary to 
be able to establish and run these Centres and deliver world class care, as mentioned by 
the Hon'ble Prime Minister when inviting TMC to set up a cancer hospital in Varanasi.  
Also, there is a need to make the Homi Bhabha National Institute (HBNI) an institution 
of national importance (INI); A proposal for the same is under active consideration by 
the Government of India.  All existing and proposed Cancer Centres under DAE/TMC 
should also be brought under HBNI - this is extremely important to create the trained 
human resources for these Centres.  
Further Comments 
1.3 The Committee seconds the view point of the Department of Atomic Energy 
that a separate budgetary head is necessary for making the funds available to 
Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) through Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) to 
establish and run the Hubs across the country to deliver world class ca ncer care 
in the country .  For the purpose, the Committee strongly feels that the 
Department of Atomic Energy should make a proposal to the Ministry of Finance 
and impress upon them to make the funds available to the TMC through DAE for 
establishing the cancer care units/Hubs for which a detailed proposal needs to be 
first prepared by the TMC highlighting the number of existing cancer cares, 
projected increase in cancer cases in the coming 10 -15 years, inadequacy of 
infrastructure to tackle these cases; funds required for setting up the Hubs, etc. so 
that the Ministry of Finance optimizes the fund requirement of TMC in a  phased 
manner.   

4 
 
 
 
 
1.4 The Committee is also hopeful that the proposal of making the HBNI an 
institute of national importance would see ligh t of the day soon and all the 
formalities related would be complete d in a timely manner so that the intended 
benefits could be yielded.   
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.5 The Committee strongly feels that the TMC should take all the stakeholders on 
board re lated to cancer treatment, and leverage some of the existing centres and 
upgrading them to TMC standards rather than building new de novo centres.  The 
Committee, therefore, opines that TMC should at the outset list out all such existing 
centres/institutions such as AIIMS, Central/State Government Hospitals/Medical 
Colleges, etc. which can be converted into either a hub or spoke, so that existing 
facilities of these centres/institutions can be optimised and made available to the 
cancer patients of that regi on/State which will further minimise their migration to 
other places. This model has been successfully evidenced in setting up the hub in 
Varanasi anchored in the Railways Hospital. The Committee further feels that 
selection of the existing centres/institutions be made cautiously and judiciously so as to 
avoid duplication of efforts, ensuring standardised care.                                 (Para 5.4) 
 
Action Taken  
1.6 Upgradation of the 29 regional cancer centres with increasing infrastructure and 
human resource would enable these centres to be hubs for cancer care.  In addition, the 
approximately 300 government medical colleges should start an oncology department 
which could serve as the spokes.  The larger government medical colleges like AIIMS 
could also be supported to be hubs.  This would cost less than 50% of setting up de 
novo new cancer centres.  This can be initiated a fter an order is passed by both the 
Central Government as well as the respective State Governments and run on the Tata 
Memorial Ce ntre model.  Government may provide funds for the first 10 years by 
which time these centres are expected to be self-sustaining.  
Further comments  
1.7 The Committee , while accepting the submission made by the DAE , feels 
that synergy and close co -ordination between the Central Government and State 
Governments holds the key in successfully rolling out hub and spoke model of 
TMC across the country.  However, the Committee would like to emphasis e on 
the fact that the Central government must take lead in the matter and make 
available the required funds for initially upgrading the 29 regional cancer centres 
to be the hubs for cancer care in the country and the intricacies involved may first 
be firmed up in co -ordination and consultation with the 29 regio nal cancer 
centres and the respective State Government s so that a clean picture can emerge 

5 
 
 
 
 
and a timeframe can be fixed for the completion of the task.   It may, therefore, be 
imperative on the part of DAE to sensitize the Ministry of Finance of the 
budgetary allocation required for the purpose.                                                          
Recommendation/ Observation  
1.8  The Committee is of the considered view that Hub and Spoke Model of TMC if 
rolled out/implemented in various parts of the country, in a phased and scientific 
manner, will surely go a long way in making available affordable cancer treatment to 
the cancer patients. The increased number of hubs and spokes will put TMC in a much 
more advantageous position to negotiate with the in dustry including pharmaceuticals 
and medical equipment providers, which in turn would further help in bringing down 
the overall cost of cancer treatment across the board.                                     (Para 5.5) 
 
Action Taken 
1.9 Department agrees.  The experience has been that the procurement price of 
drugs/consumables reduces with increased volumes.  Economies of scale would 
certainly play a part in decreasing cost of drugs.  It is also stated that governmental 
incentives for pro duction of generic drugs would also promote high quality low -cost 
drugs and consumables in healthcare.   
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.10 The Committee is also of the view that keeping prices low of medicines related to 
cancer treatment is paramount keepin g in view of the poor financial and social 
background of the patients.  To achieve this objective, the Committee hopes that there 
must be a robust mechanism to check the prices of essential medicines related to 
treatment of cancer.  These medicines must be  made available at the hubs and spokes 
at rate contract of Government.                                                                        (Para 5.7) 
 
Action Taken  
1.11 There have been many recent initiatives by the Government to cap the prices of 
essential drugs.  These will be made available at the Hubs and spokes at rate contract 
of Government.  
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.12 The Committee also notes that the proposa l of TMC for its Hub and Spoke 
Model expects that the land for setting up these hubs and spokes would be made 
available to TMC free of cost by the State Government.  The Committee, therefore 
strongly feels that a High Level Steering Committee headed by the Minister of State for 
Atomic Energy, the Chief Secretaries/Administrators of all the States and Union 
Territories as Members and Director, TMC as Member Secretary be constituted so that 

6 
 
 
 
 
all the modalities related to the adoption and rolling out of the Hub  and Spoke Model 
can be chalked out in a time bound manner in order to not only contain the patient 
migration but also to ensure that state -of-the-art facilities be made available as close 
as possible to cancer patients. This Committee may also be empowere d to evolve 
funding models that are tailored for the specific needs of States. The Committee also 
recommends additional funds for affordable accommodation and transit camps for 
patients and caregivers to ease their hardship.                                                 (Para5.8) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.13 It is a welcome suggestion.  An Advisory Group comprising of the Minister of 
State (Atomic Energy), Principal Scientific Advisor, Secretary, Department of Atomic 
Energy, Chief Secretaries of all States and Union Territories, Director, Tata Memorial 
Centre may be constituted.   
 
1.14 In addition, it is suggested that a Core Steering Committee comprising of the 
Secretary, DAE or his nominee, Director, Tata Memorial Centre with two additional 
representatives from TMC, representative from the Ministry of health  and Family 
Welfare, representative from the Finance Ministry and representative from the HRD 
Ministry be created to oversee and plan the creation of the Hubs and Spokes.  This 
committee would be primarily responsible for overseeing the entire effort, prio ritizing 
the phasing of the cancer treatment hubs, and monitoring and evaluation of progress 
with the project.  Chief Secretaries of specific states would be Special Invitees to the 
Core Committee meetings when their respective states hubs/spokes are being  planned 
and implemented.  
 
1.15 Decisions on phasing this programme would be based on estimated cancer 
burden, current availability of cancer treatment facilities and availability of 
appropriated centres to be taken over as DAE Hubs.  This Committee would  also 
ensure prompt clearances for land, water, environment and electricity for the creation 
of the Hubs.  The Department also agrees with the recommendation that all hubs and 
spokes should have arrangements/facilities for affordable accommodation for pati ents 
and their care-givers. 
 
  Further comments  
1.16 The Department, however, appears to have accepted the recommendation 
made by the Committee, yet no action seems to have been initiated thereon by the 
Department.  The Committee would have appreciated had the Department made 
earnest steps in the matter and forwarded a detailed roadmap for the purpose to 
the State Government s so that some action may have sta rted by now.                               

7 
 
 
 
 
The Committee, therefore, desires the Department to tak e up the matter with the 
State Governments and make necessary headway in the matter.  
Recommendation/ Observation  
1.17 The Committee underlines that the criteria for hubs and spokes cannot be 
determined based on population alone, as underserved regions could also be sparsely 
populated and geographically far -off from densely populated centres. Therefore, 
special attention s hould be paid to ease the hardship of cancer patients in remote 
areas.  Particularly, Dr. B Barooah Cancer Institute at Guwahati should be upgraded 
and developed as a common hub for the North Eastern states with immediate focus on 
infrastructure development and training of human resources at all levels, until similar 
hubs and spokes are set up in all North Eastern states. In addition, focused research 
must be carried out on the higher incidence of cancer in the entire region.    (Para 5.9) 
 
Action Taken 
1.18 It is stated that location of Hubs and Spokes should not be made on the 
population served alone; it should also take into account cancer incidence rates, travel 
distances, pre -existing centres capable of treating cancer in the region.   The 
Department also agree that the Dr. B. Borooah Cancer Institute in Guwahati should be 
upgraded and serve as a hub for most of the North Eastern India till other centres are 
set up.  Spokes in North Eastern India could be customized depending on the 
geographic necessit ies- e.g. creation of two smaller spokes rather than one bigger 
spoke, given the challenges of travel in the North East.  Research should also be 
initiated into the reasons for increased cancer incidence in the region.  
Recommendation/ Observation  
1.19 The Committee hopes that after materialisation of Hubs and Spoke in various 
States, Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) would be signed between the Tata 
Memorial Centre, Mumbai and respective State Governments clearly demarcating 
their roles, functions, respon sibilities, financial obligations (if any), areas of 
jurisdiction, etc.                                                                                              (Para 5.10) 
                                                                                                                           
Action Taken 
1.20 Noted.  A robust mechanism, which ensures that both the Hubs and Spokes run 
on the same model as that of Tata Memorial Centre with constant handholding and 
oversight, is important.  
 
Recommendation/ Observation  
1.21 The Committee very well understands that a project as ambitious as Hub and 
Spoke Model of TMC requires a tremendous amount of financial backing from the 

8 
 
 
 
 
Central Government for setting up hubs as well as the State Governments for land, 
infrastructure and for running the spokes in their respective States.  However, the 
Committee strongly feels that it is the responsibility of the Government to make 
available the state -of-the-art medical facilities to its citizens whe re their ailments can 
be cured and utmost care be taken of the  patients, especially when  two-thirds of the 
total expenditure for cancer treatment is currently being borne by patients.                     
The Committee, therefore, desires that a separate an d dedicated budget for setting up 
state-of-the-art cancer facilities in the form of these proposed hubs in various parts of 
the country be made available to the Department of Atomic Energy/Tata Memorial 
Centre from the Union Government without compromising  on the budget for other 
equally important activities of the DAE.                                                         (Para 5.11) 
 
Action Taken  
1.22 The Department agrees with the recommendation.  It is necessary to have a 
separate budgetary head for cancer treatment for TMC under DAE.  Keeping in view 
the increasing numbers of patients affected by cancer, this is an important investment.  
Recommendation/ Observation  
1.23 The Committee further notes that various schemes/projects/programmes are 
being run by the Union as well as State Governments for which financial 
assistance/support is also provided.  The Committee, however, is of the opinion that 
the current style of working in silos to address cancer treatment in India may not yield 
the desired resu lts and thus there should be synergy between all such 
Governments/authorities/agencies. The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that the 
Department of Atomic Energy/Tata Memorial Centre should work in tandem and close 
co-ordination with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India as 
well as State Governments so that concerted efforts are put to tackle the cancer 
burden.                                                                                                             (Para 5.12) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.24 The Department , along with TMC, would work closely with the Ministry of 
Health & Family Welfare as well as State Governments in this initiative.  
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.25 The Committee underlines the importance of human resources of the likes of 
highly qualified doctors, skilled technicians, paramedics, nursing staff and 
administrators as the backbone of the Hub and Spoke model as proposed by TMC. 
Therefore, the Committee s trongly agrees with the recommendation of TMC that the 
infrastructure and human resources must be sanctioned in tandem for the success of 
the Hub and Spoke model.                                                                               (Para 5.13) 

9 
 
 
 
 
Action Taken 
1.26 Creating human resources sufficient to manage the different Hubs and Spokes 
under this plan would take time, and sanction of manpower needs to be made along 
with the initial approval.  That wo uld provide adequate time to up -skill general 
physicians and surgeons to treat cancer as well as create human resources adequate to 
work in these Centres. 
Recommendation/ Observation  
1.27 The Committee applauds the innovative ‘share in income’ scheme of the TMC 
to incentivize highly qualified doctors to give up the private sector and serve the public 
healthcare system. The Committee also notes the tremendous research and career 
growth opportunities provided by TMC to its staff. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Union Government and Sta te Governments to adopt such innovative 
practices and also pursue other schemes that will meet the challenge of adequate 
human resources in the battle against cancer.                                                (Para 5.14) 
Action Taken 
 
1.28 Noted. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation  
1.29 The Committee strongly recommends that ‘Institute of National Importance’ 
status be granted to ‘Homi Bhabha National Institute’ through an Act of Parliament, 
since it will be the knowledge, training and research hub for human resources to 
address cancer care in India. With the status of ‘Institute of National Importance’, the 
TMC would be in a position to recruit generalists (MD General Medicine, Paediatrics, 
MS General Surgery) who will work under the supervision of trained and qualified 
medical and surgical oncologists in these hubs and spokes.  The Committee, therefore, 
urges upon the Department of Atomic Energy/Tata Memorial Centre to pursue the 
matter and impresses upon the Union Government, highlighting the significance and 
importance of Homi Bhabha Na tional Institute being granted the status of ‘Institute of 
National Importance’.                                                                                     (Para 5.15) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.30 The Department agrees.  The proposal of DAE for converting HBNI into INI 
through an Act of Parliament is under active consideration with Government of India.   

10 
 
 
 
 
CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE 
DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S 
REPLIES 
 
HUB AND SPOKE MODEL – A PROPOSAL 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.1  The Committee is of the considered opinion that since creation of infrastructure 
and research for treatment of cancer requires huge investment of money and human 
resources, the Department of Atomic Energy/TMC may chalk out strategy for linkages 
with various industries/companies for funding under Corporate Social Responsibility 
(CSR) in lieu of knowledge sharing, technology transfer etc.  The industry tie -up may 
further aid in kick starting ‘Make in India’ initiatives for pharmaceuticals and 
advanced medical equipment for cancer treatment.                                         (Para 5.6)  
 
Action Taken  
 
2.2 While some part of the investment into upgrading existing centres or 
establishing new cancer departments in medical colleges may come from CSR funds, 
this is likely to be a small proportion of overall funds required.  Meaningful 
Upgradation of existing regional can cer centers and developing oncology departments 
in government medical colleges would require funding support which will not be 
feasible by CSR funding alone.

REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE COMMITTEE 
 
HUB AND SPOKE MODEL – A PROPOSAL 
Recommendation/ Observation 
3.1 Taking note of the Hub and Spoke Model submitted by Tata Memorial Centre, 
the Committee is of the considered opinion that this model caters to not only the 
existing infrastructural requirements of the cancer patients but for the future demand 
as well. The Committee also notes that the government expenditure on TMC for cancer 
treatment is proving to be of immense value as evidenced by the rising demand from 
cancer patients all over the country for treatment at TMC.  The Committee, therefore, 
finds merit in the proposal of TMC with regard to immed iately embark on a mapping 
exercise to determine the phasing of its Hub and Spoke model, so that the first few hubs 
can be set up in the regions where incidences of cancer have been increasing and 
facilities for the cancer care is woefully inadequate.  The  Committee, therefore, urges 
upon TMC to evolve a mechanism so that the mapping exercise identifies locations 
where TMC would like to set up its hubs and recommend spokes for State Governments 
to be started and completed in a time bound manner.                                      (Para 5.3) 
Action Taken  
3.2 It is stated that TMC is also strengthening the existing system of cancer centres 
through the National Cancer Grid & a large network of 198 cancer centres, research 
institutions, patient groups and professional societies in India are already a part of this

Further comments

strengthening the existing system of cancer centres through NCG  feels that t he

therefore, reiterates its recommendation and desires TMC to initiate action and

Cancer problem in India 
1.7 The growing burden of cancer in India is a major healthcare issue. As per the 
International Agency for Research on Cancer GLOBOCAN project, it is expected that the burden 
of cancer in India will increase from an estimated incidence of 1.1 million cases in 2018 to about 
1.9 million in 2040. What is more alarming is that cancer deaths are expected to rise from 0.78 
million in 2018 to 1.3 million in 2040. The mortality: incidence ratio of 0.68 in India is far 
higher than that in very high human development index (HDI) countries (0. 38) and high HDI 
countries (0.57). While some of this disparity is because of over -diagnosis in more developed 
countries, it is also due to the unequal distribution of and lack of access to health care resources 
across India. Even among those who are able to access health care, survival is compromised by 
advanced stage at diagnosis and inability to afford optimum treatment. In addition to increasing 
awareness about cancer, augmenting infrastructure for cancer care and improving access to 
health care, one of  the key solutions is to increase the emphasis on research that can identify 
affordable, cost-effective interventions for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of common 
cancers in India. Currently, there are very few government funded cancer centres pro viding high 
quality cancer care, education and research. 
National Cancer Control Programme 
1.8 Although the National Cancer Control Program me (NCCP) has been in place since 1975, 
it has not been impactful primarily because of the lack of political support in past years. We 
propose that the NCCP be revisited under the aegis of the National Cancer Grid, a flagship 
programme of the Government of I ndia. Primarily, the focus needs to continue on prevention of 
common cancers like those of the oral cavity, cervix, lung. Early detection by increasing 
awareness amongst the lay public as well as the primary care physician (including alternative 
medicine practitioners and traditional healers) needs to be at a priority. However, there is also the 
need for augmenting treatment facilities in various parts of the country. Currently, over     two-
thirds of cancer care is provided by private sector. Increasing co sts and out of pocket expenses , 
therefore, results in close to 6% of India‟s population going below the poverty line every year. 
There is an urgent need to augment the cancer care facilities in the country. In addition, attention 
is also required in the areas of palliative care, survivorship and patient advocacy. Data collection 
and aggregation, evaluating patterns of care, and health technology assessment are also required 
to channelize scarce healthcare resources appropriately. 
A dual approach is required  for planning a systematic National Cancer Plan . First, 
existing centres should be strengthened to provide uniform standards of cancer care across the 
country. Secondly, additional Government run cancer centres need to be set up to fill the gaps in 
access across several geographies. The first approach has been successfully done by the National 
Cancer Grid, a large network of cancer centres, research institutions, patient groups and 
professional societies, with the mandate of establishing uniform standards o f patient care for 
prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of cancer, creating adequate trained human resources, and 
facilitating collaborative basic, translational and clinical research in cancer. However, there is 
still a need to create additional government-run cancer centres which can provide affordable high 
quality cancer care to all sections of society. 
 
 

4 
 
Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) 
1.9 The Tata Memorial Centre, a grant -in-aid organization under the Department of Atomic 
Energy, is the oldest and largest cancer centre in the country. Registering close to 80,000 new 
patients and over 500,000 follow ups annually, it provides high quality cancer care to patients 
from across the country regardless of socio -economic status; more than 60% of patients are 
treated almost free of cost. TMC also is the centre for cancer education in the country and trains 
over 100 students every year in various aspects of cancer including surgical, medical and 
radiation oncology. Research from TMC has addre ssed several important questions and changed 
cancer practice globally. ACTREC is the research wing of TMC and houses several cancer 
researchers working towards unravelling the biology, causes and management of cancer. In 
addition, TMC has now expanded to s ix other hospitals located in Varanasi (two), Guwahati, 
Sangrur, Vishakapatnam and Mullanpur. It is expected that TMC will treat over 150,000 new 
patients with cancer annually by the year 2022. 
The National Cancer Grid 
1.10 The National Cancer Grid, an ini tiative of the Department of Atomic Energy, 
Government of India, was created in 2012 with the broad vision of creating uniform standards of 
cancer care across India. Seven years later, it has grown to a large network of 238 cancer centres, 
research institutes, patient advocacy groups, charitable organizations and professional societies. 
Between the member organizations of the NCG, the network treats over 700,000 new patients 
with cancer annually, which is over 60% of all of India‟s cancer burden. Incorporat ing all 
stakeholders of cancer care in India, it is a strong, unified and powerful voice in the fight against 
cancer. 
NCG activities include the following: 
1. Uniform standards of care – NCG Consensus Guidelines 
2. External Quality Assurance Schemes (EQAS) 
3. Second opinion service for patients – “Navya” 
4. NCG Virtual Tumor Boards 
5. Price Discovery Cell / Group negotiation for equipment, drugs and consumables 
6. Continuing Medical Education – NCG National Cancer Library and Discovery tool 
“Akshara” 
7. Unique Educational Initiatives – “Traveling Schools of Pathology and Oncology 
Nursing” 
8. Training in Cancer Research Methods – International Collaboration on Research methods 
Development in Oncology – CreDO workshop 
9. NCG funded multicentric collaborative research 
Hub and spoke model of cancer care 
1.11 A distributed model of cancer care is required to offer patients high quality cancer care at 
their doorsteps. Common and less complex cancer care should be provided close to patients‟ 
homes (spokes) to create minimum disruption in  their lives and that of their families. Treatment 
of uncommon cancers and those with complex treatment protocols require management in expert 
centres of excellence (hubs). However, to avoid over -burdening the hubs, the spokes need to be 
reasonably capable  of handling less complex and common cancer types in the region. This 
strategy would be extremely helpful to minimize costs as well as inconvenience to patients and 
their families. We suggest a comprehensive cancer plan which will address the increasing burden 
of cancer in India by the creation of approximately 30 hubs and 120 spokes in various parts of 
the country. 
Suggested approach 
1.12 Tata Memorial Centre, a grant-in-aid tertiary cancer hospital under Department of 
Atomic Energy, Government of India has been offering state of the art cancer services for last 80 
years. We strive for excellence in cancer care, education, research, public health since our 

5 
 
inception. We hav e now set up hospitals in Sangrur, Chandigarh, Varanasi, Vishakhapatnam, 
Guwahati and Muzaffarpur. While the hospitals in Sangrur, Guwahati, Varanasi are fully 
functional, the facilities in Chandigarh and Vishakhapatnam will be fully commissioned by the 
end of this year. We also offered technical assistance to the Uttar Pradesh ( UP) Government in 
setting up State Cancer Institute at Lucknow.  
It is agreed upon that the availability of affordable cancer care is not uniformly available 
in all geographical areas of our vast country. It is ideal to establish TMC‟s hub and spoke model 
in such a way that no patient has to travel more than three hours to access basic cancer care. The 
model has been endorsed by the Parliamentary Committee on Science and Technology i n its 
report on improving cancer care and control in India. The National Cancer Grid is another 
initiative to standardize cancer care all across the nation.  
A typical hub is a tertiary care facility that has 250 beds and takes care of all specialties 
catering to a population of 4  crore. The approximate cost of setting up such a facility is Rs 700 
crore and it takes around 3 -5 years to commission the facility fully after approvals, sanction of 
funds, and statutory permissions are in place.  A typical spoke is a 100 bedded facility that takes 
care of nearly two thirds of the cancer care spectrum. The approximate cost of setting up a spoke 
is approximately Rs 385 crore and it can be commissioned in 2 -4 years after approvals, sanction 
of funds, and statutory pe rmissions are in place.The budgetary estimates are based on the 
assumption that the land required will be provided free of cost by the respective State 
Governments. Table 1 gives an overview of the sub-heads of this expenditure.

Based on the recent requests for establishment of cancer hospitals  in Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, 
Odisha, West Bengal and Goa, we would suggest the following approach. 
1. West Bengal - We suggest that TMC provide technical assistance to an existing facility in 
Siliguri in setting up a new spoke or upgrading the existing cancer  care facility.  This 
facility will serve the population of West Bengal, Sikkim, Assam, Bihar, Nepal and 
Bhutan. We are aware that Medica Cancer Hospital is an existing cancer centre at 
Rangapani (outskirts of Siliguri), and this might be an option to coll aborate with. This 
centre can be supported by our centres in Muzaffarpur and Guwahati that are 
approximately 9 hours by road from Siliguri. If we adopt this approach, we may incur an 
annual expenditure of Rs 15 crore. 
2. Chhattisgarh – On the request of forme r Chief Minister of Chhattisgarh, our team has 
visited Raipur and submitted a report on various options that State Government  can 
explore. Amongst all the available options, it appears best that we offer technical 
assistance to the BALCO hospital, a charit able cancer centre, by supporting the existing 
facility, which can be a hub. If we adopt this approach, we may incur an annual 
expenditure of Rs 30 crores. 
3. Goa: As per our assessment, the region around Karwar is deficient in good cancer 
hospitals in the vi cinity. Karwar would be a good site for a spoke as it can service 
patients from Goa as well as North Karnataka. Given the close proximity of Kaiga, this 
can be an appropriate site for a hub to be built by DAE in partnership with the State 
Government. 
4. Odisha: We are aware of an ongoing effort to establish a large cancer centre at 
Bhubhaneswar by the Odisha State Government; in addition, there is a regional cancer 
centre at Cuttack, and an AIIMS in Bhubhaneswar. It would be best that we offer 
technical assist ance to the State Government in their existing proposal of creating a 
cancer centre, which would be a hub. An annual expenditure of Rs 30 crore would be 
required to support infrastructure/ equipment upgrade and operation expenses. 
5. Rajasthan: Southern Rajas than has a scarcity of cancer centres and hence, Udaipur or 
Kota would be good choices to create hubs of cancer care. This would be a greenfield 
project with the creation of a hub. 
As mentioned above, there are two different models being proposed. In the f irst scenario, 
(West Bengal, Chattisgarh, Odisha), TMC will offer technical assistance (civil work planning, 
architectural planning, guidance on equipment purchase, human resource recruitment and 
commissioning) to an existing or upcoming facility for upgradation to a Hub or a spoke. It would 
be preferable to have the location of this facility in an existing government hospital or a 
charitable hospital. In this case, most of the capital cost will be borne by the relevant stakeholder, 
while there may be some supplementary funding for operational expenditure and upgradation of 
infrastructure / equipment from the DAE. In the second scenario (Karwar, Kota/Udaipur and any 
of the above -mentioned sites where collaboration with the suggested centres does not 
materialize), TMC would plan to establish and run the facility itself as a greenfield project. All 
facilities will be functionally and academically autonomous, run directly by TMC.

limited period of  3 years  (up to December 2023) and charges will increase by 10% every year 
and in no case , the sources will be accepted thereafter.   This one time opportunity is only for 
those sources which were imported till December 2019. 
As far as Indian origin sourced are concerned, it may be not ed that in India only BRIT/DAE can 
supply Indian origin radioactive sources. BRIT always accepts disused sources supplied by 
BRIT/DAE as per the terms and conditions of the disposal procedure. 
Recommendation/Observation  
2.7 The Committee reiterates the fact that the country has abundant availability of Thorium. 
The Committee urged the Department to find avenues for its consumption in the country as a 
substitute to the costly imported raw materials through enhanced research and development.  
                                                                                                                       (Para 6.3 ibid)    
Action Taken  
2.8 The matter pertains to find avenues for consumption of thorium in the country as a 
substitute through enhanced research & development. IREL (India) Limited as a part of  its 
mandate, extracts the thorium values from monazite and stores it in engineered trenches for 
future use in the 3rd stage of atomic power programme of the country.

SEWAGE SLUDGE HYGIENISATION  
Recommendation/Observation  
3.1 The Committee appreciates the Department for developing an indigenous technology for 
hygienisation of municipal sewage sludge. The Committee, however, finds it surprising that 
though this technology is scientifically sound, it has not been promoted to the desired level and 
only a handful of Municipalities have shown interest in the technology. The Committee is of the 
opinion that this technology can be used on a larger scale by the other Municipalities in the 
country to tackle the problem of sewage sludge.  The Committee is of the considered view that 
the success in Ahmedabad may be replicated across all the major Municipalities in the country, 
in a phased manner, and the Municipalities finding it difficult to deal with its sewage sludge 
should come forward and make best use of this technology. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should write to all State/UT Governments, apprise them the 
benefits and efficacy of this technology and ask them to impress upon all the Municipalities 
facing the problem of sewage sludge to use this technology to solve the problem faced by them.                                                                              
         (Para 4.2 of the 341st Report) 
Action Taken  
3.2 DAE has provided indirect financial support for establishing Sewage Sludge 
Hygienisation (SSH) plants in form of providing part of Co -60 source required for the plant free 
of cost. Financial assistance to the extent of 50 -60% by the Central Government soli cited to 
encourage Municipal Corporations to come forward to assimilate and adopt this technology. 
It is expected that the proposed financial assistance from Central Government will 
provide an impetus to adoption of this technology by other Municipal Corporations and will also 
help in publicity and dissemination of technology to other urban development agencies. 
Four Municipal Corporation mentioned below were apprised about the technology: 
1. Bhubaneshwar Municipal Corporation,  
2. Banaras Municipal Corporation,  
3. Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM) and  
4. Surat Municipal Corporation (SMC)  
 MCGM and SMC have shown interest in this technology. First meeting was held with MCGM 
officials in March 2021. 
Further Comments 
3.3  The Committee notes the action bei ng taken by the Department on the 
recommendation of the Committee.  The Committee is, however, of the view that the 
Department needs to scale up its action and should invariably write to all the State 
Governments highlighting the efficacy of this indigenou s technology  in solving the 
problem of sewage sludge.
