REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment & Forests 
having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present the 
Thirty-sixth Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Scientific 
and Industrial Research for the year 1996-97 (Demand No. 75). 
2. In its meetings held on 13th and 22nd August, 1996 the Committee discussed in detail 
the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research on the 
basis of documents made av·ailable to it and the submissions made before it by the Secretary 
of the Department and the other representatives of the Department. 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Department for replying to 
the clarifications sought by the Hon'ble Members and placing before it the required material 
to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of 
Scientific and Industrial Research. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 
September 3, 1996. 
5. The thrust of the programmes and activities of the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research (DSIR) is on the activities of Council of Scientific and Industrial 
Research (CSIR)- a premier Science and Technology (S&T) agency with a network of 40 
national laboratories, two complexes and 81 Extension and Regional Centres spread all over 
the country, Technology Promotion, Development, Utilisation and Transfer (TPDU) and 
National Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT). 
6. Other major programmes of the Department include Research and Development by 
Industry (RDI) consisting of in-house R & D in Industry, Scientific and Industrial Research 
Organisations (SIROs) and Fiscal ·Incentives for Scientific Research; Programme Aimed at 
Technological Self Reliance {PATSER) consisting of development of new or improved 
technologies. Development of speciaVcustom built capital goods, absorption and adaptation 
of improved technology, studies and interactions concerning Technology Evaluation and pre­
feasibility reports of major sectors/products; Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of 
Technology (SEETOT) consisting of National Register of Foreign Collaborations (NRFC), 
Industrial Technology, Transfer and Trading in Technology (TA TT), Linkages with 
International Organisations including Asian and Pacific Centres for Transfer of Technology 
(APCIT) and Promotion and Support to Consultancy Services (PSCS) including the 
Consultancy Development Centre (CDC) and two Public Enterprises viz. National Research 
Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL) engaged in the 
commercialisation of indigeneously developed technologies. 
6.1 The Committee was informed that CSIR laboratories have responded to the radical 
change and the liberalised economic policies introduced by the Government to integrate the 
Indian economy with globalisation. Consequently, successful technology transfers have taken 
place in many areas. The efforts of CSIR towards globalisation of its activities have resulted 
in entering into collaborative agreements, licensing of its technologies, and signing of MOUs 
\•.ritb international organisations like Du Pont Agricultural Products, USA; FMC 
Corporation, Commonwealth Science Council, Zymogenetics, USA; Silesia SA, South 

Africa; Chinese ~eronautical Establishment, Beijing; University of New South Wales. 
Australia; University of Lancaster, UK and Special Design Bureau, Moscow. Among the 
major industry and economy oriented programmes, those related to Drugs, Chemicals, 
Environment, Metallurgy, Agrotechnologies, Leather, Electronics, Transportation, Materials 
and Wood Substitute have made significant contributions. The collaborative efforts of 
Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants (CIMAP) and Central Drug Research 
Institute (CDRI) on arteether are about to lead to the release of a drug for the control of 
cerebral of chloroquin resistant malaria in the market. 
7. The Secretary, DSIR informed the Committee that CSIR has made significant, 
contributions in R & D and technical services resulting in industrial and socio-economic 
Development. CSIR has also achieved excellence in basic research and is creating a strong 
infrastructure in terms of S&T Manpower in the country. The attention of the Committee 
was invited towards cash flow through sponsored research and consultancy in respect of 
CSIR laboratories which was to the tune of Rs. 177 crores in 1995-96 i.e. an increase of 
Rs. 40 crores over 1994-95. If one takes into account the accomplishments like the number 
of international patents which CSIR laboratories were filling, the product value of the goods 
that were coming out as a result of research and development carried out in CSIR 
laboratories and in terms of basic science and good research publications, one could 
conclude that CSIR laboratories inspite of constraints have been making good progress. The 
Committee was informed that during 1995-96, technologies generated and patent filing 
increased by about 25%. The industrial production based on the CSIR knowhow has also 
gone up. In monetary terms the industrial production through CSIR knowhow during the 
year 1994-95 was Rs. 2600 crores. 
8. Budget Estimates of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) for 
the year 1996-97 provide Rs. 438.97 crores, of which Rs. 186.00 crores constitute the plan 
component and Rs. 252.97 crores the non-plan component. The Committee examined the 
budgetary allocations of the Department for the year 1996-97•. While considering the 
Demands for Grants of the Department, the Committee also had an opportu ~1ity to review 
the work relating to some of the projects and programmes which fall within the purview of 
the Department. 
9. On being asked about· the justification for 98% of DSIR's budget being spent as 
grants-in-aid to various organis-ations and departments, the Committee was informed that out 
of the total budgetary support of Rs. 438.97 crores to DSIR, Rs. 412.88 crores goes to 
CSIR, which being an autonomous body, receives budgetary support in the form of grants­
in-aid. The Secretary, explained that under the general financial rules any money given to 
autonomous bodies or registered societies is termed as grants-in-aid. The Secretary also 
informed that as Director General of CSIR, he is also the head of CSIR and therefore the 
fund that goes to DSIR gets transferred to CSIR, and its budget is treated as grants-in-aid in 
Parliamentary, legal and financial terms. The Committee was also informed about the issue 
of financing the laboratories and monitoring mechanisms prevailing in the Department of 
CSIR has 40 laboratories and 80 extension centres through which the research and 
development is carried out. Therefore, bulk of the expenditure is spent on funding research 
within their own laboratories. Another means of funding research is through extramural 
research, the principal of extramural research is to generate manpower in the country. 
Under this scheme examinat ions are conducted for selecting candidates who prepare for 
Ph.D., Junior Research Fellowship and Senior Research Fellowship. Besides, there is a 
•for headwise details see schedule. 

research scheme under which funds are given to graduates within the universities having linkage 
with CSIR laboratories. 
10. Asked about the monitoring mechanism the Secretary informed the Committee that the 
allocation to the laboratories is strictly monitored on the basis of specific projects having socio­
economic bearing. Since last year specific performance indicators for individual laboratories 
have been devised for optimal utilisation of the money. Accordingly, grants are linked to 
specific principles and targets. There also exists a close interaction with industry which joins to 
undertake research and development. Linkage with industry acts as a strong mechanism for 
monitoring as they are interested in achieving goals through their research. 
The Committee is of the view that with the increasing cross-linkages between industry and 
scientific research institutions/universities there is a strong possibility that it may lead to 
exclusive priority to Research and Development which may yield to immediate results. In the 
process research in pure or basic science is likely to be relegated to the background. The 
Committee therefore, observes that DSIR must put in concerted efforts to check the emergence of 
any such trend which may impair the importance of research in fundamental sciences. Besides, 
the Ministry should thoroughly monitor the projects. 
11. The Secretary, DSIR, underlined the need to modernise facilities at the national 
laboratories in order to carry out research of international standard and to be globally 
competitive. The Committee was informed that the Planning Commission had agreed to provide 
for modernisation an amount of Rs. 40 crores for 1996-97 at the time of the plan di..;cussion. 
However, the Government has pegged the current year's plan allocations for all the 
departments to the last year's level. Thus CSIR was allocated Rs. 181 crores only under the plan 
head. The Committee was apprised that the Finance Minister recognising the need for 
modernisation of the infrastructure of the laboratories has proposed in his budget speech a 
matching one time grant for the modernisation of CSIR and ICAR laboratories. However, the 
matching grant proposed by the Finance Minister would be available only from the financial 
year 1997-98 onwards. The CSIR would thus not have any plan allocations for modernisation in 
the ptesent year. The Secretary informed that a point regarding modernisation of equipment in 
the CSIR laboratories was also stressed during the meeting of the CSIR Society, which was 
presided over by the Hon'ble Prime Minister and also attended by the Finance Minister. 
The Committee observes that the yardstick adopted by the Finance Ministry ignores the 
imperative need of some of the laboratories of CSIR which need to update themselves to 
international level of research. The Committee therefore recommends that the G,)Vernment 
should restore the agreed plan allocation ofRs. 40 crores for modernisation at the earliest, say, at 
the stage of Revised Estimates for 1996-97. 
12. The Secretary, DSIR, informed that the committed liability for salary, pension and 
contingencies expenditure was expected to go up from that of 1995-96 by Rs. 32 crores in 
1996-97. Further, in 1995-96, out of the total estimated expenditure of Rs. 215 crores on pay and 
allowance Rs. 50 crores was met from the plan funds. As the Planning Commission has 
disallowed any expenditure or pay and allowance to be met from the plan funds and in'-' ted that 
the same should be met from non-plan. CSIR would be faced with a shortfall of Rs. 82 ores on 
non-plan side. 
The Committee, in its Thirteenth Report and Twenty-Fourth Report had noted that CSIR 
had been diverting funds from plan allocation to meet the expenditure in the non-plan areas. The 
Committee had recommended that enough funds be allocated to CSIR to enable it to meet its 
committed liabilities under non-plan so that the need for such diversion of plan allocation does not 
arise; and the plan funds could be utilised for their primary purpose. 

The Committee would· like to reiterate its earlier view (Twenty-Fourth Report) that 
despite a dear recommendation to make sufficient provision in the non-plan outlay of CSIR to 
meet its committed liabUity, adequate non-plan allocation has .not been made in the budget 
estimates for the year 1996-97. The Department is thus left with no alternative but to divert 
money from its plan {upds to meet its committed liabilities in non-plan areas. The Committee 
would like the Department to take up the problem with the Planning Commission and the 
Ministry of Finance so that plan funds are not diverted to non-plan activities. Such a 
diversion adversely affects the pace of R&D activities of the Department. The Committee 
therefore recommends that adequate budgetary support is made available to the Department 
at the RE stage to provide the Department with aaequate funds to meet its ·committed 
Jlabllities and thus obviate the need for diversion from plan funds. 
At the same time the Committee hopes that the Department would project its non-plan 
commitments for the Ninth Five Year Plan well in advance following the guidelines issued by 
the Planning Commission so that non-plan anomaly does not arise again. 
13. The Budget Estimates for 1996-97 for National Laboratories have shown a reduction 
from Rs. 317.53 crores in the previous year to Rs. 315.33 crores. The reduced allocation is 
of Rs. 2 crores on non-plan side. The Committee observes that the reduced allocation may 
hamper the pace of research and recommends that remedial steps should be taken say, at 
revised estimates stage to restore the allocation to last year's level. 
14. The Secretary informed· the Committee about CSIR's Technology Mission Mode 
Programmes. The mission mode programmes formulated in 1994-95 include Leather 
Technology Mission for · Sustainable Development and Clean Coal Technologies. The 
Leather Mission has been operationalised with the objective of improving the quality of 
leather produced at the grass-root level, to mitigate drudgery and improve the working 
conditions of deprived sections of the people, who are employed in tiny and small scale 
leather sectors. The Coal Mission is yet to be formally launched. Besides, CSIR has 
identified two other programmes that it proposes to implement under the Mission Mode i.e. 
development and upscaling of wood substitute materials for the building industry and 
technologies for upgrading quality of food. CSIR also continued to participate in and 
provide significant S&T inputs to two National Technology Mission Programmes viz., Rajiv 
Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission and Technology Mission on Oil Seeds and Pulses. 
The Committee observes that the Technology Mission Mode combines technology with a 
human face, CSIR should vigorously pursue the Programmes and initiate steps to launch the 
Mission on Clean Coal Technologies without further delay. 
15. It was stated that the DSIR scheme "Programme Aimed at Technological Self 
Reliance" (PA TSER) aims to promote and accelerate the efforts of industry to undertake 
Research, Design, Development and Engineering (RDDE) Projects for Domestic 
Technology Development as also for absorption and upgradation of imported technology. 
The Committee was informed that these projects have considerable commercial potential and 
relate to new or improved products/process technologies. Through this scheme, strong R&D 
linkages have been established amongst manufacturing industry, Government R&D 
laboratories and institutions as well as user/customer organisations in both the public and 
private sectors. 
It was stated that there were 57 on-going projects supported by DSIR requiring 
additional outlay of about Rs. 5 crores during 1996-97. ·Besides. about 30 new projects are 
proposed to be supported during 1996-97 involving an outlay of about Rs. 7 crores during 

1996-97. Of these new projects, 10 projects have already been approved involving an outlay of 
about Rs. 3 crores. Thus in all, there would be outflow of around Rs. 12 crores during 1996-
97. The Secretary also apprised the Committee that as the PA TSER programme is a jointly 
funded Research and Development project in industry, additional funds can be tapped from 
the venture capital funds which have been set up through public sectors .like lOBI, IFCI, and 
ICICI. This year about Rs.lOO crores has been set apart as venture capital money by lOBI. 
The Committee hopes that, by supporting an increasing number of important Research, 
Design, Development and Engineering (RDDE) projects of industry having high techno-soda­
commercial inputs, PA TSER will be able to promote and accelerate the efforts of industry in 
technology development as also involved industry in developing and commerdalising new and 
improved products or processes in various sectors of economy which would strengthen linkages 
between industry and national research organisations. The Committee feels that the allocation 
under the head is inadequate in view of the thrust of the Department in revenue generation 
through projects undertaken by the industry and the Committee recommends that the steps 
should be taken at RE stage to get the projected allocation. 
16. Asked about the policy framework for transfer of technology to oth~r countries, the 
Secretary apprised the Committee about the development of 'Artificial Heart Valve' through 
indigenous research. This artificial valve has been development Chittartirunal Institute of 
Medical Sciences and Technology, Thiruvananthapuram through funding from NRDC. This 
valve is certified for 80 million operations for a 40 year life time of a human being. The valve 
has been patented internationally and leading companies like Pfizer of Switzerland and Bayer 
of Germany are prepared to pay substantial amount for transfer of this technology but the 
matter is being reviewed in terms of national interest and commercial interests. 
The Committee is of the view that in view of the growing demand for export of our 
technology the Department should consider entering into joint ventures retaining maijority of 
the share for itself. Besides, steps be taken to protect our intellectual property rights. 
17. The public enterprises namely, National Research Development Corporation 
(NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL) attached to the Department qf Scientific and 
Industrial Research are engaged in important activities in the commercialisation of 
indigenously developed technologies. NRDC is involved in the transfer of technology from the 
laboratory to the industry and the market. NRDC acts as a technological intermediary while · 
CEL is involved in manufacturing and marketing process in Electronics, with its emphasis on 
indigenous technology, inducted both from its in-house developments and from National 
Laboratories , for its production programme in diverse high-technology areas of national 
importance. 
Asked about provision of adequate funds for Public Sector Enterprises, the Secretary 
informed the Committee that the provision is adequate and sufficient. The total investment in 
Central Electronics Limited (CEL), is to the tune of Rs. 6.10 crores ,consisting of an outlay of 
Rs.3.05 crores for equity and an outlay of 3.05 crores for loans. There is an additional , 
provision of Rs. 1 crores as support for research and development to CEL. Budgetary 
Support for NRDC is Rs. 0.40 crores as NRDC doesn't manufacture any products . 
The Committee is of the view that investments should be made in such a way that the 
public enterprises should be self-supporting and resource generating so that the provision for a 
loan Rs. 3.05 crores is avoided. Besides the Committee recommends that the time gap between 
the transfer of technology from laboratory to market should be minbnu.m to maximise the fruits 
of scientific research. 
18. While the Committee seeks to ensure that the Department of. Scientific and Industrial r 

Research is not starved of funds in order to carry out its scientific and research programmes, 
the attention of the Committee has been drawn to some of the audit observations as have 
appeared in the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for years ending 
31st March, 1993 (No. 6 of 1994) and 31st March~ 1994 (No. 6 of 1995) in respect of 
Laboratories under CSm. The objection relates to time overrun ranging from 3 to 36 months 
for in-house projects, physical non-verification of stores, idle equipment lying for want of 
inadequate manpower, unutUised equipment and the amount of demurrage being paid on 
imported consignments. The Report also mentions about the amounts lying outstanding from 
the sponsors which is to the tune of Rs. 30.71 lakhs in case of National Geophysical Research 
Institute. 
The Committee would like the Department to attend to the audit observations and report 
to the Committee unless they have been attended to in the meantime. The Commlttee 
recommends that DSIR should take steps to ensure that the Project Monitoring and 
Evaluation is effective in each organisation under DSIR so that process of Project based 
Budgeting is monitored. 
19. Asked about the outcome of CSIR's study at Jadavpur University, Calcutta on 
development of technology for Arsenic removal, the Secretary informed the Committee that 
a process has been developed for the removal of arsenic from water by first passing it 
through a composition comprising a coprecipitating agent, an oxidising agent and activated 
carbon followed by filtering through a special water filter candle. The process has resulted in 
reducing arsenic in ground water with an efficiency of better than 96%. Patents have been 
filed for the invention in India and Bangladesh. Three hundred sets of the system have been 
given to the PHED .of Government of West Bengal for field trials and evaluation and their 
reports are awaited. The Committee notes with satisfaction the contribution made by DSm to 
assist the Public Health Engineering Department of the State aimed at tackling the problem of 
Arsenic removal from water. 
20. The Committee had earlier (in its twenty fourth report) expressed its concern over 
the lack of adequate housing facilities in CSIR. Asked about the progress in this regard, the 
Secretary, DSIR informed the Committee that CSIR was fully seized of the problem and 
had accordingly set up a Committee specifically for the purpose. This Committee of CSIR 
has since submitted its report which was under examination of CSIR. The salient features of 
the recommendat~ons envisage enh~ncing the HBA ceiling upto Rs. 8 lakh, hiring/leasing of 
500 houses in endeavour to achieve accomodation satisfaction level of 70% in remote areas, 
60% in towns and 50% in metropolitan cities over the IXth Five Year Plan. CSIR has 
accordingly souglit Rs. 150 crore for this activity in the ~Xth Five Year Plan. As housing was 
a pre-requisite to attracting talented scientists the Committee recommends that CSIR should 
take action in a stipulated timeframe and endeavour to reach satisfaction level of housing on 
priority basis.

4. DEPARTMENT’S INITIATIVES ON DRUG DISCOVERY FOR MALARIA 
 4.1    The Committee, recognising the need for scientific interventions in the control and 
treatment of malaria, probed the Department about its initiatives in this re gard. The 
Department, in a written reply, brought to the attention of the Committee that CSIR has long 
standing programme/s on malaria drug discovery and development as well as parasite biology 
and drug target identification. One of the most successful outcomes of the program me 
includes discovery and development of α - β – Arteether for severe P. falciparum malaria 
including cerebral malaria as a second line treat ment for chloroquine resistant cases. Drug is 
being marketed as E MAL by the CSIR -CDRI licensee in more than 20 African & Asian 
countries. Apart from this licensee, the  α - β – Arteether is also being marketed with nearly 
400 different brand names.  
 4.2    The Committee was also informed that CSIR laboratories in collaboration with other 
Departments of the Ministry of Science and Technology are pursuing projects  related to 
development of novel oral combination formulation for the treatment of resistan t malaria, 
repurposing of Antican cer Drugs for the treatment of m alaria and other DNA & Genomic 
studies of the Malarial Parasite.  
 4.3   The Committee is cognizant of the fact that since malaria is a disease common to 
the entire country, especially in the  densely populated pockets , low cost and effective 
treatment is absolutely essential to save poor pepole’s life, loss of productive man hours 
and decrease the need for hospitalisation. In this backdrop, the Committee applauds the 
efforts of the Department in research and development of drugs for the treatment of 
malaria. The Committee observes that all scientific advancements serve their purpose 
only when those are  implemented in the welfare of the larger populace  and, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should initiate a programme on a mission mode, 
along with other stakeholder Department s/Ministries, with a target of reaching out to a 

5 
 
sizeable population in the most affected areas  and create awareness about the various 
interventions of the Department in treatment of Malaria.  
     5.   SICKLE CELL ANAEMIA (SCA) MISSION 
5.1 The Committee enquired from the  Department about its initiatives in respect of 
diagnosis, treatment and management of Sickle Cell Anaemia (SCA), especially in the tribal 
belt of the country , including Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha 
and Jharkhand. It was brought to the attention of the Committee, that a consortium of seven 
CSIR laboratories headed by CSIR - Centre for  Cellular and Molecular Biology (CSIR -
CCMB), Hyderabad is involved in research and development of technologies/interventions in 
addition to screening and testing of SCA patients using in -house developed methods and 
techniques under CSIR Sickle Cell Anaemia  Mission since 2017.  The CSIR Mission also 
involves collaboration with State Medical Colleges who are actively involved in the Mission . 
Hence, CSIR is able to reach the affected population to help the Medical Colleges with their 
expertise in screening, diagnosis and application of technological interventions that are being 
developed under the Mission.  
5.2 In a written reply to the Committee, the Department listed out the objectives of the 
Sickle Cell Anaemia Mission as follows: 
(i) Population screening, genetic testing, carrier testing, prenatal diagnosis and 
genetic counselling, treatment of identified patients, etc. 
(ii) Procurement of DCGI/CDSCO approval for dedicated use of Hydroxy urea 
therapy for patients of Sickle Cell Anaemia 
(iii) Identification of new drug molecular for the management of Sickle Cell Anaemia 
patients 
(iv) Development of genome editing approaches towards development of curative 
treatment of Sickle Cell Anaemia 
(v) Development of cheap and robust, point of care device for rapid screening of 
such patients. 
5.3  The Committee was pleased to note that about 25 lakh children have been screened in 
Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh and hundreds of target couples were identifie d; and, through 
prenatal diagnosis and counselling, birth of affected kids has been prevented. The Committee 
was also informed that one of the major achievements under the CSIR -Sickle cell Anaemia 
Mission has been in  getting the DCGI/CDSCO approval for dedicated use of Hydroxy urea 
therapy for Sickle Cell Anaemia  patients, thereby setting the stage for development of new 
formulations for effective treatment and better compliance to the Hydroxy urea usage.  
5.4  The Committee observes that the activities of SCA Mission remain confined to 
two states, i.e.  Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra in the Phase I undertaken during the 
period from 2017-2020. The SCA Mission has now been extended to Madhya Pradesh in 
Phase II  with plan s to extend the same model t o Jharkhand.  The Committee also 
observes that a programme on SCA is also executed by the Department of 
Biotechnology and, therefore, recommends the Department of Scientific and Industrial 
Research to coordinate  with the Department of Biotechnology to ensure  synergy of 
efforts and avoidance of duplicity.   
5.5 The Committee notes and appreciates the efforts of the Department towards 
early screening, treatment and management of Sickle Cell Anaemia. Since the disea se is 
endemic to many tribal areas, cost effective and efficient scientific interventions are the 
need of the hour to prevent any further prevalence of this disease  and improve the 
patient’s quality of life. The Committee, feels that identifying the carriers and avoidance 
of marriage of carrier couples may -be successful in a limited manner  to manage the 
disease. The Committee strongly recommends that appropriate interventions backed by 

6 
 
effective policy/guidelines will go a long way in not only improvi ng the quality of life of 
the SCA patients but also prevent and reduce the number of children born and affected 
by this disease. The Committee  firmly recommends that the Department should engage 
with other national and international agencies undertaking research on gene therapy 
and gene editing based treatment of Sickle Cell Anaemia.  
5.6 The Committee feels that the Department needs to take more proactive steps in 
increasing on-ground presence and collaborate with local and State level stakeholders 
so th at the solutions developed by the Department can actually reach to the affected 
masses and other intended stakeholders . To this effect, the Committee strongly 
recommends the Department to aggressively promote the use of Hydroxy urea therapy 
for the treatment of Sickle Cell Anaemia.

malaria. The Committee observes that all scientific advancements serve their pur pose 
only when those are implemented in the welfare of the larger populace and, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should initiate a programme on a mission mode, 
along with other stakeholder Departments/Ministries, with a target of reaching out to a  
sizeable population in the most affected areas and create awareness about the various 
interventions of the Department in treatment of Malaria.                                     (Para 4.3) 
     SICKLE CELL ANAEMIA (SCA) MISSION 
 The Committee observes th at the activities of SCA Mission remain confined to 
two states, i.e. Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra in the Phase I undertaken during the 
period from 2017-2020. The SCA Mission has now been extended to Madhya Pradesh in 
Phase II with plans to extend the same model to Jharkhand. The Committee also 
observes that a programme on SCA is also executed by the Department of 
Biotechnology and, therefore, recommends the Department of Scientific and Industrial 
Research to coordinate with the Department of Biotechnology t o ensure synergy of 
efforts and avoidance of duplicity.                                                                            (Para 5.4) 
 The Committee notes and appreciates the efforts of the Department towards 
early screening, treatment and management of Sickle Cell Anaemia. Since the disease is 
endemic to many tribal areas, cost effective and efficient scientific interventions are the 
need of the hour to prevent any further prevalence of this disease and improve the 
patient’s quality of life. The Committee, feels that identifying the carriers and avoidance 
of marriage of carrier couples may -be successful in a limited manner to manage the 
disease. The Committee strongly recommends that appropriate interventions backed by 
effective policy/guidelines will go a long way in not only improving the quality of life of 
the SCA patients but also prevent and reduce the number of children born and affe cted 
by this disease. The Committee firmly recommends that the Department should engage 
with other national and international agencies undertaking research on gene therapy 
and gene editing based treatment of Sickle Cell Anaemia.                                     (Para 5.5) 
 The Committee feels that the Department needs to take more proactive steps in 
increasing on-ground presence and collaborate with local and State level stakeholders 
so that the solutions developed by the Department can actually reach to  the affected 
masses and other intended stakeholders. To this effect, the Committee strongly 
recommends the Department to aggressively promote the use of Hydroxy urea therapy 
for the treatment of Sickle Cell Anaemia.                                                               (Para 5.6) 
CSIR LABORATORIES  
 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department and recommends that 
under Phase II of the CSIR - Aroma Mission, where the Department targets to add an 
additional 30,000 hectares, special emphasis should be given towards implementation of 
this programme in the aspirational d istricts. The Committee also recommends that 
mechanisms of ‘better price discovery’ be explored through enhanced marketing and 
value addition, so that farm incomes are further augmented.  Further, providing 
technical and infrastructural support to farmers/ growers will also help in generating 
employment in rural areas of the country.                                                               (Para 6.5) 

13 
 
 The Committee feels that the technological expertise of CSIR should be used to 
redress the challenges r elating to sustainable management of underground water 
resources. The Committee, therefore recommends the Department to proactively reach 
out to State Governments as well as stakeholder Ministries/Departments at the centre 
and engage in mapping of underground water resources at a large scale.           (Para 6.8) 
 Further, the Committee recommends that this information should be made 
available to the public in a user friendly manner with special focus on promoting 
ground water recharge initiatives.                                                                            (Para 6.9) 
 The Committee observes that as against a demand of Rs.5899.62 crore under the 
head ‘CSIR’ the Department has been allocated Rs.5562.76 crore in B.E. 2022-23, which 
is about Rs.300 crore less. The Committee recommends the Department to raise internal 
budgetary resources and try to offset the reduction in budgetary allocation and,  if 
required, the Department should seek additional funds from the Ministry of Finance at 
the supplementary/R.E. stage so that the Department is able to sustain its key 
programmes.                                                                                                             (Para 6.10) 
 The Committee further recommends that the Department should also constantly 
monitor the utilisation of funds under the various programmes on a quarterly basis and 
ensure optimal utilisation of funds.                                                                         (Para 6.11) 
 The Committee  observes that in the year 2020 -21, against a target of 5000 
fellowships, only 2743 fellowships were disbursed. The Department informed that due 
to COVID -19 pandemic, CSIR could conduct only one Joint CSIR -UGC JRF -NET 
exam and hence targets could not be ac hieved. The Committee further observers, that 
even-though only about 50 percent of the target set for 2020 -21 could be achieved the 
Department has completely utilised the budgetary allocation under the head for the 
same year.                                                                                                                  (Para 6.13) 
 The Committee further observes with surprise, that the Department has 
substantially reduced the targets for 2021 -22 by 60 percent, to only 2000 (as opposed to 
5000 in 2020-21) and yet the budgetary allocation under the head is higher for the year 
2021-22 as compared to 2020 -21 by 18 percent ( Rs. 75 crore). In addition to this 
counterintuitive allocation of funds, the Committee is very disturbed to note that so far 
no fellowships have been disbursed out of the target of 2000 for the year 2021-22. 
            (Para 6.14) 
 It is astonishing to note that despite this fact, the Department has indicated an 
expenditure of almost 85 percent of the budgetary allocation u nder the head for the 
year 2021 -22. It is unclear to the Committee that on one hand the Department has 
stated that out of the target of 2000 fellowships for the year 2021 -22, none could be 
disbursed so far, but on the other hand there is an expenditure of almost 85 percent 
against this head. The Committee desires to seek clarity on this aberration and demands 
that the Department must furnish a detailed note on performance during the last five 
years, including 2021 -22 clearly indicating therein, the month wi se expenditure and 
physical targets achieved under the head ‘Research Schemes, Scholarships and 
Fellowships’.                                                                                                              (Para 6.15) 
 The Committee further recommends the Department to clear any pendency in 
the disbursement of fellowships and ensure that targets set for the year 2022-23 are met. 
The Department, in collaboration with UGC, should also explore alternate methods of 
conducting the qualifying examinations so that researchers do not have to suffer in 
future.                                                                                                                        (Para 6.16) 

14 
 
 The Committee is compelled to observe, from the table above, that the number of 
patent applications filed and patents granted in India during the year 2021 -22 has been 
the lowest in the past five years.  The Committee strongly recommends the Department 
to give special emphasis in improving these numbers in the year 2022-23.       (Para 6.18) 
DISINVESTMENT OF CENTRAL ELECTRONICS LIMITED (CEL) 
 The Committee notes the details regarding CEL, the basis of decision for its 
disinvestment and the process, as appraised by the Department. The Committee 
recommends the Department that all measures to ensure the welfare of the employees 
be taken and that no employee should suffer adversely. The Committee also notes that 
CEL, with an intention to work in common areas of interest for the development of 
technology, has signed many MoUs such as with Indian Institute of Technology -
Kanpur, Naval Materials Research Laboratory –DRDO and many more. The 
Committee therefore recommends that since CEL was working in many important 
sectors in collaboration with various labora tories, the partnerships must be honoured, 
as mutually decided, in the best interest of the nation.                                         (Para 7.10)

3. NATIONAL MISSION ON INTERDISCIPLINARY CYBER PHYSICAL 
SYSTEMS (NM-ICPS)  
3.1 The Department informed the Committee that it is implementing multi -stakeholder 
National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber Physical System (NM -ICPS).  The mission was 
approved in 2018 with a total outlay of ₹3660 crore for a period of five years. The Mission aims 
at convergence of stakeholders by establishing strong linkages between academia, industry, 
Government and International Organisations. The Mission is implemented through 25 number of 
Technology Innovation Hubs (TIHs) established in the top academi c Institutes. Each TIH will 
have four major activities i.e., Technology Development, Human Resource & Skill Development 
(including development of CPS technology application tools for education at elementary and 
high school level), Innovation, Entrepreneurs hip & Start -Up Ecosystem and International 
Collaborations.  
3.2 The Committee observed that despite the importance and criticality of NM -ICPS, no 
budget was allocated to the Mission in 2021 -22. The Committee enquired the reason and impact

of this to which the Department submitted that as per approved expenditure plan for NM -ICPS, 
Rs.123.66 crore was allocated for the Year -one (2019-20) and the same was released on March 
27, 2020 at the end of financial year which was available for utilization in next FY 202 0-21. 
Also,      Rs.271.27 crore was allocated for the year 2020 -21 and approximately same amount 
was released. Since, ample amount of fund was available with supported 
organisations/institutions under the scheme NM -ICPS and there was no scope of releasing  any 
further grant to the host institutes for the financial year  2021-22, allocation for the current year

scheme with Implementing Agencies, there is no hindrance in execution of the scheme.

by not allocating budget as all TIHs had drawn up their strategies and tie -up with industries and

country at the forefron t of state -of-the-art technology research. The Committee also

capabilities in these fields and make them future -ready. The Committee thus is perturbed 
to note that the a chievement of the physical targets under NM -ICPS may get adversely 
affected due to shortage of funds.

4. SUPPORT TO STARTUPS UNDER NSTEDB AND TDB 
4.1 The Department informed the Committee that under it established the  National Science & 
Technology Entrepreneurship Development Board (NSTEDB) was established as an institutional 
mechanism to help promote knowledge driven and technology intensive enterprises. The Board 
aims to foster innovation and Start -Up ecosystem through Science, Technol ogy & Innovation 
(ST&I) interventions, capacity building, pre -incubation, incubation, acceleration and engaging 
private sector.  
4.2 The Department informed the Committee that the National Initiative for Developing and 
Harnessing Innovations  (NIDHI) is NST EDB's flagship programme for nurturing ideas and 
innovations into successful startups. NIDHI aims to nurture start -ups through scouting, 
supporting and scaling of innovations. The key stakeholders of NIDHI include various 
departments and ministries of the central government, state governments, academic and R & D 
institutions, mentors, financial institutions, angel investors, venture capitalists and private 
sectors. While NSTEDB is the funding agency, the NIDHI programmes are implemented 
through Technology B usiness Incubators (TBIs) available around the country.   The Department 
further informed that NIDHI has the following components with their corresponding 
achievements: 
i. NIDHI4COVID2.0 initative: 34 startups are being funded by DST to support startup -led 
Covid solutions making our country stronger on multiple fronts in the ongoing fight 
against COVID. 
ii. i-TBI: To increase outreach of incubation and entrepreneurship programs of DST, a new 
program has been rolled out in name of ‘Inclusive -Technology Business Incu bator’ 
(iTBI). The mandate of iTBI is to increase outreach of incubation program in terms of 
geographies, gender etc. 
iii. NIDHI-TBI: ‘National Initiative for Developing and Harnessing Innovations’ - 
Technology Business Incubators to support and nurture knowled ge driven innovative 
start-ups into successful enterprises. 4 new TBIs are being established in the country. 
iv. NIDHI COE: NIDHI - Centre of Excellences to strengthen existing capacities of 
Technology Business Incubators (TBIs) and supports potential start -ups. 2 new COEs are 
being established at FITT, IIT Delhi and T-Hub, Hyderabad.  
v. NIDHI- PRAYAS (PRomoting and Ac celerating Young and ASpiring technology 
entrepreneurs) to support young innovators turn their ideas into Proof of Concept 
(PoC)/Prototype. PRAYAS is implemented by 43 PRAYAS Centres, with 13 new 
PRAYAS centres established in FY 21-22. 
vi. NIDHI EIR (Entrepren eurs-in- Residence) to inspire and motivate graduating students to 
take entrepreneurship by providing support as fellowship. EiR is being implemented 
through 32 TBI’s, including 12 new TBI’s implementing EiR. 
vii. NIDHI Seed Support Programme to ensure timely a vailability of the seed support to the 
deserving incubate startups within an incubator. During this FY 2021 -22, a total of about 
65 startups have been supported so far.

6.1 The Committee enquired the Department about the initiatives of the Department towards 
disseminating science and technology education, research and technological interventions at the  
grass root levels, especially in the rural and backward region s. The Department submitted before 
the Committee that it has initiated a programme for holistic development of Scheduled Caste 
(SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) Communities in the Country through s ystemic interventions by 
establishing Science Technology and Innovation (STI) Hubs in different regions of the country 
with the following objectives:  
(i) To address the weakest linkages in the predominant livelihood systems through Science 
& Technology (S&T) interventions. 
(ii) Creation of social enterprises based on the strengths in livelihood systems. 
(iii) To improve the Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) through inputs of S&T

livelihood assets rather than techno -centric approach driven by the inquisitiveness of principal 
investigators. The STI Hubs will thus develop, nurture and ensure the delivery of appropriate and 
relevant technologies for inclusive socio -economic development through creation of sustainable 
livelihoods for the SC and ST population in tune to their growing aspirations. The STI Hubs are 
established in collaborative, networked and partnership framework to resolve the last mile 
problem in the introduction, delivery, management, use and extension of technology applications 
for development of target population.

REPORT  
1.1 The Government of India has set up the Space Commission and the Department of Space 
(DOS) in 1972.  The DOS is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space 
Commission.  These are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), 
Indian National Space Promotion & Authorization Centre (IN -SPACe) and the Grant -in-aid 
institutions viz., Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National Atmospheric Research 
Laboratory (NARL), North -Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE -SAC), Semi -Conductor 
Laboratory (SCL) and Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST).  
1.2 The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of  ISRO are located in 
Bangalore.  The Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarters co -ordinate the overall programmes 
like Satellite Communication, Satellite Navigation,  Earth Observation, Space Transportation 
Systems, Space Science and Planetary Exploration, Climate &  Atmospheric Programme, 
Disaster Management Support, National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS), 
International   Co-Operation, Capacity Building, Media & Public Relations, Budget & Economic 
Analysis and Human Resources Development.  
Major Centres / Units of DOS/ISRO: 
1.3 The major Centres, Units and establishments of DOS/ISRO, responsible for carrying out 
research and development activities as well as for undertaking various projects and programmes, 
are as follows: 
a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VS SC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the technology 
base for the country‟s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development; 
b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities located at Bangalore and 
Thiruvananthapuram, is responsible for development  of liquid propulsion and cryogenic 
propulsion systems for satellite and launch vehicles; 
c) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC -SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the 
spaceport of India providing launch base to indigenously built launch vehicles.  Also, i t 
provides the facilities for processing of solid rocket motors; 
d) Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) is created with the responsibility to act as the lead 
centre for Human Space Flight Program. This centre is responsible for the execution of 
Gaganyaan programme that envisages sending a crew of astronauts to space and bring back 
safely to earth.   
e) U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), Bangalore, is entrusted with the prime responsibility for 
development of satellites;      
f) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad,  carries out research and development in 
space applications as well as development of application payloads; 
g) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite data 
acquisition and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sen sing and decision support 
for disaster management.  

 
2 
 
h) The Laboratory for Electro -Optics Systems (LEOS), Bangalore has the responsibility for 
development and productionisation of electro optical sensors for satellites; 
i) ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC) located a t Mahendragiri has the responsibility for 
assembly, integration and testing of storable and cryogenic liquid rocket engines and 
stages, spacecraft thrusters testing in sea level and high altitude conditions, storage of 
liquid and cryogenic propellants and production of liquid hydrogen etc.; 
j) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC), with its ground stations at 
Bangalore, Sriharikota, Lucknow, Bearslake,  Biak (Indonesia), Brunei and Mauritius 
provides the telemetry, tracking and command support and  spacecraft mission management 
for the Indian remote sensing satellite missions, space science missions and satellite launch 
vehicle programmes; 
k) Master Control Facility (MCF) with its main facility at Hassan, Karnataka and backup 
facility at Bhopal, Madhya  Pradesh has the responsibility for control and operation of 
INSAT/GSAT/METSAT satellites; 
l) Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun is a premier training and educational 
institute set up for developing trained professionals in the field of Remot e Sensing, Geo -
informatics and  GPS Technology for Natural Resources, Environmental and Disaster 
Management.   
m) Development and Educational Communication Unit (DECU), Ahmedabad,                    is 
involved in the conception, definition, planning and socio /techno-economic evaluation of 
development communication programmes; 
n) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram, carries out research and 
development in the area of inertial systems for satellites and launch vehicles; 
Organisations receiving Grants-in-aid: 
a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution supported 
mainly by the Department of Space, carries out research in space sciences. 
b) The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki near Tirupati , 
conducts atmospheric research. 
c) The North -Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE -SAC) established as an autonomous 
body under the Department of Space provides space technology inputs for developmental 
activities in the North-Eastern Region.  
d) The Semi -conductor Laboratory (SCL) located at Chandigarh is a research and 
development society and is entrusted with the design and development of Very Large Scale 
Integrated Circuit (VLSI) devices and development of  micro-electronic systems to meet 
the strategic needs of the country.  
e) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) is an autonomous body under 
the Department with the objective of creating quality human resources tuned to suit the 
requirements of state-of-art space research programme.  The Institute offers graduate, post -
graduate and doctoral programmes in the area of space science, technology and 
applications. The annual intake of the Institute is about 150-200 students.   
 

 
3 
 
Government Companies under DOS:  
a) The Antrix Corporation Limited, Bangalore, established in 1992, is a wholly owned 
Government Company for marketing space products and services.  
b) The NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), Bangalore, is another commercial arm of Indian 
Space Research Organization, with the primary objective of enabling Indian industries to 
scale up high-technology manufacturing and production base for Indian space programme. 
NSIL was established on March 06, 2019 as a wholly owned Government Undertaking / 
Central Public Sector Enterprise, under the administrative control of Department of Space.  
Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (INSPACe) 
1.4 Recently, the space sector was opened up to promote, handhold, regulate and authorise 
private enterprises and start-ups to undertake space activities by creation of an independent nodal 
agency under Department of Space - the Indian National Space Promotion and A uthorization 
Center (IN-SPACe).  This will enhance the contribution of space technology towards bo osting 
space economy within the country.

9. General Observations/recommendations of the Committee 
9.1 The Committee notes that the Department of Space has been making efforts in 
mapping the glacial lakes which span over  more than 2.5 hectare in size and the said 
exercise has been completed in respect of the Ganga basin and Sutlej river and the data has 
already been complied in the atlas  form.  The Committee is of the view that it will be of 
great importance if an inventory about the glacier and glaci al lakes in the Himalayan 
region is documented on yearly basis .  This is crucial  in light of many  studies suggesting 
that there has been rapid increase in the number of glaci al lakes due to retreat in the 
glaciers caused by the impact of global warming and keeping into consideration the 
possible large scale flooding and destruction  that could happen i n future .                                                             
Therefore, role of the Department , in the matter becomes all the more pivotal and 
significant in light of the fact that many such glaciers are physically inaccessible for ground 
reporting.  The Committee also feels that with the modern technology and better resolution 
satellite imagery  the task of glacier lake s outburst monitoring can be done in a more 
scientific and robust manner.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to 
initiate action in this regard in a time bound manner and to make best use of its  remote 
sensing services for the purpose.  Adequate budgetary allocations should also be made for 
the same. 
9.2 The Committee further notes that the existing Institute/Centres of the Department 
are stationed in major cities and the presence of the Department appears to be negligible as 
far as the remote locations of the country are concerned.  The Committee feels that with 
the increasing demand of space based activities in various sectors, it would be justifiable to 
have Institutes/Centres spread across the country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Department to explore possibilities of establishing Institutes/Centres in these 
underserved areas so as to strengthen its base in the entire country. 
9.3 On the issue of providing assistance/su pport by the Department to the space 
industry based startups in the country , the Committee appreciates the efforts being made 

 
16 
 
by the Department in this direction.  The Committee, however, feels that in order to give 
impetus to the budding startups , more incentives may be offered by the Department which 
would have far reaching impact on the ground level .  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Department to identify the startups that would play a greater role in the 
overall growth and development of the space ecosystem in the country  and help them 
appropriately through incentives. 
          
  

 
17 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS-AT A GLANCE 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021 -22 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FIANANCIAL YEAR 2022-
23 
 The Committee observes that the Department of Space was allotted Rs.13,919.09 
crore in BE 2021 -22 which was reduced to Rs.12,642.00 crore at  RE stage 2021 -22.  The 
top three areas that suffered a drastic cut at RE 2021-22 stage are (i) Space Technology; (ii) 
Space Application; and (iii) Space Sciences.  Given the significance and importance of these 
three Central Sector Schemes/Projects in the overall growth and development of the 
country, the Committee desires to know the reasons for poor ut ilisation of the allocated 
amount.                                                                                                                             (Para 2.4) 
 The Committee makes note of the roadmap prepared by the Department for the 
year 2022-23 with a hope that the Department would strive hard to ensure that the targets 
set for the year 2022 -23 are achieved and the budgetary support provided to the 
Department would be sufficient to sustain its major projects/schemes/programmes without 
any difficulty.                                                                                                                   (Para 2.7) 
 The Committee while scrutinising the targets set and progress achieved by the 
Department during the year 2021 -22, observes that the Department had set the target of 
realisation and launch of Geo -Imaging Satellite (GISAT) for agriculture and disaster 
management applications which could not be achieved as the launch could not succeed.  
Likewise, the launch of India’s first sola r observatory Spacecraft, Aditya -L1, on -board 
PSLV was envisaged during  the year 2021 -22 which has now  been targeted during 2022 -
23. The Committee further notes that the Department had a plan to launch                         
the 3rd generation Oceanographic satellite – Oceansat-3 on-board PSLV in the year 2021-22 
which has now been rescheduled to 2022 -23. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department should strive hard to ensure that the newly set timeline for these 
components are honoured and further delay should not happen.                              (Para 2.8) 
 The Committee hopes that the recruitment drives as intended by the Department 
would be completed in a time bound manner.  The Committee also desires the Department 
to furnish its updated manpower status in the Action Taken Notes.                        (Para 2.10) 
BUDGET ALLOCATION FOR CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES/PROJECTS 
SPACE TECHNOLOGY 
 The Committee hopes that the Department would make all out efforts to ensure full 
utilisation of the budgetary allocation for the year 2021 -22 during the remaining period of 
the financial year 2021-22.                                                                                               (Para 3.3) 
 The Committee further feels that the utilisation by the Department under various 
components such as Trisonic Wind Tunnel Facility Project (TWT); Small Satellite Launch 
Vehicle (SSLV); Launch pad for SSLV;  Network for Space Object Tracking & Analysis 
(NETRA); Geo-Imaging Satellite (GISAT); Resourcesat -3S & 3SA; Development of Space 
Materials & Components; Development & Supply of Aluminium alloy tankages (Pre -
investment); and Capacity Building Programme (CBP ) could have been better.                              
The Committee, accordingly, desires the Department to revisit its fund utilisation strategy 

 
18 
 
under these components and take necessary remedial actions so that funds made available 
for them are utilised fully.                                                                                              (Para 3.4) 
SPACE APPLICATIONS 
 The Committee finds the overall financial performance of the Department under its 
‘Space Application’ Scheme satisfactory.  The Committee, however, is of the firm view that 
the Department still could have improved its performance particularly with regard to 
National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS) and Disaster Management 
Support (DMS) components where the Department  could manage to spend only 54.5 per 
cent and 61.74 per cent, respectively.                                                                             (Para 4.3) 
SPACE SCIENCES 
 The Committee observes that leaving two components viz., Sponsored Research 
(RESPOND) and Space Docking Experiment Mission, the Department could not utilise the 
funds satisfactorily.  The financial performance of the Department under this head has not 
been heartening to note.  The Committee, therefore, recomm ends the Department to 
furnish a detailed note on the reasons because of which it could not utilise the budgetary 
allocations satisfactorily.  The Committee also desires the Depar tment to apprise the 
impact of sub-optimal utilisation on the physical target s envisioned by the Department for 
the year 2021-22.                                                                                                             (Para 5.3) 
INSAT SATELLITE SYSTEMS 
 The Committee finds the overall utilisation of the budgetary allocation satisfactory.  
The Committee, howeve r, would like to highlight the sub-utilisation under GSAT -20 
Satellite, GSAT-22/23/24 Satellites and TDS-01 components.                                    (Para 6.3) 
AUTONOMOUS BODIES 
 The Committee finds that out of total funds of Rs.417.55 crore allotted in favour of 
SCL and the Centre could utilise Rs.270.00 crore only which is just about 65 per cent 
utilisation of the funds.  Given the strategic importance of SCL for the Indian Space 
Programme, the Committee feels that the Centre should have tried its level best to make 
best use of the budgetary suppor t being provided to it.  The Committee recommends that 
SCL should make sincere efforts to utilise the funds earmarked for the year 2021 -22 to 
achieve the envisaged targets.                                                                                         (Para 7.3) 
7.4 The Committee further expresses its concern over the under utilisation of the 
financial support provided to North -Eastern Space Applications Centre  (NE-SAC) and 
National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL)  during the year 2021 -22.  T he 
recommends that the Department should find out the reasons for their poor absorption 
capacity and hopes that fiscal performance of both NE -SAC and NARL would improve in 
the year 2022-23.                                                                                                              (Para 7.4) 
NEWSPACE INDIA LIMITED (NSIL) 
 The Committee is satisfied to note that the Department till 31 st January, 2022 has 
utilised Rs.700.00 crore against  the total budgetary support of Rs.744.53 crore.  The 
Committee hopes that the intended targets set for the year 2021 -22 would not only be 
achieved by the Department but also the vision and purpose with which NSIL has been 
created would also be served. The Committee recommends that the imme nse untapped 

 
19 
 
potential of commercialisation of products and services emanating from the Indian Space 
Programme should be explored optimally in the year 2022-23.                                  (Para 8.3) 
General Observations/recommendations of the Committee 
 The Committee notes that the Department of Space has been making efforts in 
mapping the glacial lakes which span over more than 2.5 hectare in size and the said 
exercise has been completed in respect of the Ganga basin and Sutlej river and the data has 
already been complied in the atlas form.  The Committee is of the view that it will be of 
great importance if an inventory about the glacier and glacial lakes in the Himalayan 
region is documented on yearly basis.  This is crucial in light of many studies  suggesting 
that there has been rapid increase in the number of glacial lakes due to retreat in the 
glaciers caused by the impact of global warming and keeping into consideration the 
possible large scale flooding and destruction that could happen in future .                                                             
Therefore, role of the Department, in the matter becomes all the more pivotal and 
significant in light of the fact that many such glaciers are physically inaccessible for ground 
reporting.  The Committee also feels that with the modern technology and better resolution 
satellite imagery the task of glacier lakes outburst monitoring can be done in a more 
scientific and robust manner.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to 
initiate action in this regard in a time bound manner and to make best use of its remote 
sensing services for the purpose.  Adequate budgetary allocations should also be made for 
the same.                                                                                                                           (Para 9.1) 
 The Committee further notes that the existing Institute/Centres of the Department 
are stationed in major cities and the presence of the Department appears to be negligible as 
far as the remote locations of the country are concerned.  The Committee feels that with 
the increasing demand of space based activities in various sectors, it would be justifiable to 
have Institutes/Centres spread across the country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Department to explore possibilities of establishing Institutes/Centres in these 
underserved areas so as to strengthen its base in the entire country.                         (Para 9.2) 
 On the issue of providing assistance/su pport by the Department to t he space 
industry based startups in the country, the Committee appreciates the efforts being made 
by the Department in this direction.  The Committee, however, feels that in order to give 
impetus to the budding startups, more incentives may be offered by t he Department which 
would have far reaching impact on the ground level.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Department to identify the startups that would play a greater role in the 
overall growth and development of the space ecosystem in the country  and help them 
appropriately through incentives.                                                                                  (Para 9.3)

11. Forest Fire Prevention and Management 
11.1 Forest fire is a major point of concern and occurs in almost every State in the country and 
some districts are more vulnerable than others.  The Committee therefore desired to know the 
mechanism put in place for detection and prevention  of forest fires. The  Ministry informed that 
Forest Survey of India (FSI) is playing a pivotal role in forest fire monitoring in the country since 
2004 when satellite data based alerts of near real time detection of active forest fires were started.  
FSI is providing various se rvices for monitoring of forest fires some of which are: (i) Pre Fire 
Alert (one week advance based on Forest Fire Danger Rating) , (ii) Large Forest Fire Monitoring, 
(iii) Near Real Time Forest Fire Monitoring and (iv) Van Agni Geoportal . Through the use of 
satellites, under a completely digital integrated system namely Near Real Time Forest Fire 
Monitoring (MODIS & SNPP – VIIRS), early warning signs can be detected which helps in 
prevention of forest fires and also aids in managing the damage caused by such fires. 
11. 2 While the Committee acknowledges the use of satellite technology for detecting 
forest fires, the Committee feels that there is need to strengthen  the ground mechanism and 
develop a well equipped and trained workforce to fight forest fires. The Committee , 
therefore, recommends strengthening post -fire assessments, inter -state knowledge sharing 
and research to understand the longer -term impacts of  forest fire which will enable to 

14 
 
identify gaps in implementation of the existing management system  and finding solutions  
thereon. 
11. 3 Tackling forest fires is important for improving the sustainability of the country’s 
forests. The Committee is happy at the increased allocation of Rs. 44.19 crore, for the 
Financial Year 2022 -23 for efficient utilisation and sufficient funding to the Ministry for 
implementation of its initiatives/ programmes for forest fire prevention and management at 
the central and State level . The Committee also urges upon the Ministry to promote 
awareness pro grammes in regions around forest areas for sensitising the concerned 
stakeholders to prevent accidental cases of forest fires.  Proper fencing of forest areas,  real 
time monitoring of illegal activities in forest areas and punitive action against the 
miscreants would further help the agencies in preventing forest fires.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take into consideration national and 
international best practices for forest fire management. 
12. Man-Animal Conflict 
12.1 During the meeting of the Committee , a number of Members pointed out the increase in 
instances of man-animal conflict which were resulting in loss of life of both humans and animals 
and loss of property . Instances of human killing and damage to the crops  were unequivocally 
referred to by many Members.  Members also pointed out that a number of wild animals, 
especially , elephants, nil gai , wild pigs, leopards  etc, were venturing out of their territory and 
entering into the surrounding areas of human habitat resulting in damage to crops and increase in 
cases of man-animal conflict . The Committee , therefore,  desired to be appr ised about the 
mechanism that has been put  in place for compensation, treatment of victims of man -animal 
conflict, early settlement of compensation and prevention of such conflicts.  
 
12. 2 Responding to the issues raised in this regard, the representative of the Ministry of 
Environment, Forest and Climate Change submitted that this is a very serious issue and needs 
immediate attention. The Committee was informed that increase in cattle population is one of the 
major reasons for activities like grazing of cattle, collection of fire wood , etc, in forests, which 
often leads to attack on humans and cattle by the wild animals.  Therefore, work is being carried 
out for demarcation of forest area and its boundaries and also electric fencing of the boundaries. 
The Committee was also informed that efforts are being made to treat man -animal conflict as a 
disaster so that early resolution to such  conflicts could be made in a coordinated manner at 
district level. Efforts are also being made to evolve a mechanism for formulating a uniform 
compensation policy for the country  and that the inclusion of NDMA into the scheme for 
prevention and management  of National Disaster at national level would further help in early 
resolution of man-animal conflict and its prevention. 
 
 
12. 3 The Committee is of the view that the cases of man -animal conflict are on the rise  
and it still remains an area of concern.  As such, there is an urgent need to minimize the 
instances of man-animal conflict that was resulting in both human and an imal killings. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take proactive steps to 
sustainably manage and minimis e man-animal conflict in a balanced manner , whereby the 
wildlife habitat is improved.  The Committee urges upon the Ministry to evolve a 
mechanism at the national level for uniform compensation, ea rly settlement of 
compensation and rehabilitation of  the victims of man -animal conflict. The Committee 
recommends that efforts should be made by the Ministry at local level and especially 
among the communities living in peripheral forest areas to sensitis e them towards 
ecological balance through co-existence with wild life. The Committee urges for creation of 

15 
 
grasslands for grazing of cattle outside the forest area to minimis e man -animal conflict.  
Further, State Forest Departments should also be advised to improve availability of fodder 
and adequate water sources in the forests, especially during summers, which would reduce 
the chances of the wildlife venturing out of their habitat in search of these basic needs.   
13. Plastic Waste Management 
 
13.1 The Committee desired to be apprised about the initiatives taken by the Ministry towards 
Plastic Waste Management and elimination of single use plastics . The Ministry informed the 
Committee that under Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2021-12, single-use plastic 
items have be en identified for prohibition by 2022 , which have low utility and high littering 
potential.  Further, Plastic Waste Management Second Amendment Rules, 2021 were notified on 
17th September 2021 with respect to use recycled plastic in food contact applicatio ns subject to 
rules and regulations framed by FSSAI.  The Committee was also informed that country wide 
awareness programmes are being run to sensitise people to avoid the use of single use plastics by 
making them aware of its harmful effects. 
 
13. 2 The Committee recognizes the importance of plastic waste management and 
elimination of single -use plastics. Single-use plastics being a bio hazard not only impact  
wild life and ecosystems  but also pollute  the environment. The Committee , therefore,  
recommends the Ministry to run awareness programmes on regular basis, to educate the 
people about the ill effects of single-use plastics and encourage them to use other sources as 
a replacement to plastic products i n day to day usage.  The Committee also recommends  
bringing stricter norms and regulations to discourage the use of single-use plastics and also 
lay down clear allocation of roles and responsibilities. 
13.3 The Committee yet again expresses its deep concern  on the issue of non -cooperative 
and unresponsive behavior of the officials dealing with environment al matters towards the 
public representatives .  The Committee reiterates its previous recommendation in this 
matter that the Ministry of Environment, Forest  and Climate Change, being the nodal 
central Ministry dealing with these matters, must impress upon the State Governments as 
well as their own officers to sensitize all the concerned authorities to accord due courtesy to 
the public representatives, attend to their grievances, respond to their communications and 
make available the information sought by them.
