Forest Conservation 
26. The Forest Conservation (Act), 1980 was enacted with a view to check indiscrimi­
nate deforestation and diversion of forest land for non-forest purpose. The Act was amended 
in 1988 to make it more stringent. The Advisory Committee with representation of eminent 
personalities was set up under this Act. At field level there are six regional offices situated 
at I3angalore, Lucknow, Shillong, Bhopal, Bhubaneshwar and· Chandigarh with Headquar­
ters at New Delhi. These offices were set up to monitor cases under Forest (Conservation) 
Act. Later, in 1988 these offices were strengthened and also entrusted with the responsibility 
of monitoring cases under Environment (protection) Act. Under the revised guidelines, the 
regional offices have been empowered to decide cases involving diversion of forest land for 
non-forest purposes up to the extent of 5 ha. except mining and regularization of 
encroachments and examine cases of 5 to 20 ha. in consulation with State Advisory Board.

celsius in 1970 to plus 0.3 in 1990. One of the factors responsible for this is the record-level 
use of fossil fuels which boosts the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide, which traps 
heat to increasing heights. Last year alone, carbon emissions from burning fossils and fuels all 
over the world reached 6.1 billion tonnes which marl<s an increase of one million tonnes over 
1991. The Committee has been given to understand that most Governments of industrialised 
countries are failing to meet the goal of limiting carbon set by the Framework Convention on 
climate change signed at the earth summit in 1992. The Committee is of the view that curbs 
on carbon emission are necessary. Even though the scientific concept of a friendly 
environment is relatively new to us something drastically needs to be done by the Ministry in 
this regard with a view to control the environmental pollution. 
The Committee has been given to understand that according to a WHO report released at 
the conference tropical diseases like malaria, dengue and cholera will rise sharply in Africa 
and Asia. Besides, malnutri ·tion and water scarcity will affect many more families ·. Changes in 
h)·drological cycle will alter rainfall patterns in many areas. Many inland areas in the tropics 
may insteud face droughts and drying up o'f rivers. According to a study 3 to 4 degrees 
warming may eliminate up to 85 of the remaining wetlands, wipling out many birds and turtle 
species. 
67. The Committee agrees tliat ther-e is thus an urgent need to bring about a consensus to 
finally reduce emissions by 50 to 70 per cent over the next few decades by taking steps to 
increase energy efticiency, limit carbon consumption and encourage transition to renewables . 
This is all the more necessary because scientific studies advocate a stabilisation target of 450 
PPI\1 by 2100 A.D., where eco-systems could naturally adapt to climate change . 
The Committee further agrees that access to emironment friendly technology and finance 
is critical for countries like China and India which are stated to be fourth and fifth largest 
producers of Green House Gases (GIIGs) respectively to curb their emissions. The Committee 
recommends that Government should join the attempts to activate the Global Environment 
Facility (GEF) , a multilateral fund set up by affluent nations to meet obligations under the 
UN climate ~hange convention and lend budgetary support. 
(>S. The Committee notes that the l\linistry 's record in utilisation of budgetary support on 
conservation programmes in the last two )'cars has been poor. In 1995-96, the Ministr y 
utilised Rs. 6.31 crores out of the budget prO\'ision of Rs. S uores which is about 80% . ln 
199-J-95 the l\linistry utilised Rs. -L56 crorcs out of a pro\i ~ i on of Rs. ~ cron:s i.e., 50.7%. 
The Committee observes that the l\linistry should widen its hori,_,nl and should concentrate on 

urgent areas of Consevation Programme. This would also ensure optimum utilisation of 
budgetary support. 
69. As regard the dependence of the country's rural population on forest resources the 
Committee's attention has been drawn to a su~:vey conducted by Self-employed Women's 
Association (SEW .t\) in some villages in Sabarkanth~ District in Gujarat where 93% of the 
families live below poverty-line. These women have to pay 200 to 300 per cent more than what 
paper mills pay for the same forest produce. Besides, the Adivasi women who are at best 
semi-literate and who tap gum are also required to obtain licence. Another agony of these 
women is that they are required to sell their produce to Government agencies at one-fourth of 
the ,market price. In the process when these women were operating 'illegally' they could earn 
Rs. 25'- per day but now as SEW A members when they wish to operat~ 'legally' they earn 
Rs. 121-per day with longer working hours and with the additional help of c,hildren who have 
to leave school to provide the necessary supportive labour. 
The Committee therefore, feels that a line has to be drawn on the exploitation of forest 
wealth by the tribal ' and rural population on the one hand and unauthorised exploitation for 
commercial purposes. 
70. Another important aspect related to the preservation of forests is the large scale 
devastation by fire. This aspect, the Committee feels, is being neglected due to lack of modern 
fire fighting systems and insufficient control, monitoring and communication system to contain 
and prevent such fires. 
71. This is one of the projects for which budget estimates for 1996-97 provide an amount 
of Rs. 44 crores. Already till 1995-96, an amount of Rs. 89 crores has been released to the 
ICEF by the Ministry. The objective or the ICEF is to enhance the capacity of Indian 
institutions and organisations to promote and deli~er sustainable development programmes. 
For this purpose the priority areas identified under ICEF are the following projects: 
(i) Enhancing the capacity : of Indian private and public sector institutions and 
organisations to undertake environmentally sustainable development and 
management of energy and water resources. 
(ii) Providing support for programms which specifically address the inter-relationship 
between poverty .and environmental degradation, especially as it affects women, in 
energy, land and water management activities at the community and village level. 
(iii) Providing support for public awareness of environmental issues, community 
participation and community-based management of energy, land and water 
resources. 
72. The Committee feels that there is no correlation between the goals set forth, the 
projects identified and the amount of funds provided to these projects. It is also not clear how 
the funds spent on these projects ultimately benefit women engaged h~ energy, land and water 
management activities at the community and village_ level and provide support for public 
awareness of environmental issues etc. Among the beneficiaries are certain institutions like 
M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation Project entitled "Coastal Wet Lands Mangrove 
Conservation and Management". The Committee is not aware whether there is any 
mechanism to monitor the satisfactory utilisation of funds by such beneficiaries. Further, 
certain amounts realised from the sale of commodities donated by the Canadian Government 
are also channelised to projects under ICEF. The Committee has not been apprised as to what 
are the commodities donated by the Canadian Government and how they are sold and the 
receipts accruing thereform are channelised to the project. Prima facie there seems to be a 

case for further investigation into the entire project and utilisation of the funds earmarked for 
the project. 
73. One of the projects under the head forestry is the Project Elephant for which the 
budgetary support amounted to Rs. 5 crores each year in the last three years namely 1993-94, 
1994-95, 1995-96. While the actual expenditure during 1993-94 was Rs. 5.69 crores, in 
1994-95, it went down to Rs. 4.80 crores and declined further to Rs. 3 •• 4 crore in 1995-96. 
The Committee was informed that the large portion of the funds were provided to the State of 
Kerala for providing an 'Elephant Corridor' in ldukki and Parambikulam. The amount was 
disbursed to the State Government through District Collector and so far about 60 hectares of 
land had been taken over by the Ministry for the establishment of corridor in Kerala. The 
Committee was also informed that they have planted trees on an area of 400 acres of land. 
While the total budgetary provision for the project is Rs. 23 crores of which the corridor will 
require roughly an amount of Rs. 4 crores 25 per cent of the amount is to be spent on 
strengthening of infrastructure namely specialy wireless stations as elephant is considered to 
be a wide ranging animal. Asked about the details of the project and the number of trees etc. 
planted all these years in the elephant corridor, the Ministry could not furnish details. 
Besides, it was stated that a census was conducted for estimation of elephant population by 
direct count and index count in different parts of the country during 1992 and 1993. The 
habitat restoration and improvement activities have resulted in reduction of the period of 
man-elephant encounters thus mitigating the man-elephant conflict in such areas. 
74. The Committee is not happy with the progress made by the Ministry in the Project 
Elephant. Despite whatever has been done by the Ministry, one elephant is killed everyday. 
The generation of elephants appears to have completely stopped. There are no details 
provided by the Government indicating whether life of any elephant has been saved anywhere 
as a result of large amounts spent by them under the scheme. The Committee feels that the 
figures furnished by the Government regarding increase in the population of elephants from 
23,000 in 1989 to 25,000 in 1993 are not realistic. On the other hand, a large number of 
elephants die for reasons other than poaching. The Committee recommends that tliis project 
should be closely monitored and detailed notes on action taken with results, indigenous species 
planted with survival rate, number of wireless sets given, etc. should be furnished to the 
Committee. 
. 
75. The Animal Welfare Board has been provided with budgetary support of Rs. 1.64 
crores in the budget estimates for 1996-97 of which Rs. 1.30 crores in on plan side an~ 0.34 
crores on the non-plan side. The budgetary allocation during the last three years ranged from 
LO to 1.5 crores (plan as well as non-plan) and it was largely over-spent. The Committee 
observes that there is a considerable scope for enhancing the budgetary support under this 
head for stopping rabies in the country, for providing rearing homes for cows, for health care 
and sterilisation of animals and for prevention of cruelty to animals. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the budgetary support in respect of Animal Welfare Board needs 
to be considerably enhanced to say, Rs. 10 crores, for catering to the needs of the animals. At 
the same time , Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry to ensure that the 
enhanced budgetary support, if provided, are spent really for the benefit of the animals and 
not on illusory overheads . 
76. Central Zoo Authority incurred an expenditure of Rs. 3 crores equal to the amount 
provided as budgetary support. The budgetary provision in 1993-94 and 1994-95 ranged from 
Rs. 1.5 crore to Rs. 3 crores and it was over-spent . A budgetary provision of Rs. 3 crores has 
been made in the budget estimates for 1996-97 also. The Committee observes that the 
budgetary support is not spent Jor the purpose for which it is intended otherwise the death 

rate of 15 to 20 per cent of animals due to gastroenteritis in Indian zoos would not have been 
there. The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry that the animals should be 
protected from heatstroke. They should be provided with good food and safe drinking water 
so that the death of animals on these counts are avoided. Steps should also be taken to 
provide a trained cadre of officers for management of zoos. The Committee is constrained to 
observe that a sum of Rs. 3 crores spent on evaluation of zoos was not properly spent as 
nothing appears to have been spent for rehabilitation purposes. In Committee's view there is a 
strong case for enhancing the budgetary allocation, say, Rs. 10 crores for Central Zoo 
Authority to say Rs. 10 crores so that the programmes relating to the welfare of the animals 
as also the creation of a cadre comprising of trained officers can be taken care of. 
77. A provision of Rs. 106 crores has been made in the budget estimates for 1996-97 in 
respect of Ganga Project Directorate. The main objective of GAP Phase-! is to improve the 
water quality of river Ganga. To that end, sewage generated from 25 class I towns 
(populations above 1 lakh) in U.P., Bihar, and the West Bengal is intercepted, diverted and 
treated before its final disposal either back in the river or for irrigation purposes. 261 
schemes of pollution abatement have been sanctioned which include interception and diversion 
of sewage, sewage treatment plants, low cost toilets, electric crematoria and bathing ghats, in 
the States of U.P., Bihar and the West Bengal. The action plan envisages diversion and 
treatment of 873 million litres per day of sewage from the above towns. Out of this, a capacity 
of 654 million Jitres per day has already been created. 
It has been stated that 244 schemes have been completed, the remaining 17 are in 
progress and expected to be completed by 31.03.1997. Of the 35 sewage treatment plants 
proposed to be constructed, 26 are functional and remaining 9 are in their final stages of 
completion. The project has tieen delayed due to reasons such as inexperience in the kind of 
work required, inordinate delays in land acquisition for certain schemes, litigation and court 
cases in Kanpur, Allahabad in U.P. and in West Bengal encroachment of sites of major 
projects in Calcutta and Patna, tendering and retendering of certain schemes due to 
contractual problems, delay in the external aid component of ·Kanpur and Mirzapur and 
diversion of funds by State Governments of U..P. and Bihar and consequent delayed release of 
the Central funding to the States for implementation of certain programmes. 
78. The Committee has been informed that the Ganga Action Plan Model with necessary 
corrections on the basis of lessons learnt and experience gained has been applied to all the 
major rivers of the country un,der the two schemes of GAP Phase-11 and the NRCP. It would 
take- about 10 years of time to complete these works. 
79. The Committee notes that a sum of Rs. 18.70 crores was surrendered against GAP 
Phase-1 and Rs. 70 crores in GAP Phase-11 Rs. 14 crores on NRCP and Rs. 3.30 crores on 
establishment. The Committee expresses its concern on the non-utilised component of the 
Ganga Action Plan. The Committee observes that non-utilisation/surrender of funds at least 
on some programmes could have been visualised and corrections made accordingly. Further, 
the Committee would like to be apprised of the mechanism put in place to monitor the 
working of various plants set up under the GAP, Phase-1 and whether any provision was 
incorporated in the contracts with contractors for liquidated damages for failure/delay in 
execution of contracts. 
80. On the basis of the oral evidence tendered before the Committee and the written 
submissions made, the Committee has regretfully come to the conclusion that the functioning 
of the Ministry of EnYironment and Forests is far from satisfactory. The Committee had 
asked for detailed and comprehensive notes on some of the issues like modern fire-fighting 

controls including helicopters and aircrafts, the Project Elephant and Ganga Action Plan and 
certain other issues. While notes have been supplied but those are not very detailed and lack 
critical analysis. For example, note on Project Elephant had no details on the issues the 
Committee had specifically asked for. The Committee had also asked for details of the 
indigenous species of plants planted and how bad they been received by the local people? 
Similarly, no details of the equipment etc. supplied under this project have been furnished. 
81. A large amount of expenditure of the Ministry is by way of grants-in-aid to the 
various State Governments and Non-Government Organisation (NGOs). It therefore becomes 
incumbent on the part of the Ministry to interact more closely with the grantee states and 
NGOs to ensure that the grants made available are in fact used for the purpose for which 
these are being made available. The Committee, however, feels that this part of the activity 
has not been taken seriously. In fact, whenever explanations and details were asked for during 
the course of oral evidence, the Committee was told that the same was under the State 
Government and the Ministry had no control over it. The Committee is unable to accept this 
explanation and recommends greater monitoring on the funds made available to different 
State Governments and NGOs. 
82. The Committee has also noted the delays in completion of various civil works 
undertaken by the l\linistry. The Committee would like to emphasise the importance of their 
timely completion so as to avoid cost-overruns and delays in the projects. 
83. The attention of the Committee has also been drawn to some of the observations in 
respect of review of various projects, as have appeared in the Report of the Comptoller and 
Auditor General of India, for the year ended 31st March, 1993 (No. 6 of 1994). Some of these 
observations are reproduced below:-
Under 'National social forestry project', aided by World Bank and the United States 
Agency for classification resulting in non-reimbursement (Himachal Pradesh), excess purchase 
of polythene granules, non-transfer of plantation areas to gram panchayats (Rajasthan), non­
compliance with orders resulting in loss of revenue, non-conformity to norms of World Bank 
resulting in non-reimbursement and excess procurement of vehicles (Uttar Pradesh) were 
notices in audit. World Bank's assessment of project weaknesses in Uttar · Pradesh indicated 
lack of marketing information system, problems in supply of seedlings, ineffective monitoring 
and analysis of project research . and its use in project management decisions. 
There were dalays in completion of Ganga Action Plan (GAP) programme in the 
'Integrated sanitation works in Kanpur and 1\·lirzapur'. Effective performance of the upflow 
anaerobic sludge blanket system is dependent upon the adoption of technology for chromium 
recovery from tanneries' discharges. A mid-term evaluation report (February · 1992) revealed 
that only 26 out of 151 tanneries were likely to adopt chromium recovery thereby affecting the 
performance of upflow anaerobic sludge blanket system. The technology for post-treatment of 
effluents from upflow anaerobic sludge blanket system was still in an experimental stage in 
Netherlands and therefore could not be adopted in India. 
Non-installation of equipments, training details not being available, delays in planning, detailed 
review not having been conducted were somt of the problems that affiicted the project: in respect of 
'Technical assistance and equipments' aided by Unitt>d Kingdom no details of the aid received were 
available. 
Aid provided by Governm'ent of Sweden for 'Strengthening of Indian Institute of Forest 
Management' could not be utilised substantively because of management problems, infighting in the 
faculty, problems in design of management development programmes etc. 
The project progress review report in its analysis also indicated lack of clarity in planning, 

problems in management and co-ordination by Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and problems 
in co-ordination between Indian Authorities and German Technical Co-operation Agency (GTZ) head 
office. No details of the aid received were available. 
Similar observations have appeared in respect of review covering the implementation of Schemes of 
Ganga Action Plan Phase-1 and an appraisal of its achievements at selected cities of Uttar Pradesh 
(U.P.), Bihar and West Bengal (W.B.) and Forest Survey of India (F.S.I.) as have appeared ln the 
Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, for the year ended 31st March, 1994 (No. 6 
of 1995). These are only a few of the observations. The list is endless. 
84. The Committee observes that these observations should be implemented expeditiously. The 
Committee would also take the opportunity to emphasise that foreign aid lo any form should be 
avoided where in all such cases the indigenous resources can be utilised.

REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change  deals with the 
action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the contained in its „Three 
Hundred Sixty Second Report‟ on „Demands for Grants (2022-23) of the Department of Space‟.  The 
Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 15th March, 2022. 
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from Department of Space in respect of all 
the fifteen recommendations/observations contained in the „Three Hundred Sixty  Second Report ‟. 
The replies of the Department of Space have been categorized as follows:- 
Chapter I:        Recommendations/Observations which have been accept ed by the 
Government:  
Para Nos.:- 2.7, 2.8, 2.10, 3.3, 3.4, 4.3, 6.3, 7.3, 7.4, 8.3, 9.1, 9.2 and 9.3  
 Total recommendations – 13 accepted. 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Department has accepted its  thirteen 
recommendations/observations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report.  
Chapter II:       Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies:  
Para Nos.:- 2.4 and 5.3  
Total recommendations – 02 Not to be pursued further. 
The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Department 
and, therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendations further. 
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted by the Committee: ‘Nil’ 
Chapter IV:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: ‘Nil’ 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding chapters.  
 
  

2 
 
CHAPTER - I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021 -22 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FIANANCIAL YEAR 2022-23 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.1 The Committee makes note of the roadmap prepared by the Department for the year       
2022-23 with a hope that the Department would strive hard to ensure that the targets set for the 
year 2022 -23 are achieved and the budgetary support provided to the Department would be 
sufficient to sustain its major projects/schemes/programmes without any difficulty. 
(Para 2.7 of the 362nd Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2 The observations of the Committee are noted.   
Recommendations/Observations 
1.3 The Committee while scrutinising the targets set and progress achieved by the Department 
during the year 2021-22, observes that the Department had set the target of realisation and launch 
of Geo -Imaging Satellite (GISAT) for agriculture and disaster management applications which 
could not be achieved as the launch could not succeed. Likewise, the launch of India's first solar 
observatory Spacecraft, Aditya -L1, on-board PSLV was envisaged during the year 2021 -22 which 
has now been targeted during 2022 -23.  The Committee further notes that the Department had a 
plan to launch the 3rd generation Oceanographic satellite - Oceansat-3 on-board PSLV in the year 
2021-22 which has now been rescheduled to 2022 -23. The Committee, theref ore, recommends that 
the Department should strive hard to ensure that the newly set timeline for these components are 
honoured and further delay should not happen.                                                             (Para 2.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.4 The recommendations of the Committee regarding launch of Aditya -L1 and Oceansat-3 are 
noted.  The Department will take necessary steps to ensure the timely launch of these satellites. 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.5 The Committee hopes that the recruitment drives as intended by the Department would be 
completed in a time bound manner. The Committee also desires the Department to furnish its 
updated manpower status in the Action Taken Notes.                                                  (Para 2.10 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.6 Presently, the men -in-position at various DOS / ISRO Centres / Units is 16077 against the 
Sanctioned strength of 19610. The recruitment activities in DOS/ISRO were greatly affected by 
Covid-19 induced restrictions during last two years. Further, Department was in the process of 
carrying out detailed assessment of S&T manpower in ISRO, while factoring the impact of reforms. 
Based on this, necessary guidelines have been issued to initiate recruitment actions in campaign 
mode. 
 
 

3 
 
 
BUDGET ALLOCATION FOR CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES/PROJECTS 
SPACE TECHNOLOGY 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.7 The Committee hopes that the Department would make all out efforts to ensure full 
utilisation of the budgetary allocation for the year 2021 -22 during the remaining period of the 
financial year 2021-22.                                                                                                   (Para 3.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.8 At the end of the Financial Year 2021 -22, the actual expenditure of the Department under 
the head “Space Technology” was Rs.8873.63 crore with an utilisation factor of 99.34 % of RE 
allocations. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.9 The Committee further feels that the utilisation by the Department under various 
components such as Trisonic Wind Tunnel Facility Project (TWT); Small Satellite Launch Vehicle 
(SSLV); Launch pad for SSLV; Network for Space Object Tracking & Analysis (NETRA); Geo -
Imaging Satellite (GISAT); Resourcesat -3S & 3SA; Development of Space Mate rials & 
Components; Development & Supply of Aluminium alloy tankages (Pre -investment); and Capacity 
Building Programme (CBP) could have been better. The Committee, accordingly, desires the 
Department to revisit its fund utilisation strategy under these com ponents and take necessary 
remedial actions so that funds made available for them are utilised fully.                    (Para 3.4 ibid)

1.21 The Committee is satisfied to note that the Department till 31st January,  2022 has utilised

1.22 During the year, NSIL has taken several important steps to commercialise the products and 
services emanating from the Indian Space Programme for the benefit of the users.  Some of the

1. NSIL‟s 1st De mand Driven Satellite Mission, namely GSAT -24 Communication satellite

In addition, NSIL has signed four PSLV Launch Service agreements for launching 
international customer satellites.  Of this, one dedicated PSLV launch for Singapore  satellite

GENERAL OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.23 The Committee notes that the Department of Space has been making efforts in mapping the 
glacial lakes which span over more than 2.5 hectare in size and the said exercise has been 
completed in respect of the Ganga basin and Sutlej river and the data has already been complied in 
the atlas form. The Committee is of the view that it will be of great importance if an inventory about 
the glacier and glacial lakes in the Himalayan region is documented on yearly basis. This is crucial 
in light of many studies suggesting that there has been rapid increase in the number of glacial lakes 
due to retreat in the glaciers caused by the impact of g lobal warming and keeping into 
consideration the possible large scale flooding and destruction that could happen in future.  
Therefore, role of the Department, in the matter becomes all the more pivotal and significant in 
light of the fact that many such gl aciers are physically inaccessible for ground reporting. The 
Committee also feels that with the modern technology and better resolution satellite imagery the 
task of glacier lakes outburst monitoring can be done in a more scientific and robust manner. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to initiate action in this regard in a time bound 
manner and to make best use of its remote sensing services for the purpose. Adequate budgetary 
allocations should also be made for the same.                                                               (Para 9.1 ibid)  
 
 
 
 

8 
 
Action Taken 
1.24   i. As an implementing agency under the National Hydrology Project (NHP) of M inistry of 
Jal Shakti, National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC)/ ISRO mapped Glacial lakes of size 
greater than 0.25  ha in Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river basins of Himalaya 
(including transboundary catchment flowing into Indian region), along with associated 
characteristics describing geometry, hydrology, topographic, etc., using Resourcesat -2 
LISS4 MX data. 28,043 such lakes have been mapped across these basins, and 
corresponding atlases have been published. Mapping and attribute assignment of  these 
Glacial lakes took nearly 3 years. 
 ii.  
(a) Glacial lake formation is a slow process and generally extends over long duration, 
except in cases like landslide dammed lakes. Considering the dynamicity of the 
glacial lakes and availability of usable (due to issues such as cloud, snow cover, 
shadow etc.) high resolution satellite data, it is desirable to ha ve Glacial lake 
inventory updation at periodicity around 3-5 years. 
Periodic updation of Glacial lake database can be taken up by the following 
Organisations: 
o Central Water Commission/NWIC 
o State Disaster Organisations/State Remote Sensing Centres 
NRSC/ ISR O would build capacity for the concerned Organisations and extend 
technical handholding. 
(b) In case of Glaciers, the dynamism (changes in glacier surface area; volume etc.) may 
not be perceivable on an annual basis, even on high resolution satellite data. Mos t of 
the Himalayan glaciers are covered with rock debris partially in their ablation zones 
which makes it difficult to monitor the changes in ice surface area of glaciers. 
Glacier mapping is practically done by visual interpretation, which would take more 
than a year for covering the entire Himalaya, using High resolution satellite data.   
Also, usable (cloud/snow -free) high resolution satellite data for the entire Himalaya 
may not be available every year.  
Monitoring of Glacier mass balance can also be done using geodetic methods such as 
DEM differencing. This has been done by many foreign researchers, which has 
established thinning of glaciers in the Himalaya. These assessments have been done 
for decadal or coarser time intervals.  
Glacier inventory and ch ange assessment have been done by Space Applications 
Center (SAC)/ ISRO over different time periods in the Himalaya (Annexure-I). 
Based on these experiences and scientific knowledge, it is proposed that inventory of 
Glaciers in the Indian Himalayan regions  would be required at time intervals of 10 -
15 years. This could be taken up by SAC/ ISRO, on demand from the concerned 
Ministry/ Department; such as Ministry of  Environment, Forests and Climate 
Change, Ministry of Jal Shakti etc.   
 
 
 

9 
 
iii. 
(a) Glacial Lake Monitoring by Central Water Commission (CWC)/NWIC 
o Central Water Commission (CWC) is mandated by Government of India to provide 
Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) early warning. 
o NRSC/ ISRO imparted necessary training & technical handholding to Morphology & 
Climate Change Directorate, Central Water Commission, during 2015 for monitoring 
of glacial lakes using satellite data. Morphology & Climate Change Directorate, 
CWC is internally carrying out the monitoring Glacial lakes (>50ha) using satellite

(http://www.cwc.gov.in/glacial-lakeswater-bodies-himalayan-region). 
o NRSC/ISRO further conducted one -week training to CWC Officials in 2021 on 
“Monitoring of Glacial Lakes using Satellite Remote Sensing Data. Updat ed Glacial 
lake data base (size GT 0.25a) prepared by NRSC/ ISRO under NHP is also shared 
with CWC for use in monitoring of glacial lakes. 
o Hence, it is suggested that CWC may continue to monitor glacial lakes using updated 
glacial lake database provided by NRSC/ ISRO. 
(b) Glacial Lake Monitoring by State Organisations /State Remote Sensing Centres 
o State Government Departments located in Himalayan region can monitor glacial 
lakes concerned to their geographical region on regular basis for better and efficient 
management of glacial lake floods.  
o NRSC/ ISRO can build capacity and extend technical handholding for the concerned 
State Organisations on monitoring of glacial lakes using satellite data. 
o It is also informed that the Power Organisations such as NHPC, SJVNL , etc. are also 
gearing up for periodic monitoring of Glacial lakes using satellite data 
(c) GLOF studies at ISRO 
Glacial lake outburst flood modelling of prioritised glacial lakes are being done by 
NRSC/ ISRO, under NHP. 
Further, SAC/ISRO would carry out rese arch on developing method to identify potential 
areas around the lakes which could create temporary damming, and could lead to GLOFs. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.25 The Committee further notes that the existing Institute/Centres of the Department are 
stationed in major cities and the presence of the Department appears to be negligible as far as the 
remote locations of the country are concerned.  The Committee feels that with the increasing 
demand of space based activities in various sectors, it would be justifiable to have Institutes/Centres 
spread across the country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to explore 
possibilities of establishing Institutes/Centres in these underserved areas so as to strengthen its 
base in the entire country.                                                                                               (Para 9.2 ibid)

across the country. So far, there are  24 R&D cells instituted at premier academic institutions like

research potential.

1.27 On the issue of providing assistance/support by the Department to the space industry based 
startups in the country, the Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department in this

Annexure-I 
Glacier inventory was carried out by SAC/ISRO over Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins 
using IRS P6  satellite data of (AWiFS and LISS -III sensor) for the periods; 2004 -2007 and 2007 -
2010. During Phase-I of the project, inventory was generated for all the glaciers in the Indus, Ganga 
and the Brahmaputra basins encompassing the Himalayas, Trans -Himalaya and Karakoram regions 
on 1: 50,000 scale using Resourcesat -1 satellite data of 2004 –2007 period. The results show that 
there are 32, 392 glaciers covering 71,182 sq. km area in the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins 
draining into the Indian territory. Duri ng Phase-II, the work was extended to map glaciers of West 
Indus basin which are draining into neighbouring countries. Thus the total glacier inventory data for 
all the three Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins show that there are 34919 glaciers covering 7 5, 
779 sq. km area. An updation of the Glaciers‟ inventory is proposed systematically; selectively over 
Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins with the help of collaborating agencies in respective states 
with recent satellite images. 
Glacier monitoring has be en carried out for select Glaciers using satellite data at SAC/ 
ISRO, which may represent the general trend of the Glacier dynamics. Changes in area of glaciers 
for the time period of 1962 – 2001/04/05 were mapped for 2630 glaciers. Glacier extents for 196 2 
were taken from Survey of India (SOI) topographical maps on 1:50,000 scale as reference and that 
of 2001/04/05 timeframe were taken from satellite data. This study showed a total loss of 13.4 % in 
area of glaciers. In continuation, monitoring of change i n extents of 2018 glaciers was carried out 
from IRS LISS III data of year 2000/01/02 and 2010/2011. The monitoring showed that 87% of the 
glaciers had no change, 12% have retreated and 1 % glaciers have advanced. This gives a net loss of 
20.94 sq. km in th e total area of 10,250.68 sq. km for all the monitored glaciers mapped in the year 
2000/01. Net change in glaciated area varies from region to region.  
Further, 5234 glaciers were monitored between the years 2001 and 2017/2018 across 
Himalayan –Karakoram ( H-K) region from Kashmir to Sikkim using IRS LISS III and limited 
Landsat data. These 5234 ice bodies included 3435 debris free glaciers also. In Karakoram region 
(north of Indus river), 2058 glacier bodies were checked and mapped. In this region, gain in area 
(0.056 %) has been observed in the area coverage of 17902.95 Km 2. The loss observed in rest of 
Himalayan region varies from 0.751 % for sub -basins south of Indus river (or in rest of Jammu and 
Kashmir and Ladakh states), 2.32 % in Himachal Pradesh or in Chenab and Sutlej basins, 0.84 % in 
Uttarakhand, 2.164 % in parts of Nepal, and 2.147 % in Sikkim or Tista sub -basin. SAC/ ISRO has 
taken up glacier monitoring using recent satellite images.

FOREST FIRE PREVENTION AND MANAGEMENT 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.31 While the Committee acknowledges the use of satellite technology for detecting forest 
fires, the Committee feels that there is need to strengthen the ground mechanism and develop a 
well equipped and trained workforce to fight forest fires. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
strengthening post -fire assessments, inter -state knowledge sharing and research to understand 
the longer-term impacts of forest fire whi ch will enable to identify gaps in implementation of the 
existing management system and finding solutions thereon.                                  (Para 11.2 ibid)                                                                                                                                                                       
 
Action Taken 
 
1.32 The number of incidences of forest fire in the country varies from year to year and occurs 
during fire season from November to May every year due to various natural and anthropogenic 
reasons including accumulation of inflammable materials such as dry leaves, twigs, pine needles 
etc. Most of the forest fires in the country are ground fires in which ground vegetation, etc. get 
burnt. 
 
1.33 Ministry prepared a National Action Plan on Forest  Fire in April 2018  after several 
rounds of consultations with all the States and Union Territories. The objective of this Plan is to 
minimize forest fires by informing, enabling and empowering forest fring e communities and 
incentivizing them to work in tandem with the State Forest Departments. The Plan also intends to 
substantially reduce the vulnerability of forests across the diverse forest ecosystems in the 

8  
country against  fire hazards, enhance the capab ilities of forest personnel and institutions in 
fighting fires and speed up recovery after a fire event. 
 
1.34 The Ministry issues advisories to all State and UT Governments before the start 
of fire season for adequate preparedness for effective prevention and management of forest fire. 
 
1.35 Forest Survey of India (FSI), Dehradun, an organization under the Ministry disseminates 
the satellite-based forest fire alerts to the State Forest Departments and other registered mobile 
users whenever forest fires are detected. Till date, around 1.30 lakh users have been registered to 
receive the fire alerts from FSI. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.36 Tackling  forest fires is important for improving the sustainability of the country’s forests. 
The Committee is happy a t the increased allocation of Rs. 44.19 crore, for the Financial Year 
2022-23 for efficient utilisation and sufficient funding to the Ministry for implementation of its 
initiatives/ programmes for forest fire prevention and management at the central and St ate level. 
The Committee also urges upon the Ministry to promote awareness programmes in regions 
around forest areas for sensitising the concerned stakeholders to prevent accidental cases of 
forest fires. Proper fencing of forest areas,  real time monitorin g of illegal activities in forest 
areas and punitive action against the miscreants would further help the agencies in preventing 
forest fires. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take into 
consideration national and international best practices for forest fire management.  
          (Para 11.3 ibid)                                                                                            
Action Taken 
 
1.38 FSI is currently working on a system similar to Canadian Forest Fire Danger  Rating 
System (CFFDRS), based on Fire Weather Index (FWI) for fire danger rating in India. 
Additionally, Forest Type Layer information and Forest Fire Archival information are also being 
used to generate Forest Fire Danger Rating. The parameters are quant ified and overlaid on grids 
of 5 km x 5 km. 
1.39 FWI consists of six components that account for the effects of fuel, moisture and weather 
conditions on fire behaviour. The first three components are fuel moisture codes, which are 
numeric ratings of the mo isture content of the forest floor and other dead organic matter. Their 
values rise as the moisture content decreases. The remaining three components are fire behaviour 
indices, which represent the rate of fire spread, the fuel available for combustion, an d the frontal 
fire intensity; these three values rise as the fire danger increases.  
1.40 All information regarding FWI is downloadable from GEOS-5 (Goddard Earth Observing 
System Model, Version -5) daily data from NASA’s GFWED database  (Global Fire Weather  
Database), which is satellite calibrated weather data. The FWI values from GEOS -5  daily 
database from NASA’s GFWED database are downloaded and thresholds are customized for 
different physiographic zones of the country using past archive data on a weekly basis. The Fire 
Danger Rating is categorized into five classes, which are Extreme Risk, Very High Risk, High 
Risk, Moderate Risk and Low Risk and uploaded as Web Map Service (WMS) in the Van Agni 
Geo-portal of FSI. 
1.41 During Fire season, the Extreme Risk  and Very High Risk categories of Forest Fire 
Danger Rating based on FWI values are disseminated as Pre -Fire Alerts (PFA) on every 
Thursday of the week to State Forest Departments ( SFDs). PFA’s are disseminated through e -
mail as KML (Keyhole Markup Languag e) file, which is Google Earth compatible file, to 

9  
Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Head of Forest Force) and Forest Fire Nodal Officer of 
the State Forest Departments. 
1.42 The Ministry supports the efforts of State Governments/Union Territory Admi nistration 
in prevention and control of forest  fire by providing financial assistance for various 
forest fire prevention and management measures such as creation and maintenance of fire lines in 
forest areas, engagement of  fire watchers, creation of water storage structures in forest areas, 
strengthening of forest infrastructure, procurement of firefighting equipment, soil and moisture 
conservation works in high risk areas, awareness creation, incentivizing villages/communities for 
protection against forest  fire etc. During the curr ent financial year Rs. 44.19 crore  has been 
allocated to all the States /UTs under Forest  Fire Prevention and Management Scheme.    A sum 
of about Rs.113.1322 cr ore have been released to the States in last year (2019 -20 to 2021 -22) 
under this scheme. 
MAN-ANIMAL CONFLICT 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.43 The Committee is of the view that the cases of man -animal conflict are on the rise and it 
still remains an area of concern.  As such, there is an urgent need to minimize the instances of 
man-animal conflict that was resulting in both human and animal killi ngs. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take proactive steps to sustainably manage and 
minimise man-animal conflict in a balanced manner, whereby the wildlife habitat is improved. 
The Committee urges upon the Ministry to evolve a  mechanism at the national level for uniform 
compensation, early settlement of compensation and rehabilitation of the victims of man -animal 
conflict. The Committee recommends that efforts should be made by the Ministry at local level 
and especially among the communities living in peripheral forest areas to sensitise them towards 
ecological balance through co -existence with wild life. The Committee urges for creation of 
grasslands for grazing of cattle outside the forest area to minimise man-animal conflict. Further, 
State Forest Departments should also be advised to improve availability of fodder and adequate 
water sources in the forests, especially during summers, which would reduce the chances of the 
wildlife venturing out of their habitat in search of these basic needs.                  (Para 12.3 ibid)                                                                      
Action Taken 
 
1.44 To minimize the instances of man -animal conflict, following procedure/advisory/SOPs 
are followed by the Ministry: 
 
I   Project Tiger 
 
1.45 The Government of India, through the National Tiger Conservation Authority, has 
advocated a three pronged strategy to manage human-tiger negative interactions as follows: 
 
(i)  Material and logistical support:  Funding support through the ongoing Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme of Project Tiger, is provided to tiger reserves for acquiring capacity in terms of 
infrastructure and material, to deal with tigers dispersing out of source areas. These are solicited 
by tiger reserves through an Annual Plan of Operation (APO) every year which stems out from an 
overarching Tiger Conservation Plan (TCP), mandated under Section 38 V of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972.  Inter alia,  activities such as payment of ex -gratia and compensation, 
periodic awareness campaigns to sensitize, guide and advise the general populace on man -animal 
conflict, dissemination of information through various forms of media, procurement of 
immobilization equipment, drugs, training and capacity building of forest staff to deal with 
conflict events are generally solicited. 

10  
 (ii) Restricting habitat interventions:  Based on the carrying capacity of tigers in a tiger 
reserve, habitat interventions are restricted through an overarching TCP. In case tiger numbers are 
at carrying capacity levels, it is advised that habitat interventions should be limited so that there is 
no excessive spill over of wildlife including tigers thereby minimizing man -animal conflict. 
Further, in buffer areas around tiger reserves, habitat interventions are r estricted such that they 
are sub -optimal vis -à-vis the core/critical tiger habitat areas, judicious enough to facilitate 
dispersal to other rich habitat areas only. 
 
 (iii)  Standard Operating Procedure (SOPs):  The National Tiger Conservation Authority has  
also issued three SOPs to deal with human -animal conflict which are available in public domain. 
These are as under: 
 
i        To deal with emergency arising due to straying of tigers in human dominated landscapes 
ii       To deal with tiger depredation on livestock 
iii     For active management towards rehabilitation of tigers from source areas at the landscape  
level 
 
II Project Elephant 
 
(i) To address issue of human elephant conflict, the states have resorted to capture of 
problematic elephants and the  funds needs to be augmented for the establishment of 
rescue/rehabilitation centres for permanent or temporary housing of wild elephants. 
 
(ii)  Critical elephant habitats are notified as ‘Elephant Reserve’ (ER) for focus and synergy in 
elephant conservation and to reduce conflict. The notification is carried out with the approval of 
Steering Committee formed in the Ministry. So far 31 ERs have been established in 14 major 
elephant States in which 10 ER's are from North Eastern States such as Assa m, Arunachal 
Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland. 
 
 (iii)  A guideline for Management of Human Elephant Conflict has been issued by the 
Ministry on 6.10.2017 and elephant range States have been requested for implementation of the 
same. 
 
III Development of Wildlife Habitats 
 
1.46 The Ministry is implementing CSS -Development of Wildlife Habitats under which 
financial assistance is provided to State/UTs for the protection and conservation of Wildlife

Ministry to run awareness programmes on regular basis, to educate the people about the ill 
effects of single-use plastics and encourage them to use other sources as a replacement to plastic

roles and responsibilities.                                                                                      (Para 13.2 ibid)

(v) The enforceable prescription of minimum level of recycling of plastic packaging waste 
collected under EPR by producer, importers & brand -owners will strengthen circular 

12  
economy of plastic packaging waste. 
(vi) The guidelines on EPR mandate use of recycled plastic content in plastic packaging by 
the industry. This step will generate demand for recycled plastic material. 
(vii) Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has laid down guidelines for use of 
recycled plastic content in food contact applications, after the notification of Plastic 
Waste Management Second Amendment Rules, 2021 on 17th September 2021. 
(viii) The EPR guidelines will strengthen circular economy of plastic packaging waste, and 
promote development of new alternatives to plastics and move towards sustainable 
plastic packaging. 
(ix) Steps have been taken for undertaking large scale awareness generation activities at 
national level, State and UT level and local authority/district level with respect to the 
upcoming ban and alternatives available. 
Recommendation/Observations 
1.48 The Committee yet again expresses  its deep concern on the issue of non -cooperative and 
unresponsive behavior of the officials dealing with environmental matters towards the public 
representatives.  The Committee reiterates its previous recommendation in this matter that the 
Ministry of En vironment, Forest and Climate Change, being the nodal central Ministry dealing 
with these matters, must impress upon the State Governments as well as their own officers to 
sensitize all the concerned authorities to accord due courtesy to the public represe ntatives, 
attend to their grievances, respond to their communications and make available the information 
sought by them.                                                                                                      (Para 13.3 ibid)

(i) States/UTs have been requested to constitute a Special Task Force under Chairpersonship 
of Chief Secretary/Administrator for elimination of single use plastics and effective 
implementation of PWMR, 2016.  Thirty four States/UTs have constituted the Special 
Task Force till date. 
(ii) A National Level Taskforce has been constituted by the Ministry for monitoring and 
reviewing action plans of States/UTs and Union Ministries for elimination of single use 
plastic. 
(iii) The State /UT Governments and concerned Central Ministries/Departments have been 
requested to develop a comprehensive action plan and implement it in a time bound 
manner. 
(iv) Committees have been established at the National, State and District/City level. These 
Committees are requested to consider the publi c representations and address the 
issues/concerns raised by them.

REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change  deals with the

„Three Hundred Sixty Fourth Report‟ on “Demands for Grants (2022-23) of the Ministry of Earth

15th March, 2022.

in respect of all the thirteen recommendations/observations contained in the „Three Hundred Sixty

pursue in view of the Government’s replies: Para Nos.:-3.7 and 6.4

 The Committee is convinced with the explanations furnished by the Ministry and 
therefore, does not want to pursue the recommendations further. 
Chapter III:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: Nil 
Chapter IV:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still  awaited: Para  Nos.:- 4.2, 5.4 an d 5.5  To be pursued 
further 
 Total recommendations – 03 
The Committee desires that the Ministry should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of recommendations/observations made in 
Chapter IV of the Report.

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2021 -22 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FIANANCIAL YEAR      
2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 The Committee finds that against the total budg etary support of Rs.2369.54 crore for the 
year 2021 -22, the Ministry could utilise Rs.1379.98 crore only which is just 58.23 per cent 
utilisation of the funds made available.  The Committee, thus, summarises that despite having 
higher allocation in certain components at RE stage, the overall utilisation of the same by the 
Ministry has not b een very encouraging.  The Committee observes that had the increased funds 
allocated to the Ministry at RE stage been given at  BE stage itself then the utilisation by the 
Ministry could have been better.                                                              (Para 2.3 of the 364th Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.2 Allocation of the Ministry was enhanced at RE stage to Rs.2369.54 crore against BE of            
Rs.1897.13 crore.  Enhanced allocation included allocation of Rs.671.01  crore for new services/ 
instruments (DOM & Satellite rent lease payment. The approval for 2nd and 3rd supplementary was 
received only in last week of February and 3 rd week of March respectively.  Expenditure incurred 
as on 31 st March, 2022 was Rs.2190.42 crore against the allocation of Rs.2369.54 crore which is 
92.44% of RE.  Agreed with the observation of the Committee. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3 The Committee  further finds that the utilisation of the funds has been significantly low 
under the Head „Establishment Expenditure of the Centre‟ where the Ministry could manage to 
spend 43.64 per cent only of the total funds made available.  Further, utilisation under „Central 
Sector Schemes‟ has been to the tune of 66.99 per cent.  Given the budgetary allocation utilisation 
capacity of the Ministry, the Committee hopes that the Ministry would increase its absorption 
capacity in order to utilise the total budgetary allocation made for the year 2021 -22 optimally.  
The Committe e, therefore, desires that the details of the action taken for the purpose may be 
intimated for the consideration of the Committee along with the detailed reasons for unutilised 
funds, if any.                                                                                                                 (Para 2.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.4 Allocation for establishment expenditure was enhanced at RE stage to Rs.1064.96 crore 
from Rs.517.96 crore at BE stage.  The enhanced allocation included Satellite lease rent payment 
of    Rs.521.01 crore for which necessary approval could be obtained only by 22nd March 2022.   
1.5 As on 31 st March 2022, utilization under the Head “Establishment Expenditure of the 
Centre” was Rs.1030.41 crore which is 98.94 % of RE 2021-22. 
Details of Action taken: 
1.6 Ministry expedited re-appropriation proposal for 2 nd & 3rd supplementary.  For payment of 
lease rent for Oceansat -II Satellite to ISRO, Ministry of Earth Sciences pursued with M inistry of 
Finance for necessary approval which enabled utilization of funds.   
1.7 For procurement of High Performance Computing System ( HPC), the complex Request 
for Proposal (RFP) in terms of technical specification was finalized and vetted by a committee 
constituted by the Ministry which facilitated timely concurrence by Integrated Finance Division  

3 
 
 
(IFD) and Ministry of Earth Sciences for floating of RFP in Central Public Procurement ( CPP) 
portal.  
1.8 For acquisition of land from ONGC under Deep Ocean Mission, necessary negotiation 
with ONGC was done by the Ministry/NIOT.  
Detailed reasons for unutilized funds: 
1.9 Under Establishment expenditure, IMD could not util ize Rs.30 crore due to resignation of 
newly recruited official in the cadre of SA/Admin and recruitment of Scientists could be finalized 
by IMD for which budget was projected by IMD. 
1.10 Under Deep Ocean Mission, Rs.30 crore under Capital Section could no t be utilized as 
MoU with ONGC for acquisition of Land could not be finalized. 
1.11 Last date for submission of technical & financial bids was extended by 5 days as requested 
by the bidders and due to complexity of the tender, evaluation reports (Technical & Financial) 
was submitted only by 30 th March 2022.  Therefore , Rs.90 crore earmarked for payment of 
advance could not be utilized.  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.12 The Committee notes the roadmap shared by the Ministry for the year 2022 -23 and also 
the fact that against the projected demand of Rs.3144.56  crore only Rs.2653.51 crore has been 
allocated to the Ministry in BE 2022 -23 registering a total reduction of Rs.491.05 crore.                      
The Committee feels that the budgetary allocation of Rs.2653.51 crore at BE 2022-23 stage would 
be sufficient initially  to take care of the financial requirement of the Ministry under its various 
schemes/ projects/ programmes and if required, the Ministry  would seek higher allocation at RE 
stage specifically under the Deep Ocean  Mission (DOM) and Polar and Cryosphere Resea rch 
(PACER) components so that the objectives envisaged for the year 2022 -23 could be realised.     
The Committee, therefore, desires the Department to take necessary action in order to optimise 
the allocation made in BE 2022-23.                                                                            (Para 2.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.13 Noted for compliance.  BE of Rs.2653.51 crore allocated during Financial Year 2022-23 
will be sufficient. 
Details of Action taken: 
1.14 Ministry is ensuring on -time concurrence of approval of proposals for timely release of 
funds. 
UMBRELLA SCHEMES OF MINISTRY OF EARTH SCIENCES 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.15 The Committee observes that the overall financial performance (upto January, 2022) of 
the Ministry under the Centre Sector Schemes has not been very encouraging.  Out of the total 
budgetary allocation of Rs 2369.54 crore, the Ministry could utilise Rs.1379.98 crore only which 
is just 58.23 per cent utilisation of the RE allocation of funds made available to the Ministry for 
the year 2021 -22.  The Committee, however, hopes that the Ministry would be able to utilise 
optimally the remaining funds of Rs.989.56 crore during the remain ing period of the financial 
year 2021-22.                                                                                                               (Para 3.4 ibid)   
 Action Taken 
1.16 As on 31 st March 2022, the Ministry could utilize 92.44% of RE.  Expenditure is            
Rs.2190.42 crore against RE of Rs.2369.54 crore. 
1.17 Detailed reason for un-utilization is as indicated in Ministry‟s response of the Committee‟s  

4 
 
 
recommendation as contained in Para 2.4 of the 364th the Report (Para 1.4 of this Report). 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
1.18 The Committee during the meeting held on 14 th February, 2022 was given to understand 
by the Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences that the Ministry would be making a payment of      
Rs.521.01 crore to the Department of Space as lease rental for Oceansat -3 Satellite.  It was also 
informed that the concerned file for making the payment of Rs.521.01 crore is yet to be approved 
by the Ministry of Finance.  The Committee feels the timely payment of the dues by the Ministry 
will not only help it utilising the funds for the intended purpose but will also imp rove its financial 
performance.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Ministry to take up the matter with 
the Ministry of Finance on top priority so as to ensure timely payment to the Department of 
Space.                                                                                                                           (Para 3.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.19 As suggested by the Committee, Ministry pursued the matter with the Ministry of Finance 
and got its approval by 22nd March 2022 which enabled timely payment to Department of Space. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.20 The Committee also notes that the financial performance of the Ministry under the Capital 
allocation with specific reference to O -SMART, ACROSS and SAGE Schem es has not been upto 
the mark.  The Committee underlines the importance of the Capital Budget which is meant for 
creating new assets as well as improving the existing ones.  Therefore, any complacency on this 
count is not heartening to note.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to 
make earnest efforts for making optimal utilisation of the funds earmarked under these Schemes to 
reap the desired benefits.                                                                                             (Para 3.6 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.21 The point raised by the Committee is very pertinent. The expenditure was less than the 
planned expenditure, mainly due to deferment in taking up some works and delay in supply of 
equipment owing to COVID restrictions.  Since the COVID -19 pandemic is now in declining 
phase, Ministry will make all efforts to utilize the funds fully.   
1.22 Capital Expenditure under ACROSS -IMD: All efforts are being made to fully utilize the 
Capital allocation under ACROSS-IMD. During FY 2021-22, out of an allocation of Rs.77.0 crore 
(R.E.), an expenditure of Rs.73.19 crore (approx. 95%) was incurred under ACROSS -IMD 
(Capital). 
1.23 Furthermore, during current FY 2022 -23, the entire capital allocation of Rs.66.0 crore 
received under ACROSS-IMD is likely to be fully utilized. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
1.24 The Committee further notes that the total financial outlay under this Mission is             
Rs.4077.00 crore for a period of 5 years (2021 -26) out of which Rs.2823.40 crore has been 
estimated for the first phase for the 3 years (2021 -24).  Given the envisaged objectives of the 
Mission, it is imperative to make full and optimal utilisation of the budgetary support by the 
Ministry which in turn would ensure achiev ement of the envisioned targets.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Ministry to leave no stone unturned to make best use of the funds being 
allocated under the Mission.                                                                                       (Para 3.8 ibid)                                                                                                                              
Action Taken 
 
1.25 The point is well noted. The Ministry will make all efforts to utilize the allocated funds  
under Deep Ocean Mission. 
 

5 
 
 
WEATHER BASED AGRO ADVISORY SERVICES 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.26 The Committee while making note of the efforts being made by the Ministry under its 
weather based agro advisory services expresses its satisfaction towards the overall progress 
achieved against the physical targets for the year 2021 -22.  The Committee, however, observes 
that the progress of the Ministry on many counts such as number of District Agro -meteorological 
Field Units (DAMU); installation & commission ing of Doppler Weather Radars; installation of 
Automatic Weather Stations (AWS); number of Climate Reference station s set up by IITM/IMD; 
number of X-band radars installed/commissioned; establishment of Doppler Weather Radars over 
North Eastern Region etc., has been sluggish.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to revisit 
its performance in terms of realisation of physical targets set under ACROSS Scheme and strive 
hard to improve it. Steps taken in this regard may be intimated to the Committee.                                
The Committee also recommends that climate hazards and vulnerability atlas be prepared 
State/UT-wise for the entire country and disseminated to the farmers at ground level on priority 
basis.                                                                                                                            (Para 5.2 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.27 Establishment of District Agro-metrological Field Units (DAMUs): In the year 2021-22, a 
total of 3 DAMUs were established at Kupwara in J& K and Almora and Pithoragarh in 
Uttarakhand against the target of 20 DAMUs. As of now IMD has established a total of 199 
DAMUs in the country. The pace of growth of DAMU network  was affected due to limited funds 
available for this. Keeping funds availabili ty into consideration, it has been planned  to set up 
additional 100 DAMUs in the premises of Krishi Vigyan Kendras ( KVK) at district level in next 
four years i.e. 2022 -23-2025-26. This expansion will help to improve the quality of weather 
services for farmers by rendering block-level advisories in these districts. 
1.28 Installation & commissioning of Doppler Weather Radars (DWRs): Installations of Radars 
have been taken up on priority basis in Himalayan States. 6 DWRs have been installed at 
Mukteshwar, Kufri, Jammu, Leh, Surkanda Devi and Ayanagar , Delhi. DWRs will be installed 
soon at Lansdowne, Murari Devi, Jot and Banihal top.   
1.29 Initiatives have been taken for Radar coverage of North-Eastern States. Tender has been 
issued for commissioning of 08 Nos. X -Band DWRs for North East region and technical 
evaluation of bids is under process.  Revised tender for 03 Nos. SSPA based C -Band DWRs has 
been issued and technical evaluation of bids is under process.   An expert committee has been 
constituted for eva luation of choice of technology (SSPA or Klystron) for further weather radars 
in IMD. As per decision, tender process for procurement of 08 Nos. C -Band DWRs will be 
initiated. Process has also been initiated for replacement of 04 Nos. S -Band DWRs at Chenna i, 
Kolkata, Vishakhapatnam  and Machhilipatnam. 
1.30 Installation of Automatic Weather Stations (AWS):  IMD‟s existing Automatic Weather 
Station (AWS) and Automatic Rain Gauge (ARG) network comprises of 727 AWS and 1382 
ARGs. Further augmentation of network is underway on a large scale. The installation of 200 
Agro-AWS was completed on 27 th April, 2022. The procurement process for another 330 Agro 
AWS is in progress. Another project for installation of 400 AWS all over India is under process. 
IMD is establishing a network of 10 AWS in Ladakh UT.  Besides, process has been initiated for 
installation of AWS, ARG and ASG in NW Himalayan region, major Urban centres and Schools. 
1.31 Expansion of observational network over North East India: Tendering process is underway 
for procurement of 8 DWRs for NE India. Sites are already selected at Jorhat, Tezpur, Lengpui, 
Kohima, Guwahati, Imphal, Silchar. Site selection is underway at Itanagar/ Holongi airport.  For 
augmentation of AWS network, one AWS is already installed in Guwahati city. 10m mast & 
accessories (15nos) for installation of AWS has been sent to Imphal for installation at Manipur, 
Mizoram & Nagaland. Procurement of AWS/ARGs for Arunachal Pradesh and other sites in NE  

6 
 
 
India is being carried out through rate contract. Besides, 7 AWS/ ARG are likely to be installed at  
Indo-China border during June/July, 2022. 
1.32 Climate hazards and vulnerability Atlas: From the web version of climate hazards and 
vulnerability Atlas, State-wise Atlas has been prepared in soft form (pdf). Already it has been sent 
to some of the States like Maharashtra, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand etc. The Atlas will be sent 
to all the regional offices of IMD shortly for onward communication to State authorities and other 
users. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

7 
 
 
 
CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
2.1 As regards the total fund allocation of Rs.150.00 crore under the Deep Ocean Mission 
(DOM) to the Ministry for the year 2021 -22, the Committee notes that the funds have been 
provided to the Ministry at RE stage only.     The Committee, however, is surprised to observe that 
not a single penny has been utilised by the Ministry till 31 st January, 2022.  The Committee takes 
serious note of the lackadaisical approach of the Ministr y towards the funds allotted under the 
DOM Scheme and, accordingly, recommends the Ministry to apprise it of the reasons in detail due 
to which it could not utilise the funds satisfactorily.                              (Para 3.7 of the 362nd Report)          
 
 Action Taken 
2.2 Rs.150 crore was allocated for the Deep Ocean Mission at the RE Stage. An amount of       
Rs.120 crore was re-appropriated to Deep Ocean Mission vide Om dated 17th February, 2022. Out 
of the total Rs.150 crore provided, Rs.119 crore was utilized by 31st March 2022.  
2.3 The remaining Rs.30 cr ore was for purchase of land in Goa for the proposed marine 
station activities under Deep Ocean Mission. ONGC was approached to transfer/lease out the land 
at the campus of Institute of Petroleum Safety Health and Environment Management ( IPSHEM), 
Goa to Ministry of Earth Sciences. The issue was discussed in the ONGC Board and few queries 
were raised. After clarification and discussion, the ONGC Board approved the lease of land only 
on 30 th March 2022.  Subsequently, a detailed survey of the land allocated by ONGC at the 
campus of IPSHEM, Goa was undertaken before finalization of lease deed. It was found that 
about more than 60% of land come s under steep slope and is absolutely not suitable f or any 
purpose. The said issue was brought to the notice of the officials of ONGC. Hence, the matter 
needs to be discussed and resolved with ONGC on providing suitable land to an extent of                       
40 acres. If not possible, M inistry of Earth Sciences will explore alternative location of Marine 
Station. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
AUTONOMOUS BODIES 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.4 The Committee notes with satisfaction the financial performance of the Autonomous 
Bodies under the aegis of the Ministry. The Committee hopes that the budgetary allocation of 
Rs.199.07 crore in BE 2022 -23 would be sufficient to cater to the financial requi rements of these 
Institutes and the targets set for the year 2022-23 would be realised fully. 
(Para 6.4 of the 362nd Report) 
Action Taken 
2.5 The budgetary allocation of Rs.199.07 crore in BE 2022 -23 would be sufficient to cater to 
the financial requirements of the five autonomous institutes of the Ministry.

CHAPTER – IV

REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT ARE STILL AWAITED 
 
AVAILABILITY OF HUMAN RESOURCES 
Recommendation/ Observation 
4.1 The Committee notes with concern that the Ministry is facing challenges on account of 
availability of trained manpower to further strengthen its R&D activities.  The Committee is of the 
firm opinion that even if the Schemes/programmes/activities of the Min istry are adequately 
funded, the desired results cannot be achieved without having trained manpower to take up R&D 
at par with international standards.  Therefore, it is imperative to take necessary interventions on 
immediate basis so that the required man power (scientific/technical/administrative) could be 
made available to the Ministry.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Ministry to take 
necessary action so as to ensure that the R&D activities of the Ministry are not halted for want of 
skilled workforce.  The steps undertaken by the Ministry for the recruitment and training of the 
additional 500 manpower may also be intimated to the Committee.                           (Para 4.2 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
4.2 The Ministry has taken up the case for sanctioning of the permanent manpower, as per the 
approved schemes, with Dep artment of Expenditure, Min istry of Finance. In the meantime, the 
required manpower is hired under project mode. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.3 The Committee while taking note of the action taken by the Ministry  desires that it 
should make sincere efforts to complete the process in a time bound manner.  
WEATHER BASED AGRO ADVISORY SERVICES 
Recommendation/ Observation 
4.3 The Committee appreciates the sentiments expressed by the Ministry and the problems 
being faced by it in acquiring a PRV.  It is painful to learn that despite having two stations in 
Antarctica and one in the Arctic of greater strategic significance and importance with specific 
reference to the climate change, India does not have a PRV.  The reasons for delay in acquiring a 
PRV are well understood but the Ministry should not lose sight of its determination of acquiring 
one.  The Committee strongly supports the Ministry in the matter and recommends it to tighten the 
loose knots and make earnest efforts in getting the required funds for the purpose.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry of Earth Sciences to take up the matter 
appropriately with the Ministry of Finance to make the funds available so th at the purpose of 
having these stations could be achieved fully.                                                             (Para 5.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
4.4 Ministry carried out revised cost estimation as per prevalent market conditions through 
Indian Maritime University (IMU) and arrived at an estimated cost of USD 317 million USD. 
Currently, Ministry is in the process of preparing a Note for in -principle approval of Dep artment 
of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.5 The Committee notes that the Ministry is in the process of preparing a Note for        
in-principle approval of Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance. The Committee 
would like the Ministry to intimate it of the further development in the matter. 
 
 

10 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
4.6 Further, the Committee notes the impressing need for replacement/upgradation of the 
Maitri Station especially in light of the fact that the Station has not only outlived its life and its 
structural integrity is very much compromised which needs immediate replacements but also the 
Station is not environment friendly and the same has been commented upon by various 
international committees, as informed by the Ministry. The Committee is happy to note that the 
Ministry is already seized of the matter and making efforts in this direction.  The Committee hopes 
that the proposed new Station referred to as “Maitri -II” would be completed as per the timeline 
fixed for the purpose and the Ministry would be duly supported financially to meet this target. 
                                                                                                                                     (Para 5.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.7 Maitri, the second Indian Research Station which was commissioned in 1988, has outlived 
its useful life but continues as the mainstay for Indian scientists till date.   It was designed for an 
estimated life of 10 years. Much beyond the duration of the origi nal design, the station has served 
as a permanent and continuous Indian Antarctic base for the last 34 years. It is proposed to 
construction of a new Maitri Station at Schirmacher Oasis, cDML, East Antarctica (Maitri -II) as a 
replacement for existing struc tures however could not be initiated for want of funds. The 
estimated cost of this is about INR 900 crore. Ministry is in the process of preparing a Note for in-
principle approval of Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.8 The Committee notes that the Ministry is in the process of preparing a Note for        
obtaining in-principle approval of the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to apprise it of the further developments with regard to 
completion of ‘Maitri-II’ Antartica Station.
