REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
 The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), came into being on August 3, 1954, and has been 
engaged in the development of nuclear power technology, application of radiation technologies in the 
fields of agriculture, health care, industry and basic research. 
1.2  The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) is the apex body for formulation of policies and 
direction of the programmes. The Commission implements its policies and programmes through the 
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). The programmes of  DAE have been divided into four sectors 
viz. Research and Development, Industries, Minerals and Power Sector. 
1.3  The programmes being followed by DAE, can be briefly summed up as follows: 
 Increasing the share of nuclear power through deployment of indig enous and other proven 
technologies and also developing fast breeder reactors and thorium reactors with associated fuel 
cycle facilities; 
 Building and operation of research reactors for production of radioisotopes; developing 
radiation technology applications in the field of health care, agriculture and industry, cancer 
care, water related technology, waste management etc.; 
 Designing and developing advanced technologies such as accelerators, lasers, supercomputers, 
advanced materials and instrumentation and encouraging transfer of technology to industry; 
 Providing support to basic research in nuclear energy and related frontier areas of science; 
interaction with universities and academic institutions; supporting academic programmes 
having a bearing on DAE’s activities; and International co -operation in related advanced areas 
of research and contribution to national security. 
1.4 DAE’s programmes are multidisciplinary in nature. For their execution, DAE has evolved 
abroad based organizational structur e comprising research centres, industrial units, public sector 
undertakings and fully aided institutions, along with service organizations. These organizations are 
engaged in research, technology development and commercial operations in the areas of nuclea r power 
and associated technologies, radiation technologies and their applications, basic research and academic 
programmes. 
1.5 The Department is also engaged in the development of radiation technologies and their 
applications for better crop varieties, te chniques for crops protection, radiation based post -harvest 
technologies, techniques for radio -diagnosis and radiotherapy of diseases particularly cancer, 
technologies for safe drinking water, better environment and industrial growth. 
1.6 Over the years, t he Department has been able to establish a network of institutions engaged in 
R&D as well as industrial activities and acquired expertise in all aspects of the nuclear fuel cycle. The 
first stage of the nuclear power programme is in commercial domain and t he second stage has been 
launched with the ongoing construction of 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR). 
1.7 Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) formed in 1987, is a Public Sector 
Enterprise under the administrative control of DAE. NPCIL is responsible for siting, design, 

2 
 
construction, commissioning and operation of nuclear power reactors. Safety is given overriding 
priority in all facets of nuclear power reactors. At presents, NPCIL is operating 22 nuclear power 
reactors with an installed capacity of 6780 MW. 
1.8 DAE has under its aegis – 
1. Six Research Centers: - 
 
i) Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) – Mumbai

matrix of the country, it is high time that the contribution from nuclear power is increased 
substantially. This is not just crucial from a point of view of environment but also to ensure the 
country's energy security in times of ever increasing power consumption.

objectives in increasing nuclear power production through commissioning of more nuclear power

recommends the Department to study the reasons for thi s anamoly and also apprise the 
Committee of its findings. Further, the Committee recommends that the Department devices a 
strategy to install higher production capacity power units so that the unit cost comes down and 
nuclear power becomes more affordable.

7. TATA MEMORIAL CENTRE  – IN NATION’S SERVICE AS A PRIMER CANCER 
CARE INSTITUTE IN THE COUNTRY 
The Committee, with  a view of highlighting the activities and impact of the Tata Memorial 
Centre, sought a note on the same from the Department. The information received from the Department 
is as below: 
The Tata Memorial Centre, a grant -in-aid organization under the Departme nt of Atomic 
Energy (DAE) is the oldest and largest cancer centre in the country. Registering close to 80,000 new 
patients and over 650,000 follow ups annually at Mumbai alone, it provides high quality cancer care to 
patients from across the country regard less of socio economic status and their ability to pay; more 
than 60% of patients are treated almost free of cost. The centre runs an active Bone Marrow 
Transplant (BMT) program with a 6 bedded BMT unit performing 60 to 70 transplants every year. 
Twenty-five percent of all transplants are funded by the institute so that patients who otherwise would 
not have been transplanted undergo this expensive but life saving treatment. 
7.2 TMC is the largest centre for cancer education in the country and trains close t o 200 students 
every year in various aspects of cancer including surgical, medical and radiation oncology, pathology, 
radiology and anesthesiology amongst others. TMC’s educational activities are affiliated to the Homi  
Bhabha National Institute (HBNI) Mumb ai – a deemed university of the DAE. Besides academic 
courses such as MCh, DM, MS, MD, PhD, MSc, etc. the center organizes various training programs, 
fellowships, and short courses for continuing education.  Some innovative courses started at TMC in 
the pa st 5 years include Masters in clinical research, patient navigation (Kevat) and physician 
assistants. These courses have had major impact on the conduct of cancer research and the holistic 
approach to patient care. 
7.3 The focus of TMC’s research remains t he identification of gaps in cancer management, 
addressing them by conducting high quality clinical trials, and finding cost effective solutions to cancer 
problems relevant to the region. While the Tata Memorial Hospital remains at the forefront of clinica l 
cancer research, ACTREC, the research wing of TMC houses several basic and translational scientists 
working towards unravelling the biology of cancer. The Centre for Cancer Epidemiology conducts field 
studies on various aspects of causation of cancer in addition to organizing regular cancer awareness 
and prevention programmes. 
7.4 Responding to the national need for more centres of excellence for cancer treatment like TMH 
and ACTREC in Mumbai, TMC embarked on a major expansion plan that will quadruple its  patient 
care capabilities as well as broaden its geographic presence in the country. TMC has now expanded to 
six other hospitals located in Varanasi (2), Guwahati, Sangrur, Vishakapatnam, Chandigarh and 
Muzaffarpur. ACTREC, which had 100 beds till 2020, i s now a 500-bedded facility, and will expand to 
900 beds by end -2023, offering cutting -edge treatment with dedicated facilities for solid tumor 
chemotherapy, hematolymphoid cancers management, treatment with radionuclide isotopes, and the 
first Proton Beam therapy unit in the government sector.  
7.5 Starting from 840 beds in 2017, TMC has grown to 2200 beds (in 2022) and will further 
increase its capacity to 2800 beds by the end of 2023, and 3400 beds by the end of 2026. Currently, 
TMC treats about 125,000 new patients with cancer annually (approximately 10% of all of India’s 

19 
 
cancer burden). The hub and spoke model of cancer care has been successfully implemented in Punjab 
and in Uttar Pradesh. In addition, a proposal is being considered for a cancer hospita l in Odisha 
(NISER campus of DAE), which is at a fairly advanced stage of discussion with joint funding from DAE 
and the Tata Trusts. TMC is also planning an Integrated Centre for Treatment, Research and 
Education in cancer at Khopoli, Maharashtra which wi ll house a medicinal plant facility, and include 
infrastructure and resources for cancer research involving traditional Indian systems of medicine 
(AYUSH). 
7.6 With the expansion envisioned with the creation of these new hospitals, it is expected that TMC 
will soon treat close to 200,000 new patients with cancer annually, which will account for 
approximately 12 -15% of all patients with cancer diagnosed in the country every year. TMC also 
provides technical support to several state governments with their can cer treatment facilities including 
Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir amongst others. 
TMC’s increasing capacity to train individuals in all branches of oncology will ensure that there are 
adequate human resources to run these centres.  
7.7 The following chart shows the number of patients covered under affordable cancer care during 
F.Y. 2021-22 and F.Y. 2022-23 (till Dec. 2022) in 6 regional cancer care hospitals under DAE: 
 
7.8 The National Cancer Grid, an initiative of the Tata Memorial Centre, was created in 2012 with 
the broad vision of creating uniform standards of cancer care across India. Ten years later, it has 
grown into the world’s largest cancer network with 289 members , comprising cancer centres, research 
institutes, patient advocacy groups, charitable organizations and professional societies. The mandate 
of the NCG is establishing uniform standards of patient care for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment 
of cancer, cre ating adequate trained human resources, and facilitating collaborative basic, 
translational and clinical research in cancer. Between the member organizations of the NCG, the 
network treats over 750,000 new patients with cancer annually, which is over 60% o f all of India’s 
cancer burden.

7.9 Some of the activities of the NCG include: uniform standards of care – resource stratified 
guidelines for cancer management, External Quality Assurance Schemes (EQAS), training in Quality 
Improvement through the EQuIP program, institutional peer review, online second opinion service for 
patients, multidisciplinary Virtual Tumor Boards, Price Discovery Cell / Group negotiation for 
equipment, drugs and consumables, National Cancer Library resources, unique educational ini tiatives 
– “Traveling Schools of Pathology and Oncology Nursing”, training in cancer research methods – the 
International Collaboration on Research methods Development in Oncology – CreDO workshop and 
NCG funded multicentric collaborative research. With th e creation of NCG “Vishwam”, the 
international component of the NCG, the network is rapidly being acknowledged as one of the most 
influential organizations in global cancer care. 
7.10 During the meeting of the Committee, the Department informed that TMC ha s conducted three 
trials that can be implemented immediately: 
 The first on Yoga in breast cancer tested , adding Yoga to standard surgery, radiotherapy and 
chemotherapy show ed improvement in quality of life, compliance to treatment and a 15% 
reduction in deaths due to breast cancer.  
 The other two trials tried two low cost interventions in the form of injections that saved 29% 
and 26% lives in breast cancer. Both these injectio ns are available across India as part of 
arogya shree as well as state insurance schemes. The cost of these injections is Rs25 and Rs 
2000/- only.  
7.11 In summary, the Tata Memorial Centre has spearheaded major advances in patient care, 
training, research , public health and policy in cancer over the past decade in India. TMC has 
expanded its scope, presence and influence across the length and breadth of the country through its 
own expansion and the development of the National Cancer Grid. Over the next dec ade, TMC will 
remain at the forefront of all aspects of cancer management - provision of high-quality evidence-based 
cancer care to all strata of the population, creating human resource adequate to tackle the growing 
burden of cancer in the country, conduct meaningful, cost effective, contextually relevant research, and 
help frame and advance India’s cancer policy. 
7.12 The Committee lauds with a full heart, the efforts of Tata Memorial Centre as well as the 
Department for anchoring the various aspects of cancer diagnosis, treatment, management and 
cutting edge research. It also highlights the stellar service that TMC has provided to this country 
in terms of serving the needy by delivering  high impact low cost cancer care. TMC’ s hub a nd 
spoke model is exemplary in terms of the geographical expanse it covers, number of patients it 
treats and the quality & standards of care it maintains. The Committee would like to 
congratulate TMC and the Department along with a request to identify more  underserved 
regions and reach out.  The Committee would like to extend its full support to TMC for all its 
future endeavours.

OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022-23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2023-24 
From Chart 1, the Committee observes a general increasing trend in B.E. allocations for 
the Department. While the B.E. allocation for 2021 -22 was at Rs. 27,795 crore, it has been 
increased by about 21 percent in B.E. 2023 -24. Similarly, for the past two ye ars, i.e. 2021-22 and 
2022-23, the Department has been getting an additional allocation at the R.E. stage. The 
proposed B.E. allocation for 2023 -24 was Rs. 42,092.20 crore but the Department was allocated 
only Rs. 35, 262.49 crore in 2023-24. This is a shortfall of Rs. 6,829.71 crore.                    (Para 2.6) 
                                        
 From Chart 2 which depicts the share of Revenue and Capital allocation in B.E. 2023 -24 
of the Department, across its various key sectors, the Committee obs erves that while the share of 
revenue and capital expenditure allocations is almost equal in the total budget, capital 
expenditure is almost twice that of revenue for the Power Sector. On the other hand, revenue 
expenditure is more than thrice of the capital expenditure allocation under the R&D Sector.   
                (Para 2.7) 
     
 From the submission of the Department the Committee feels that the Department may 
face challenges especially in its initiatives relating to Nuclear Recycle Board (NRB),Tata 
Memorial Centre (TMC), Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL), Heavy Water  
Board (HWB) and Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC).                                         (Para 2.11) 
 The Committee underlines the requirement of an additional budg etary allocation of Rs. 
3,150 crore over and above the B.E. 2023-24 quoted by the Department and recommends that the 
Department be given the additional allocation for them to continue with their set goals and 
objectives and ensure a timely and effective co mpletion.  The initiatives of the Department under 
TMC, NPCIL and BARC, amongst others, are crucial to the energy needs of the country as well 
as in many healthcare and societal applications. It is also necessary to ensure that the activities of 
the Depart ment do not suffer due to any lack of funds as it will have a bearing on India’s 
strategic nuclear capacity.                                                                                                      (Para 2.12) 
 The Committee also recommends that the Department should reach out to the Ministry of 
Finance for additional funds at the R.E./ Supplementary stage and also look for raising the same 
either through internal revenue or through reallocating funds from heads which have excess 
allocation, if any.                                                                                                                     (Para 2.13) 
 The Committee therefore recommends that the Department be diligent in managing the 
expenditure as well as achieving the physical targets that it has set out for itself for 2023 -24. The 
Committee further recommends that while ensuring that the physical targets are accomplished 
the Committee would also like to recommend that the Department should ensure optimum 
utilisation of these funds.                                                                                                        (Para 2.17) 
 
 

22 
 
 The Committee observes from Chart 7, that while there has been a general uptrend in the 
overall allocations to the Department in B.E. 2021 -22 to 2023 -24 as well as in the capital 
allocation component of the same period, the establishment expenditure has not shown a similar 
trend. The Establishment expenditure increased in 2022 -23 over 2021 -22 allocation but in 2023 -
24 it has shown a slight reduction. The Committee enquired the Department about the reasons 
for this increase in Establishment Expenditure (especially during R.E. 2022 -23) and was 
informed that the increase is on accounts of payment of arrears of Magnesium Di-uranate (MDU) 
to M/s UCIL due to revision of rate pertaining to 2018-19 onwards.                                 (Para 2.19) 
 The Committee recommends the Department to identify more such areas where payment 
towards arrears is yet to be made. This is shal l be in the fitment of things as delayed payments 
and uncertain cash outflows may hamper the planned activities of the Department as well as it's 
various stakeholders.                          (Para 2.20) 
 The Committee is of the view that even though an i ncrease of 40 percent, i.e. from 4780 
MW to 6780 MW is substantial, it is not commensurate with the need of the country for more 
clean energy. With nuclear energy having a share of only about 3 percent in the total energy 
matrix of the country, it is high time that the contribution from nuclear power is increased 
substantially. This is not just crucial from a point of view of environment but also to ensure the 
country's energy security in times of ever increasing power consumption.                      (Para 2.25) 
 The Committee, while being optimistic that the Department shall seek it's above stated 
objectives in increasing nuclear power production through commissioning of more nuclear power 
plants, hopes that these projects will be implemented on war footi ng and are not delayed or fall 
short of their objectives in any way.                                                 (Para 2.26) 
 The Committee observes and highlights the fact that even though India's rank is 6th in 
terms of numbers of nuclear power react ors being operated, we are still at number 11 and 14 
when it comes to nuclear power produced and installed capacity respectively. This is indicative of 
the fact that the production capacity per power plant is low. The Committee therefore 
recommends the Dep artment to study the reasons for this anamoly and also apprise the 
Committee of its findings. Further, the Committee recommends that the Department devices a 
strategy to install higher production capacity power units so that the unit cost comes down and 
nuclear power becomes more affordable.       (Para 2.27) 
 The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should take utmost care in 
ensuring proper utilisation of funds and that the Department should take extra efforts to ensure 
optimum utilisation under the three heads 'BARC', 'IGCAR' and 'Nuclear Fuel Complex'.  
   (Para 2.30) 
BHAVINI- BHARATIYA NABHIKIYA VIDYUT NIGAM LTD. 
 The Committee observes from Chart 9, that the allocations made under BHAVINI have 
varied from year to year depending upon the need of projects, research and development of 
reactors and associated technologies. The highest allocation since 2020 -21 was made in the year 
2021-22 – of Rs. 550 crore at the R.E. 2021 -22 stage. While the actual expenditure under this 

23 
 
head (till January 2 023) has been Rs. 200 crore, the Department sought an allocation of Rs. 400 
crore in B.E. 2023 -24 but has been allocated Rs. 200 crore in B.E. 2023 -24 allocations. There is 
thus, a shortfall of Rs. 200 crore in budgetary allocations.                                                 (Para 3.5) 
 The Committee, acknowledging the extremely critical task carried by BHAVINI in terms 
of indigenisation of technologies relating to nuclear power reactors, recommends that the 
Department be given the extra budgetary allocation over and above B.E. 2023 -24 so that none of 
the activities planned by the Department under this head are adversely affected. The Committee 
also recommends that the Department should reach out to the Ministry of Finance for additional 
funds at th e R.E. / Supplementary stage and also look for raising the same either through 
internal revenue or through reallocating funds from heads which have excess allocation, if any. 
                             (Para 3.7) 
 The Committee heartily appreciates the p rogress made by the Department so far. It also 
acknowledges the fact that the research and development of a nuclear fuel reactor is an intense 
scientific and engineering process, and hence recommends the Department to take all possible 
steps in resolving all technical challenges ensuring that the commissioning of fast breeder reactor 
in the most efficient manner. The Committee also recommends the Department to prepare digital 
content around this fantastic achievement and create awareness amongst the citizen ’s especially 
students about this wonderful feat. This shall not just further the endeavour to promote scientific 
temper but shall also motivate students to opt careers in STEM domain.                         (Para 3.10) 
ECIL- ELECTRONICS CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD. 
 The Committee, while underlining the importance of the activities and achievements of 
ECIL, appreciates its vision in attaining self -reliance in the strategic electronics design and 
manufacturing sector. The Committee also appreciates the fact that ECIL is doing cutting edge 
research and development of key electronic components which are crucial for India’s energy and 
defence security. The Committee is pleased to observe that while the Expenditure has remained 
almost the same, the revenue and th e profit before tax earned by ECIL has been constantly 
increasing.                                                                                                                                  (Para 4.5) 
 The Committee is perturbed to note the low percentage of physical targets achieved by the 
Atomic Minerals Directorate especially under Heliborne Survey and Augmentation of Uranium. 
While under Heliborne Survey, it could achieve only 40 percent, 65 percent and 56 percent of 
targets in the last three year s respectively, under Augmentation of Uranium this figure 100 
percent, 68 percent and 41 percent respectively. AMD plays a crucial role in the front end fuel 
cycle and is tasked with key objectives relating to survey and exploration of atomic minerals. In 
this backdrop, for AMD to miss its targets shall have direct impact on nuclear fuel sufficiency 
and achieving self-reliance. The Committee therefore strongly recommends that the Department 
should take necessary steps in ensuring that the physical targets f or the year 2023 -24 set by 
Atomic Minerals Directorate are achieved.                                                                            (Para 5.3) 
 Further, the Committee desires that a status update on the targets achieved by the end of 
second quarter of F.Y. 2023-24 be furnished.                                                                          (Para 5.4) 

24

 The Committee observes from Chart 11 that while during the years 2020 -21, 2021-22 and 
2022-23 the revenue generated and the gross budget of the Department has constantly increased,

1. INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1  The Department of Biotechnology was set up as an independent Board in 1982, and thereafter 
became a full -fledged Department under Ministry of Science & Technology in 1986. The mandate of 
the Department is given below: 
 
- To evolv e policies and integrated programmes in biotechnology and ensure their 
implementation and monitoring. 
- To identify specific programmes of Research and Development and manufacturing in 
biologicals and biotechnology and oversee the initiation and pursuit of r elated research and 
manufacturing activities. 
- To identify, set up and support Centers of Excellence for Research and Development in 
biotechnology and ensure proper dovetailing of their activities as per national priorities and 
objectives. 
- To act as a scree ning, advising and approving agent of the Government with regard to import 
and transfer of new technologies for the manufacture of biologicals, biotechnological products 
and their intermediates. 
- Evolve safety guidelines for Biotechnology Research and Devel opment and manufacturing in 
India. 
- To act as the central agency for the import of genetically manipulated materials, culture, cells, 
specimens, tissues and biotech products including DNA and RNA of any type or size and for 
promoting their production in the country. 
- Serve as the inter -ministerial and interagency nodal point for all specific international bilateral 
and multilateral Research and Development collaborations and agreements in the area of 
Biotechnology, act as the nodal point for all technology tr ansfers in the area of biotechnology. 
Manufacture and ensure application of recombinant, cell -based and DNA vaccines, diagnostics 
and other biotechnological products. 
- To evolve programmes for Human Resource Development in the area of biotechnology. 
- Serve a s an administrative and implementing Department of agencies, commissions, boards, 
etc. specifically formed by the Government for fulfilling the national objectives in 
biotechnology and also to serve as the nodal point for Bio -informatics including training  and 
creation of infrastructure, collection, dissemination and exchange of information relating to 
biotechnology.

3. BIOTECHNOLOGY RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT – MAJOR INITIATIVES 
3.1 The Committee sought to know from the Department the major initiatives during the year in the 
field of research and development.   In response, the Department informed that the major  thrust areas 
for the year 2022 -23 and 2023 -24 include agriculture, affordable healthcare and  medical technology, 
food and nutritional security, animal biotechnology, environmental safety,  clean energy a nd bio-fuel, 
and bio-manufacturing. The research projects related to basic, discovery and translational research in 
the areas of agriculture and allied areas including Animal Biotechnology and Aquaculture, Healthcare 
including vaccine, drugs, medical devic es and implants, Bio -engineering, Food and  Nutrition, 
Environment and Clean Energy and Industrial Biotechnology have been considered for support.  
3.2 On the basis of the information provided by the Department, some of the major 
programmes/initiatives and the achievements under them are: 
- The Department in partnership with DARE/ICAR is implementing three Mission programmes, 
namely Mission programme on minor pulses, Mission programme on oilseeds of Indian  origin 
(sesame, niger, safflower and linseed) and Miss ion programme on characterization of  genetic 
resources (rice, wheat, chickpea). These programmes are aimed at screening genetic resources 
for abiotic and biotic stresses and finding new genes which can be utilized for developing 
climate and pathogen resilient varieties for future. In addition, the Department is implementing 
network projects in ICAR institution/SAU‟S in rice which have led to development of varieties 
in rice tolerant to submergence, salinity and drought. Researches supported by the Departmen t 
have led to development of varieties by various institutions, which have  been released to  small 
and marginal farmers through extension network of ICAR/SAU‟s as well as Biotech -Kisan 
programme of the Department. A programme on plant biotechnology catering to engineering of 
smart plant types for enhanced  productivity under a range of environmental conditions as 
well as R&D projects to improve stress resilience in cereals, vegetables, pulses, etc., have been 
supported. 
- Plant genome editing being amongs t one of the most promising technologies with a huge 
economic potentia l in a wide range of sectors, D BT proactively initiated the development of 
draft „Guidelines for the safety assessment of Genome Edited Plants’, which were notified in May, 
2022. The Departme nt ha s notified the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for regulatory 
review of Genome Edited Plants under Site Directed Nuclease -1 (SDN -1) and SDN -2 
categories for enabling regulatory streamlining of genome edited plants and resilient crop s for 
future. These SOPs shall be applicable to all organizations involved in R&D and handling of 
the Genome Edited Plants under these categories. 
- India‟s first  indigenously developed quadrivalent Human Papilloma Virus (qHPV) vaccine,  
CERVAVAC, against cervical cancer s upported by the Department and BIRAC through the 
pioneering partnership  programme „Grand Challenges India‟, received market authorization  
from DCGI in 12th July, 2022. The affordable vaccine is effective against HPV serotypes 6, 11, 
16, and 18, which are responsible for most of the invasive cervical cancer cases. This is fitting 
example of the Government‟s focus on „Preventive Healthcare‟. 
- Through Translational  Research Platform for Veterinary Biologicals (TRPVB), which was  
established to develop cutting ed ge technologies such as next generation  diagnostics, vectored 

10 
 
vaccines etc., a vaccine candidate for Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) virus in cattle has been 
identified. The virus isolates have been transferred to M/s  Biovet Pvt Ltd, Bangalore for 
developing a live attenuated vaccine. The live attenuated Theileria annulata vaccine technology 
which is at TRL-6 level has been transferred to M/s Hester Biosciences Pvt Ltd., Ahmedabad. 
- Study of a large  cohort of patients with Covid-19 was undertaken through the Transl ational 
Research in Health Science and Technology Institute (THSTI), Faridabad, for understanding the 
durability of immunity and risk of re -infection and long  COVID. The study establishes how 
inactivated vaccine BBV152/Covaxin induces robust immune memory to SARS -CoV-2 and 
variants of concern (VOCs) by novel mechanisms involving follicular T -helper cells having B 
cell help potential. The study revealed that majority of the participants have persistent 
antibodies for more than 8 months after vaccination/infe ction; majority of them have increased 
antibody titres post omicron which neutralize all subvariants of omicron; and T -cell responses 
persist in most even though antibody is negative.  
- Genome India, a pan India multi -institutional project, was first implemented by the Department 
in 2020 to build an exhaustive catalogue of genetic variations (common, low frequency, rare, 
SNPs and structural variations) and construct a reference genome and haplotype structure, by 
performing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of 10,000 individuals representing the Indian 
population diversity. The project spanning across 20 institutions envisages the creation of 
national resource of  genetic information and also caters to build capacity in the country in the 
areas of whole genome  sequencing, data analysis, and methods development for high 
throughput genomic studies and  analysis. The whole genome sequencing for 6305 individuals 
has been completed and 8065  genome wide genotyping accomplished. Analyses of joint 
genetic variants calling in these genomes have been carried out for 3966 sequences. 1297 
sequences have been analyzed after joint calling using DRAGEN analysis pipeline. 
- Human Microbiome Initiative, implemented in 2020, is aimed to map the reference microbiome 
of 3400  healthy indivi duals across 11 non-tribal and 6 tribal communities spread across the 
country. Considering the geographic, ethnic and dietary diversity of Indian population, the 
study envisages  the association of „Genetics, biogeography and diet with Microbiome‟. The 
project also looks at the microbiome various with respect to Ayruvedik Prakriti. Complete 
microbiome profiling of 2181 individuals and  partial microbiome profiling of 789 subjects has 
been completed. Diet showed highest influence on microbiome followed by ethn icity and 
geography. Ayurvedic prakriti assessment of  993 subjects by  Ayurvedic physicians has also 
shown high correlation with human microbiome.  
- A network Mission Program on Pediatric Rare Genetic Disorders has been initiated to study  
disease-associated novel genetic variations and development of new genomics-based 
diagnostic tests for pediatric  rare genetic disorders  that are relatively more prevalent in  India. 
The Mission aims to analyze a total of 6000 individuals (2000 patient-parent trios) over 5 years, 
to identify the cause  of undiagnosed genetic  diseases, and to reduce the burden of genetic 
diseases in India by the joint efforts of doctors, scientists and citizens. 
- Under the programme on Energy Biosciences/Biofuels & Waste  to Value, a facility of 1,00,000 
L scale for cultivation of marine algae has been created at Mumbai coast, using a  custom-made 
sunlight-distributed algal growth system for improved algal biomass and lipid  productivity. A 

11 
 
microalgae-based sewage treatment plant (photobioreactor facility) has also been commissioned 
at BPCL Campus, Mumbai to clean sewage at 2,00,000 liter/day scale. 
 
3.3 The Committee was informed that the Department has so far sanctioned a total of 1146 new 
proposals and supported 7,056 ongoing proposals for undertaking innovative research and development 
activities in the areas of Biotechnology. This  support has resulted in about 8343 publications and 
development/commercialization of 567 technologies.  
3.4  The Committee appreciates the achievements of the Department under the various 
programmes/schemes towards Biotechnology Research and Development––especially 
development of the qHPV vaccine CERVAVAC, and hopes that the Department would be able to 
achieve its targets for 2023 -24, through judicious and efficie nt use of  the budget allocation for 
this period.  
3.5  The Committee is of the considered view that setting of realistic and achievable targets, 
both short term and long term, as well as existence of a robust monitoring mechanism to monitor 
and review the  progress of ongoing schemes and programmes, are extremely crucial. The 
Committee recommends that the Department of  Biotechnology should ensure an  effective 
monitoring and periodic review of all its schemes and programmes and take corrective measures, 
wherever required, so that they proceed as per schedule. 
3.6 The Committee recommends more collaboration with DARE/ICAR to accelerate the R&D 
in agriculture, especially plant genomes, so that more productive, drought and flood resistant 
varieties of various important crops can be developed in the next 3-5 years. 
4.  HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
4.1 The Committee asked the Department about its initiatives towards development of human 
resources and capacity building. The Department informed that capacit y building, competence building 
and skill development in broad areas of biotechnology are the key verticals defining the mandate of 
Human Resource Development (HRD) programmes of the Department. Recognizing the need for 
nurturing large pool of skilled and dynamic human capital which are critical for success in building of 
Indian innovation ecosystem as well as fostering the growth of the Indian Biotechnology industry, DBT 
has been supporting several human resource development programmes for promoting and su pporting 
students, research scholars, faculty, scientists, entrepreneurs, etc. DBT‟s National Biotechnology 
Development Strategy 2021 -2025 also places strong emphasis on creating high quality scientific and 
technical human resource in the country. Accordin gly, the Department has been supporting 
programmes and taking initiatives towards human resource development and capacity building as well 
as activities of skill development and academic outreach in the areas of biotechnology under its 
umbrella scheme „Biotechnology Research & Development‟.

7.   HUMAN GENETICS & GENOME ANALYSIS 
7.1. Considering the importance and scope of genetic res earch, the Committee, in its endeavour to 
know about the initiatives  taken by the Department in this direction and the progress  
made by the Department, has been given to understand that the  Department is making efforts in this 
field. The Committee was info rmed that an important programme of the Department, viz., Human  
Genetics & Genome Analysis program supports basic, translational and clinical research, to generate 
knowledge about how to use genomic information to advance medical care.  This  program, which  

19 
 
primarily addresses issues  related to inherited diseases, supports research and development activities 
across the spectrum: basic, translational and clinical research to establish how to use genomic 
information to advance medical care. The diseases which have been studied through ongoing and new 
projects under this programme include: pediatric rare genetic disorders, lysosomal storage disorders, 
Covid – 19, beta thalassaemia, schizophrenia and Parkinson‟s disease, hemophilia, congenital 
nonsyndromic deafne ss, primary cardiomyopathies, monogenic diabetes, movement disorders, celiac 
disease, etc. 
7.2 The Department submitted that, a bout 25 research publications emanated from the R&D 
activities supported under this programme, and more than 150 human resources have been trained in 
this area. It has also established research platform and National Genomics Core, to facilitate pursuit of 
biomedical genomics at the national level by opening up its core facilities of genome sequencing and 
analysis to universities and  other national labs. The Department also informed the Committee that, for 
the first time, a novel gene therapy using cutting -edge biotechnology for hemophilia A, a rare blood 
disorder, has  been developed by the team of researchers from the Centre for Stem  Cell Research 
(CSCR), Christian Medical College, Vellore. Regulatory approval for conducting Phase -I clinical trial 
of gene therapy has been given by the Central Drugs Standard Control  Organization (CDSCO), and the 
clinical trial has been initiated at CMC, Vellore with the first subject recruited in May, 2022.  
7.3 During the financial year 2023-24, the Department plans to provide continued  support to R&D 
projects under the human genetics and  genome analysis program; support cross -disciplinary proposals 
having near-term translational potential; initiate  R&D activities  and support  projects/activities in 
thematic areas and facilitate creation of biorepositories/biobank, for various human genetic disorders. 
7.4 The Committee recognizes the immense potential that genetic research and gene therapy 
hold for altering the treatment paradigm of many genetic diseases, including those that are 
currently incurable. However, as it is a relatively new field of medical science, the many 
challenges still associated with it are not lost on the Committee. Despite the existing challenges, 
such as issues regarding delivery methods, safety and effectiveness concerns, potential long -term 
effects of genetic modification, high costs of developing and administering the therapy making  it 
inaccessible to masses, etc., the potential benefits are far too significant to ignore and, therefore, 
it is highly essential to prioritize research in the area.  
7.5 The Committee appreciates the ongoing efforts of scient ists and researchers in this f ield. 
The Committee recommends the Department to undertake deeper research in collaboration with 
other institutes under the government and private sector, explore avenues for using latest 
emerging technologies including Artificial Intelligence (AI), in ord er to  fully explore the 
untapped potential of genetic research. The Committee also recommends that adequate funds be 
earmarked for the purpose, so that financial constrain ts do not hinder the much-needed R&D. 
The Committee would also like  to be kept informed about the progress made by the Department 
in this regard.

INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is one of the three Departments of 
the Ministry of Science and Technology. It was established on 4 th January, 1985, for the promotion of 
industrial research through indigenous technology promotion, develop ment, utilization and transfer. 
The allocation of business shown under this Department in the Notification is as under: 
(i) All matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR). 
(ii) All matters relating to National Research Development Corporation (NRDC). 
(iii) All matters relating to Central Electronics Limited (CEL). 
(iv) Registration and Recognition of R&D Units. 
(v) Matters relating to UNCTAD and WIPO. 
(vi) National Register for Foreign Collaborations. 
(vii) Matters relating to creation of pool for temporary placement of Indian Scientists and 
Technologists. 
1.2. The primary endeavor of DSIR is to foster development of state -of-the-art technologies and 
products through research and development (R&D), encourage industry to increase their share in the 
country‟s R&D expenditure, support industrial units in developing competitive technologies of high 
commercial potential, catalyze faster commercialization of labor atory-scale R&D, and strengthen 
consultancy and technology management capabilities. 
1.3. The DSIR has two autonomous institutions, viz., CSIR and Consultancy Development Centre 
(CDC) and two public sector undertakings, viz., NRDC and CEL, under its administrative control. The 
Department also provides institutional host facilities to Asian & Pacific Centre for Transfer of 
Technology (APCTT). 
1.4. The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests an d Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research in its meeting held on 22nd February, 2023.

allocation of ₹ 5941.61 crore, over B.E. 2022 -23 allocation of ₹ 5636.46 crore. The Committee also 
observes that that overall financial performance of the Department during 2022 -23 is, by and large, 
satisfactory as it has achieved an overall utilization of 83.6 per cent of its R.E alloc ation for this period. 
However, the performance in respect of the Central Sector Schemes/Projects, which comprises of major 
schemes „Industrial Research & Development‟ and „Assistance to PSEs for Other Scientific Research‟, 
is far from satisfactory . The Department has been able to spend an abysmal 40.6 % of its revised 
allocation under this head. 
2.3 The Committee appreciates  the overall satisfactory financial performance of the 
Department. At the same time, the Committee expresses concern over the sub -optimal utilisation 
in respect of the Central Sector Schemes/Projects, as over 50 per cent of the funds allocated 
under this r emain to be utilized within the remaining quarter of the current financial year . The 
Committee, therefore, urges the Department to ensure optimal utilization of funds during th e 
course of the financial year. In future, periodic monitoring preferably on qua rterly basis may be 
undertaken to facilitate the same. 
2.4 The Committee inquired about the budgetary allocation proposed by the Department vis-à-vis 
the amount actually allocated to it for t he year 2023 -24. The Department  informed that against a 
proposal of Rs. 6871.77 crore, an amount of Rs. 5746.51 has been allocated, which is about 16 per cent 
lesser than its budgetary demand. There is an overall shortfall of Rs. 1125.26 crore in actual allocation 
to the Department. 
2.5 In response to a query about the likely impact of this shortfall in actual allocation over the 
proposed budget and the strategy of the Department for dealing with the challenges arising thereof, the 
Department submitted that -

financial planning and participative performance of R&D projects in general.

S&T areas. A contemporary R&D organization having pan -India presence, CSIR has a dynamic

R&D expertise and experience is embodied in about 3439 active scientists supporte d by about 
4193 scientific and technical personnel, along with about 2514 administrative staff. 
4.2. CSIR has two non -Central Sector Schemes, viz., (i) National Laboratories Scheme; and (ii)  
Capacity Building and Human Resource Development. While the former covers a wide range of R&D

and S&T aspects, latter deals with human resources and different awards. 
4.3 The Committee desired to know about the major achievement s of CSIR during the ye ar. 
The Department informed , during the meeting, that CSIR national labs are grouped together under 
eight sector-specific theme based clusters, with each cluster under a separate directorate. A few of the 
major achievements under these eight verticals during the year are as follow:-   
 
(i) HANSA-NG, India‟s first all -composite single engine light aircraft for flying, training, 
sport and hobby flying designed and developed by CSIR-NAL, successfully completed in-
flight engine relight test on 17 th May, 2022. The 2 -seater, low noise emissio n aircraft has

CSIR‟s production partner, has received order worth Rs. 220 crore  from HAL to make 
composite parts of series of Light Combat Aircraft Mk1A. Besides, CSIR developed multi-
copter drones which were utilized  during Covid times for drug delivery, are now also being 
utilized for fertilizer spray.   
(ii) As a part of its endeavo ur to address water security, CSIR has undertaken High Resolution 
Aquifer Mapping & Management in Arid Regions of North Western India to augment the 
groundwater resources. The Heli -borne geophysical  mapping technology of CSIR  which 
provides high resolution images enables mapping of water-rich areas as also arid regions. In 
phase –I, mapping of priority areas covering an area of 1 lakh sq.kms. has been completed. 
The ultimate a im of the project is to map potential sites for groundwater withdrawal and 
conservation. Further, CSIR is in the process of developing an integrated SMART water 
management system. 
(iii) In the area of energy – including generation, conversion and storage, CSIR has made 
significant strides. A CSIR -Innovation Centre for Next Generation Energy Storage Facility 
is being developed to meet the country's requirement for batteries, which aims to be the 
first in India to demonstrate Lithium battery fabrication up to 100  Mega Watt capacities. 
Once developed, it would help the Indian  industry to come up with Lithium battery 
fabrication facilities with environment -friendly, cost-effective, and energy-efficient 
technology. The proposed  facility would leapfrog next-generation technologies such as 
Sodium-ion, Lithium-sulfur and Solid-state batteries. The lead laboratory is  in the process 
of identifying the industrial partner. 
(iv) In view of the country‟s huge dependence on import of many chemicals, special ity 
chemicals and Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs), CSIR is giving special importance 
to speciality chemicals including leather and petrochemicals. Recently, one manufacturing 
unit of Hydrazine Hydrate in Gujarat was dedicated to the nation by the Prime Minister of 
India. CSIR has also made significant progress with respect production of Azelaic Acid and 
Isobutylene-based derivatives. 
(v) CSIR has developed a tissue culture technology for virus free apple root stock, which 
reduced the chilling time from 1,100 hours to 400 hou rs. These low chilling varieties of 
apple, which were earlier confined only to the Himalayan region, are now being 
popularized in the North -Eastern Region . Further, CSI R‟s „Purple  Revolution‟ under its 
Aroma Mission for introduction and promotion of Lavender  cultivation in  Jammu & 
Kashmir, is now in the process of being expanded to other states like Uttarakhand and 
Himachal Pradesh.  
(vi) After successful development of DNA v accines for the Covid – 19 pandemic, CSIR is 
slowly expanding interest towards mRNA vaccines, which will find application in respect 
of other diseases too, including cancer. CSIR is in the process of completely indigenizing 
the platform by means of which u pcoming pandemics can be easily understood, 

8 
 
predicted/forecast at the shortest possible time.

from distillery, industrial solid waste, brine sludge, e-waste, coal-based power industry

technologies have been transferred to more than 50 licencees and are at various stages of 
implementation with MSMEs, industries and other partners.  
4.4 The Committee applauds the contribution of the Department through CSIR and its 
network of laboratories in the pursuit of excellence across all sectors of scientific research and 
development. The Committee also notes that these endeavours of CSIR are  well-aligned to the 
economic, industrial and social priorities of the nation, as exemplified by their convergence with 
the Government's Mission Programmes  such as Atma Nirbhar Bharat, Make in India, Startup

6.1 The Committee was informed that, in 2023-24, the Department plans to launch a Mission Mode 
project through CSIR, to address a variety  of industrial and other crucial waste management issues 
with their proper disposal, including fossil fuel waste, biotic waste, metallic waste, non -metallic waste, 
and electronic  waste. The Mission is also  in alignment with the United Nation‟s „Sustainable 
Development Goals‟  and the Government‟s commitments towards environment conservation , 
mitigating climate change and adapting approaches of sustainable development. 
6.2 The Department, in the meeting, mentioned about some of the waste -to-wealth technologies 
developed by CSIR for converting various types of wastes into high, value added -end products. The 
Committee evinced keen interest in the success stories of the Department in this area, and sought to 
know more about the technology developed for conversion of steel slag as road making aggregates. In a 
written reply, the Department informed that , under the R&D project sponsored by Ministry of Steel 
along with four major steel industries, CSIR -Central Road Research Institute (CRRI), New Delhi 
developed customized steel slag valorisation technologies for conversion of different types of steel slag 
as processed steel slag aggregates for road making. The design and construction methodology for its 
utilization have been devised after various intrinsic challenges associated with the slag conversion and 
its possible environmental impacts were successfully addressed. 
6.3 Using this technology, India‟s first steel slag road (1.2 km long six lane) has been constructed at 
Hazira Surat. The road has 32% reduced thickness than conventional bituminous road section, with its 
structural strength four times better despite reduced thickness and caters to heavy commercial traffic 
without any sign of distress. Further, the construction cost is around 40 % cheaper than conventional 
bituminous road. So far, the technology has been used for construction of steel slag roads in other areas 
too, including the Sino -India Border Road in Aru nachal Pradesh (1 km. long, two lane); Jharkhand 
(six-lane road on NH -33 connecting Jamshedpur to Ranchi); Maharashtra (1 km. six lane road on 
Mumbai-Goa highway and another six lane Bhadara Bypass Section of NH -53); and Gujarat (NH -53, 
near Abhava village junction and Khajod village junction at Surat). 
6.4 The Committee was informed that there are many key benefits of thi s technology, such as eco -
friendly sustainable utilization of steel slag waste (19 million tons generated annually through various 
steel plants in the country, which will increase to 45 million tons by 2030); saving of natural aggregates 
and reducing unsustainable quarrying and mining; reduction of GHG emissions and carbon footprint of 
road construction, improved durability of road with better service life; higher load resistance capacity, 
etc. As per directives of Niti Aayog and Ministry of Steel, CSIR is preparing a comprehensive design 
guidelines and specifications for utilization of steel slag in road constructions. Apart from road 
projects, there are immense future prospects for using steel slags in construction of civil and defence 
runways and for usin g it as Railway Ballast. CSIR -CRRI is focused towards promotion of sustainable 
utilization side by side with upgradation of the technology for better outcomes, and aiming to extend 
this technological support to various SAIL and other steel plants in the country.

solvents, salts and the excipients essential for drug formulations. Hence, there is an urgent necessity to 
invest in R&D not only to achieve greater heights in this field, but to sustain current levels of business. 
7.2 The Department informed that, so far,  CSIR has developed cost -effective processes for various

pharmaceutical companies for production and commercialization. CSIR -Indian Institute of Chemical 
Technology (IICT), Hyderabad has established a kilo -lab facility which soon will be made a GMP 
accredited lab. Similarly, CSIR ha s stepped forward in developing indigenous, innovative and novel 
chemical processes to produce intermediates and final APIs and also repurposing drugs for Covid-19 
towards affordable health care. 
7.3 To continue R&D in this crucial domain,  CSIR has propose d to take up a Mission P roject on 
APIs, with an objective to develop viable, non -infringing routes of synthesis for selected APIs using 
advanced instruments such as automation, flow chemistry and follow ing green chemistry principles. 
The Government of Indi a had, during the beginning of Covid -19 pandemic, shortlisted close to 60 
APIs/bulk drugs for which the Indian pharma industry was critically dependent on imports of raw 
materials or Key Starting Materials (KSMs). Under the proposed Mission project on APIs , priority is 
being given to these KSMs depending upon essentiality, availability of raw -materials and supply chain.

down the cost of production through proce ss optimization to enhance productivity and robustness. The 
efforts will be focused on developing alternate synthesis with the use of indigenous and renewable 
sources of raw materials and flow synthesis. Based on their need for the country, around 20 APIs are 
being taken up for process development under the proposed mission project.  The project aims to serve 
the country with its contributions to „Make in India‟ program and towards better health for the society.

industry. The Committee, therefore, expresses its wholehearted support towards CSIR’s 
proposed Mission Project on APIs, and wishes the Department a speedy progress in this 
direction.

INTRODUCTION 
The Department of Science & Technology (DST) is the nodal agency in the country for 
strengthening science, technology and innov ation, identifying gap areas in S&T sectors, making 
planning and policy to meet the societal needs, promoting new areas of S&T in view of future 
demands. DST also serves in connecting the science and technology sectors with different Government 
horizontals and verticals, academia, R&D labs /institutions and industries. With the objective to 
strengthen the national S&T capacity and capability, DST provides the largest extramural research and 
development support in the country to scientists cutting across institutions and disciplines through a  
competitive mode reinforcing our country’s education system, scientific and industrial R&D and the 
overall Science, Technology and Innovation landscape of the country.  
1.2 The Department has been continuing efforts towards strengthening the national STI ecosystem 
to emerge as a forerunner to play a critical role in science and technology for bringing positive 
transformations towards a safe, secure, better society, and be well prepared for future disruptions.  
1.3 The Department also administers 25 autonomous bodies and two statutory bodies, namely 
Science & Engineering Research Board (SERB) and Technology Development Board (TDB). The 
autonomous bodies include 16 research institutions, 4 specialized knowledge and S&T service 
organizations and 5 profe ssional bodies. These institutions, with long and cherished history and their 
variety of activities, occupy an important place in the S&T eco-system of the country. 
1.4 The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the 
Department of Science & Technology in its meeting held on 21st February, 2023.

3.  KEY ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT DURING 2022-23 
 
3.1 The Department of Science & Technology has four Central Sector Schemes/Project s, namely, 
Science and Technology Institutional and Human Capacity Building; Research and Development; 
Innovation, Technology Development and Deployment; and National Mission on Interdisciplinary 
Cyber Physical System (NM -ICPS). The Department implements its wide -ranging programmes under 
these schemes. The Department, through written replies and presentation during the meeting, submitted 
some of the key achievements across its various programmes during the year 2022-23, as below – 
- The Fund for Improvement of S&T Infrastructure in Universities and Higher Educational 
Institutions (FIST)  programme has been restructured to orient it towards  the goal of 
Atmanirbhar Bharat. During the year, 525 fresh proposals were received in seven subject areas , 
out of which 90 projects have been recommended. With support pro vided by the 15 
Sophisticated Analyti cal Instrument Facilities (SAIFs ) in the country , approximately 2400 
research papers were published and about 33,000 users across India utilized and be nefitted from 
these facilities. Under Synergistic Training program U tilizing the Scientific and Technological 
Infrastructure (STUTI) , a total of 192 training programs were organized and around 6,500 
researchers have been trained. Similarly, u nder State S&T Programme, 31 S&T Councils are 
supported currently. Two Policy Research Cells (PRC s) have also been supported and around  
19 DST-STI fellows received fellowship under the DST-STI fellowship programme.  
- Under Promotion of University Research and Scientific Excellence (PURSE) , four new 
Universities have been identified for support. The Department also announced a special call for 
the unserved regions in the country, to provide basic infrastructure for promoting R&D 
activities in new and emerging areas, in the universities of North Eastern Region, Jammu & 
Kashmir, Chhattis garh, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Bihar, Haryana, Telangana, Himachal 
Pradesh and Rajasthan. Under the special c all, 12 new universities have been identified for 
support.  
- Under Women in Science & Engineering - Knowledge Involvement in Research Advancement 
through Nurturing ( WISE-KIRAN), a total of 293 projects out of 990 proposals have been 

7 
 
selected in 5 different streams under Women Scientists Scheme – A (WOS -A), while under 
WOS-B grant has been released for 9 ongoing projects  and more than 30 publications  have 
come out from these projects. A new post -doctoral fellowship for women has also been 
launched under the Women Scientists Scheme - Professional Development of Women in 
Science (WISE  - PDF). VigyanJyoti programme, which aims to encourage girls to pursu e 
higher education and career in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM)  has 
been extended to 200 districts (including 13 aspirational districts) of 34 states/UTs of the 
country, thereby benefitting  approximately 18,000 girls. 
- Two national missions on climate change viz., National Mission on Strategic Knowledge for 
Climate Change (NMSKCC) and National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem 
(NMSHE) are being implemented  under the Climate Change Programme . Four new State 
Climate Change Cells (SCCCs) have been established, each in Goa, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh 
and Chandigarh (UT) resulting in the presence of SCCCs in 28 states/UTs across the country. 
- Under National Supercomputing Mission (NSM), five new installations of supercomputers have 
been successfully completed at IIT Roorkee, NIT Trichy, IIT Gandhinagar, IIT Guwahati, IIT 
Mandi. So far, 28 supercomputers have been installed while a n indigenously developed Rudra 
server is getting ready for use.

during 2022, out of which 7 were sanctioned.  Several new dimensions were added to the Clean

issues through the Water Technology Initiative.

new program called National Initiative for Developing and Harnessing Innovations (NIDHI) – 
Inclusive Technology Business Incubators (i-TBI) has been initiated to ensure inclusiveness of 
innovation and entrepreneurship across the country and to foster innovation and startup culture.

established. A new Centre of Excellences ( CoE) at T -Hub, Hyderabad, Telangana has been

submitted that, this year, it proposes to have a full scal e implementation of the mission in terms of 
technology development, setting up startups, employment creation, industry connect, etc., in key 
priority areas of cyber physical technologies to make India globally competitive.

5.4 The Committee, taking cognizance of the consistent and widespread public demand for 
increasing the amount  of various scholarships/fellowships, particularly Junior Research Fellowship, 
asked the Department if any action is being taken in this regard . In its re sponse, the Department

Ministerial Committee under the Chairmanship of the Secretary, DST, is being set-up to undertake a 
holistic examination of the same. Ce rtain issues including the basis/formula  for raising the amount, 
shortage of funds of some Departments, the huge financial implication of such an increase  in the 
emoluments of various fellowships, etc., are being examined and sorted out. 
5.5 Taking cognizance of the importance of human resource development and capacity 
building for a nation, the Committee commends the efforts of the Department towards this end. 
The Committee, however, feels that much more needs to be done, especially for a country li ke 
ours which is endowed with adequate human resource to be developed, trained, harnessed and 
empowered. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should set defined 
targets across all its programmes , in quantifiable terms to the extent poss ible, and steadfastly 
work towards achieving them. The Committee  further recommends that a robust mechanism 
should be put in place for monitoring the progress of each programme. 
 
6. WOMEN IN SCIENCE AND ENGINEERING (WISE) 
6.1 The Committee was informed that the Department is implementing a dedicated scheme known 
as ‘Women in Science & Engineering - Knowledge Involvement in Research Advancement through 
Nurturing (WISE-KIRAN)’ to promote women in Science & Te chnology (S&T) domain . Under this 
umbrella Scheme, various women centric programmes like Women Scientists Scheme (WOS) to 
promote women researchers; Consolidation of University Research for Innovation and Excellence

under-represented areas of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) ; Gender 
Advancement for Transforming Institutions (GATI), a recent initiative to transform institutions for 
gender sensitive approach to achieve gender equality at institution level, etc. are under implementation.  
6.2 The Committee was further informed that, in the last three years, 838 women have benefitted 
from the WOS, while 25 Women Post -graduate Colleges have been supported  under C URIE. More 
than 30,000 girls of Class IX -XII have benefitted from the various i nterventions under VigyanJyoti, 
while 30 Indian institutions of national importance and higher education have be en selected to

6.3 During the meeting, t he Committee inquired from the Department about the overall enrolment 
of women in science education in the country. The Department informed that the number of women till 
graduation level is, in fact, higher than men – the enrolment ratio being about 52 per cent female and 
48 per cent male at present. While this percentage declines slightly at the post -graduate level, it drops

students pursuing higher education in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM), the 
Department stated that it had undertaken a study on this issue and found that, apart from economic and 
social factors such as marriage, parental influence etc., there are several other reasons such as the lack 
or absence of institutes of higher learning in rural areas where they can pursue studies at home, among 
others. The Department mentioned that steps are being taken through its various programmes to 
address th e challenges, including scaling up of the VigyanJyoti programme during 2023 -24 and

parity in S&T through various  interventions, the Department should endeavour to  maintain the

7. NATIONAL RESEARCH FOUNDATION 
7.1 On scrutiny of budgetary allocations of the Department for the financially year 2023 -24, it is 
observed that Rs. 2000 crore, i.e., almost 25 per  cent, has been earmarked for the head ‘National 
Research Foundation (NRF)’. The Committee sought details about the aims, objective and activities 
being planned under this head. In a written reply, the Department submitted that NRF is envisioned as a 
body with a mandate to set the overall research agenda at the national level and it will seed, grow and 
promote research and development (R&D) and foster a culture of research and innovation throughout 
India’s universities, colleges, research institutions and R&D laboratories. In addition, NRF will create a 
vibrant R&D framework for industries and other organizatio ns to work closely with academic and 
research institutions. Its objectives and goals include: 
- funding of competitive peer -reviewed grant proposals to indivi duals or groups of individuals 
across all S&T disciplines in all types of institutions;  
- assist in setting up research infrastructure and environment for scientific pursuit;  
- increase India’s role and participation in key areas of national and global importance;  
- coordinate across Ministries, State Governments, Industries, etc. to document and analyse 
expenditure on science research as well as their outcomes during each financial year; and 
- serve as a high -level think tank for the coordination and short -and long -term planning of 
research in the country  
 
7.2 The Department further submitted that NRF has a broad-based strategy to enlarge the scope of 
research funding and promote/facilitate growth in research in academic institutions across the country. 
Seeding research at State Universities and colleges at rural settings has been given top priority. 
Research Mentors (in the form of ‘NRF Professorships’) at Universities and Colleges where research is 
currently in a nascent stage, particularly State Universities, will be created by utilizing the expertise of 
serving or retired faculty. Bringing in young research talent will be key to developing research cultures 
at educational institutions. For this purpose, NRF will launch a large and prestigious system of 
postdoctoral fellowships to be used in our academic systems. Creating Centers of Excellence (CoE) & 
National Mission Projects are some other modes to develop and support areas o f  critical national 
importance, such as A rtificial Intelligence (AI) , Machine Learning, Environmental Science, Climate 
Change etc. Many of these  Centres will aim to work in an interdi sciplinary manner, while d edicated 
R&D platforms will be created in partnership with industry to support and improve linkages between 
R&D, academia and industry. 
7.3 The Department informed that the following programmes will be initiated during 2023-24: 
(i) Seeding Research at State Universities through NRF Professorships: One of the foremost aims 
of the NRF will be to seed research at Universities and Colleges where research is currently 
non-existent or in nascent stages, particularly State Universities, whe re over 90% of the 
country’s faculty and students work and study. 
(ii) Postdoctoral Fellowships: The NRF will initially select and fund Postdoctoral Fellowships to 
outstanding researchers across S&T fields. 
(iii) Centers of Excellence (CoE) & National Mission Projects: Each year, proposals will be invited 
for establishing Centres of Excellence/ National Mission Projects at academic institutions and 
National Labs in areas of critical national importance, such as Machine Learning, 
Environmental Science, etc. Many of these Centres will aim to work in an interdisciplinary 
manner. 
(iv) Funding of Grants: A major goal of the NRF will be to fund competent people with good ideas, 

13 
 
across fields, wherever they may be located. Proposals will be invited by the NRF from 
individuals and groups of individuals across institutions. The aim will be to increase the 
resource absorption capacity for high-quality research in the nation, over a period of time. 
7.4 Both domestic and International Projects will be undertaken under the Grant sy stem. Broadly 
these projects would have defining characteristics such as individual centric, competitive funding; high 
priority research around established research groups with complementary experti se from different 
departments/institutes; t ransformative a nd disruptive research concepts based on innovative and 
unproven hypothesis, possessing a high degree of uncertainty, yet having conviction to produce a 
lasting impact across discipline boundaries ; gender parity oriented; equity and e mpowerment focused; 
thematically oriented ; and State University/ College centric promotional competitive projects . In 
addition, there will be special window for addressing and funding industrial research engagement. 
Performing scientists will be recognized through National Fellowships. 
7.5  The Department submitted that the tentative physical targets for financial year 2023 -24 include 
- 10 NRF Professorships; 500 Postdoctoral Fellowships; a minimum of one CoE & National Mission 
Project; competitive funding of 1000 projects; Early  Career Research Support to 500 regular 
faculty/scientists; sanctioning of Homecoming Fellowship to  100 scientists from abroad; 100 Science 
Excellence Fellowships; 300 gender parity oriented programmes; 100 Special calls; and 50 Priority 
Research projects. 
7.6 The Committee desired to know as to what would be the nature of relationship between the 
Department of Science & Technology  and NRF, as also of other bodies under the Department such as 
the Technology Development Board (TDB) and Science and Engineeri ng Research Board (SERB) . In 
its response, the Department informed that NRF will be established as a statutory body through an Act 
of Parliament. While NRF will serve as a high-level think tank for coordination and short and long -
term planning of research in the country, funding of grant proposals to individuals, groups or 
institutions across all S&T disciplines in all types of institutions will be synergized with the EMR 
funding schemes of the Department . Further, considering that NRF has an expanded mandate covering 
activities over and above the activities of SERB, it is proposed SERB will be subsumed in NRF. 
7.7 The Committee takes due note of the visions, objectives and purpose of creation of the 
National Research Foundation. It believes that a cent rally established NRF that transparently 
seeds, funds, and coordinates research across institutions in the country - in all disciplines, in an 
integrated manner, with a special mandate to foster research and innovation in universities and 
colleges, includi ng inter -disciplinary research to provide practical solutions to societal, 
developmental, financial, techno -economic challenges of the nation,  is a much needed 
overarching mechanism. The Committee recommends that , in the process of implementing this 
programme, special consideration should be given towards under-funded as well as new and 
emerging areas of research, while also keeping under-served regions of the country in mind.

 The Committee notes the overall increase in the budgetary allocation of the Department

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
 The Government of India set up the Space Commission and the Depa rtment of Space (DOS) in 
1972. Department of Space is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space 
Commission. These are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), Indian 
National Space Promotion & Authorization Centre (IN -SPACe) and the Grant -in-aid institutions viz., 
Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), North -
Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC), Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL) and Indian Institute 
of Space Science and Technology (IIST). 
1.2 The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located in 
Bengaluru. The Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarte rs co -ordinate the overall programmes like 
Satellite Communication, Satellite Navigation, Earth Observation, Space Transportation Systems, 
Space Science and Planetary Exploration, Climate & Atmospheric Programme, Disaster Management 
Support, National Natur al Resources Management System (NNRMS), International Co -Operation, 
Capacity Building, Media & Public Relations, Budget & Economic Analysis and Human Resources 
Development. 
1.3 The activities of Department of Space (DOS) are broadly organized und er four umbrella 
schemes namely 
 Space Technology - development of launch vehicles, satellites, manned space mission, R&D in 
Space Technology such as propulsion, navigational satellite systems, indigenization of Space 
materials & components, etc.  
 
 Space Applications - major Projects/activities such as Earth Observation Navigation Missions, Tele-
medicine, Tele-education, Disaster Management Support,etc are undertaken. 
 
 Space Sciences - projects towards Space sciences and planetary exploration are undertaken. Major 
projects undertaken under the scheme include Indian Lunar Mission - Chandrayaan-3, Aditya -L1 
mission, XPoSat, Space Docking Experiment.  
 
 INSAT Satellite Systems - This programme is envisaged to provide satellite based communication 
services in the country. 
1.4 Major Centres / Units of DOS/ISRO: 
a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the technology base for 
the country‟s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development 
b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities locat ed at Bengaluru and 
Thiruvananthapuram, is responsible for development of liquid propulsion and cryogenic 
propulsion systems for satellite and launch vehicles 
c) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the spaceport of 
India providing launch base to indigenously built launch vehicles.  Also, it provides the facilities 
for processing of solid rocket motors 
d) Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) is created with the responsibility to act as the lead centre for 
Human Space Flight Progra m. This centre is responsible for the execution of 
Gaganyaanprogramme that envisages sending a crew of astrounauts to space and bring back 
safely to earth.   
e) U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), Bengaluru, is entrusted with the prime responsibility for 
development of satellites

f) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad 
g) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite data acquisition 
and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision s upport for disas ter 
management 
h) The Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bengaluru  
i) ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC), Mahendragiri 
j) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC) 
k) Master Control Facility (MCF), Hassan 
l) Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun  
m) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram  
1.5 Organisations receiving Grants-in-aid: 
a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution supported mainly 
by the Department of Space, carries out research in space sciences. 
b) The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki near Tirupati, 
conducts atmospheric research. 
c) The North -Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE -SAC) established as an autonomous body 
under the Department of Space provides spac e technology inputs for developmental activities in 
the North-Eastern Region.  
d) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) is an autonomous body under the 
Department with the objective of creating quality human resources tuned to suit the requirements 
of state-of-art space research programme.    
1.6 Government Companies under DOS:  
a) The Antrix Corporation Limited, Bengaluru, established in 1992, is a wholly owned 
Government Company for marketing space products and services.  
b) The NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), Bengaluru, is another commercial arm of Indian Space 
Research Organization, with the primary objective of enabling Indian industries to scale up high-
technology manufacturing and production base for Indian space programme.  
1.7 Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (INSPACe) 
Recently, the space sector was opened up to promote, handhold, regulate and authorise private 
enterprises and start-ups to undertake space activities by creation of an independent nodal agency under 
Department of Space - the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (IN -SPACe). 
This will enhance the contribution of space technology towards boosting space economy within the 
country.

2.13 The Committee makes note of the variation in budgetary allocations across key schemes of 
the Department  and the reasons pertaining to disruption of the global supply chain. The 
Committee also makes note of the fact that Semi -Conductor Laboratory which is responsible for 
design and development of crucial electronic components has been transferred to the Ministry of 
Electronics and Information Technology. The Committee highlights that a significant inventory 
of components used in satellites and launch vehicles are imported as they are not manufac tured 
in India.  
2.14 While the challenges to domestic manufacturing of electronic chipsets, solar panels, 
atomic clocks and other crucial components are varied, ranging from availability of raw material 
to expertise in design and high scale -cost effective  and precise manufacturing, the Committee 
recommends that the Department should take necessary steps in maintaining an inventory of 
these crucial components and engineer the supply chain in such a manner that it remains 
immune to such geo -political hurdles, to the largest extent possible. Further, the Committee also 
recommends that s teps be taken to achieve higher indigenization in pro duction of some key 
components.2.15
