REPORT 
Necessity is the mother of invention. The history of mankind is full of examples where 
scarcities and shortages led to inventions. The men behind these inventions were not always 
intellectuals hailing from affluent families. Instead, they came from ordinary walks of life and in 
many cases were illiterate and so poor that they did not have even two square meals a day. They 
burnt mid-night oil in order to help the mankind with the benefit of their inventions. They 
followed the ideals enshrined in what Sir Winston Churchill described in following woi:ds:-
"Heights of the great men were not attained in a single flight, they came up toiling upwards when 
their companions slept in the night" 
The domain of inventions is thus not the property of any intellectuals or enlightened or 
affluent sections of the Society alone. It belongs to one and all. 
Shri P. Ramar Pillai who shot in the news sometime back comes from ordinary walk of life. 
He was reported to have invented what he described as "Herbal Fuel". This gave him a world­
wide publicity, for his experiment could open. new vistas for the worlq and save the mankind 
from the near crisis in the field of energy with which we are confronted today. It has often been 
projected and rightly so that the oil reserves were not going to last long. It is thus incumbent on 
all of us to conserve · the oil resources in the best possible manner and at the same time our 
endeavour should be to aim at inventing the alternative and new sources of energy. 
It was in this background, that Shri P. Ramar Pillai of Kamrajar district, Tamil Nadu, 
attracted attention world-wide about his production of herbal fuel. History tells us that to Dr. 
Isaac Newton, it was a rude jolt by a falling apple which made him ponder about earth's 
gravitational pull whereas young Ramar did not have to undergo such an ordeal with the nature 
when the green leaves burnt with a frenzy, he knew they belonged to an extraordinary genre. 
According to Shri Ramar Pillai, while taking part in an annual picnic to the Western Ghats 
with other students of Mamsapuram's Sivanthi Petty Nadar High School, he had noticed that in 
the rice they had just cooked, a spark fell on the leaves and they caught fire. While this set him 
thinking, his other classmates were not carried by the significance that Shri Ramar Pillai 
attached to the event. He drew his classmates' attention to it but they ignored him. It is stated 
that in the years that followed, the 'leaf-hunt' became such an obsession that Shri Ramar Pillai 
failed to clear the Xth standard. His wandering ways made follow.ed, the 'leaf -hunt ' became 
such an obsession that Shri Ramar to earn his bread, he started collecting firewood from the 
forest. Finally in 1987, he identified the plant and had a hunch that it could be converted into a 
fuel. None believed him except a school-mate of Ramar, Poonkani, who ultimately became his 
foster sister. Then began a series of trial and error experiments. They studied the effect of 
different materials on the herb after grounding it into a paste. Poonkani remembers that though 
they knew about the power of the herb all along, it was, however, on November 20, 1992, only 
that they made a definite breakthrough. When they mixed Sodium Chloride to a certain kind of 
fruit essence there was a reaction and a lot of smoke. They then mixed this with the herb and 
started heating , they got a semi-solid mixture, the precursor of the fuel that they claim to have 
made. By 1993, they had refined it to its present form resulting in the first official demonstration _ 
of the production of herbal fuel at the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras on 30th June, 1995. 
News agencies splashed that the ''herbal fuel" produced has been tested by Dr. V. Ganesan an 

expert at the Madras liT's Internal Combustion ·Engines Lab, who found that the oil is just 
as good, if not better, as a fuel for two stroke and four stroke engines. 
Dr. Ganesan, like some other scientists is stated to have wondered: From where does 
Ramar get the carbon to make his "Petrol"?" Ramar makes 400-750 ml. of his fuel from two 
litres of water using about 30 gm. of the herb. Even if the herb were full of carbon , and one 
gets maximum efficiency from it, it would take about 175 gm. of carbon to get so much fuel. 
While water, salt and lemon do not contain carbon, he uses just 5 gm. of the catalyst. 
Even the Secretary, DST was initially stated to have reacted to Ramar's experiment 
saying, "I. would neither believe it nor disbelieve it till I know the full details. But I would 
say that v':hat he showed was very interesting and significant and I have no reason to assume 
that he was doing any magic or fraud". A scientist whose scooter had run out of petrol 
decided to do the first verification outside the laboratory . After getting a refill of Ramar's 
fuel he m:1de several rounds on his campus and even rode home nine kms. away. This along 
with resu :ts of the test was telecast by Doordarshan. 
Then ·after, Shri P. Ramar is stated to have written a letter to the Secretary, 
Departme 1t of Science & Technology on 1st December, 1995 claiming to have developed a 
fuel from herbal mixture for two-wheelers. In order to substantiate his claim emission test 
reports of the Madras liT's IC Engine Laboratory were also stated to have been enclosed. 
He had a')pealed that he should be helped to set up production facility centres in his 
hometown in Tamil Nadu . 
Accordingly Shri P. Ramar was invited to demonstrate his production process again to a 
team of Scit-ntists and patent experts in Madras on 25th September, 1996. All the u"'""'~'"m 
equipments to carry out the demonstration were provided by the liT , Madra s. However, 
Shri P. Ramar, it is stated could not successfully demonstrate the process of producting fuel 
from plants in front of the team of Scientists. 
Controversies gained momentum from both the sides when Department of Science & 
Technology dropped patent formalities as the demonstration could not establi sh the validity 
of Shri Ramar 's claim of "herbal fuel" and accused that Shri P. Ramar had used "dishonest 
means" to prod uce the herbal fuel. But Shri Ramar denied that he had used any "dishonest 
means" to produce his fuel an~ explained that he was prepared to prove his claim true. 
The Committee was informed that the Department of Science & Technology, however, 
sought to keep an open· mind to investigate and give Shri Ramar another chance. The 
Secretary explained that it was quite possible that Shri Ramar had not used all the 
ingredients in rhe demonstration at the liT, Madras in his anxiety not to let anyone 
including top sc.ientists from gettiug to kno·w all his secrets. 
When the is ~ ue of production of what was described as herbal fuel assumed a national 
debate·, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & 
Forests discussed t.he issue with the Secretary, Department of Science & Technology during 
the Committee's visit to Thiruvananthapuram on 12th OctQ_ber, 1996. During the course of 
deliberations, the S'ecretary informed the Committee about th~ significance of demonstration 
in a controlled condition and therefore, it was decided to have the demonstration before the 
Committee at Indian Institute of Petroleum, Dehradun on 15th November, 1996. 
Accordingly, the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee met in 
Dehradun at the Indian Institute of Petroleum on 15th November, 1996 at 3.00 p.m. to have 
a demonstration from Shri P. Ramar Pillai about his claim for producing herbal petrol. The 
Committee discussed with the Secretary, Department of Science and Technology and 

Director, Indian Institute of Petroleum, Dehraduo, the arrangements made in connection 
with the demonstration for production of 'herbal fuel'. The Committee was informed that 
the arrangements made for the demonstration under controlled . laboratory conditions were to 
the satisfaction of Shri Ramar. Thereafter, the Committee discussed with Shri Ramar about

satisfaction.

sample obtained during the demonstration experiment for preparation of 'herbal fuel' on 
15th November, 1996 at Indian Institute of Petroleum, Dehradun clearly shows that it is a 
mixture of hydrocarbons boiling in kerosene range with dissolved camphor. 
The Committee has been further informed that the Indian Institute of Petroleum 
conducted a confirmatory experiment on 19th November, 1996 in order to further confirm 
the formation of the 'herbal fuel'. The steps followed were the same as in the demonstration 
experiment (Ramar experiment) carried out on 15th November, 1996. The data obtained in 
the confirmatory experiment as well as in the demonstration experiment of the 'herbal fuel' 
of Shri Ramar (15/11/96) are quite comparable in all respects including the change in the 
local volumes and burning characteristics. The Indian Institute of Petroleum has thus arrived 
at the following conclusions:-
(i) The 'Herbal Fuel' obtained in the demonstration experiment (Ramar experiment) 
was separated into the solid and liquid portions. This step became necessary since 
separation of solid wall observed when the 'Merbal Fuel' was allowed to cool to 
ambient temperature. Detailed analysis has been carried out on the solid and liquid 
portions. 
(ii) The laboratory analysi.s by liP established that the product produced during the 
Ramar experiment is a mixture of hydrocarbons boiling in the kerosene range with 
dissolved camphor. 
Going by the analysis of the Ramar's end product the expectations of finding an 
indigenous and economical solution to the energy crisis facing the mankind may 
have been belied for a while, the Committee nonetheless feels that it is not the end 
of the road. The Government should liberalise research and should extend all help 
to Scientists coming forward with their experiments. The Committee feels that there 
is no adequate infrastructure obtaining at the learning stages say at schools and 
colleges where Scientists/Officers/Researchers can conduct experiments on their 
findings. The Government should endeavour to provide the necessary infrastructure 
and throw it open to students and non-students in order to encourag e s cientific 
temper and research.

The data obtained in the confirmatory experiment as well as in the demonstration 
experiment of what was described herbal fuel of Mr. Ramar (15.11.1996) are quite 
comparable in all respect s including the change in the liquid volumes and burning 
characteristics. 
7. Final Conclusions 
1. "Herbal fuel" obtained in the demonstration experiment (Ramar experiment) was 
separated into the solid and liquid portions. This step became necessary since separation of 
solid was observed when the so called herbal fuel was allowed to cool to ambient 
temperature. Detailed analysis has been carried out on the solid and liquid portions. 
2. The laboratory analysis by liP established that the product produced during the 
Ramar experime nt is a mixture of hydrocarbons boiling in the kero10ene range with disolved 
camphor. 
3. Although, the nature of the inputs to the Ramar experiment were not allowed to be 
analysed , based on the fact that the solid input smelled strongly like camphor and the liquid 
input (so called essence) smelled strongly like kerosene, it is most likely that Ramar 
provided kerosene and camphor as inputs. Camphor dissolved in kerosene during the Ramar 
experiment with resultant increase in the volume of liquid. 
4. The hypothesis in Shri Ramar's experiment above was verified by liP in a 
confirmatory experiment where the same amount of Camphor was mixed with the same 
amount of kerosene under the same experimental conditions leading to the same increase in 
volume with liquid having the same property to burn as the so called herbal fuel produced in 
the Ramar experiment.

each year, however, the  Department has been  sanctioned additional  funds through Supplementary 
Demands for Grants at RE stage. The current shortfall of  Rs. 6,829.71 crore alongwith any further  
additionality, based on the budgetary requirements,  shall be sought at RE stage. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.3 From the submission of the Department the Committee feels that the Department may  face 
challenges especially in its initiatives relating to Nuclear Recycle Board (NRB), Tata Memorial Centre  
(TMC), Nuclear Power  Corporation of India Limited  (NPCIL), Heavy Water  Board (HWB) and 
Bhabha Atomic Research  Centre (BARC).                                                                        (Para 2.11 ibid) 
 
1.4 The Committee underlines the requirement  of an additional budgetary allocation of Rs.3,150 
crore over and above  the BE 2023-24 quoted by the Department  and recommends that the Department 
be given the additional alloca tion for them to continue with their set goals and  objectives and ensure a 
timely and e ffective completion.  The initiatives of the Department under TMC, NPCIL  and BARC, 
amongst others, are crucial to the energy needs of the country  as well  as in  many healthcare and 
societal applications.  It is also necessary to ensure tha t the activities  of the Department do not suffer 
due to any lack of funds as it will have a bearing on India's strategic nuclear capacity.  
                                                                                                                                    (Para 2.12 ibid) 
 
1.5 The Committee also recommends  that the Department should reach  out to the  Ministry of 
Finance for additional funds  at the RE/Supplementary stage and al so look for  raising the same  either 
through internal revenue or  through reallocati ng  funds from heads which have  excess al location, if 
any.                                                                                                                                    (Para 2.13 ibid)                                                                                                                         

3 
 
                                                                                                                             
Action Taken 
1.6 As advised by the Hon'ble Committee the Department shall  seek the additional funds of         
Rs.3,150 crore at the RE 2023-24/ Supplementary  Demands for Grants and ensure that the set Goals 
and objectives of the Department are achieved. 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.7 The Committee therefore recommends  that the Department be  diligent in managing  the 
expenditure as well as achieving the physical targets  that it has set out for  itself for  2023-24. The

these funds.                                                                                                                        (Para 2.17 ibid)

1.8 As recommended by the Hon'ble Committee,  the Department shall ensure that the physical  
targets indicated in  the major thrust areas of the Department/deliverables are acc omplished with the

CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE 
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES  
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIA L YEAR 2022 -23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR 20 23-24 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.1 From Chart 2 which depicts the share of Revenue and Capital allocation in BE 2023 -24 of the 
Department, across its various key sectors, t he Committee  observes that while the  share of revenue 
and capital expenditure allocations is almost  equal in the  total budget, capital  expenditure is  almost 
twice that of revenue for the Power Sector. On the other hand,  revenue expenditure is more than thrice  
of the capital expenditure  allocation under R&D Sector.                          (Para 2.7 of the 373rd Report) 
 
Action Taken 
2.2 Power Sector: The Department  provides Gross Budgetary Support under Capital Division for 
Power Sector  towards – Loans and Investments in PSUs.  Whereas, the Department  provides limited 
budgetary support under Revenue Division for Operation &  Maintenance purpose for e.g. Fuel 
Inventory, Interest on Heavy Water Pool Management etc. A  major portion of Revenue expenditure is 
incurred by the Power Sector  PSUs through internal sources. The Budgetary allocations under Capital 
Division (Loans and Inve stments) have increased due to the upcoming  Projects. Hence,  the Capital 
expenditure is  almost twice of the Revenue for the  Power Sector i.e.  NPCIL (Rs.6364  crore), 
Investments in NPCIL (Rs.3046  crore) and Loans to BHAVINI (Rs.200 crore). 
 
2.3 R&D Sector: The revenue expenditure of R&D sector comprises of Establishment expenditure 
(Rs.4410.80 crore) of all R&D Units viz. BARC, IGCAR, AERB, AM D, DCSEM, GSO, RRCAT and  
VECC. Grants to Autonomous Bodies and Aided Institute s (Rs.3240.40  crore) and Contribution to 
IAEA & Anunet charges (Rs.62.43 crores). As the employee strength in R&D units is 65% of the total 
staff strength of the Department, the establishment expenditure are commensurately on the higher side. 
Further, O&M expenditure of the  running Pl ants/R&D Reactors is also booked under  the Revenue 
Division. The allocations under the Capital  Division of R&D Sector are towards the ongoing  R&D 
Projects of BARC, IGCAR, RRCAT, VECC, GSO, AERB, DAE, DCSEM, and AMD as  per the 
budgetary requirements. Hence, the allocations towards revenue expenditure  are more than  thrice of 
the Capital expenditure under R&D Division. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.4 The Committee observes and highlights the fact that even though India's rank is 6th in terms of 
numbers of nuclear power reactors being operated, we are still at number 11 and 14 when it comes to 
nuclear power produced and installed capacity respectively. This  is indicative of  the fact that the 
production capacity  per power plant is low. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to 
study the reasons for  this anomaly and also apprise the Commi ttee of  its findings. Further, the 

7 
 
Committee recommends that the  Department devices a  strategy to install higher production capacity 
power units so that the unit cost comes down and nuclear power becomes more affordable.    
                                                                                                                                           (Para 2.27 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.5 The small  size (200-220 MW) reactors were set up  in the early days of  the nuclear power 
programme in the country due to the limited capacity of the then existing regional electricity grids. 
Following the imposition of  international technology denial  and embargo regime in 1974, India placed 
thrust on achieving self-reliance in this high technology area. India mastered Pressurized Heavy Water 
Reactor (PHWR) technology,  evolved a standard 220 MW PHWR design and  setup a number of fully 
indigenous 220 MW reactors. With the evolution of the capacities of the Indian electricity  grids, a 540 
MW PHWR was designed in the 1980s and the first  540 MW PHWR commenced operation in 2005.  
Following the successful operation of the 540 MW size PHWRs, a larger  unit size - the indigenous 700 
MW standard design has been evolved and  the first  700 MW PHWR is  connected to  the grid, 
generating power.  Fifteen more reactors of 700MW size  PHWRs are under construction/pre-project 
activities, to be progressively commissioned  by 2031-32. These reactors will form the mainstay of the 
rapid expansion of  nuclear capacity in the  country in the near future. Large size reactors which were 
setup in some countries of the world in the 1980s and 1990s  could not be setup in India due to the 
technology denial  and embargo regime. However, with the fruition of international cooperation in 
nuclear energy and entering into of relevant agreements, large size reactors of 1000 MW capacity are 
being setup at Kudankulam in cooperation with Russian Federation . Discussions are also in progress 
with France and the USA to arrive  at project  proposals to  setup large size reactors at  Jaitapur, 
Maharashtra and Kovvada, Andhra Pradesh respectively. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.6 The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should take utmost care in ensuring 
proper utilization of  funds and that the Department should  take extra effort to ensure optimum 
utilization under the three heads 'BARC', 'IGCAR'  and 'Nuclear Fuel Complex'.             (Para 2.30 ibid) 
 
Action Taken

REVENUE GENERATION BY THE DEPARTMENT  
 
Recommendation/Observation

same trends is not seen in terms of percentage  profit (% of Gross budget). The Commi ttee is aware of

resources in terms of research, development and deployment and hence relationship between budget 
spent, revenue generated and profits earned may not be as linear as it is in the classical sense. The

REPORT 
 
 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the action taken by  
the Government  on the recommendations/observations of the Committee contained in its ‘Three 
Hundred Seventy Fourth Report’ on ‘Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the Department of 
Biotechnology’. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha on the 15 th March, 2023 and laid on the 
Table of Lok Sabha on the 20th March, 2023.  
2. Action Taken Note s (ATNs) ha ve been received from the Department of Biotechnology  in 
respect of all the 21 recommendations/observations contained in the ‘Three Hundred Seventy Fourth 
Report’. The replies of the Department of Biotechnology have been categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 
Para Nos. 2.15, 3.5, 3.6, 4.9, 4.10, 5.6 and 6.2. 
 Total recommendations – 07  
Chapter II:    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government’s replies: 
Para Nos. 2.4, 2.9, 2.19, 3.4, 4.3, 4.4, 4.8, 5.7, 6.6, 6.7, 6.8, 6.9, 7.4 and 7.5. 
 Total recommendations – 14   
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted by the Committee: ‘Nil’ 
Chapter IV:   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: ‘Nil’ 
 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters. 

2 
 
CHAPTER – I  
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022-23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2023-24. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.1 The Commi ttee recognises the important contributions of the Department of Biotechnology 
across crucial sectors and the need for an additional allocation of at least Rs. 350 crore, over and 
above to the allocation of Rs. 2683.86 crore in B.E. 2023 -24, to sustain its  key programmes. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may approach the Ministry of 
Finance/Department of Expenditure for seeking the requisite additional allocation of funds at the R.E. 
stage. The Committee further recommends that the D epartment should strive for greater revenue 
generation in the long term, especially through equity stake in incubated startups and through 
commercialization of products developed by the Department, and explore options to facilitate 
financing of some of its important projects and schemes through them.   (Para 2.15 of the 374th Report)  
Action Taken 
 
1.2 Department is thankful to the Committee for recognizing the important contributions of the 
Department across crucial sectors. As recommended by the Committee , the Department depending on 
the pace of expenditure may request for an additional allocation at the R.E. stage.   
1.3 With respect to revenue generation, it is submitted that the Department through its Public 
Sector Undertaking Biotechnology Industry Res earch Assistance Council (BIRAC) provides equity 
based funding to startups.  BIRAC has supported more than 140 startups through equity support under 
SEED and LEAP schemes. Out of these startups, more than 60% have raised follow on funding 
amounting to more  than INR 1000 Cr. There is an increasing number of startups getting investments 
from Angels, High Net Worth Individuals (HNIs), and early -stage Venture Capitals (VCs) contributing 
to the growth story of biotech industry. 
 
BIOTECHNOLOGY RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT – MAJOR INITIATIVES 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.4 The Committee is of the considered view that setting of realistic and achievable targets, both 
short term and long term, as well as existence of a robust monitoring mechanism to monitor and review 
the progress of ongoing schemes and programmes, are extremely crucial. The Committee recommends 
that the Department of Biotechnology should ensure an effective monitoring and periodic review of all 
its schemes and programmes and take corrective measures, wh erever required, so that they proceed as 
per schedule.                    (Para 3.5 ibid) 

3 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.5 The Committee’s suggestion is well appreciated. It is submitted that the Department’s schemes 
and programmes undergoes both mid -term review during the finance commission period as suggested 
by DoE amd NITI Aayog. Further, the programs are being reviewed time to time by the respective 
expert committees. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.6 The Committee recommends more collaboration with DARE/ICAR to acc elerate the R&D in 
agriculture, especially plant genomes, so that more productive, drought and flood resistant varieties of 
various important crops can be developed in the next 3-5 years.              (Para 3.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.7 The recommendations of the Committee have been noted. It is submitted that the Department is 
already collaborating with ICAR/NARs/SAU through its mission programmes and projects. In 
collaboration with ICAR institutions/SAU’s network projects are being funded towards development of 
drought and flood resistant varieties. 
 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.8 While noting the not -so-encouraging fluctuations in figures of 2020 -21 and 2021 -22, the 
Committee is delighted to observe that, during 2022 -23, the Department has been able achieve its 
targets against almost all of the indicators, except just three parameters i.e., number of publications, 
number of genomes sequenced under Genome India and number of NE -specific germplasm collected. 
The Committee, in particular, takes note of the achievements in respect of the number of patents 
filed/granted and products/technologies developed, transferred or commercialized, as these are an 
acknowledgement of the fact that expenditure on research and development translate into benefits for 
wider industry and society as a whole. At the same time, the Committee underlines the importance for 
the Department to perform much better in parameters such as number of acclaimed publications and 
the number of genomes sequenced.                 (Para 4.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.9 The concern of the Committee for the parameters where achievement is low has been noted. 
The Department will take requisite steps for achieving the targets during in FY 2023-24. 
 

4 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.10 The Committee recommends that the Department should strive hard to continue to sustain this 
momentum, intensify its R&D activities along with initiatives towards development of human resources 
and capacity building during 2023 -24, and significantly focus the expansion of the overall network in 
Tier II and Tier III cities going forward.              (Para 4.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.11 The suggestions of the C ommittee are well noted by the Department.  It is submitted that 
Department has already taken several steps to increase the representation of students from the Tier II 
and Tier III cities in all HRD programs. The Program Division has developed data analytics on number 
of applications received from Tier II and Tier III cities and the same is shared with expert committee in 
order to sensitize them towards the needs/challenges of candidates from Tier II /III cities. Additionally, 
the Department has also been conducting outreach programmes in remote and under -represented 
regions to rais e awareness about various schemes of the Department in order to improve the 
participation of students and researchers from under-represented cities, states and regions. 
 
AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.12 The Committee acknowledges  the immense contribution of the autonomous institutions and 
PSUs under the Department of Biotechnology in the advancement of biotechnology sector in the 
country and their crucial role in the implementation of the various policies and programmes of the 
Department towards fostering a culture of innovation and research, support and promotion of 
entrepreneurship, commercialization of biotechnological advancements, etc.           (Para 5.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13 Department gratefully acknowledges the observat ion of the Committee. It is submitted that the 
approved Cabinet Note for the r ationalization of DBT AIs has a para on retaining the distinct research 
mandates of the various institutes. All efforts are being made to build synergy through mutual 
collaboration for developing, joint, integrated research programs fulfilling national missions.  The 
institutes will also coordinate with each other in the proposed new education programs being developed 
on the lines of NEP. 
 
SUPPORT TO STARTUPS AND SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SMES) 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.14 The Committee observes with appreciation the continuous upward trend in the number of 
startups and SMEs being supported over the years. In particular, it is pleased to note that for 2022 -23, 
the number of startups and SMEs supported by the Department (i.e, 3251) is nearly four times the 
annual target (i.e, 850). Interestingly, however, for the same period, the target in respect of number of 

5 
 
startups getting follow-up funding has not been met. The Committ ee hopes that this target will be met 
within the remaining quarter of the current financial year.              (Para 6.2 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.15 Department gratefully acknowledges the observation of the Committee. Following points with 
respect to follow on funding are submitted: 
 Follow on funding for biotech startup beneficiaries of BIRAC is influenced with market 
dynamics. 
 35 startups received INR 1878 Cr. as follow on funding in 2022-23. 
 This is lower in terms of number of startups but higher against the quantum of funds received in 
previous year 2021-22 i. e., INR 1028 Cr.

TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022-23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2023-24. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.1 The Committee notes the reasons cited by the Department for the reduction of allocation for the 
year 2022-23 at R.E stage. The Committee also not es that the allocation to the Department in B.E. 
2023-24 has been marginally increased by around 4 per cent over B.E. 2022 -23, which will be utilized 
for implementation of ongoing programmes and also for initiation of new activities. 
          (Para 2.4 of the 374th Report) 
Action Taken 
 
2.2 Department gratefully acknowledges that the Committee accepted the reply furnished by the 
Department. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.3 The Committee expresses concern over the sub -optimal utilization of funds by the D epartment, 
particularly with respect to the two Central Sector Schemes - ‘Biotechnology Research & 
Development’ and ‘Industrial and Entrepreneurship Development’, and urges the Department to fully 
utilize the funds by the end of the financial year. The Com mittee also recommends that the Department 
should take appropriate measures to ensure optimal utilization of the funds allocated to it in B.E. 2023-
24.                               (Para 2.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.4 The Department is also concerned about t he sub-optimal utilization of funds in FY2022 -23. As 
a matter of fact, in FY 2022-23, the Department could spend more than 95 % of allocation with respect 
to RE 2022 -23 of the  two Central Sector Schemes - ‘Biotechnology Research & Development’ and 
‘Industrial and Entrepreneurship Development’ 
2.5 The revised process flow of funds is still a major roadblock like  in FY2022-23 and the 
Department is currently working with D/o Expenditure to streamline the utilization of funds optimally. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.6 The Committee is of the considered opinion that analysing trends in the budgetary allocations 
over the years, the factors for variations and its implications etc., are important to fully gauge the 
performance of the Department, both in terms of a chieving its financial and physical targets. The 
Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department of Biotechnology to undertake a detailed 

7 
 
analysis of its budgetary allocation and utilization trends for the last ten years at least, for a healthy 
assessment of its overall performance. In addition, the Department should indicate the breakup of 
expenditure towards various fields for eg. health, agriculture, energy and so on.         (Para 2.19 ibid) 
Action Taken

BIOTECHNOLOGY RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT – MAJOR INITIATIVES 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.9 The Committee appreciates the achievements of the Department under the various

HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.11 The Committee observes from the above table that achievement of physica l targets in respect of 
Postgraduate Teaching Programme, DBT -JRF Programme and Tata Innovation Fellowship are 
satisfactory. However, in case of DBT -Research Associateship and Bhan Young Researchers 
Fellowship, the Department has not been able to achieve ev en half of its physical targets for the year. 
Further, the Committee is constrained to note that, in case of at least three of its fellowship 
programmes, selection of candidates is still under process even at the last quarter of the financial year, 
which d oes not augur well to achieve the objective of developing human capit al for research and 
innovation.                    (Para 4.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.12 It is submitted that Post -doctoral fellowships such as, DBT -RA and MK Bhan fellowship are 
provided on ly to meritorious scholars who submit high quality research proposals based on 
scientifically sound hypothesis and methodology. These applications are screened and evaluated by the 
expert committee, consisting of eminent scientists from all major areas of Biotechnology. The 
Department supports all the cases of fellowship as recommended by the expert committee. For the lack 
of sufficient number of high -quality proposals, sometimes, the expert committee does not recommend 
as many cases as available number of fellowships resulting in some vacancies. 
2.13 It is further clarified that these are not rigid physical targets but the maximum number of 
fellowships available. The actual number of fellowships supported by the Department will depend upon 
the number of applications recommended by the expert committee after rigorous evaluation keeping in 
mind their previous research experience, scientific quality, methodology and novelty etc.  
2.14 It is further submitted that delay in selection of fellows in some schemes is  due to the fact that 
many of the schemes such as, Ramalingaswami Re -entry fellowship, Har -Gobind Khorana IYBF and 
DBT-BioCare have undergone significant reviews which includes several rounds of deliberations. 
These are time-consuming exercises which somet imes led to delay in selection process and the 
Department strives to improve the cycle period. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.15 The Committee strongly recommends that the Department should review its existing mechanism 
for monitoring the progress of its  programmes and take appropriate measures to ensure no delay 
whatsoever in the selection of fellows and the disbursement of fellowships.            (Para 4.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.16 The recommendation by the C ommittee is well noted. As elaborated in the l ast section, the 
delay in selection of fellows in few schemes was due to the review of the program by expert 
committee. Additionally, the disbursement of fellowships during the last financial year was delayed 
due to implementation of a revised flow of fund  through Zero Balance Subsidiary Account (ZBSA) by 

9 
 
Ministry of Finance, which mandated that each institution has to open a ZBSA account to receive any 
grant w.e.f 1st April, 2022 onwards. There was further delay  on the part of institutions to provide their  
banking details to the Department. However, from next year the system is likely to be stabilized and 
delays are expected to be minimized. 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.17 The Committee is pleased to note that, in as many as half of the above indicators,  the 
Department has been able to consistently achieve its targets during the last three years which include 
the number of patents filed/granted, products or technologies developed/transferred/commercialized, 
Centres of Excellence (CoEs) and Bioinformatics Centres supported, Databases/softwares developed, 
number of women and tribal farmers beneficiaries, number of successful bio -entrepreneurs developed 
and QA/QC Facilities set up in NER. The Committee applauds the work done and progress achieved by 
the Department against these indicators.                (Para 4.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.18 The Department thankfully acknowledges the observation of Committee.

Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.19 The Committee takes note of the restructurin g process being brought in place for streamlining 
these autonomous institutions and expresses its best wishes for realizing the objectives of this policy 
reform. At the same time, the Committee recommends that, as informed by the Department, the distinct 
research mandates of these institutions are maintained and their capacities are not negatively 
impacted, but rather leveraged through the inter -disciplinary interactions and research synergies thus 
created. The Committee hopes that this becomes an important  step towards catapulting the country to 
the position of a global leader in the field of biotechnology.              (Para 5.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.20 Department gratefully acknowledges the observation of the Committee. It is submitted that the 
approved Cabinet Note for the rationalization of DBT AIS has a para on retaining the distinct research 
mandates of the various institutes. All efforts are being made to build synergy through mutual 
collaboration for developing, joint, integrated research programs fu lfilling national missions. The 
institutes will also coordinate with each other in the proposed new education programs being developed 
on the lines of NEP. 
 
SUPPORT TO STARTUPS AND SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SMES) 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.21 The Committee commends the work being done by BIRAC towards promoting entrepreneurship 
by empowering start-ups and SMEs in the country.               (Para 6.6 ibid) 

10 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.22 Department gratefully acknowledges the appreciation of the Committee. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.23 The Committee is of the firm belief that the development of an entrepreneurial ecosystem is 
critical for any country's economic growth and prosperity, for which support to start -ups and SMEs is 
a must. The Committee, therefore , recommends that the Department should make concerted efforts 
towards fostering a thriving ecosystem of entrepreneurship in the country. The Department should 
strive towards better collaboration with other stakeholders to create a supportive policy enviro nment, 
build a culture of innovation, provide access to funding, develop infrastructure to support new 
ventures/startups/SMEs, collaborate with other incubation and mentorship programmes of the 
government etc., all of which will go a long way in achieving the objective of fostering a thriving 
ecosystem of entrepreneurship in the country.               (Para 6.7 ibid)  
Action Taken 
 
2.24 Biotech sector is a knowledge -based niche domain that has distinct requirements of 
infrastructure, equipment, technical expertise, regulatory compliance requirements, etc. The concerned 
industry base, Angels/VCs investor pool are also domain centric rather than generic. Therefore, only 
6300+ biotech startups are there out of 95,000+ startups in the country. 
2.25 BIRAC’s model, best practices are shared and followed by peer ministries/departments at both 
Centre and State level. Duplication of efforts is avoided by having representation of officials in the 
monitoring and selection committees. BIRAC has an active engagement with all relevant National 
Mission programs. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.26 The Committee especially recommends that the Department should ensure equitable 
distribution of resources/initiatives across the country, so that the benefits of its programmes aim ed at 
supporting start-ups and SMEs can reach the under-served regions of the country as well. 
          (Para 6.8 ibid)  
Action Taken 
 
2.27 Biotechnology Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) under the BIG programme has been 
instrumental in spurring the cre ation of biotech startups. More than 800 innovative ideas have been 
supported out of 10,000 applications received from across the country. The scheme has been able to 
aspire entrepreneurs across the country. The spread of aspirants covers 550+ cities and 3 8 aspirational 
districts pan India. More than 50% of the applications under BIG are from Tier 2 and 3 cities. 
2.28 BioNEST Bioincubation centres setting up is an ongoing activity. Currently, 75 incubation 
centres are located in 21 States/UTs. In the last f ew years, the numbers of new B ioincubation centres 
seeded in the Tier 2/3 cities have also increased significantly. 

11 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.29 The Committee recommends that the Department must carry out a detailed analysis on the 
investment in R&D over the last 10 years, the financial value created by the products, the potential 
revenue generated and the multiplier effect in the market.              (Para 6.9 ibid)  
Action Taken 
 
2.30 The recommendations of the Committee have been noted. Make -In-India Cell at Biotechnology 
Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) has been mapping India’s BioEconomy since 2018 and 
publishes a professional India BioEconomy Report (IBER). This has monitored the growth from 
$44.47 Bn in 2017 to $93+ Bn in 2022. The I ndia Bioeconomy Report helps to determine the growth 
trajectory, and importantly set the target for India’s bioeconomy for 2025 as $150 Bn; for 2030 as $300 
Bn and 2047 as $3 trillion USD. 
 
 
HUMAN GENETICS & GENOME ANALYSIS 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
 
2.31 The Committee recognizes the immense potential that genetic research and gene therapy hold 
for altering the treatment paradigm of many genetic diseases, including those that are currently 
incurable. However, as it is a relatively new field of medical science, the many challenges still 
associated with it are not lost on the Committee. Despite the existing challenges, such as issues 
regarding delivery methods, safety and effectiveness concerns, potential long -term effects of genetic 
modification, high costs of developing and administering the therapy making it inaccessible to masses, 
etc., the potential benefits are far too significant to ignore and, therefore, it is highly essential to 
prioritize research in the area.                (Para 7.4 ibid) 
                 
Action Taken 
 
2.32 The Department has been facilitating research in this domain to make cell and gene therapy 
affordable. Since past one decade, the Department supported gene therapy programme, which led to the 
first-in-human gene therapy phase-I clinical trial for Hemophilia A patients.  Proof -of-concept studies 
have also been completed for development of novel lentiviral vectors which can be employed for gene 
addition (beta or gamma globin genes); gene modulation (BCL11A gene); and gene editin g approaches 
using CRISPR-Cas9 and base editing technologies. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.33 The Committee appreciates the ongoing efforts of scientists and researchers in this field. The 
Committee recommends the Department to undertake deeper researc h in collaboration with other 
institutes under the government and private sector, explore avenues for using latest emerging 
technologies including Artificial Intelligence (AI), in order to fully explore the untapped potential of 
genetic research. The Commi ttee also recommends that adequate funds be earmarked for the purpose, 
so that financial constraints do not hinder the much-needed R&D. The Committee would also like to be 
kept informed about the progress made by the Department in this regard.            (Para 7.5 ibid) 

12 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.34 Department of Biotechnology under the Competitive Research Grant program considered 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the promising niche area and is supporting projects for application 
of AI in healthcare sector in t he areas of Cancer, Tuberculosis and Pulmonary Diseases, Diabetes & 
Cardiovascular Diseases, Ophthalmological Diseases, Neurological Disorders and Drug Development.

REPORT 
 
 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the action taken by  
the Government  on the recommendations/observations of the  Committee contained in its ‘Three 
Hundred Seventy Fifth Report’ on ‘Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research (DSIR)’ . The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha on the 15 th March, 2023 and 
laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 20th March, 2023.  
2. Action Taken Note s (ATNs) ha ve been received from the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research (DSIR) in respect of  all the 15 recommendations/observations contained in the 
‘Three Hundred Seventy Fifth Report’ . The r eplies of the Department of Scientific and Industrial 
Research have been categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 
Para Nos., 2.8, 4.5, 5.7, 5.9, 5.11, 6.5 and 7.5  
 Total recommendations – 07  
Chapter II:    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government’s replies: 
Para Nos. 2.3, 2.9, 3.5, 4.4, 5.5, 5.6 and 7.4  
 Total recommendations – 07   
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted by the Committee: ‘Nil’ 
Chapter IV:   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited:  
Para No. 3.6  
 Total recommendation- 01 
 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022 -23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR 2023-24. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.1 The Committee finds merit in the Department’s request for an additional budgetary allocation 
to the tune of ₹1048.26 crore, over and above the provision made in B.E. 2023 -24. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department may seek the requisite additional allocation from the 
Ministry of Finance at the R.E. stage. Further, the Committee recommends that,  apart from re -
appropriation of CSIR internal resources to supplement CSIR -driven projects, the Department should 
explore options for more collaborations with other Departments/Ministries as well as the private 
sector, through enhanced outreach and dissemi nation of information about i ts activities and 
achievements.                  (Para 2.8 of the 375th Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.2 Department thankfully acknowledges the Committee’s recognition towards need for an 
additional allocation to the tune of ₹1048.26 crore, over and above the provision made in B.E. 2023-24. 
As per recommendations of the Committee, Department will seek additional funds from the Ministry of 
Finance at the R.E. stage to sustain its key programmes/initiatives. 
1.3 Department will also follow the directions of the Committee regarding exploring options for 
more collaborations with other Departments/Ministries as well as the private sector through enhanced 
outreach and dissemination of information about its activities and achievements . Department has 
already started stakeholder discussions with Industry to take their views on increasing collaboration 
with them in the areas of support to in -house R&D, more Technology Transfers & Commercialization, 
and their suggestions to create a vibrant R&D ecosystem in the c ountry.  Additionally, Department 
would also like to submit that: 
 CSIR Labs have been engaged in attracting funds from other available sources including efforts 
have been made for obtaining contributions under Corporate Social Resp onsibility (CSR) f rom 
eligible Indian Corporates/Industries for undertaking R&D projects for promotion of SDGs; 
 CSIR Labs have been interacting with stakeholder Ministries such as MoEF & CC etc. to make 
them aware of capabilities of CSIR while undertaking projects in areas of mutual interest. CSIR 
Labs are also engaged with Industries and undertakes R&D projects of global 
competitiveness/national relevance; and  
 CSIR Labs have been interacting with many Industries from India and abroad to promote CSIR 
knowledge base. Many such industries are financially supporting CSIR R&D projects f or 
development of technologies/products of their interest. 

3 
 
 
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR) 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.4 The Committee is of the view that , although many new initiatives are being undertaken, a lot 
more needs to be done in order to successfully meet the challenges of the future. The Committee 
recommends that the Department should undertake meaningful initiatives to establish strong 
foundations to enable the country to become a global leader in scientific research and development. 
While sufficient allocation of funds is an obvious pre -requisite to effectively pursue this goal, the 
Committee feels that it is essential to let more private sector /industries on board to play a greater role 
in contributing to R&D in the country. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that more 
representatives of industries/companies should be motivated to partake in this endeavour, especially by 
way of capital investments.                  (Para 4.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.5 Department sincerely acknowle dges the C ommittee’s recommendations and will follow the 
directions of the Committee. The Department has been constantly working to promote in -house R&D 
activities of t he industry through Recognition/Registration, Certification of R&D Expenditure of the 
industry for weighted tax deductions under Section 35 (2AB) of IT Act 1961 among others. It is further 
submitted that the Department understands the requirement of transl ational R&D in terms of 
collaboration with relevant industries and getting financial support for a certain portion of R&D 
expenditure from them. CSIR has been constantly working towards this goal and is taking up a lot of 
initiatives such as NMITLI, One Week One Lab, CSIR Societal Portal, iConnect, etc. Though, with 
these efforts, there has been a great response from the industrial fraternity. However, CSIR will 
continue to explore all possible dimensions to convert the industry interests to capital investm ent in 
CSIR R&D works. Department has tasked IIM Calcutta to conduct a detailed study/evaluation of the 
ongoing Fiscal Incentive Scheme of the Department and to explore the possibility of improvement of 
industrial R&D ecosystem in the country under the aeg is of DSIR. Department has also started 
stakeholder discussions on R&D (with various industrial sectors) to take their feedback and 
suggestions on the required new initiatives for strengthening of scientific and industrial research in the 
country to make it a global leader. 
 
CAPACITY BUILDING AND HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT OF CSIR 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.6 Further, the Committee takes note of the status of CSIR award schemes, which are yet to be 
declared even at the last quarter of the current finan cial year, and recommends that appropriate and 
expeditious action may be taken to complete the process.              (Para 5.7 ibid) 
 

4 
 
Action Taken 
1.7 Department will follow the directions/recommendations of the Committee. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.8 The Committee observes that the figures for patent applications filed and granted and papers 
published during 2022 -23, are lower than those of the preceding year. As these are key indicators of 
the scientific and technological advancements of a country,  the Committee exhorts CSIR to intensify its 
efforts towards improving these numbers during 2023-24.              (Para 5.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.9 Department will follow the directions of the Committee. It is humbly submitted that CSIR is the 
only R&D orga nization filing, prosecuting and maintaining its patents In -house in India. CSIR 
centrally as well as at lab level is increasing awaren ess through webinars/workshops/ seminars related 
to importance of filing of patents, design, copyrights and other forms of  IP. CSIR is having dedicated 
IP co-ordinators in each of its laboratories helping scientists in securing of IP. IP awareness programs 
are also conducted at the lab level. CSIR through all these interventions is trying to improve its number 
of filings not only in patents but also in other forms of IP. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.10 The Committee applauds the efforts made by CSIR for revenue generation, and recommends the 
Council to set targets in this regard and, accordingly, explore more avenues for h igher revenue 
generation during the next financial year.              (Para 5.11 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.11 Department thankfully acknowledges the Committee’s recognition and appreciation towards 
efforts made by CSIR for revenue generation. Department will f ollow the recommendations of the 
Committee. 
 
CSIR MISSION MODE PROJECT ON ‘WASTE TO WEALTH’ 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.12 The Committee highly commends the efforts of the Department in the field of waste 
management and, in particular, is pleased to le arn about the technologies developed for converting 
various wastes to wealth. Taking cognizance of the need for a well coordinated waste management 
strategy in the country for various types of wastes, the Committee recommends that the Department 
should make concerted efforts to ensure that the Mission project on waste to wealth is implemented 
with all sincerity and in a holistic manner. Apart from sufficient budgetary allocations towards the 
project, efforts should be made to involve other stakeholders as w ell. Further, thrust should be given to 
research and development of more waste -to-wealth technologies including for electronic wastes – the 
management of which is becoming an important issue for the country.            (Para 6.5 ibid) 

5 
 
 
Action Taken 
1.13 Department thankfully acknowledges the Committee’s recognition and appreciation of 
Department’s efforts and contribution in the field of waste management.  Department will fol low the 
recommendations of the C ommittee. It is humbly submitted that a new waste -to-wealth mission is 
under formulation by CSIR and will be launched in the FY 2023 -24 to address a variety of industrial 
and other important waste management issues, including fossil fuel waste, biotic waste, metallic waste, 
non-metallic waste, and electronic waste. 
 
MISSION PROJECT ON ACTIVE PHARMACEUTICAL INGREDIENTS (APIs) 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.14 The Committee recommends that specific targets, both short term and long term, should be set 
for reducing the dependence on imported raw materials fro m around 80 per cent at present, to 30 or 
40 per cent in the next five years. To achieve this, the Committee recommends that the proposed 
Mission project should be dovetailed with the initiatives being undertaken in this area by other 
Ministries/Departments and the private sector, adequate funds should be earmarked for the purpose so 
that financial constrains do not hinder the much needed research work, and options should be explored 
for benefiting from latest emerging technologies such as Artificial Intell igence (AI), with the overall 
objective of achieving the desired outcomes within the shortest possible timeframe. The Committee 
would also like to be kept abreast of the progress made by the Department in this regard.  
          (Para 7.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.15 Department will follow the directions/recomm endations of the C ommittee. It is kindly 
submitted that CSIR has excellent expertise in organic synthesis, process chemistry and chemical 
engineering.  With this expertise, CSIR has developed cost -effective processes for various APIs and 
their intermediates. Such developed processes have been successfully transferred for few molecules 
like α -Lipoic acid, Azelaic Acid and Paracetamol to pharma companies for production and 
commercialization.  A pilot plant fo r paracetamol has been erected and commissioned in 2019 at NCL. 
Similarly, CSIR contributed in repurposing of drugs for COVID -19 towards affordable health care, 
which include Remdesivir, Molnupiravir, Umifenovir, Favipiravir. Favipiravir, transferred to M/s Cipla 
Ltd, Mumbai, is commercialized in the name of “CIPLENZA”.  It is also submitted that CSIR -IICT, 
Hyderabad has already established a kilo -lab facility, which shall soon be GMP accredited lab. To 
continue R&D in this important domain and direction, a  mission project on APIs is under formulation 
with primary aim to develop viable, non -infringing synthesis routes for selected APIs, based on their 
need for the country and broadly for cardiovascular, respiratory diseases and Diabetes.  CSIR efforts in  
the domain of APIs/KSMs aspire to serve the country by aiming at import substitution and contributing 
to ‘Make in India’ program.

CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE 
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022 -23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR 2023-24. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.1 The Committee appreciates the overall satisfactory financial performance of the Department. 
At the same time,  the Committee expresses concern over the sub -optimal utilisation in respect of the 
Central Sector Schemes/Projects, as over 50 per cent of the funds allocated under this remain to be 
utilized within the remaining quarter of the current financial year. The  Committee, therefore, urges the 
Department to ensure optimal utilization of funds during the course of the financial year. In future, 
periodic monitoring preferably on quarterly basis may be undertaken to facilitate the same. 
          (Para 2.3 of the 375th Report) 
Action Taken 
2.2 Department sincerely acknowledges the Committee’s recommendation and will follow the 
directions of the Committee. Also, as advised by the Committee, the Department will undertake 
periodic monitoring on quarterly basis to ensure  optimal utilization of funds during the course of 
the financial year. Department also thankfully acknowledges the Committee’s recognition towards 
satisfactory financial performance of CSIR.  Further, NRDC, a PSE with DSIR would also do the 
needful in ensuring complete utilization of funds for its respective schemes in the CFY 2023-24. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.3 The Committee underscores the criticality of timely completion of projects and, therefore, 
recommends the Department to undertake regular r eview of its financial and physical targets, in order 
to make a practical assessment of any further corrective measures which may be required to overcome 
the challenges in the way of achieving set targets.                        (Para 2.9 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.4 Department duly acknowledges the observation and concern of the Committee. Department 
would like to submit that constant monitoring/review is being made in DSIR & CSIR for the ongoing 
projects against their financial and physical targets. 
2.5 It is humbly submitted that CSIR has devised a strong monitoring mechanism for its project/s 
which is as given below:  
 The project is technically evaluated by the monitoring committee which comprises domain experts 
and evaluates the projects half -yearly and also  by the Mission/Theme Director who monitors the 
project regularly.   

7 
 
 Further, to evaluate the financials of the project there is both an internal CSIR audit and a CAG 
audit; and  
 In addition to this, the coordinating lab Director reviews and monitors the p rogress on monthly 
basis and all the administrative bottlenecks faced by the project are reviewed and handled weekly 
during the Lab Strategic Group (LSG) Meeting. 
2.6 Projects supported by NRDC are also regularly reviewed and adequate assessment is made to  
ensure timely completion and in achieving set targets and milestones.  
 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES/PROJECTS 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.7 The Committee s takes note of the important initiatives undertaken through the umbrella 
schemes of the Department, and expresses its appreciation for the significant work being done through 
them. However, given the abysmal actual utilization of funds during 2022 -23 under these schemes, as 
has been pointed out at para 2.3, the Committee is constrained to observe that a be tter monitoring 
mechanism needs to be put in place to ensure an effective check on its physical and financial 
performance. Concomitantly, the Department should also indicate and quantify, to the extent possible, 
physical targets it aspires to achieve across all the schemes/sub-schemes.            (Para 3.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.8 Department appreciates the observation of the Committee regarding fixing of targets and for 
setting up a monitoring framework. In this regard, it is informed that targets are fixed  as per the 
approved Standing Finance Committee. In addition  to this, the targets and the achievements against 
each of these targets is monitored by Niti Aayog through the Output Outcome Monitoring framework 
office. The physical targets and the a chievements in all the schemes/ sub-schemes is also monitored by 
the concerned officer heading the program divisions in the Department. CSIR & NRDC have also set 
targets for the activities to be carried out under the schemes for the year 2023 -24 and the achievement 
in terms of physical and financial performance is regularly monitored. 
 
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR) 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.9 The Committee applauds the contribution of the Department through CSIR and its network of 
laboratories in the pursuit of excellence across all sectors of scientific research and development. The 
Committee also notes that these endeavours of CSIR are well -aligned to the economic, industrial and 
social priorities of the nation, as exemplified by their conv ergence with the Government's Mission 
Programmes such as Atma Nirbhar Bharat, Make in India, Startup India, Swachh Bharat, focus on 
green growth, etc.                   (Para 4.4 ibid) 
 

8 
 
Action Taken 
2.10 Department thankfully acknowledges the Committee’s r ecognition and appreciation towards 
Department’s contribution through CSIR and its network of laboratories in the pursuit of excellence 
across all sectors of scientific research and development including their convergence with the 
Government’s Mission Programmes. 
 
CAPACITY BUILDING AND HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT OF CSIR 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.11 Recognizing the criticality of human capacity building and development, the Committee 
appreciates the work being done by the CSIR towards this end. Howeve r, the Committee notes that the 
scholarships/fellowships are provided to students mostly at higher levels. Options may, therefore, be 
explored for instituting scholarships/fellowships at lower/entry levels too, such as graduation or even 
senior secondary level, in order to encourage the youth of the country to pursue science studies. 
(Para 5.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.12 It is humbly apprised to the Committee that Department of Science and Technology, Ministry 
of Science and Technology under its INSPIRE Scheme  provides scholarship to schools stude nts for 
higher studies. Further, the Department of Higher Education instituted “NSP Central Sector Scheme of 
Scholarship for college and university students” for pursuing graduation, BE/B.Tech and PG.   
2.13 The sugges tion of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee for institutin g 
scholarships/fellowships by CSIR at lower /entry levels too, such as graduation or even senior 
secondary level has been noted. Department will take the suitable needful actions if budgetary 
allocations are provided by the Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure to meet the expenses 
on such scholarships. 
2.14 It is also kindly submitted that graduates in Science and Engineering are eligible for JRF 
through the CSIR -UGC National Eligibility Test (NET). Apart from JRF -NET, CSIR also offer s JRF 
fellowship to engineering and pharmacy graduates under its JRF-GATE scheme. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.15 The Committee is of the considered opinion that, apart from awarding some 
fellowships/scholarships, there is a need to nurture and groom young students to become future 
scientists. CSIR, with its vast chain of scientific labs and strong team of scientists, can play a major 
role in this direction. The Committee, therefore, recomm ends that the Department should also work 
towards introducing various policies and programmes to attract, harness and retain the youth in the 
field of science.                   (Para 5.6 ibid) 
 
 
 

9 
 
Action Taken 
2.16 It is kindly submitted that CSIR has been  engaged in connecting school students with scientists 
through its “Jigyasa” (student -scientist connect) program since 2017. The programme envisages 
opening up the national scientific facilities to school children, enabling CSIR scientific knowledge base 
and facility to be utilized by school children to develop ‘Scientific Temper’ in the young minds thereby 
attracting school children towards science. The Jigyasa program is being implemented through CSIR 
laboratories wherein more than 5,25,000 students and m ore than 45,000 teachers across the country 
have benefitted, directly since 2017. CSIR has signed MoU with Kendriya Vidyala Sangathan, 
Navodaya Vidyalaya Samithi, NITI Aayog, Karnataka Science & Technology Agency, Chief 
Development Officer Bulandshahr, Ind ian Institute of Technology -Bombay, National Council of 
Science Museums (NCSM) for collaboration in Scientist -Student connect under “Jigyasa” platform of 
scientific social responsibility. 
2.17 CSIR has also developed and launched a Virtual Lab Platform und er Jigyasa.  With the launch 
of Virtual Lab Platform, CSIR had organized Bootcamps and virtual National Level Scientific 
Creativity competitions. 15 bootcamps were organised that had an outreach of more than 20,000 
students. Prize awards to the top 75 cont ents created in comics, science fiction, infographics, videos, 
app development and animation were provi ded by Hon’ble Minister of S&T.  Moving ahead, Jigyasa 
has also developed mobile app for better linkage of students with scientists. 
 
MISSION PROJECT ON ACTIVE PHARMACEUTICAL INGREDIENTS (APIs) 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.18 The Committee is fully aware of current state of huge dependence of the Indian Pharmaceutical 
industry on import of majority of raw materials used in the pharmaceutical industry. T he Committee, 
therefore, expresses its wholehearted support towards CSIR’s proposed Mission Project on APIs, and 
wishes the Department a speedy progress in this direction.              (Para 7.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.19 Department thankfully acknowledges t he Committee’s recognition and support for 
Department’s proposed Mission project on APIs. These recognitions will fuel the on -going R&D 
activities on APIs to get great momentum and result in new technological breakthroughs.

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the action taken by  
the Government  on the recommendations/observations of the Committee contained in its ‘Three 
Hundred Seventy Sixth Report’ on ‘Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the Department of Science and 
Technology’. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha on the 15 th March, 2023 and laid on the Table 
of Lok Sabha on the 20th March, 2023.  
2. Action Taken Note s (ATNs) ha ve been received from the Department of Science and 
Technology in respect of  all the 10 recommendations/observations contained in the ‘Three Hundred 
Seventy Sixth Report’. The r eplies of the Department of Science and  Technology have been 
categorized as follows:-  
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 
Para Nos. 2.4, 2.12 and 7.7 
 Total recommendations – 03  
 
Chapter II:    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee do es not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government’s replies: 
Para Nos. 2.8, 2.17, 3.2, 4.4, 4.5 and 6.4 
 Total recommendations – 06   
 
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government 
have not been accepted by the Committee:  
Para No. 5.5 
Total recommendations – 01  
 
Chapter IV:   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: ‘Nil’ 
 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters. 

2 
 
CHAPTER – I  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022 -23 (BE, RE & ACTUAL 
EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2023-24. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.1 The Committe e duly takes note of the reason cited by the Department regarding the under -
utilization of the budgetary allocations, and the adverse affect of introduction of the new payment 
system on implementation of its various activities/projects, as also achievement  of their physical and 
financial targets. However, the Committee is constrained to observe that the ground cited by the 
Department is primarily administrative and procedural in nature. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends that the matter should be  addressed with utmost urgency and the system streamlined at 
the earliest, so that no further negative impact percolates to the next financial year.  
          (Para 2.4 of the 376th Report)  
Action Taken 
1.2 The issues r elated to new payment system have  already been sorted out. Further, despite the 
adverse effect of introduction and implementation of the new payment system, Department of Science 
and Technology was able to spend  ₹ 4744.78 crore against the RE of  ₹ 4907.17 crore, which is 
96.69% of RE for FY 2022 -23, by taking various proactive initiatives and concerted monitoring of 
expenditure. However, the recommendations of Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.3 The Committee notes the overall increase in the budgetary all ocation of the Department for the 
financial year 2023 -24, and urges the Department to ensure optimal utilization of funds during this 
period. To achieve this, the Committee recommends that periodic monitoring of the progress w.r.t 
achievement of targets may be made at least on a quarterly basis.           (Para 2.12 ibid)  
Action Taken 
1.4 On basis of recommendation of the Committee, the Department has already prepared quarterly 
plan for regular and continuous monitoring for optimal utilization of allocated  funds and to ensure 
achievement of targets and the same will be followed rigorously. 
 
NATIONAL RESEARCH FOUNDATION 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.5 The Committee takes due note of the visions, objectives and purpose of creation of the National 
Research Foundation. It believes that a centrally established NRF that transparently seeds, funds, and 
coordinates research across institutions in the country - in all disciplines, in an integrated manner, 

3 
 
with a special mandate to foster research and innovation in u niversities and colleges, including inter -
disciplinary research to provide practical solutions to societal, developmental, financial, techno -
economic challenges of the nation, is a much needed overarching mechanism. The Committee 
recommends that, in the pr ocess of implementing this programme, special consideration should be 
given towards under-funded as well as new and emerging areas of research, while also keeping under -
served regions of the country in mind.                (Para 7.7 ibid)  
Action Taken 
1.6 The National Research Foundation  (NRF) is currently under the process of approval and the 
above recommendations have been noted for compliance during implementation. 
 
 

4 
 
CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE 
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022 -23 (BE, RE & ACTUAL 
EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2023-24. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.1 The Committee observes that, in fact, the Departm ent has been allocated an additional amount 
of Rs. 800.25 crore over and above its demand for the year 2023-24. This amount is more than the bare 
minimum requirement (i.e, Rs.500 crore) projected by the Department, in the event of a reduction in 
the actual budgetary provision. In view thereof, the Committee feels that the Department should be in a 
comfortable position to sustain its key programmes and even take up additional projects during the 
year without seeking any further support to augment its budget.           (Para 2.8 of the 376th Report)  
Action Taken 
2.2 The Department of Science and Technology has proposed ₹ 7132.00 crore for FY 2023 -24 
wherein no budget was sought from National Research Foundation (NRF). In the allocated budget of 
₹7932.25 crore, there is provision of ₹ 2000.00 crore for National Resear ch Foundation which is 
proposed to be created during the current fiscal year. The rest of the allocation under BE, i.e., Rs. 
5932.25 for ongoing activities of the Department, is lesser than the BE projection of Rs.7132.0 crore. 
Considering the above, the D epartment will try to work to optimize its resources for the ongoing 
activities and may request for additional allocation as part of RE allocation for 2023-24. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.3 The Committee expresses the view that administrative and proce dural matters do not become 
major reasons for hampering the planned activities of the Department in the long run. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department should ensure due diligence in its management of 
expenditure to ensure optimal utilization for 2023-24 as well as achievement of set targets. Besides, the 
Committee desires that all efforts should be made during the year to compensate for the mediocre 
performance during the financial year 2022-23.              (Para 2.17 ibid)  
Action Taken 
2.4 The Department has taken necessary step to streamline the administrative and procedural issues 
and the same will not impact the performance of the Department in future to achieve the set targets. 
 
KEY ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT DURING 2022-23 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.5 The Committee notes the achievements of the Department across its various schemes and 
programmes during the year, and appreciates its varied contributions for furthering scientific and 

5 
 
technological progress of the country. Th e Committee desires that the Department should focus its 
resources on more projects and programmes which align with the national priorities. The Committee 
further desires that year-wise information/data pertaining to the targets and achievements in respect of 
each major head and the various programmes under them, should be maintained in a consolidated 
manner and updated whenever required, so as to enable a wholesome assessment of their performance 
across periods.                    (Para 3.2 ibid)  
Action Taken 
2.6 The Department has already initiated few steps towards optimizing its resources aligning with 
the national priorities. During recent years, the Department has introduced a new model of S&T 
equipment facility named SATHI, an independently operated facility accessible for all the stakeholders, 
including the industries and SMEs. Similarly, the VigyanJyoti programme has been initiated for 
empowering girl students in the underrepresented STEM areas. To deal with the COVID -19 pandemic, 
a dedicated programme called CAWACH was launched to support the entire value chain of innovations 
and start-ups that addresses COVID -19 challenges. The Department has been consolidating year -wise 
information/data pertaining to the targets and achievements under the programm es and shall put 
concerted efforts to strengthen the existing mechanism in the above regard. 
 
NATIONAL MISSION ON INTERDISCIPLINARY CYBER-PHYSICAL SYSTEMS (NM-ICPS)  
Recommendations/Observations 
2.7 The Committee underlines the physical achievements of the  Department under NM -ICPS in 
almost four years of its inception. Given the fact that the Mission has been implemented with a vision 
of five years and an outlay of Rs.3660 crore, the Committee hopes that the Department will continue its 
efforts in furthering the development of Technology, Entrepreneurship and Human Resources through 
this mission.                     (Para 4.4 ibid)  
Action Taken 
2.8 The Mission is continuing its efforts in furthering the development of Technologies, 
Technology Products, Entrepreneurship and Human Resource in the areas of Cyber Physical Systems.

innovation, and product/technology development, and equip them with the necessary expertise to be 
job-ready for the future. 
 
WOMEN IN SCIENCE AND ENGINEERING (WISE) 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.13 The Committee notes the efforts being made by the Department to promote women in the area 
of science and technology through its various women centric programmes. In order to make the 
programmes more effective, the Committee recommends that the Department should clearly quantify 

7 
 
its targets in respect of each programme. As the primary focus is on improving gender parity in S&T 
through various interventions, the Department should endeavour to maintain the same enrollment rate 
of graduation level, at the higher levels.                          (Para 6.4 ibid)
