RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE  
GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.1 Taking cognizance of the importance of human resource development and capacity building for 
a nation, the Committ ee commends the efforts of the Department towards this end. The Committee, 
however, feels that much more needs to be done, especially for a country like ours which is endowed 
with adequate human resource to be developed, trained, harnessed and empowered. T he Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department should set defined targets across all its programmes, in 
quantifiable terms to the extent possible, and steadfastly work towards achieving them. The Committee 
further recommends that a robust mechanis m should be put in place for monitoring the progress of 
each programme.                 (Para 5.5 of the 376th Report) 
Action Taken 
3.2 The Department has been implementing Human Resources Development programmes at 
various levels such as the MANAK programm e (targeting students from class VI -XI), INSPIRE 
scholarship for higher education (SHE) at undergraduate level, INSPIRE fellowship for doctoral 
students, SERB-NPDF supporting the Post-doctoral students and INSPIRE Faculty for young scientists 
to start their career. The Department is making sincere efforts to increase the beneficiary base under all 
the programmes. All the programmes including the human resource development programmes of the 
Department are being monitored through an Outcome Output Monitoring Framework (OOMF) devised 
by the NITI Aayog. Targets in quantifiable terms are being defined for all the programmes and their 
achievements are monitored quarterly which is accessible through online dashboard. 
 
Further Recommendations/Observations 
3.3 While taking note of the reply of the Depar tment of Science and Technology, the 
Committee desires that a more comprehensive response detailing the various HRD programmes 
of the Department, the targets defined for each programme and the status of achievement of the 
same, may be shared in detail with the Committee.  
3.4 Further, the Committee recommends that a more holistic approach  needs to be evolved 
w.r.t the HRD programmes  encompassing not only academic education but also skill 
development, vocational training and entrepreneurship, by duly recognizing the importance of 
addressing the broader range of skills and competencies required in toda y's rapidly changing job 
market. Enhancing the reach and accessibility of these programmes should also be prioritized, so 
that beneficiaries from all socio -economic backgrounds and regions of the country have equal 
access to them.

Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.1 The Committee makes note of the variation in budgetary allocations across key schemes of the 
Department and the reasons pertaining to disruption of the global supply chain. The Committee also 
makes note of the fact that Semi -Conductor Laboratory wh ich is responsible for design and 
development of crucial electronic components has been transferred to the Ministry of Electronics and 
Information Technology. The Committee highlights that a significant inventory of components used in 
satellites and launch vehicles are imported as they are not manufactured in India.  
        (Para 2.13 of the 377th Report) 
1.2 While the challenges to domestic manufacturing of electronic chipsets, solar panels, atomic 
clocks and other crucial components are varied, ranging f rom availability of raw material to expertise 
in design and high scale-cost effective and precise manufacturing, the Committee recommends that the 
Department should take necessary steps in maintaining an inventory of these crucial components and 
engineer the supply chain in such a manner that it remains immune to such geo-political hurdles, to the 
largest extent possible. Further, the Committee also recommends that steps be taken to achieve higher 
indigenization in production of some key components.                                                    (Para 2.14 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3 As recommended by the Committee, the Department shall ensure the inventory of key 
components/materials required for its on -going projects/programmes to mitigate the effects of 
disruptions in supply chain in future.  
 
1.4 The Department is pursuing Indigenis ation programs for critical technologies such as 
Travelling Wave Tube Amplifiers, Electronics packaging including LTCC (Low temperature co -fired 
ceramic) & HTCC (High temperatur e co -fired ceramic) package technology for RF, Optical, and 
Digital systems, ASICs (Application Specific Integrated Circuits), detectors. In addition, currently 
imported items are published in the Procurement Live Register  (PLR) portal of ISRO website to i nvite 
Expression of Interest (EoI) from Indian Industries for indigenous development. The indigenously 
developed atomic clock has been realized and flown in recent navigation satellite (NVS-01).

Action Taken 
2.2 The substantial reduction in RE 2022 -23 to Rs. 10,530.04 Crore from B.E. of Rs. 13,700 Crore 
is mainly attributable to programmatic realignment of satellite and launch vehicle programmes due to 
revised mandate of the Department, global supply chain issues, shortage in semiconductors and geo -

2.3 The allocations made in BE 2023 -24 is adequate to meet the committed liabilities and for

MAJOR ACHIEVEMENTS IN THE RECENT PAST 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.18 Considering the immense potential of downstream data applications across various fields of 
governance and public service delivery such as MG -NREGA, DBT, Survey and Monitoring of land, 
location based services, domestic navigation, disaster warning, etc. the Committee recommends that 
the Department collaborates with more stakeholders, service providers and data distribution platforms 
so that more people can benefit from data based service  delivery and also add to the revenue of the 
Department.                                                                                                                          (Para 3.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.19 Following steps have been taken by the Depar tment to ensure broad -based penetration of 
downstream services:  
(a) For greater interaction amongst various user departments, an inter-ministerial mechanism called 
Space Applications Management System (SAMS) has been established by Government, for identif ying 
the requirements of space based services, and to recommend necessary space technology interventions 
to ensure its maximal utilisation in the respective thematic domains. SAMS framework comprises of a 
Planning Committee (PC -SAMS) as its apex body and i s supported by ten theme -specific Standing 
Committees (SCs). PC -SAMS oversees the SAMS activities, provides policy guidelines and 
recommends suitable funding mechanism to realize space assets & associated ground segment, in line 
with the space sector reforms announced by the Government. 
(b) As per the Space Policy 2023, ISRO’s remote sensing data of spatial resolution >=5m is to be 
made accessible on free & open basis to all, while remote sensing data of resolution <5m is to be made 
available free of cost t o Government entities and at fair & transparent pricing to non -governmental 
users. ISRO has established a web -based data dissemination system called Bhoonidhi Geoportal for 
hassle-free dissemination of remote sensing data to the users. 
(c) Interaction with non-governmental entities and academia with reference to Earth Observation 
data utilization & applications is promoted through the IN-SPACe mechanism.  
(d) Capacity building of the stakeholders is also being carried out regularly, for enabling their 
significant involvement in the utilisation of space based inputs.  
(e) In order to provide PNT service to strategic users, Department of Space is working closely with 
the users for building robust space and ground segments and for ensuring comprehensive deploym ent 
in strategic user segment. 
(f) In transportation sector, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has mandated 
panic button and location tracking device in all public and commercial vehicles to ensure safety of 

10 
 
passengers and timely help during distress. NavIC has been identified as an essential PNT system for 
vehicle location tracking. Additionally, MoRTH is in consultation with the Department for establishing 
the overall framework of NavIC/GNSS-based tolling in the country. Indian Railways has been utilising 
NavIC and GAGAN based devices for Real -time Train Information System (RTIS). Department is in 
consultation with the stakeholders in maritime domain, including Ministry of Shipping (MoS), for 
introducing NavIC in the maritime equipments. Depa rtment had successfully demonstrated NavIC 
based vessel positioning system to MoS. Recognition of NavIC by the International Maritime 
Organisation (IMO) has been possible due to combined efforts of the Department and MoS. 
Department is in regular consultation with Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) for adoption of GAGAN 
in civilian aircrafts. Also, MoCA has recommended NavIC as the PNT system in Drone Rules 2021. 
(g) Department is working closely with the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) for 
integrating NavIC in Aadhaar enrolment devices. Department has facilitated successful conduction of 
field trials, and is providing technical expertise in finalisation of procurement specification of the 
devices.  
(h) Department is working with Department o f Consumer Affairs (DoCA) and National Physical 
Laboratory (NPL) for the implementation of country -wide IST dissemination system. Department is 
providing technical expertise and in-house developed software for building the system.  
(i) Department is in con sultation with telecom OEMs and chipset manufacturers for ensuring 
seamless adoption of NavIC in mobile handsets in the country. The interaction is facilitated by 
Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY) and Department of Telecom (DoT). Industry has already 
indicated willingness and readiness for incorporating NavIC in 5G handsets.  
(j) Department has supported National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) for utilising NavIC 
as an alert dissemination system for major natural disasters like landslides, earthquak es, floods, 
avalanches, etc. Indian National Centre for Ocean Information System (INCOIS) already utilises 
NavIC to broadcast cyclones, high waves, and tsunamis alert messages for fishermen venturing into 
deep sea. 
(k) Department is engaged with the Indian  industry, startups, and academia for promoting NavIC -
based PNT ecosystem in the country. This engagement is through technology transfers, test facility 
support, startup challenges, student hackathons, and workshops. Department also works in close 
coordination with the industries in formulating various standards applicable to the PNT domain. Some 
of the standards bodies that are actively working on NavIC standards are the Bureau of Indian 
Standards (BIS), Telecom Standards Development Society (TSDSI), Telec om Engineering Centre 
(TEC), Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), Radio Technical Commission for Maritime 
Services (RTCM), International Electrotechnical Committee (IEC), and International Standards 
Organisation (ISO).

INDIGENISATION 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.23 The Committee notes that the current import dependencies in satellite systems are to the tune of 
45-50 percent and that the Department is making earnest efforts in achieving higher indigenization. 
The Committee recommends that the Department collaborates more intensel y with the Indian industry 
as well as with the Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology in finding out solutions towards 
creating the support ecosystem that enables domestic manufacturing of critical electronics 
components. This shall not only save  expensive foreign reserves but also shuttle India into the orbit of 
semiconductors and related critical technologies.                                (Para 6.4 ibid)

2.2 It is submitted that DOE vide OM’s dated 27.03.2021, 09.03.2022, 15.03.2022, 23.03.2022 and 
02.12.2022 revised the procedure for release of funds under Central Sector Schemes (CS) and Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes (CSS) and monitoring procedure for utilization of the funds released. The critical 
components of these instructions are as under: 
 
(i)  For each Central Sector Schemes (CS), the concerned Mi nistry will designate an Autonomous 
Body as the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) to implement the scheme. 
 
(ii)  Every State Government will designate a Single Nodal Agency (SNA) for implementing each 
CSS. The SNA will open a Single Nodal Account for each CSS at the State level in a Scheduled 
Commercial Bank authorized to conduct government business by the State Government. 
 
(iii)  In the beginning of a financial year, the Ministries/ Departments will release not more than 25% 
of the amount earmarked for a State for a CSS for the financial year. Additional central share 
(not more than 25% at a time) will be released upon transfer of the stipulated State share to the 
Single Nodal Account and utilization of at least 75% of the funds released earlier (both Central 
and State share) and compliance of the conditions of previous sanction. However, this provision 
will not be applicable in case of schemes w here a different quantum of release has been 
approved by the Cabinet. 
 
(iv)  After opening of Single Nodal Account of t he scheme and before opening zero balance 
subsidiary account of IAs or assigning those drawing rights from SNA’s account, the IAs at all 
levels shall return all unspent amount lying in their accounts to the Single Nodal Account of the 
SNA. It will be the r esponsibility of the State government concerned to ensure that the entire 
unspent amount is returned by all the IAs to the Single Nodal Account of the SNA concerned. 
For this, the State Government will work out the modalities and the timelines and will wor k out 
Central and state share in the amount so available with IAs. SNA will keep a record of unspent 
balance lying in the account of IAs and the amount refunded by IAs. 
 
(v)  The State Government will transfer the Central share received in its account in t he RBI to the 
concerned SNA’s account within a period of 21 days of its receipt. The Central share shall not 
be diverted to the Personal Deposit (PD) account or any other account by the State Government. 

5 
 
Corresponding State share should be released as earl y as possible as and not later than 40 days 
of release of Central share. The funds will be maintained by the SNA in the Single Nodal 
Account of each CSS. State Governments/ SNAs/ IAs shall not transfer scheme -related funds to 
any other bank account, except for actual payments under the Scheme. 
 
(vi)  Corresponding State share in full has been credited to by the State Government to the Single 
Nodal Account of the SNA. 
(vii) The amount released in one installment shall not be more than 25% of the amount earma rked 
for the State/ UT for a CSS for the financial year 2022-23.

Taken Report (ATR), preparing ATR Review Report etc. Based on the inspection reports received

Protection Act, 1986; as amended.

1 
 
 
REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with the 
action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the Committee 
contained in its ‘Three Hundred Seventy Ninth Report’ on “Demands for Grants (202 3-24) of the 
Ministry of Earth Scienc es”.  The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha on the 15th March, 2023 
and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 20th March, 2023. 
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from Ministry of Earth Sciences  (MoES) 
in respect of all the 14 recommendations/observations contained in  the ‘Three Hundred Seventy 
Ninth Report’. The replies of the Ministry of Earth Sciences have been categorized as follows:- 
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos.:- 2.8, 2.10, 2.11 and 2.21  
 Total recommendations – 04 
Chapter II: Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies:  
  Para Nos.:- 2.9, 2.17, 2.19, 2.20, 2.22, 2.27, 3.7, 3.9, 3.10 and 4.2 
  Total recommendations – 10  
Chapter III:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: NIL 
Chapter IV:  Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: NIL 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters.  
  

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2022-23 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2023-24 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 Not being able to procure critical components such as high power computing devices, 
research vessels and other infrastructure has led to a reduction in allocation at the R.E. 2022 -23 
stage. This reflects poorly on the Ministry’s commitments towards its obj ectives. Further, the 
Ministry’s response that most of these schemes have a long term horizon and hence any missed 
opportunities shall be compensated for in the coming years is not satisfactory. The Committee 
therefore recommends that the Ministry should t ake all necessary steps towards dissolution of 
such hurdles and ensure that the progress on its various initiatives is not compromised. 
(Para 2.8 of the 379th Report) 
Action Taken 
1.2 Noted for compliance. The annual acquisition plan under all the schemes has been 
finalized. The order for the procurement of High Performance Computing (HPC) system has been 
placed in May 2023. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3 Chart 2 depicts the variation in Capital Expenditure and Overall Budget in B.E. & R.E. 
2022-23 and B.E.  allocations for 2023-24. The Committee observes that the Capital expenditure 
in B.E. 2022 -23 was Rs. 450 crore which was revised down by about 59 per cent to Rs. 188.65 
crore at R.E. 2022 -23 stage. The allocation for Capital expenditure in R.E. 2022 -23 w as Rs. 
188.65 crore which has been substantially increased by about 257 percent to Rs. 673.81 crore in 
B.E. 2023 -24. The Ministry, while replying to a query of the Committee submitted that the 
increased Capital allocations during B.E. 2023 -24 will be used in Procurement of HPC, 
Acquiring of Land for setting up of Advanced Marine Biology Station and Construction of NCS 
building.                                                                                                                     (Para 2.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.4 Noted. The order for the procurement of High Performance Computing (HPC) system has 
been placed in May 2023. The design of the NCS building has been completed and will be 
submitted to the concerned authority for approval. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.5 The Committee notes the reasons for increase in capital expenditure as well as overall 
budgetary allocation for B.E. 2023 -24 and recommends that the Ministry should take all steps 
possible in ensuring the procurement of high performance co mputing devices and other such 
infrastructure necessary for achieving the desired outcomes under the flagship schemes of the 
Ministry. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should actively pursue with the 
Department of Space to ensure timely c ompletion and launch of the INSAT 3D satellite and that 
any value added –data based services that can be made available to the general public, service 
delivery institutions, government and law enforcement, etc., shall be done with priority.  
 (Para 2.11 ibid) 
  

3 
 
Action Taken 
1.6 Noted for compliance. The order for the procurement of High Performance Computing 
(HPC) system has been placed in May 2023. The Ministry will actively pursue with the 
Department of Space to ensure timely completion and launch of the INSAT 3D satellite. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.7 The Committee therefore strongly recommends that the Ministry should do a thorough 
analysis of the reasons and areas of improvement to ensure that t he funds available to the 
Ministry are deployed towards achievement of the physical targets set and that the flagship 
schemes of the Ministry do not lose its objective and importance due to these inordinate delays. 
Further, the requirements in terms of Com puting Capacity, vessel related equipment and other 
research related inventory should be planned and orders be placed well in advance, so that the 
crucial initiatives of the Ministry are not stalled.                                                      (Para 2.21 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.8 Noted for compliance. The annual acquisition plan under all the schemes has been 
finalized. The order for the procurement of High Performance Computing (HPC) system has been 
placed in May 2023. 
 
  

4 
 
CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1 As regards B.E. 2023 -24 allocations, the Committee observes that the Ministry has been 
given Rs. 3319.88 crore for  2023-24 which is about 25 percent more than the corresponding 
allocation in 2022 -3. To understand the reason for this substantial increase, the Committee 
sought details from the Department. In a written reply, Committee was informed that that the 
increased allocation under the sub -head Secretariat is for the rental charges of about Rs.520 
crore for the INSAT 3D satellite charges to be given to Department of Space for making and 
launching the satellite.                                                                         (Para 2.9 of the 379th Report) 
Action Taken 
2.2 Noted. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.3 The Committee emboldens the fact that the role of Ministry of Earth sciences has become 
more profound in the current context of climate change as well as in acting as an enabler of the 
Blue Economy through access to the vast oceanic resources and knowledge. Further, the 
increasing number of episodes of extreme weather phenomena has further highlighted the need 
for enhanced accuracy in prediction and diss emination of weather updates. The quest for 
knowledge concealed in the Polar Regions, is not just crucial for maintaining scientific database 
but also of great interest in protecting and furthering for India’s security interests. The deep 
ocean preserves i n itself vast resources which can be boon for our country’s economic progress 
and can prove to be a substitute for many imports which cost dearly to the country’s foreign 
reserves. In this backdrop, it is of utmost importance that the tasks at hand with th e Ministry be 
executed with great vigour and efficiency.                                                                (Para 2.17 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
2.4 The Ministry thanks the Committee for its advice. All efforts will be made during 2023 -24 
to improve the weather, climate and ocean services. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.5 The Committee observes, with dismay, that under the head ‘O -SMART’ the Ministry was 
granted Rs. 340 crore in R.E. 2022-23 against which it could spend only Rs. 143.48 crore, thereby 
achieving only 29 percent utilisation (till January 2023). Similarly under another flagship scheme 
of the Ministry –REACHOUT, a sum of Rs. 63.13 crore was allocated in R.E. 2022 -23 against 
which the Ministry could utilise only Rs. 27.43 crore or just 43 pe rcent. Deep Ocean Mission, for 
which the Ministry was granted Rs. 300 crore during R.E. 2022 -23, it is observed that the 
Ministry could spend 61 percent of the allocation i.e. Rs. 184.39 crore. Further, as against an 
R.E. allocation of Rs. 400 crore the Ministry could spend Rs. 209 crore only, about 52 percent. 
(Para 2.19 ibid)  
Action Taken 
2.6 At the end of the FY 2022 -23, the expenditure under O -SMART was Rs. 250.20 (73.59% 
of the RE) and under REACHOUT was Rs. 60.55 Cr (95.91% of RE). 
 

5 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.7 The Committee is disheartened to see such drastic under -utilisation of allocations made to 
the Ministry under all of its flagship schemes. The severe utilisation across all flagship schemes of 
the Ministry is indicative of the fact that the  Ministry has not been able to achieve its physical 
targets that it had earlier set out. Further, the Ministry’s explanation to the Committee’s concern 
on such gross under -utilisation and subsequent reduction is not reassuring and recommends the 
Ministry to ensure optimal utilisation of funds for allocation made in F.Y. 2022 -23 as well as in 
2023-24.                                                                                                                     (Para 2.20 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.8 Noted for compliance. All efforts will be made during 2023 -24 for the optimal utilization 
of funds and achieve the physical targets. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.9 The Committee would also like to emphasize that the Ministry should chart out a detailed 
action plan  on integrating with the private sector in augmenting the reach and efficacy of the 
services offered by the Ministry especially in the field of weather forecast, disaster management, 
fisheries, etc. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should ex plore the possibilities 
of manufacturing crucial equipments domestically so that the dependencies on import and 
therefore the lead time as well as the cost, may be reduced. This shall also strengthen the Indian 
industry in manufacturing high end telemetric  equipments which shall have a huge spin -off 
advantage for other sectors as well.                                                                          (Para 2.22 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.10 Noted for compliance. India Meteorological Department (IMD), under  MoES is exploring 
the possibilities of engaging Start-ups for the development of met sensors/ software/ application/ 
dissemination tools through an MoU. The National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) till date 
has signed 32 technology licensing agreements with Indian industries and is in the process of few 
more agreements in the current financial year NIOT is in the process of forming a Section 8 
Company, The proposed Marine Gate Incubation Centre (MAGIC) by NIOT will be first in the 
country which will deal exclusively in the area of ocean/marine technology. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.11 The Committee notes the physical targets set in by the Ministry under its flagship Scheme 
ACROSS and acknowledges that Atmospheric modelling and observation systems are crucial for the 
country in terms of accurately predicting weather patterns not just for  the benefit of the farming 
community but also for city administration. The increasing instances of flash floods, long dry spells, 
rapid temperature change has put pressure on the city administration since they are now tasked with 
making adequate arrangeme nts for mitigation. In such a scenario, advance forecasts shall be of 
utmost importance and should enable farmers, service providers, first responders as well as the 
general public to accordingly plan and minimize inconvenience and losses.                 (Para 2.27 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.12 The Ministry thanks the Committee for its advice. All efforts will be made during 2023 -24 
to improve the weather and climate services. 
  

6 
 
DEEP OCEAN MISSION 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.13 As regards physical targets and achievement, the Committee observed that the physical 
performance of the Ministry has been extremely disheartening. The Ministry could achieve only 7 
per cent against 15 per cent physical targets proposed for Deep Ocean Surv ey and Exploration. 
The Ministry has also achieved only 5 per cent against 20 per cent physical targets proposed for 
Establishment of an Advanced Marine Station for Ocean Biology. The Committee recommends the 
Ministry to revisit its performance in terms of  realisation of physical and financial targets set 
under Deep Ocean Mission Scheme and strive hard to improve it. Steps taken in this regard may 
be intimated to the Committee. The Committee also hopes that the Ministry, with the help of its 
periodic review s of the financial and physical performance of this Scheme, will strive hard to 
achieve the targets set for the year 2023-24.                                                               (Para 3.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.14 The physical and financial targets  couldn’t be achieved due to effect of Pandemic in 
realization of certain components and challenges in demonstration of technologies due to ocean 
weather. All efforts will be made during 2023-24 to achieve physical and financial targets. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.15 The Committee is constrained to take serious note of the reasons provided by the Ministry 
for sub -optimal utilisation of funds and recommends the Ministry to expedite the process of 
tendering with an aim of materializing the tender in this  financial year itself. The Committee also 
expresses its concern over the missed opportunity during the year and recommends that the 
Ministry should ensure that any loss in achievements of physical targets for the year 2022 -23 is 
compensated for in 2023 -24. Further, the Ministry should take all necessary steps to ensure that 
targets set for a particular year are met in that year itself, without having to be carried over to the 
next year.                                                                                                                      (Para 3.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.16 Noted for compliance. The annual acquisition plans under all the schemes have been 
finalized. All efforts will be made during 2023-24 to achieve physical and financial targets. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.17 Blue Economy is crucial for India’s position as the net security as well as prosperity 
provider in the Indian Ocean region and therefore, the Committee while emboldening the 
importance of the Deep Ocean Mission, re commends the Ministry to play a larger role in acting 
as the backbone of this cause.                                                                                    (Para 3.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.18 The Ministry thanks the Committee for its advice and recommendation. 
  

7 
 
INITIATIVES FOR SOCIETAL BENEFITS 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.19 The Committee underlines the priceless services that the Ministry provides in the interest 
of the Nation. These services are crucial not just for the common citizen to lead a more 
productive, safe and prosperous life but also essential for the protection of environment and vast 
natural resources of the country. The Committee also acknowledges the value addition the 
Ministry has provided over the years to a plethora of se ctors including agriculture & fisheries, 
weather forecast and early warning systems, survey of mineral resources, coastal and oceanic 
research, etc.                                                                                                                (Para 4.2 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.20 The Ministry thanks the Committee for its advice and recommendation.

INTRODUCTION 
 The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), came into being on August 3, 1954, 
and has been engaged in the development of nuclear power technology, application of 
radiation technologies in the fields of agriculture, health care, industry and basic 
research. 
1.2  The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) is the apex body for formulation of 
policies and direction of the programmes. The Commission implements its policies and 
programmes through the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). The programmes of 
DAE have been divided into four sectors viz. Research and Development, Industries, 
Minerals and Power Sector. 
1.3  The programmes being followed by DAE, can be briefly summed up as follows: 
 Increasing the share of nuclear power through deployment of indigenous and 
other proven technologies and also developing fast breeder reactors and thorium 
reactors with associated fuel cycle facilities; 
 Building and operation of research reactors for production of radioisotopes; 
developing radiation technology applications in the field of health care, 
agriculture and industry, cancer care, water related technology, waste 
management etc.; 
 Designing and developing advanced technologies such as accelerators, lasers, 
supercomputers, advanced materials and instrumentation and encouraging 
transfer of technology to industry; 
 Providing support to basic research in nuclear energy and related frontier areas 
of science; interaction with universities and academic institutions; supporting 
academic programmes having a bearing on DAE’s activities; and International 
co-operation in related advanced areas of research and contribution to national 
security. 
1.4 DAE’s programmes are multidisciplinary in nature. For their execution, DAE 
has evolved abroad based organizational structure comprising research centres, 
industrial units, public sector undertakings and fully aided institutions, along with 
service organizations. These organizations are engaged in research, technology 
development and commercial operations in the areas of nuclear power and associated 
technologies, radiation technologies and their applications, basic research and academic 
programmes. 
1.5 The Department is also engaged in the development of radiation technologies 
and their applications for better crop varieties, techniques for crops protection, radiation 
based post-harvest technologies, techniques for radio-diagnosis and radiotherapy of 
diseases particularly cancer, technologies for safe drinking water, better environment 
and industrial growth.

1.6 Over the years, the Department has been able to establish a network of 
institutions engaged in R&D as well as industrial activities and acquired expertise in all 
aspects of the nuclear fuel cycle. The first stage of the nuclear power programme is in 
commercial domain and the second stage has been launched with the ongoing 
construction of 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR). 
1.7 Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) formed in 1987, is a 
Public Sector Enterprise under the administrative control of DAE. NPCIL is responsible 
for siting, design, construction, commissioning and operation of nuclear power reactors. 
Safety is given overriding priority in all facets of nuclear power reactors. At presents, 
NPCIL is operating 22 nuclear power reactors with an installed capacity of 6780 MW.

2.5 The Committee recommends that the DAE should adopt a more robust 
approach to financial planning and forecasting by incorporating detailed risk 
assessments and contingency allocations into the initial budget estimates. The 
Committee notes that the Revised Estimates have consistently exceeded the Budget 
Estimates. The Committee therefore urges the Department to implement regular 
internal and external audits and to ensure transparent reporting of any mid-year 
adjustments, with clear justifications for deviations from the initial allocations. 
Furthermore, it is recommended that standard operating procedures for urgent 
procurement and maintenance should be established to pre-empt emergency 
expenditures, while also integrating anticipated costs for global collaborations and 
new technologies into the budgetary framework.  
2.6 The Committee expresses major concern over the substantial gap between 
the budgetary allocations and actual utilization by the DAE. In 2023-24, the actual 
expenditure of ₹35,885.93 crore was closely aligned with the RE. However, in 
2024-25, actual expenditure stood at ₹29,051.95 crore, a mere 80.34% utilization of 
BE allocations, falling significantly short of both BE and RE by nearly ₹7,500 
crore. The Committee acknowledges that the Ministry of Finance imposed a 
budgetary cut of 13.47% on the proposed RE for 2024-25 which led to reduction in 
the allocation from the projected ₹42,256.77 crore to ₹36,564.24 crore. The 
Department informed the Committee that it has sought additional funds through the 2nd 
batch of Supplementary Demand for Grants (SDG), which, if fully allocated, would 
allow the Department to incur an expenditure of up to ₹37,362 crore during the fiscal 
year. A significant portion of the additional funds requested under the SDG is 
earmarked for critical payments, including ₹1,710.43 crore for the procurement of 
nuclear fuel from M/s TVEL, Russia, ₹595.42 crore towards India's commitments to the 
International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) project, and ₹5,900 crore for 
committed liabilities of various units, aided institutions, and Public Sector Undertakings 
(PSUs) under the capital and revenue sections. 
2.7 The Committee recommends that the Department continue to streamline 
fund disbursal processes to ensure optimal utilization of allocated resources, 
particularly for multi-year atomic energy projects. The Committee also 
recommends that a more robust financial strategy be adopted, incorporating 
contingency planning to mitigate the impact of unexpected budget cuts. 
Additionally, the Committee urges the Ministry of Finance to consider the critical 
nature of the Department’s commitments, particularly those related to nuclear 
fuel procurement and international obligations, and to ensure that adequate 
funding is provided in a timely manner. The Committee urges upon the 
Department to implement these measures with immediate effect to restore the 
expenditure trajectory to match both the budget estimates and the requirements of 
multi-year projects. The Department took note of Committee’s observations and 
assured that the Department would fully utilize the allocations by the end of FY 2024-
25 and the actual expenditure would correspond with the figures for the last three years.

2.12  Upon enquiry by the Committee on the impact of shortfall in budgetary 
allocations for the year 2025-26, on the activities of the Department, the DAE stated 
that the substantial reduction in budgetary allocation will slow down activities related to 
basic research and derail the progress achieved over the years which shapes up into 
technologies over a considerable period of time. The DAE further stated that reduction 
in fund allocation would impact the high priority activities of developmental nature 
which have potential in transforming rural or industrial landscape. In response to these 
challenges, DAE outlined several mitigation strategies. The Department has committed 
to prioritising high-impact and time-sensitive projects, ensuring that operational power 
plants and essential fuel cycle activities continue without disruption. It also plans to 
optimise costs by reallocating resources within its existing budget, implementing 
austerity measures to minimise the financial strain. Furthermore, DAE explained to the 
Committee that it is exploring Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) for infrastructure 
development, particularly in the Bharat Small Reactors (BSR) initiative, to attract 
private investment into the nuclear sector. 
2.13 The Committee recognises the critical role of nuclear energy in India's energy 
security, scientific progress, and healthcare advancements. While DAE has outlined 
strategies to mitigate the impact of budget shortfalls, the risks posed by inadequate 
funding remain significant. The Committee acknowledges the fact that slowdown of 
nuclear research, isotope production, and uranium exploration may have lasting 
consequences on India’s scientific progress and energy security. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends immediate action to restore essential funding, 
support nuclear research, and ensure uninterrupted progress in India’s nuclear 
energy and medical applications. The Committee recommends urgent restoration 
of at least ₹5,933.62 crore, particularly for the R&D and I&M sectors, to ensure 
continued progress in nuclear technology development and fuel production.

3.1 BHABHA ATOMIC RESEARCH CENTRE (BARC) 
 The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is India's premier 
multidisciplinary nuclear research institution under the Department of Atomic Energy 

13 
 
(DAE). Established in 1954 as the Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay (AEET) and 
renamed BARC in 1966 in honour of Dr. Homi Bhabha, it has been instrumental in 
advancing nuclear science, technology, and energy security in India. BARC plays a 
crucial role in India's three-stage nuclear power programme, covering nuclear reactor 
research, fuel fabrication, waste management, isotope applications, and nuclear safety. 
The centre is also responsible for healthcare, agriculture, water purification, and 
radiation technology applications, reinforcing its impact beyond energy production. 
BARC is central to the implementation of India’s indigenous three-stage nuclear 
programme, designed to achieve energy security through the optimal utilisation of 
nuclear fuel resources. 
Stage I – Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs): BARC develops 
reactor safety technologies, nuclear fuel fabrication, and in-service reactor 
inspection tools to enhance the efficiency and safety of PHWRs. 
Stage II – Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs): The centre contributes to spent fuel 
reprocessing, sodium-cooled fast reactor technology, and advanced fuel 
fabrication to sustain the second stage of the programme. 
Stage III – Thorium-based Reactors: BARC plays a vital role in research on 
Advanced Heavy Water Reactors (AHWRs) and Thorium fuel cycle 
technologies, leveraging India's vast thorium reserves. 
BARC has designed and operates research reactors such as Dhruva, Apsara-U, 
and KAMINI, which are essential for neutron beam research and isotope production. 
The centre is actively developing high-temperature gas-cooled reactors (HTGRs), 
molten salt reactors, and small modular reactors (SMRs) to explore future nuclear 
energy possibilities.BARC develops uranium and thorium fuel fabrication techniques, 
supporting India's expanding nuclear power infrastructure.The centre operates 
reprocessing plants for recovering plutonium and uranium, crucial for Fast Breeder 
Reactor technology. 
BARC is responsible for managing several research and industrial facilities that 
contribute to nuclear technology and allied fields. 
 (i) Research and Development Centres 
Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR): Focuses on Fast 
Breeder Reactor (FBR) technology, materials science, and reactor engineering. 
Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT): Specialises in 
lasers, accelerators, and advanced optics for nuclear applications. 
Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC): Engaged in particle accelerator 
research, medical isotope production, and high-energy physics. 
(ii) Industrial and Service Organisations 
Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC): Manufactures fuel bundles for PHWRs and 
BWRs, producing fuel components for India's nuclear power plants. 
Heavy Water Board (HWB): Manages the production and supply of heavy 
water (D2O) for nuclear reactors and industrial applications. 
Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT): Engages in radioisotope 
production, nuclear medicine, and radiation technology applications for 
agriculture and healthcare. 
 
 
 

14 
 
(iii) Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) Under DAE 
Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL): Responsible for the 
construction and operation of commercial nuclear power plants in India. 
Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI): Develops and 
operates Fast Breeder Reactors, essential for India's nuclear energy future. 
Uranium Corporation of India Limited (UCIL): Engaged in uranium mining 
and processing, a critical part of the nuclear fuel supply chain.

3.19 Heavy Water Facilities 
The Heavy Water Board (HWB) under the DAE plays a critical role in India's 
nuclear programme by ensuring a steady supply of heavy water (D₂O) for Pressurised 
Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs). These reactors constitute a major portion of India's 
nuclear power generation capacity, and any disruption in heavy water supply could 
affect reactor operations and power generation. HWB is also involved in the production 
of deuterium-based pharmaceuticals, enriched boron, and nuclear solvents, which are 
essential for fuel reprocessing, radiation shielding, and medical applications. The 
Department informed the Committee about the key activities undertaken in 2024-25 and 
planned for 2025-26, the notable ones being: 

18 
 
(i) Modernisation and Expansion of Heavy Water Facilities 
Upgrading ageing H₂S-based heavy water plants, including the retrofit of 
pipelines, exhaust systems, and heat exchangers, has been prioritised to enhance 
operational efficiency. 
Recommissioning of Heavy Water Plant, Tuticorin, in April 2025 is expected to 
increase India's domestic heavy water production capacity. 
Expansion of nuclear solvent production facilities, including TBP, D2EPHA-II, 
and TOPO at HWP, Tuticorin, to support fuel reprocessing and industrial 
applications. 
(ii) Research & Development in Deuterium-Based Pharmaceuticals 
Development of deuterated analogues of anti-cancer drugs, with biological 
evaluation in collaboration with ACTREC, Mumbai. 
Studies on deuterium-depleted water (DDW) for cancer treatment to explore its 
potential as a novel therapeutic agent. 
(iii) Expansion of Boron Enrichment Facilities 
Installation of high-vacuum induction furnaces and CNC grinding machines at 
HWP, Manuguru, to increase the production of boron carbide pellets for the Fast 
Breeder Reactor (FBR) programme.

3.39 Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd (BHAVINI) 
Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI) is a Government 
Company under the administrative control of the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) 
incorporated on 22nd October, 2003 as Public Limited Company under the Companies 
Act, 1956 with the objective of constructing and commissioning the first 500 MWe Fast 
Breeder Reactor (FBR) at Kalpakkam in Tamilnadu and to pursue construction, 
commissioning, operation and maintenance of subsequent Fast Breeder Reactors for 
generation of electricity in pursuance of the schemes and programmes of Government 
of India under the provisions of the Atomic Energy Act,1962. BHAVINI is currently 
constructing a 500MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, 70 Kms 
away from Chennai. The PFBR is the forerunner of the future Fast Breeder Reactors 
and is expected to provide energy security to the country. The PFBR is being built with 
the design and technology developed at the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research 
(IGCAR) located at Kalpakkam. The PFBR is a First-Of-Its-Kind (FOAK) reactor, 
designed to utilise plutonium-based mixed oxide (MOX) fuel and sodium as a coolant, 
paving the way for large-scale deployment of Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) in India. 
The objectives of BHAVINI emanate from the following mandate: 
Providing energy security for the nation through Fast Breeder Technology based 
power stations commencing with 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor. 
Demonstrating the techno-commercial viability of Fast Breeder Technology based 
nuclear power stations. Strengthening the public awareness programmes for enhancing 
and improving the public perception of Nuclear Power in the country. Strengthening the 
QA activities relating to Fast Breeder Technology based nuclear power programme 
within the organization and those associated with it and increasing the overall share of 
nuclear power. 
  BHAVINI’s 500 MW PFBR is in the advanced stage of integrated 
commissioning, with expected first criticality by 2025-26. Some of the key 
accomplishments are: 
 (i) Completion of major structural work: Reactor containment, sodium cooling loops, and steam 
generator systems have been installed.  
 (ii) Modifications to reactor components: 376 subassemblies were modified to address higher 
extraction force issues and ensure seamless handling.  
(iii) Deployment of high-temperature materials: Advanced materials have been incorporated to 
enhance reactor efficiency and safety.  
(iv) Operationalisation of the Demonstration Fast Reactor Fuel Reprocessing Plant (DFRP): 
This facility, capable of handling both carbide and oxide fuels, was commissioned in 2024 and has 
successfully completed two fuel reprocessing campaigns. 
(v) Indigenous production of medical isotopes (Strontium-89): The PFBR has been used for the 
pilot-scale production of radioisotopes, contributing to nuclear medicine and cancer treatment.

4. 100 GW Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat 2047 
The Secretary, Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) made a presentation before 
the Committee, outlining the 100 GW Nuclear Energy Mission, an ambitious plan to 
achieve 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047 in alignment with India’s energy 
security and decarbonization goals. The Committee was informed that this mission aims 
to leverage private sector participation, streamline regulatory frameworks, and scale up 
nuclear power production to meet India’s increasing energy demands. The Committee 
recognizes the strategic importance of this initiative in ensuring a sustainable, low-
carbon energy future but acknowledges significant challenges that need to be 
addressed to make this target achievable. 
4.2 The Department in a written reply informed the Committee that the present 
installed nuclear power capacity stands at 8.18 GW, with an additional 7.3 GW under 
construction/commissioning and 7 GW already sanctioned and currently undergoing 
pre-project activities. Upon completion of these projects, India’s nuclear power capacity 
is expected to reach 22.48 GW by 2031-32. Beyond this, NPCIL plans to add another 
15.4 GW through indigenous Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) and 17.6 
GW through Light Water Reactors (LWRs) with foreign cooperation, bringing the total 
installed capacity to 55 GW. Additionally, BHAVINI is expected to contribute 3.8 GW 
through Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs), while the remainder of the capacity will come 
from Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), Bharat Small Reactors (BSRs), and other 
advanced nuclear technologies developed with private sector collaboration. The 
Committee notes that scaling up from the projected 55 GW to 100 GW by 2047 
will require substantial investment, regulatory reforms, and policy interventions. 
4.3 On being asked about the capital investments in the 100 GW Mission, the 
Department informed that around 50% of the 100 GW target is expected to come from 
Public-Private Partnerships (PPP). However, the exact public-private and indigenous-
imported mix will emerge as amendments to the Atomic Energy Act and Civil Liability 
for Nuclear Damage (CLND) Act are introduced, along with necessary regulatory 
reforms. 
4.4 The Committee acknowledges that achieving 100 GW of nuclear capacity 
by 2047 requires a structured and phased approach. Instead of focusing solely on a 
long-term 100 GW target, the Committee recommends phased capacity additions, 
with clear short-term (2030), medium-term (2040), and long-term (2047) 
milestones. The Committee recommends that 2031-32 projection of 22.48 GW 

25 
 
should serve as a baseline, with subsequent capacity additions planned in 
alignment with investment inflows, policy reforms, and domestic manufacturing 
capabilities. 
4.5 The Committee notes that nearly 50% of the 100 GW capacity is expected 
to come from private sector participation and recommends establishing a robust 
financial model that includes Government incentives, Viability Gap Funding 
(VGF), and sovereign guarantees to attract both domestic and foreign investments. 
The Committee suggests that legislative amendments to the Atomic Energy Act 
and Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act should be expedited to encourage 
private investment in nuclear power generation. 
4.6 The Committee emphasizes the importance of Small Modular Reactors 
(SMRs) and Bharat Small Reactors (BSRs) in achieving the 100 GW target. The 
Committee recommends that SMRs and BSRs should be deployed in remote 
regions and industrial zones to support decentralized energy generation. The 
Committee also urges the Department to accelerate Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) 
deployment, with the 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) expected 
to attain first criticality by March 2026 and completion by September 2026. 
5. Nuclear Energy Mission for R&D of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) 
Secretary, DAE made a presentation before the Committee on Nuclear Energy 
Mission for R&D of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), a dedicated programme with an 
allocated budget of ₹20,000 crore, focusing on the development, testing, and 
deployment of small nuclear reactors. The Committee was informed that the 
programme aims to build at least five indigenously developed SMRs by 2033 and 
includes the development of Bharat Small Modular Reactors (BSMR), Gas-Cooled 
Micro Modular Reactors (GCMMR), and 50 MWe SMRs. 
5.2 On being asked about the specific research priorities for Small Modular 
Reactors (SMRs) under the ₹20,000 crore R&D initiatives and the technology 
development road map for SMRs, the Department in a written reply stated that research 
priorities will include R&D of fuel cycle and installation & commissioning of 
demonstration plants of (i) 200 MWe Loop Type BSMR demonstration plant (ii) 5 
MWth gas cooled reactor (hydrogen generator) demonstration plant.The Department 
has planned design and development of SMRs keeping in mind three broad purposes: 
(i) Re-purposing of the aging thermal power plants (ii) Captive power generation aimed 
at the energy intensive domestic heavy industry such as steel and aluminum industry 
with a rated power around 200 MWe (iii) Small power plants, typical rating of 50 
MWe, meant for remote locations. The Committee was informed that BSMR & SMR 
designs are pressurized water reactors and they have significant technological readiness 
for indigenous realisation. Design and developments for other candidate SMR design 
such as gas cooled reactors has been initiated for realization in the long-term. The 
Department in its written reply has stated that there are nearly 80 SMR designs being 
pursued world-wide. Only a very few of them are seen to be actually realized and 
working. LWR based SMRs are relatively easy to develop owing proven operating 
experience of LWRs world-wide. It is seen that in general SMRs do not have the benefit 
of economy of scale like large nuclear power plants but they have innovative designs 
and small foot print. The Department informed the Committee that Ownership of 
nuclear fuel in general will be with the government. A few SMR designs have 
envisaged proliferation resistant fuels and SMRs utilizing traditional fuels will have to 
be placed under nuclear safe guards. SMRs by virtue of their smaller power rating will 
produce relatively smaller quantities of nuclear waste. India requires a closed nuclear 

26 
 
cycle for sustainability and hence policy of reprocessing of spent fuel will result in 
reduced radioactive inventory. The Committee recognises SMRs as a potential 
breakthrough in nuclear technology, offering advantages such as scalability, enhanced 
safety features, and suitability for decentralised power generation. The Committee 
agrees that these reactors are particularly well-suited for energy-intensive industries, 
such as steel and aluminium production, as well as remote locations where large nuclear 
plants are not feasible. 
5.3 To support SMR development, the Committee recommends prioritizing 
demonstration projects, ensuring that the first set of SMRs is successfully deployed 
and operational before scaling up production. Furthermore, international 
collaboration with established nuclear agencies should be pursued to adopt best 
practices in reactor design and safety protocols. The Committee also recommends 
prioritising domestic SMR research and pilot projects to ensure economic 
viability. 
5.4 The Committee recommends that initial funding should focus on BSMR 
and GCMMR demonstration plants before large-scale commercialisation.

infrastructure  
The Bharat Small Reactors (BSR) initiative is a key step towards expanding

Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) for the development and deployment of small-
scale nuclear reactors through a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model, with bid

initiative aims to accelerate nuclear capacity expansion and encourage private 
investment, it introduces significant challenges that require careful regulatory oversight. 
The funding for BSR development is expected to come from a mix of public and private 
investments, with financial incentives for private players. The Committee was informed 
that Viability Gap Funding (VGF) and long-term Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) 
will be crucial to attracting private investments. Key focus areas for BSR development 
includes integration with industrial hubs to provide stable base load power for sectors 
like steel, aluminium, and chemicals, repurposing ageing coal-fired thermal power 
plants to ensure efficient land use and development of  decentralised nuclear power 
solutions for remote and underserved areas. 
6.2 The Committee acknowledges that private sector involvement in nuclear energy 
presents security, regulatory, and operational risks. The Committee notes that the 
existing Atomic Energy Act and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act have 
been revised to facilitate private participation while ensuring safety and security 
standards are met. However, the Committee notes that several key concerns still 
remain. The Committee observes that ensuring strict compliance with nuclear 
safety protocols, waste management regulations, and radiation protection 
measures is crucial to avoid potential hazards. The Committee expresses concern 
that regulatory uncertainties regarding liability and risk-sharing mechanisms 
could deter private investors.  
6.3 The Committee also stresses that India’s strategic control over critical 
nuclear technologies must not be compromised through excessive reliance on 
private enterprises. To mitigate these risks, the Committee recommends that the 
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) be strengthened to enforce stringent

compliance measures for private sector entities. The Committee recommends that

Government-supported clinical trial funding should be enhanced, ensuring greater 
participation in global cancer research initiatives. The Committee firmly believes 
that TMC and DAE must adopt a multi-faceted approach to enhance cost-effective 
cancer treatment and therapies in India. Sustained government support, increased 
corporate participation, and advancements in research will ensure that high-
quality cancer treatment remains accessible to all sections of society.

8.2 The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) plays a critical role in advancing 
India's nuclear research, energy generation, and scientific innovation. However, a 
review of its workforce distribution by the Committee reveals significant vacancies 
across its various units, which could affect efficiency and operational effectiveness. As 

31 
 
observed by Table 4 above, one of the most crucial institutions under the DAE, the 
Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), has a sanctioned strength of 14,445 
personnel, but only 10,604 employees are currently in position, leaving 3,841 
vacancies. This results in a vacancy rate of 26.6%, indicating a substantial shortage of 
skilled personnel in key research and technical positions. Similarly, the Indira Gandhi 
Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), which is responsible for advanced nuclear 
research and fast breeder reactor development, has 2,134 employees in position against 
a sanctioned strength of 2,730, leaving 596 vacancies. This 21.8% vacancy rate could 
slow down research projects and affect the development of next-generation nuclear 
technologies. An even more concerning situation exists in the Heavy Water Board 
(HWB), which is responsible for producing and supplying heavy water for nuclear 
reactors. With a sanctioned strength of 3,872 personnel, only 2,015 employees are in 
position, leaving 1,857 vacancies. This represents a staggering 48% vacancy rate, which 
could impact reactor operations and nuclear fuel production. 
8.3 NPCIL which operates India’s nuclear power plants, has a sanctioned workforce 
of 15,088 employees, but only 10,745 are in position, leading to 4,343 vacancies. This 
represents a 28.8% vacancy rate, which could affect the efficiency and safety of nuclear 
power plant operations. The Atomic Minerals Directorate (AMD), responsible for the 
exploration of atomic minerals such as uranium and thorium, also faces significant 
shortages. With 2,495 sanctioned posts, only 1,699 employees are in position, leaving 
796 vacancies, translating to a 31.9% vacancy rate, which could impact India's ability to 
expand its nuclear fuel reserves.A notable concern is the vacancy rate at the Tata 
Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), which is one of India's leading scientific 
research institutions. With a sanctioned strength of 1,448 employees, only 609 are in 
position, leaving 839 vacancies. This results in a 58% vacancy rate, reflecting a 
significant shortfall in scientific manpower. Such a high vacancy rate suggests that 
TIFR is heavily reliant on contractual and research-based staff rather than regular 
employees. Given the institute's crucial role in fundamental research, this issue requires 
immediate attention to ensure stability in long-term scientific projects. 
8.4 The Tata Memorial Centre (TMC), India's premier cancer treatment and 
research institution under the DAE, has a sanctioned strength of 6,229 personnel, with 
5,052 in position, leaving 1,177 vacancies. This results in a vacancy rate of 18.9%, 
which, although lower compared to other DAE institutions, still reflects a shortage of 
medical professionals and researchers who are essential for providing comprehensive 
cancer care and advancing oncology research. 
8.5 The DAE informed the Committee in its written reply that it has initiated a 
recruitment drive to mitigate workforce shortages. A Central Recruitment Agency 
(CRA) has been set up in the year 2022 to streamline recruitment across all DAE units. 
The Department further informed that a mission-mode recruitment drive in 2023-24 led 
to the hiring of 3,200 personnel, including scientific officers, technical staff, and 
administrative personnel. Trainee Scientific Officers (TSOs) are recruited annually for 
BARC Training Schools, and 180 officers were inducted in August 2024. The 
Department emphasized that Recruitment of Technical Officers, Scientific Assistants, 
and Paramedical Staff is ongoing, with empanelment of 2,269 technicians and 1,206 
scientific assistants. However, the Committee observes that recruitment delays still 
persist, and several advertised posts remain unfilled. 
8.6 The high vacancy rates across DAE institutions raise serious concerns 
about workforce planning, recruitment efficiency, and the overall sustainability of 
nuclear and research projects in India. The Committee expresses its concerns over 
these vacancies, especially in key operational areas such as nuclear power 
generation, research, and mineral exploration. The shortage of skilled personnel 
could lead to delays in research and development, inefficiencies in plant 
operations, and constraints in nuclear fuel production, ultimately affecting the 

32 
 
country's nuclear energy programme. To address this issue, the Committee 
strongly recommends an immediate recruitment drive to fill the existing vacancies. 
It is imperative that recruitment processes be streamlined to ensure timely hiring 
of personnel in technical, scientific, and operational roles. A review of existing 
workforce policies should be undertaken to identify areas where delays occur in 
the hiring process, and necessary reforms should be implemented. The DAE must 
adopt modern human resource management strategies to attract and retain talent, 
ensuring competitive salaries, career progression opportunities, and research 
grants for professionals in nuclear science, energy, and advanced research. 
8.7 The Committee observes with great concern contractual employment and 
temporary staffing, particularly in research institutions such as TIFR. The 
Committee urges a review of these employment practices and recommends 
converting long-term contractual positions into permanent roles wherever 
necessary. The Committee recommends that regularisation of employment will not 
only enhance job security for researchers and scientists but also ensure continuity 
in long-term research projects. Additionally, for institutions such as TMC, where 
medical professionals are in high demand, the Committee recommends expanding 
recruitment efforts and increasing budgetary support for healthcare staff and 
researchers.

 The Committee also urges the Department to strengthen NFC’s domestic 
production capabilities and recommends scaling up indigenous manufacturing of 
nuclear fuel materials to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The Committee 
recommends the Department to invest in R&D for next-generation nuclear fuels, 
including Thorium-based fuel fabrication for India’s three-stage nuclear program.  
(Para 3.38) 
 The Committee notes that, for BE 2025-26, BHAVINI has been allocated 
₹374 crore, significantly lower than the ₹600 crore in Revised Estimates (RE) for 
2024-25. This marks a reduction of ₹226 crore. However, the Committee observes 
that, in 2024-25, BHAVINI's actual expenditure of ₹390 crore was lower than RE 
of ₹600 crore, indicating underutilization of funds due to delays in commissioning 
process.                                                                                                            (Para 3.41) 
 The Committee urges the Department that BHAVINI should prioritise 
remaining integrated commissioning activities and ensure that criticality is 
achieved by 2025-26. Acknowledging the reduction of ₹226 crore in 2025-26 
allocations from ₹600 crore in RE 2024-25, the Committee recommends additional 
financial support at the RE stage to facilitate smooth commissioning and post-
criticality testing.                                                                                          (Para 3.42) 
100 GW Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat 2047 
The Committee recognizes the strategic importance of this initiative in 
ensuring a sustainable, low-carbon energy future but acknowledges significant 
challenges that need to be addressed to make this target achievable.         (Para 4.1) 
 

41 
 
The Committee notes that scaling up from the projected 55 GW to 100 GW 
by 2047 will require substantial investment, regulatory reforms, and policy 
interventions.                                                                                                     (Para 4.2) 
The Committee acknowledges that achieving 100 GW of nuclear capacity 
by 2047 requires a structured and phased approach. Instead of focusing solely on a 
long-term 100 GW target, the Committee recommends phased capacity additions, 
with clear short-term (2030), medium-term (2040), and long-term (2047) 
milestones. The Committee recommends that 2031-32 projection of 22.48 GW 
should serve as a baseline, with subsequent capacity additions planned in 
alignment with investment inflows, policy reforms, and domestic manufacturing 
capabilities.                                                                                                       (Para 4.4) 
 The Committee notes that nearly 50% of the 100 GW capacity is expected 
to come from private sector participation and recommends establishing a robust 
financial model that includes Government incentives, Viability Gap Funding 
(VGF), and sovereign guarantees to attract both domestic and foreign investments. 
The Committee suggests that legislative amendments to the Atomic Energy Act 
and Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act should be expedited to encourage 
private investment in nuclear power generation.                                          (Para 4.5) 
 The Committee emphasizes the importance of Small Modular Reactors 
(SMRs) and Bharat Small Reactors (BSRs) in achieving the 100 GW target. The 
Committee recommends that SMRs and BSRs should be deployed in remote 
regions and industrial zones to support decentralized energy generation. The 
Committee also urges the Department to accelerate Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) 
deployment, with the 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) expected 
to attain first criticality by March 2026 and completion by September 2026.  
                                                                                                                            (Para 4.6) 
 
NUCLEAR ENERGY MISSION FOR R&D OF SMALL MODULAR 
REACTORS (SMRS) 
 To support SMR development, the Committee recommends prioritizing 
demonstration projects, ensuring that the first set of SMRs is successfully deployed 
and operational before scaling up production. Furthermore, international 
collaboration with established nuclear agencies should be pursued to adopt best 
practices in reactor design and safety protocols. The Committee also recommends 
prioritising domestic SMR research and pilot projects to ensure economic 
viability.                                                                                                             (Para 5.3) 
The Committee recommends that initial funding should focus on BSMR 
and GCMMR demonstration plants before large-scale commercialisation.  
 (Para 5.4) 
 
BHARAT SMALL REACTORS (BSR) AND PUBLIC-PRIVATE 
PARTNERSHIP IN INFRASTRUCTURE 
The Committee notes that the existing Atomic Energy Act and the Civil 
Liability for Nuclear Damage Act have been revised to facilitate private 
participation while ensuring safety and security standards are met. However, the 
Committee notes that several key concerns still remain. The Committee observes 
that ensuring strict compliance with nuclear safety protocols, waste management 
regulations, and radiation protection measures is crucial to avoid potential 

42 
 
hazards. The Committee expresses concern that regulatory uncertainties 
regarding liability and risk-sharing mechanisms could deter private investors.  
                                                                                                                (Para 6.2) 
                                              
The Committee also stresses that India’s strategic control over critical 
nuclear technologies must not be compromised through excessive reliance on 
private enterprises. To mitigate these risks, the Committee recommends that the 
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) be strengthened to enforce stringent 
compliance measures for private sector entities. The Committee recommends that 
the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) must enforce compliance measures 
for private players. The Committee urges the Department to develop clear 
contractual frameworks and risk-sharing mechanisms. The Committee also 
suggests that clear contractual frameworks may be developed, ensuring 
transparent agreements that prioritise safety, security, and accountability in 
nuclear energy projects.                                                                                   (Para 6.3) 
TATA MEMORIAL CENTRE (TMC) 
The Committee notes that TMC's actual expenditure for 2023-24 was 
₹1688.93 crore, reflecting higher-than-expected financial utilisation. For 2024-25, 
the Revised Estimate (RE) was ₹1439.02 crore, with actual utilisation already 
reaching ₹1746.27 crore by January 2025, indicating an increase in spending on 
cancer care and research. The proposed BE 2025-26 for revenue (salary) was 
₹1164.55 crore, but only ₹980 crore was sanctioned, leading to a shortfall of 
₹184.55 crore. The Committee also notes that ₹1034.30 crore was proposed by the 
Department for BE 2025-26 but only ₹550 crore were sanctioned, reflecting a 
shortfall of ₹484.30 crore.                                                                                (Para 7.4) 
 The Committee acknowledges the effective financial management by TMC 
and recommends sustained funding to support ongoing and future initiatives. The 
Committee also recognises the importance of expansion of new cancer hospitals 
across the country and urges for timely completion of ongoing projects. The 
Committee commends TMC’s leadership in oncology research and recommends 
continued government funding for R&D.                                                      (Para 7.5) 
 The Committee recognises the Tata Memorial Centre’s outstanding 
contributions to India’s cancer care landscape. With consistent financial backing 
from DAE, TMC has expanded its network of cancer hospitals, pioneered new 
research in oncology, and strengthened preventive care initiatives. However, 
increasing cancer incidence necessitates further expansion of healthcare 
infrastructure, sustained investment in R&D, and enhanced public outreach 
programmes. The Committee urges the Government to ensure continued support 
for TMC’s initiatives to make cancer care affordable and accessible to all. 
(Para 7.6) 
 The Committee recommends increased Government funding for subsidised 
cancer treatment at TMC hospitals and affiliated institutions. The Committee also 
recommends that the National Cancer Grid (NCG) should be strengthened to 
ensure uniform pricing policies for cancer care across all NCG-affiliated hospitals 
to avoid cost disparities. The Committee urges the DAE that R&D in indigenous 
pharmaceutical production should be prioritised, focusing on generic versions of 
expensive cancer drugs to reduce dependence on costly imports. The Committee is 
of the opinion that TMC and the DAE should collaborate with Indian 
pharmaceutical industries to develop cost-effective versions of immunotherapy 
drugs, targeted therapies, and biologics for affordability.                           (Para 7.7) 

43 
 
 The Committee taking note of advancements in the field of radiotherapy, 
recommends increased investment in R&D under TMC and DAE for next-
generation chemotherapy and radiotherapy innovations to improve treatment 
outcomes and affordability. The Committee also recommends that Proton Beam 
Therapy (PBT) and Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) should be 
expanded, as these offer precise tumour targeting with fewer side effects, reducing 
long-term treatment costs.                                                                               (Para 7.8) 
 The  Committee strongly recommends that TMC and DAE should engage 
with corporate entities and industry leaders to create dedicated CSR funds for 
subsidising cancer treatments.The Committee recommends introduction of 
Corporate-sponsored free treatment schemes, where large private enterprises can 
support treatment for underprivileged cancer patients in TMC hospitals. The 
Committee recommends fast-tracking the establishment of new TMC-affiliated 
cancer hospitals in tier-2 and tier-3 cities, ensuring better regional access to 
quality cancer care.                                                                                          (Para 7.9) 
 The  Committee recommends increased budgetary allocations to DAE and 
TMC for advanced oncology research, particularly in nuclear medicine, gene 
therapy, and radio-immunotherapy. The Committee urges the DAE to encourage 
institutional research collaborations between TMC, IITs, and AIIMS to develop 
low-cost, high-efficacy cancer treatments. The Committee also observes that 
Government-supported clinical trial funding should be enhanced, ensuring greater 
participation in global cancer research initiatives. The Committee firmly believes 
that TMC and DAE must adopt a multi-faceted approach to enhance cost-effective 
cancer treatment and therapies in India. Sustained government support, increased 
corporate participation, and advancements in research will ensure that high-
quality cancer treatment remains accessible to all sections of society.      (Para 7.10) 
 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
  
However, the Committee observes that recruitment delays still persist, and 
several advertised posts remain unfilled.                                                       (Para 8.5) 
 
The high vacancy rates across DAE institutions raise serious concerns 
about workforce planning, recruitment efficiency, and the overall sustainability of 
nuclear and research projects in India. The Committee expresses its concerns over 
these vacancies, especially in key operational areas such as nuclear power 
generation, research, and mineral exploration. The shortage of skilled personnel 
could lead to delays in research and development, inefficiencies in plant 
operations, and constraints in nuclear fuel production, ultimately affecting the 
country's nuclear energy programme. To address this issue, the Committee 
strongly recommends an immediate recruitment drive to fill the existing vacancies. 
It is imperative that recruitment processes be streamlined to ensure timely hiring 
of personnel in technical, scientific, and operational roles. A review of existing 
workforce policies should be undertaken to identify areas where delays occur in 
the hiring process, and necessary reforms should be implemented. The DAE must 
adopt modern human resource management strategies to attract and retain talent, 
ensuring competitive salaries, career progression opportunities, and research 
grants for professionals in nuclear science, energy, and advanced research.  
(Para 8.6) 
  

44 
 
The Committee observes with great concern contractual employment and 
temporary staffing, particularly in research institutions such as TIFR. The 
Committee urges a review of these employment practices and recommends 
converting long-term contractual positions into permanent roles wherever 
necessary. The Committee recommends that regularisation of employment will not 
only enhance job security for researchers and scientists but also ensure continuity 
in long-term research projects. Additionally, for institutions such as TMC, where 
medical professionals are in high demand, the Committee recommends expanding 
recruitment efforts and increasing budgetary support for healthcare staff and 
researchers.             (Para 8.7)
