1. INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Department of Science & Technology (DST) stands as the premier nodal agency in 
India dedicated to fortifying the nation's Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) landscape. It 
plays a pivotal role in identifying critical gaps within the S&T sectors, formulating strategic plans 
and policies to address societal needs, and fostering emerging areas of science and technology to 
meet future demands. DST acts as a vital bridge, connecting the science and technology domains 
with various Government horizontals and verticals, academia, Research and Development (R&D) 
laboratories, institutions, and industries, ensuring a cohesive and collaborative ecosystem. 
1.2 With the overarching goal of enhancing India's S&T capacity and capability, DST 
spearheads the largest extramural R&D support in the country. This is achieved through three 
comprehensive umbrella schemes: (i) Science and Technology (S&T) Institutional and Human 
Capacity Building, (ii) Research and Development, and (iii) Innovation, Technology Development, 
and Deployment. These schemes are designed to empower scientists across diverse institutions and 
disciplines through a competitive framework, thereby reinforcing India's education system, 
scientific and industrial R&D. 
1.3 In a significant move to streamline operations and enhance flexibility in fund allocation, 
these three umbrella schemes have been consolidated into a single, unified initiative named ‘Vigyan 
Dhara’. This integration ensures a more efficient and adaptive flow of resources across programs, 
fostering greater innovation and impact. 
1.4 DST remains steadfast in its mission to strengthen the national STI ecosystem, positioning 
India as a global leader in science and technology. By driving positive transformations, DST aims 
to contribute to a safer, more secure, and prosperous society, while proactively preparing for future 
challenges and disruptions. Through its relentless efforts, DST continues to catalyze advancements 
that not only address current societal needs but also pave the way for a sustainable and 
technologically advanced future. 
1.5 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the 
Department of Science & Technology in its meeting held on 19th February, 2025.

4.4 On scrutiny of budgetary allocations of the Department, it is observed that ₹ 2000 crore was 
allocated in B.E. 2024-25 under the head ‘National Research Foundation (NRF)’ which was 
revised to ₹ 200 crore at R.E. stage. It is further observed that no amount was spent under the head 
till 31st January, 2025. The Committee sought reasons for nil expenditure in 2024-25. In a written 
reply, the Department submitted that the provisions of the ANRF Act were notified on 5th 
February, 2024 and with this the ANRF came into existence. After operationalization, the 
Executive Council (EC) and the Governing Board (GB) of ANRF were constituted and notified by 
the Government on 29.06.2024. The first meeting of Executive Council (EC) of ANRF and the 
Governing Board (GB) of ANRF were held on 22.08.2024 and 10.09.2024 respectively. 
Thereafter, ANRF initiated call for online proposals during the period from October, 2024 to 
February, 2025 under the following new ANRF schemes; namely (i) Prime Minister Early Career 
Research Grant (PMECRG) (ii) Mission for Advancement in High-impact Areas (MAHA): EV-
Mission, (iii) Inclusivity Research Grant (IRG) and (iv) Partnerships for Accelerated Innovation 
and Research (PAIR) and these research proposals are under scrutiny/finalization at various stages 
for funding by ANRF. The Department further informed that as only two months (February-
March) were left during FY 2024-25, the budget allocation, was reduced from ₹ 2000 crore (BE 
2024-25) to ₹ 200 crore in RE 2024-25, keeping the financial prudence in mind. For the Financial 
Year 2025-26, the Department will ensure that the entire budget allocation of ₹ 2000 crore (BE 
2025-26) be utilized fully for funding the schemes already initiated and the new schemes to be 
introduced during the year 2025-26. 
4.5 The Committee acknowledges and appreciates the establishment of the Anusandhan 
National Research Foundation (ANRF) as a significant and progressive initiative to 
strengthen research and innovation in the country. However, the Committee is of the view 
that the Department could have demonstrated greater foresight in expediting the procedural 
formalities and operationalization of the ANRF. With better planning and timely execution, a 
portion of the allocated funds could have been effectively utilized during the financial year. 
The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to ensure a more structured and time-bound 
approach in the future to optimize the utilization of budgetary allocations, thereby facilitating 
the timely implementation of research initiatives under ANRF. 
 
5. NATIONAL QUANTUM MISSION (NQM)  
5.1 The Department informed the Committee that one of the thrust areas for the year 2025-26 is 
National Quantum Mission (NQM). It was approved by the Union Cabinet on 19th April 2023 at a 
total cost of ₹6003.65 crore for a period of eight years from 2023-24 to 2030-31.  
 
5.2 Under the Mission, four Thematic Hubs comprising of 14 Technical Groups having 17 
Project Teams across India, involving nearly 152 researchers from 43 institutions have been 
established, each dedicated to a specific technology vertical:  
(i) Quantum Computing at IISc. Bengaluru; 
(ii) Quantum Communication at IIT Madras in association with C-DOT, New Delhi; 
(iii) Quantum Sensing & Metrology at IIT Bombay; and 
(iv) Quantum Materials & Devices at IIT Delhi 

10 
 
5.3 The Mission objectives include developing intermediate-scale quantum computers with 20-
50 physical qubits in 3 years, 50-100 physical qubits in 5 years and 50-1000 physical qubits in 8 
years in various platforms like superconducting and photonic technology. Satellite-based secure 
quantum communications between ground stations over a range of 2000 kilometers within India, 
long-distance secure quantum communications with other countries, inter-city quantum key 
distribution over 2000 km as well as multi-node Quantum networks with quantum memories are 
also some of the deliverables of the Mission. The National Quantum Mission will focus on 
developing magnetometers with high sensitivity in atomic systems and atomic clocks for precision 
timing, communications, and navigation. It will also support the design and synthesis of quantum 
materials such as superconductors, novel semiconductor structures, and topological materials for the 
fabrication of quantum devices. Single photon sources/detectors, and entangled photon sources will 
also be developed for quantum communications, sensing, and metrological applications. The 
Mission would greatly benefit various sectors including communication, health, financial, energy 
with applications in drug design, space, banking, security etc. The Mission will also provide a huge 
boost to National priorities like Digital India, Make in India, Skill India and Stand-up India, Start-
up India, Self-reliant India and Sustainable Development Goals (SDG). 
5.4 The Committee enquired about the physical achievements of the Mission, and was informed 
that IIT Bombay has established the section – 8 Company in the area of Quantum Sensing & 
Metrology namely Qmet Tech Foundation in October 2024. Similarly, IIT Madras in association 
with C-DoT, New Delhi has established IITM CDOT Samgnya Technologies Foundation in 
December 2024 in the area of Quantum Communication. 
5.5 The Committee notes that the ₹ 427 crores were allocated in B.E. 2024-25 which were 
significantly reduced to ₹ 86 crores and Department could spent only 64.30 per cent of the 
R.E. till 31st January, 2025. Even after such gross under-utilization of funds, ₹ 600 crores has 
been allocated for this Mission in B.E. 2025-26. The Committee enquired about the increased 
budget allocation for the National Quantum Mission (NQM) in B.E. 2025-26 and the 
Department informed that the increased allocations will play a pivotal role in expanding and 
scaling up ongoing initiatives while accelerating the development of a robust quantum 
technology ecosystem in India. A significant portion of this funding will be dedicated to 
strengthening the four established Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs), each focused on a key vertical—
Quantum Computing, Quantum Communication, Quantum Sensing & Metrology, and 
Quantum Materials & Devices. The enhanced funding will empower these T-Hubs to fulfill 
their mandates effectively by: Technology Development, Human Resource Development, 
Entrepreneurship Development and Industry Collaborations and International 
Collaborations. 
5.6 The Committee acknowledges that the launch of a dedicated Mission for research in 
Quantum Technologies is a strategic and forward-looking initiative, aligning with global 
technological advancements. However, the underutilization of allocated funds raises concerns 
about the Department's commitment and operational efficiency. The Committee emphasizes 
the need for the Department to adopt a more proactive and results driven approach to ensure 
the Mission's success. Rather than merely playing catch-up to Google’s Willow and 
Microsoft’s Majorana 1, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department adopt an 
ambitious vision to position India as a global leader in Quantum Technology.

Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute of Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) is actively

Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) is a specialized R&D institute in the field of Astronomy,

D. Raman Research Institute (RRI), Bengaluru 
The Raman Research Institute (RRI) was founded by Indian Science Nobel Laureate Sir C V 
Raman in 1948, marking 2023 as its Platinum Jubilee Year (PJY). The research at the Institute 
spans mind-boggling spatial and temporal scales from the very large- galaxies, galaxy clusters and 
beyond, to the very small – on the scale of atoms; from processes that happen over millions and 
billions of years to ultrafast processes that occur in attoseconds. The Institute has designed and built 
POLIX, world's first instrument designed to operate in the medium X-ray band of 8 to 30 kilo 
electron Volt (keV) energy. It was launched onboard XPoSat mission by ISRO on 1st January, 2024. 
It is designed to detect the scattered X-rays, enabling X-ray polarisation measurements. After initial 
calibrations and tests, the first light was obtained in early February and since then, the instrument 
has been making scientific observations. 
6.12 The Committee commends the Raman Research Institute (RRI) for its outstanding 
contributions to scientific research across vast spatial and temporal scales, from cosmology to 
atomic physics.  
6.13 The successful design and development of POLIX, the world's first instrument

The Committee appreciates the Institute’s efforts in pioneering X-ray polarisation

requested to comply with the Karmayogi Guidelines vide DO letter from Secretary, DST. 
V. Two Immersion programmes for newly recruited scientists have been conducted. 

19 
 
VI. Quarterly incentive for top three karmayogis has been introduced. 
VII. Conducted multiple workshops for enhancing skills of its Office. 
7.6 The Committee observes that the existing provisions for capacity building and skill 
enhancement are inadequate in effectively cultivating scientific talent. To address this gap, the 
Committee strongly recommends that the Department formulate a comprehensive policy 
dedicated to capacity building programs for its staff. This policy should focus on structured 
training initiatives, skill development, and continuous learning opportunities. Additionally, 
the Department should actively explore and establish collaborations with internationally 
renowned scientific institutions to facilitate knowledge exchange, exposure to global best 
practices, and advanced research training. 
 
 
  

20 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS-AT A GLANCE 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2025-26. 
 
A significant restructuring has taken place in the funding mechanism for institutional 
and human capacity building. The previously existing three schemes under this category have 
been merged into a single entity called 'Vigyan Dhara,' which has now been allocated ₹1,425 
crore for the upcoming year. This consolidation suggests a move towards greater efficiency in 
fund utilization and streamlined administration. While this restructuring is intended to 
simplify processes, it will be crucial to ensure that it does not lead to disruptions in existing 
projects.                                                                                                                                (Para 2.8) 
 
The Committee emphasizes the need to ensure that administrative and procedural 
challenges do not become significant obstacles to the Department's planned activities in the 
long term. It, therefore, recommends that the Department exercise due diligence in 
managing its expenditures to guarantee optimal fund utilization for 2025-26 while ensuring 
the successful achievement of its set objectives. Furthermore, the Committee urges the 
Department to make every possible effort in the current financial year to compensate for the 
suboptimal performance recorded during 2024-25.                                                    (Para 2.10) 
  
RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT & INNOVATION FUND 
Although the Committee acknowledges the bold initiatives undertaken by the 
Department to encourage private sector participation in cutting-edge research in deep tech 
and sunrise sectors, it also recognizes certain concerns. These include the potential risk of 
fund misallocation, the competence of fund managers in identifying suitable recipients and 
impactful projects, implications for national security, the limited rate of return on investment, 
the possibility of private entities benefiting disproportionately at the Government's expense, 
and the extent to which the outcomes of such research will ultimately benefit the common 
citizen. The Committee is also concerned that such a substantial allocation of funds could 
have yielded a significant impact if directed towards government institutions. Therefore, the 
Committee strongly recommends that the Department should consider these apprehensions 
while formulating the detailed framework and guidelines to implement this scheme. (Para 3.6) 
ANUSANDHAN NATIONAL RESEARCH FOUNDATION  
The Committee acknowledges and appreciates the establishment of the Anusandhan 
National Research Foundation (ANRF) as a significant and progressive initiative to 
strengthen research and innovation in the country. However, the Committee is of the view 
that the Department could have demonstrated greater foresight in expediting the procedural 
formalities and operationalization of the ANRF. With better planning and timely execution, a 
portion of the allocated funds could have been effectively utilized during the financial year. 
The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to ensure a more structured and time-bound 
approach in the future to optimize the utilization of budgetary allocations, thereby facilitating 
the timely implementation of research initiatives under ANRF. 
                                                                                                                                   (Para 4.5) 
NATIONAL QUANTUM MISSION (NQM)  
 
The Committee notes that the ₹ 427 crores were allocated in B.E. 2024-25 which were 
significantly reduced to ₹ 86 crores and Department could spent only 64.30 per cent of the 
R.E. till 31st January, 2025. Even after such gross under-utilization of funds, ₹ 600 crores has 

21 
 
been allocated for this Mission in B.E. 2025-26. The Committee enquired about the increased 
budget allocation for the National Quantum Mission (NQM) in B.E. 2025-26 and the 
Department informed that the increased allocations will play a pivotal role in expanding and 
scaling up ongoing initiatives while accelerating the development of a robust quantum 
technology ecosystem in India. A significant portion of this funding will be dedicated to 
strengthening the four established Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs), each focused on a key vertical—
Quantum Computing, Quantum Communication, Quantum Sensing & Metrology, and 
Quantum Materials & Devices. The enhanced funding will empower these T-Hubs to fulfill 
their mandates effectively by: Technology Development, Human Resource Development, 
Entrepreneurship Development and Industry Collaborations and International 
Collaborations.                                                                                                                     (Para 5.5) 
The Committee acknowledges that the launch of a dedicated Mission for research in 
Quantum Technologies is a strategic and forward-looking initiative, aligning with global 
technological advancements. However, the underutilization of allocated funds raises concerns 
about the Department's commitment and operational efficiency. The Committee emphasizes 
the need for the Department to adopt a more proactive and results driven approach to ensure 
the Mission's success. Rather than merely playing catch-up to Google’s Willow and 
Microsoft’s Majorana 1, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department adopt an 
ambitious vision to position India as a global leader in Quantum Technology.            (Para 5.6) 
PERFORMANCE OF THE AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS UNDER THE 
DEPARTMENT DURING 2024-25 
 
The Committee commends the efforts of Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute of Medical 
Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) in advancing biomedical technology development, 
fostering industry collaboration, and translating research into commercially viable products. 
The successful development and market launch of innovations such as the AG Chitra 
Tuberculosis Diagnostic Kit, Titanium Nitride (TiN) coated coronary stent, Automatic 
Contrast Injector, and Automated Trolley e-drive highlight the Institute’s significant 
contributions to the healthcare sector.                                                                              (Para 6.6) 
 
Given the impact of these developments, the Committee recommends that the 
Department extend greater financial and infrastructural support to SCTIMST to further 
strengthen its research and development capabilities. Additionally, the Committee urges the 
Department to facilitate wider adoption and deployment of these indigenous technologies 
across healthcare institutions in India, ensuring affordability, accessibility, and scalability. 
The Committee also emphasizes the need for an enabling ecosystem to promote industry 
partnerships and expedite regulatory clearances, thereby accelerating the commercialization 
of innovative medical technologies for the benefit of the healthcare sector and the common 
citizen.                                                                                                                                   (Para 6.7) 
 
The Committee acknowledges the significant contributions of the International 
Advanced Research Centre for Powder Metallurgy and New Materials (ARCI) in advancing 
research across critical domains such as energy storage, nanomaterials, engineered coatings, 
additive manufacturing, and advanced powder metallurgy. The successful development and 
technology transfer of battery-grade Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) as a cathode material for 
Li-ion batteries to M/s. Altmin Pvt. Ltd., Hyderabad, marks a commendable step towards 
strengthening India's indigenous battery manufacturing capabilities.                         (Para 6.8) 
 
In view of the growing demand for energy storage solutions, the Committee 
recommends that the Department provide enhanced support to ARCI for scaling up its 
research and accelerating commercialization efforts in battery technology and other advanced 

22 
 
materials. The Committee also emphasizes the need for wider industry collaboration, strategic 
partnerships, and policy interventions to facilitate domestic production, reduce import 
dependency, and position India as a global leader in energy storage technologies. 
Furthermore, it is imperative to ensure that such technological advancements are leveraged 
for broader industrial applications and made accessible to multiple stakeholders, thereby 
fostering self-reliance and sustainability in the sector.                                                    (Para 6.9) 
 
The Committee recognizes the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) as a premier 
institution dedicated to research and development in Astronomy, Astrophysics, and 
Astronomy Instrumentation. The successful fabrication and verification of the first 1.44-
meter mirror segment for the international Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) at the India-TMT 
Optics Fabrication Facility is a significant achievement, demonstrating India's capability in 
high-precision optics and advanced astronomical instrumentation.                            (Para 6.10) 
The Committee recommends that the Department extend continued support to IIA for 
the successful completion of India’s commitments to the TMT project and other international 
collaborations in astrophysics. Additionally, the Committee urges the Department to explore 
opportunities for further strengthening indigenous expertise in astronomical instrumentation, 
including the development of next-generation telescopes and space-based observational 
facilities. Ensuring adequate funding, infrastructure, and skilled workforce development will 
be crucial for positioning India as a global leader in cutting-edge astronomical research and 
technology.                                                                                                                          (Para 6.11) 
 
The Committee commends the Raman Research Institute (RRI) for its outstanding 
contributions to scientific research across vast spatial and temporal scales, from cosmology to 
atomic physics.                                                                                                                   (Para 6.12) 
The successful design and development of POLIX, the world's first instrument 
operating in the medium X-ray band (8 to 30 keV), and its launch onboard ISRO’s XPoSat 
mission on 1st January 2024, is a remarkable achievement in space-based X-ray astronomy. 
The Committee appreciates the Institute’s efforts in pioneering X-ray polarisation 
measurements, which hold immense potential for advancing our understanding of high-
energy astrophysical phenomena. In light of these achievements, the Committee recommends 
that the Department provide continued support to RRI for further advancements in space-
based astronomy and astrophysics. Strengthening collaborations with national and 
international agencies, investing in cutting-edge instrumentation, and facilitating knowledge 
transfer will be crucial in reinforcing India’s leadership in high-energy astrophysics research. 
The Committee also emphasizes the need for sustained funding, enhanced infrastructure, and 
skilled human resources to propel future discoveries and innovations in this critical domain.  
(Para 6.13) 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING  
The Committee expresses deep concern over the significant number of vacancies in the 
Department, as well as in the Autonomous Institutions (AIs) under its administrative control. 
It is particularly dismayed by the persistent reliance on contractual appointments as a 
stopgap measure to address short-term manpower shortages. The Committee firmly believes 
that a highly skilled and dedicated workforce is the cornerstone of any scientific institution’s 
success and output. Therefore, it strongly recommends that the Department adopt a mission-
mode approach to expeditiously fill all vacant positions. This will ensure the availability of a 
competent and stable workforce, essential for advancing scientific research and institutional 
excellence.                                                                                                                            (Para 7.4) 

23 
 
The Committee observes that the existing provisions for capacity building and skill 
enhancement are inadequate in effectively cultivating scientific talent. To address this gap, the 
Committee strongly recommends that the Department formulate a comprehensive policy 
dedicated to capacity building programs for its staff. This policy should focus on structured 
training initiatives, skill development, and continuous learning opportunities. Additionally, 
the Department should actively explore and establish collaborations with internationally 
renowned scientific institutions to facilitate knowledge exchange, exposure to global best 
practices, and advanced research training.                                                                       (Para 7.6)

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
 The Government of India has set up the Space Commission and the Department of 
Space (DOS) in 1972. Department of Space is responsible for implementing the policies 
framed by the Space Commission. These are carried out through the Indian Space Research 
Organisation (ISRO), Indian National Space Promotion & Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe) 
and the Grant-in-aid institutions viz., Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National 
Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-
SAC), Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL) and Indian Institute of Space Science and 
Technology (IIST). 
1.2 The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located 
in Bangalore. The Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall 
programmes like Satellite Communication, Satellite Navigation, Earth Observation, Space 
Transportation Systems, Space Science and Planetary Exploration, Climate & Atmospheric 
Programme, Disaster Management Support, National Natural Resources Management System 
(NNRMS), International Co-Operation, Capacity Building, Media & Public Relations, 
Budget & Economic Analysis and Human Resources Development. 
1.3 The activities of Department of Space (DOS) are broadly organized under four 
umbrella schemes namely 
 Space Technology - development of launch vehicles, satellites, manned space mission, 
R&D in Space Technology such as propulsion, navigational satellite systems, 
indigenization of Space materials & components, etc.  
 
 Space Applications - major Projects/activities such as Earth Observation Navigation 
Missions, Tele-medicine, Tele-education, Disaster Management Support, etc are 
undertaken. 
 
 Space Sciences - projects towards Space sciences and planetary exploration are 
undertaken. Major projects undertaken under the scheme include Indian Lunar Mission - 
Chandrayaan-3, Aditya-L1 mission, XPoSat, Space Docking Experiment.  
 
 INSAT Satellite Systems- This programme is envisaged to provide satellite based 
communication services in the country.  
1.4 Major Centres / Units of DOS/ISRO: 
a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the 
technology base for the country’s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development 
b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities located at Bangalore and 
Thiruvananthapuram, is responsible for development of liquid propulsion and 
cryogenic propulsion systems for satellite and launch vehicles 
c) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the 
spaceport of India providing launch base to indigenously built launch vehicles.  Also, 
it provides the facilities for processing of solid rocket motors 

2 
 
d) Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) is created with the responsibility to act as the 
lead centre for Human Space Flight Program. This centre is responsible for the 
execution of Gaganyaan programme that envisages sending a crew of astrounauts to 
space and bring back safely to earth.   
e) U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), Bangalore, is entrusted with the prime 
responsibility for development of satellites     
f) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad 
g) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite data 
acquisition and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision 
support for disaster management 
h) The Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bangalore  
i) ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC), Mahendragiri

a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution

Tirupati, conducts atmospheric research. 
c) The North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC) established as an 
autonomous body under the Department of Space provides space technology inputs 
for developmental activities in the North-Eastern Region.

under the Department with the objective of creating quality human resources tuned to 
suit the requirements of state-of-art space research programme.

a) The Antrix Corporation Limited, Bangalore, established in 1992, is a wholly owned 
Government Company for marketing space products and services.  
b) The NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), Bangalore, is another commercial arm of 
Indian Space Research Organization, with the primary objective of enabling Indian 
industries to scale up high-technology manufacturing and production base for Indian 
space programme.  
1.7 Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (INSPACe) 
Recently, the space sector was opened up to promote, handhold, regulate and 
authorise private enterprises and start-ups to undertake space activities by creation of an 
independent nodal agency under Department of Space - the Indian National Space Promotion 
and Authorization Center (IN-SPACe). This will enhance the contribution of space 
technology towards boosting space economy within the country.

4.  Establishment Expenditure of the Centre 
4.1    IN-SPACe 
  The Department in a written reply informed the Committee about the vision, mission 
and objectives of INSPACe. IN-SPACe aims to boost private sector participation in space 
activities, strengthen India’s space economy, and promote self-reliance in space technology. 
As a single-window agency, it facilitates start-ups, MSMEs, industries, and academic 
institutions in innovation and commercialisation within the space sector. Its key functions 
include:  
 
(i) Enabling private sector involvement in launch vehicle and satellite development. 

20 
 
(ii) Granting access to ISRO’s infrastructure for research, manufacturing, and testing. 
(iii) Overseeing the establishment of new space facilities by private players while ensuring 
compliance with safety and statutory guidelines. 
(iv) Facilitating launch campaigns and satellite registration for Indian private entities. 
(v) Encouraging technology sharing and collaboration to strengthen India’s space 
ecosystem. 
(vi) Managing an integrated launch manifest to align priorities of ISRO, public sector 
units, and private entities. 
(vii) Providing affordable access to ISRO’s high-tech facilities for private sector research 
and   development. 
The Department further informed that IN-SPACe actively promotes skill development 
and talent acquisition through short-term training courses in satellite technology, propulsion, 
and space communications to bridge industry skill gaps; academic partnerships with IIT 
Roorkee and universities to integrate space technology education; Pre-Incubation 
Entrepreneurship (PIE) Program, launched in June 2024, to mentor and support early-stage 
start-ups and recognition by NCVET as an awarding body, setting industry standards for 
space-related vocational education and training. 
4.2 The Department of Space highlighted the following key initiatives/actions under taken 
to support & enable the private-sector engagement in space activities:  
i. Regulatory and Policy Framework for Indian Space Sector 
Indian Space Policy – 2023 (ISP-2023) was brought out in April 2023, has identified 
the range of Space Activities undertaken by private players that require Authorization 
by IN-SPACe. 
Subsequently, IN-SPACe has brought out the Norms, Guidelines and Procedures 
(NGP) document for streamlining the authorization processes. 
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy provisions for the Space sector have been 
liberalized in prescribed sub sectors/activities, to attract potential foreign investors to 
invest in Indian companies in space sector. 
ii Enabling Access to Critical Infrastructure & Technical Facilities 
IN-SPACe enables & facilitates NGEs to access ISRO’s capital intensive testing 
facilities and launch infrastructure. IN-SPACe also facilitates NGEs to access & 
utilize standard test facilities at the IN-SPACe Technical labs established exclusively 
for developing and testing their technologies. All these facilities are offered to the 
Start-up and MSME at a price support. 
IN-SPACe in collaboration with ISRO, facilitates the opportunity to host payloads on 
POEM (PSLV orbital experimental module) platform to strengthen / complement the 
space-based research activities taking place in industry/academia within the country. 
IN-SPACe has also setup mechanisms to provide expert mentorship, and guidance to 
help NGEs develop & commercialize space technologies. 
iii Financial Support & Handholding for Space Startups and MSEs 
To accelerate promising start-ups, IN-SPACe had launched Seed Fund scheme to 
provide initial financial assistance to Indian early-stage space start-ups through a 

21 
 
grant of up to INR 1 cr. Under this scheme so far six (06) start-ups qualified for seed

Venture Capital Fund for Indian Space Sector: RFP for selection of Fund Managers to 
manage ₹1,000 Crore Venture Capital Fund for the Indian Space Sector issued in 
November-2024. Four (4) bids are received and are under evaluation. 
Technology Adoption Fund (TAF), a scheme to promote Indian Enterprise towards 
commercialization of early-stage technologies in the space sector is announced.

marginally by 4.88% from ₹226.08 crore in RE 2024-25 to ₹215.05 crore in BE 2025-26. The 
Committee inquired into the factors that have contributed to this reduction. The Committee 
asked the Department the manner in which it plans to optimize costs and maintain efficiency 
in ISRO’s administrative and operational activities despite the reduced allocation. The 
Department in a written reply informed that the marginal decrease in allocation under the 
subhead ISRO headquarters is mainly on account of reduced requirement towards online 
subscriptions in light of implementation of one nation one subscription by MHRD. The 
Department further informed the Committee that the ISRO Headquarters coordinates and 
administers the activities of ISRO Centres / Units and projects and provides programmatic 
directions for different verticals of space programme such as space transportation systems, 
space infrastructure, satellite communication, navigation, human space programme, capacity 
building, and space applications. Key activities undertaken by ISRO headquarters includes 
annual budget preparation and expenditure monitoring, setting up of common IT 
infrastructure, support for conference / symposia, capacity building and outreach activities. 
The Department assured the Committee that it has adequate provisions to cater to 
administrative and operational activities of ISRO headquarters. In case of additional 
requirements, the Department would approach the Ministry of Finance for additional funds at 
RE stage and through the mechanism of supplementary Grants. 
4.11  The Committee recommends that ISRO Headquarters should continue 
streamlining expenditure through improved cost optimisation measures, particularly in 
areas such as IT infrastructure, subscriptions, and operational expenses. The 
Committee notes the Department’s assurance that, if needed, it will seek additional 
funds through the Revised Estimates (RE) stage or Supplementary Grants. The 
Committee recommends that the Department continuously assess evolving needs and 
make timely requests to the Ministry of Finance to prevent any disruptions to ISRO’s 
core functions.

PRL serves as India’s premier institute for space and planetary sciences, conducting 
cutting-edge research in astrophysics, planetary exploration, and quantum technologies. 
Recent accomplishments include Discovery of exoplanets using the indigenous PARAS 
spectrograph, positioning India among a select group of nations with exoplanet detection 
capabilities; PRL’s Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) on Chandrayaan-3’s Pragyan 
rover providing critical evidence supporting the Lunar Magma Ocean Hypothesis; Pioneering

energy photonics;Research contributions in geochemical analysis confirming the ancient 
Saraswati River’s existence during the Harappan period. The future plans of PRL include 
active participation in Chandrayaan-4, Venus, and Mars missions, expanding quantum 
computing research, and advanced atmospheric modelling. The following table shows the

5.3   National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL)  
NARL conducts advanced research in atmospheric and space sciences, focusing on 
monitoring atmospheric processes, high-resolution weather modelling, and scientific 
observations to support space missions and other applications. It has developed high-power 
radio and optical instruments, many of which have been patented and transferred to industry. 
The Department informed that observatories in Hyderabad and Kolkata have been established 
to study key national issues, while the Venus Advanced Radar and Differential Absorption 
Lidar have been developed for planetary and atmospheric studies. NARL has also introduced 
AI/ML-based techniques for weather forecasting and atmospheric data analysis, built GNSS 
receiver networks for ionospheric and meteorological research, and improved rocket launch 
weather forecasting models. The airglow laboratory in Hyderabad and spectrograph in 
Gadanki contribute to studying atmospheric dynamics and space weather. Over 6.8 TB of 
climate data has been shared with scientists, and 184 research papers have been published in 
peer-reviewed journals. The institute has produced 17 PhDs and 97 dissertations, with many 
faculty members receiving national and international honours, including recognition from 
Stanford University, INSA, and the International Commission for Optics. Looking ahead, 
NARL aims to expand its research facilities, setting up more observatories across the country 
and establishing a national-level observational network. It seeks to develop indigenous 

26 
 
ground-based and space-borne instruments, enhance weather forecasting through water 
vapour and ionospheric mapping, and study the impact of rapid urbanisation on atmospheric 
conditions. The institute is also committed to strengthening collaboration with academic and 
national laboratories to achieve significant advancements in atmospheric and space research.

6. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Activities in the Department of Space 
The Committee notes that Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) activities within the 
Department of Space are carried out by two Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), 
namely Antrix Corporation Ltd and NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), in compliance with the 
Companies Act, 2013. Both entities allocate CSR funds to various social development 
projects, following strict guidelines to ensure transparency, accountability, and effective 
implementation. 
6.2 Antrix primarily implements its CSR projects through State Government 
Departments, allocating over 75% of its CSR funds for such initiatives. The selection of 
implementing agencies is conducted through rigorous due diligence, ensuring proven 
experience in social issues, strong governance, financial transparency, and robust monitoring 
mechanisms.  
6.3 NSIL, on the other hand, has established a Corporate Social Responsibility and 
Sustainable Development (CSR & SD) Committee, responsible for recommending CSR 
expenditure, monitoring CSR policies, and formulating an annual action plan. The selection 
of CSR projects follows a structured approach, including inviting proposals through its 
website and from ISRO centres/units. The approval of CSR projects is based on the 
feasibility of implementation, availability of skilled manpower, and previous experience. 
CSR activities may be carried out by the company itself or registered entities such as trusts, 
societies, or government-established organisations that meet the necessary legal and financial 
criteria. 
6.4 The Committee appreciates the structured approach adopted by both Antrix and 
NSIL in implementing CSR initiatives. However, it recommends that greater emphasis 
be placed on monitoring and evaluating the long-term impact of these projects. Given 
that Antrix spends the majority of its CSR funds through State Government 
Departments, the Committee recommends that a performance assessment framework 
be developed to track the effectiveness of these projects. 
6.5 The Committee acknowledges the role of the CSR & SD Committee in 
streamlining CSR initiatives under NSIL but recommends greater outreach to 
underrepresented communities, particularly in rural areas, to ensure that space 
technology and innovation contribute to broader societal benefits. The Committee also 
urges greater collaboration between NSIL and academic institutions, start-ups, and 
ISRO units to leverage space-based applications for social development projects. 
Furthermore, the Committee highlights the importance of ensuring that all CSR-
implementing agencies maintain high standards of governance, transparency, and 
efficiency. The Committee recommends that third-party audits and impact assessments 
be conducted regularly to ensure CSR funds are being utilised effectively and delivering 
measurable outcomes.

7.2 The Committee inquired into the manner in which this shortage will affect the 
efficiency and performance of ISRO and its affiliated PSUs, CPSEs, and Autonomous Bodies 
and the measures being taken to ensure that the Department's missions and projects are not 
impacted due to manpower shortages. The Department acknowledges the pressing issue of 
manpower shortages across ISRO, PSUs, CPSEs, and Autonomous Bodies, which currently 
stands at 3,927 vacancies. The Department informed the Committee that this shortage has 
impacted the operational efficiency and timely execution of projects, particularly as ISRO 
gears up for major missions such as the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), lunar sample 
return, and human spaceflight to the Moon by 2027. The Department informed the 
Committee that the accumulation of vacancies was primarily due to disruptions caused by 
COVID-19, sectoral reforms, and recruitment policy revisions, leading to a one-year delay in 
hiring. Additionally, security concerns in examination halls led to a four-month halt in 
recruitment activities in 2023, further compounding the backlog. The Department highlighted 
the key measures taken to expedite filling of vacancies which are as follows: 

30 
 
(i) The Department has initiated actions to fill about 1,950 posts before June 2025, with 
written tests and interviews for 1,060 posts underway and reporting planned for 889 selected 
candidates. However, administrative vacancies remain significantly high (2,008 out of 3,062 
positions), indicating challenges in processing personnel recruitment. 
(ii) To  meet the rising demands of space exploration and mission complexity, ISRO has 
proposed augmenting its workforce by at least 500 additional S&T personnel and increasing 
IT personnel by 80 posts to strengthen cyber security monitoring. 
(iii) The Department has implemented a centralised recruitment process under which 
hiring for general disciplines is conducted annually, covering about 70% of staffing needs. 
Additionally, quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises have been introduced to identify and 
resolve bottlenecks in hiring. 
7.3 The Committee recommends expediting the recruitment process to ensure that 
vacant posts, particularly for Scientists/Engineers and technical staff, are filled within 
the next six months. A dedicated recruitment task force should be established to oversee 
hiring efficiency, identify process bottlenecks, and ensure compliance with recruitment 
timelines. The Committee recommends that the Department must develop a structured 
workforce planning model, forecasting staffing needs for the next decade in alignment 
with ISRO’s Vision 2047. The Committee is concerned about the high vacancy rate in 
NSIL and Antrix, as it may impact India’s growing commercial space sector. It 
recommends an industry-specific recruitment approach to attract talent from both 
public and private space technology domains, ensuring that PSEs remain competitive 
and capable of supporting ISRO’s missions. 
7.4 The Committee supports the Department’s plan to engage S&T personnel on a 
tenure basis but recommends that flexible hiring models be expanded to include 
project-based contracts for emerging space technologies. 
7.5 The Committee notes that the backlog in hiring was caused partly due to delays 
during the COVID-19 period and recruitment policy revisions. It recommends 
increasing the frequency of centralised recruitment drives to ensure that vacancies do 
not accumulate in the future. Quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises should be 
conducted to track hiring progress and address any procedural challenges.

avoid delays in project execution and infrastructure development.                     (Para 3.7) 
 The Committee notes that the allocation for Space Applications has increased 
from ₹1,527.97 crores in R.E. 2024-25 to ₹1,706.79 crores in B.E. 2025-26.        (Para 3.8) 
The Committee appreciates the establishment of a data-sharing mechanism 
under the Indian Space Policy-2023 and recommends that the Department should 
expand access to high-resolution EO data for academic institutions, start-ups, and 
industry partners to encourage innovation in remote sensing applications. The 
Committee recommends that the Department should continue to enhance automated 
crop mapping, soil moisture analysis, and hydrological modelling to support accurate 
agriculture and water resource planning. The Committee also recommends 
collaborations with State Governments to ensure effective use of EO data for 
agricultural policy and climate resilience initiatives. The Committee supports the 
continuous development of the Bhoonidhi and Bhuvan portals and recommends user-
friendly enhancements to enable better data visualisation and integration with 
Government schemes.                                                                                             (Para 3.10) 

36 
 
     The Committee commends the Department’s role in providing over 300 flood 
maps and implementing flood early warning for the Godavari and Tapi rivers. The 
Department should extend this capability to more river basins, ensuring nationwide 
flood risk mitigation. Given the increasing incidents of forest fires and extreme weather 
events, the Committee recommends improving real-time forest fire monitoring and 
expanding the lightning observation system for better early warning. The Committee 
notes ISRO’s contribution to global disaster response efforts and recommends 
strengthening collaboration with international agencies to leverage EO data for 
humanitarian assistance and disaster management globally. The Committee encourages 
the Department to increase training programmes for disaster response agencies at 
national and state levels to ensure better utilisation of space-based disaster monitoring 
tools. The Committee supports the expansion of tele-education and telemedicine services 
and recommends prioritising remote and underserved areas, ensuring that satellite-
based communication bridges connectivity gaps in healthcare and education. 
 (Para 3.11) 
   The Committee observes that actual expenditure has consistently fallen short of 
budget estimates in recent years, with only ₹1,116.83 crore spent as of December 2024. 
The Committee recommends that the Department must strengthen financial planning 
and ensure timely fund utilisation to prevent delays in project execution. The 
Committee acknowledges the ₹178.82 crore increase in the BE 2025-26 allocation and 
supports the new R&D initiatives and facility expansions. The Committee urges the 
Department to ensure timely implementation of Geo-spatial database projects for land 
cover and land use monitoring, providing accurate and real-time information for 
environmental planning and disaster risk management. The Committee also 
recommends that the Department should provide detailed project-wise financial 
reporting, ensuring funds are allocated efficiently and spent according to planned 
objectives.                                                                                                                 (Para 3.12) 
   The Committee notes the substantial increase in the budgetary allocation 
under ‘Space Sciences’ from ₹127.24 crore in RE 2024-25 to ₹371.00 crore in BE 2025-
26, primarily allocated for the realisation of Chandrayaan-4, Venus Orbiter Mission, 
and TRISHNA, along with sponsored research activities at academic institutions. The 
Committee appreciates the Department’s efforts in advancing India's planetary 
exploration and scientific missions.                                                                       (Para 3.15) 
 The Committee recommends that the increased budget should be utilised 
effectively for timely development, testing, and execution of Chandrayaan-4, 
Chandrayaan-5, and Venus Orbiter Missions. Given the success of Mangalyaan (Mars 
Orbiter Mission - MOM), the Committee urges the Department to fast-track the 
approval and implementation of the Mars Lander Mission. The Committee 
recommends that ISRO should enhance international partnerships for planetary 
research and engage global space agencies and scientific institutions to maximise the 
scientific output from these missions.                                                                    (Para 3.16) 

37 
 
 The Committee appreciates the successful deployment of Aditya-L1 at Lagrange 
Point 1 and recommends that additional research projects should be initiated based on 
the data collected from the mission. The Committee acknowledges with pride that India 
is now the second country globally to launch an X-Ray polarimetry satellite. The 
Committee recommends ISRO to actively promote the use of XPoSat’s scientific data 
among astronomers and space research institutions.                                          (Para 3.17) 
 The Committee notes that the Chandrayaan-3 mission successfully completed its 
14-day operational period on the Moon in September 2023 and the global release of 
Chandrayaan-3’s scientific data on August 23, 2024, has further strengthened India’s 
contributions to lunar research. The Committee recommends that ISRO continue to 
build on Chandrayaan-3’s findings in its upcoming lunar exploration missions, 
particularly Chandrayaan-4 and Chandrayaan-5.                                              (Para 3.18) 
   The Committee expresses concern that actual expenditure has consistently been 
lower than budget estimates, with only ₹69.71 crore spent as of December 2024. The 
Committee recommends that the Department must streamline financial planning and 
ensure timely fund disbursement for approved projects. The Committee recommends 
that future space science budget allocations be linked to specific mission milestones, 
ensuring optimal resource utilisation.                                                                   (Para 3.19) 
  The Committee notes with concern that allocation under the Scheme- ‘INSAT 
Satellite Systems’ has decreased from ₹218.44 crore in R.E. 2024-25 to ₹207 crore in 
B.E. 2025-26.                                                                                                            (Para 3.20)  
The Committee acknowledges that the reduction in allocations under the 
Scheme’ ‘INSAT Satellite Systems’ is due to the programmatic realignment under the 
Indian Space Policy 2023. However, it recommends that the Department should review 
budgetary needs periodically to ensure that adequate funds are available for the 
development and launch of new satellites, particularly for Government and strategic 
users. While NSIL is responsible for building newer communication satellites, the 
Committee recommends that ISRO should continue developing advanced satellite 
technologies, to maintain India’s leadership in satellite-based communications. Since 
NSIL has been entrusted with commercial exploitation of GSAT/INSAT satellite 
capacity, the Committee recommends periodic evaluation of NSIL’s commercial 
performance and investment strategies to ensure that public resources are effectively 
utilised.                                                                                                                     (Para 3.21) 
The Committee recommends that the Department should actively involve private 
industry in the design, manufacturing, and deployment of communication satellites, 
ensuring a robust ecosystem for satellite-based services in India.                      (Para 3.22) 
 

38 
 
ESTABLISHMENT EXPENDITURE OF THE CENTRE 
      The Committee acknowledges the significant strides made by IN-SPACe in 
promoting private sector participation in the Indian space sector. The Committee 
recommends that IN-SPACe should develop a structured framework for private sector 
access to ISRO’s infrastructure, including transparent guidelines on facility usage 
charges, eligibility criteria, and priority allocation for research and commercial 
activities. In view of the fact that 75 Technology Transfer (ToT) agreements have been 
signed since 2020, the Committee recommends that IN-SPACe should expand its 
industry outreach, conduct awareness programs, and streamline ToT processes to 
increase private sector adoption of ISRO-developed technologies. The Committee notes 
that IN-SPACe has issued 56 authorisations and received 480 applications from 382 
Indian entities. To streamline processes and ensure timely approvals, the Committee 
recommends that IN-SPACe should establish clear timelines, a digital tracking system, 
and a public dashboard for real-time updates on authorisation requests and approvals.  
(Para 4.5) 
The Committee acknowledges the Decadal Vision and Strategy for the Indian 
Space Economy released by IN-SPACe and urges that it be translated into specific 
policy measures, investment plans, and regulatory refinements to accelerate the growth 
of India’s space sector.                                                                                              (Para 4.6) 
   The Committee appreciates IN-SPACe’s Seed Fund Scheme, which provides 
financial assistance of up to ₹1 crore to early-stage space start-ups in areas like 
agriculture, disaster management, urban development, and marine applications. Given 
its success, the Committee recommends expanding the scheme to include new focus 
areas such as defence applications, space-based AI analytics, and deep-space 
exploration. Additionally, the Committee acknowledges the announcement of a ₹1,000 
crore Venture Capital Fund and the Technology Adoption Fund (TAF) with ₹500 crore 
to transform early-stage technologies into market-ready products. The Committee 
recommends fast-tracking the operationalisation of these funding schemes, ensuring 
broad industry participation and transparent selection processes. The Committee 
appreciates IN-SPACe’s partnerships with IIT Roorkee and other universities for space 
technology education. The Committee recommends that similar collaborations should 
be extended to more universities and technical institutes, incorporating space research 
into engineering and science curricula. The Committee suggests that IN-SPACe should 
launch awareness campaigns, roadshows, and workshops to attract more start-ups, 
investors, and industry players to the Indian space sector.                                   (Para 4.7) 
 The Committee notes IN-SPACe’s ongoing efforts to establish space-based Earth 
Observation (EO) services under a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model and the 
development of common technical facilities in space manufacturing clusters with a 
funding cap of ₹100 crores per state. The Committee recommends that modalities for 
these initiatives should be finalised at the earliest and that a structured implementation 
roadmap with periodic progress reports should be made available. The Committee also 

39 
 
recommends that the Investment Incentive Scheme for private-sector manufacturing of 
space systems should be formulated with clear eligibility criteria and incentive 
structures.                                                                                                                   (Para 4.8) 
   The Committee observes that several Indian start-ups, supported by IN-SPACe, 
have begun competing globally, offering cost-effective satellite solutions, space-based 
data services, and launch capabilities. However, to enhance their competitiveness, the 
Committee believes that more structured support, funding mechanisms, and 
international collaborations are required.                                                              (Para 4.9) 
 The Committee recommends that ISRO Headquarters should continue 
streamlining expenditure through improved cost optimisation measures, particularly in 
areas such as IT infrastructure, subscriptions, and operational expenses. The 
Committee notes the Department’s assurance that, if needed, it will seek additional 
funds through the Revised Estimates (RE) stage or Supplementary Grants. The 
Committee recommends that the Department continuously assess evolving needs and 
make timely requests to the Ministry of Finance to prevent any disruptions to ISRO’s 
core functions.                                                                                                          (Para 4.11) 
AUTONOMOUS BODIES 
 However, the Committee expresses concern over fund utilisation trends, 
particularly in FY 2024-25. As of December 2024, only ₹168.50 crore had been utilised 
against a RE allocation of ₹220.08 crore, indicating slower-than-expected project 
execution. The Committee notes PRL’s contributions to advanced atmospheric 
modelling and its relevance for climate change studies. The Committee urges the 
Department to strengthen collaborations between PRL and national meteorological 
agencies to leverage its expertise in climate forecasting. Given the low fund utilisation 
rate in FY 2024-25, The Committee recommends that PRL should adopt a quarterly 
financial review system to track spending progress and ensure that funds are allocated 
efficiently. The Committee also recommends a faster procurement and project 
execution mechanism to prevent delays in research infrastructure and laboratory 
expansions.                                                                                                                 (Para 5.2) 
 The Committee recommends that NARL should expedite the expansion of its 
research infrastructure by setting up additional atmospheric observatories across 
different parts of the country. Given the growing importance of self-reliance in space-
based atmospheric research, the Committee urges NARL to accelerate the development 
of indigenous ground-based and space-borne instruments. The Committee notes that 
the gap between budgetary allocations and actual expenditure by NARL. The 
Committee recommends that NARL should adopt a structured financial planning model 
to improve fund utilisation, streamline project timelines, and ensure the timely 
execution of approved research activities.                                                                                                          
             (Para 5.4) 

40 
 
 The Committee notes the declining trend in actual expenditure compared to 
budgetary allocations under NE-SAC. In 2022-23, only ₹24.27 crore was spent against a 
budget estimate (BE) of ₹37.50 crore, and in 2024-25, actual expenditure as of 
December 2024 remains significantly low at ₹29.46 crore against a BE of ₹51.49 crore. 
This pattern suggests delays in project execution and resource deployment. The 
Committee recommends better financial planning and faster project implementation to 
ensure that allocated funds are fully utilised. NE-SAC should adopt a structured 
approach for project execution timelines and establish quarterly performance reviews 
to track progress. The Committee recommends closer engagement with state 
governments, local research institutions, and universities to improve the adoption of 
NE-SAC’s geospatial data for policy-making. The Committee suggests that NE-SAC 
integrate AI and machine learning (ML) technologies to enhance land-use analysis, 
climate modelling, and hydrology mapping.                                                           (Para 5.6) 
 The Committee recommends strengthening IIST’s partnerships with industry 
and start-ups, particularly in emerging fields such as AI-driven space applications, 
quantum computing, and advanced propulsion systems. The Committee recommends 
that IIST streamline fund utilisation processes, implement quarterly financial reviews, 
and set clear milestones for research projects to ensure that resources are effectively 
utilised. As IIST plans to align its academic structure with the NEP, the Committee 
recommends integrating interdisciplinary studies and flexible credit-based learning 
systems to offer students broader exposure to space policy, commercial space 
operations, and emerging technologies. The Committee recommends that IIST expand 
incubation support for deep-tech start-ups, encourage student-led space ventures, and 
facilitate technology transfer from ISRO to start-ups to enhance the commercialisation 
of space-based applications.                                                                                      (Para 5.8) 
CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY (CSR) ACTIVITIES IN THE 
DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
 The Committee appreciates the structured approach adopted by both Antrix and 
NSIL in implementing CSR initiatives. However, it recommends that greater emphasis 
be placed on monitoring and evaluating the long-term impact of these projects. Given 
that Antrix spends the majority of its CSR funds through State Government 
Departments, the Committee recommends that a performance assessment framework 
be developed to track the effectiveness of these projects.                                      (Para 6.4) 
The Committee acknowledges the role of the CSR & SD Committee in 
streamlining CSR initiatives under NSIL but recommends greater outreach to 
underrepresented communities, particularly in rural areas, to ensure that space 
technology and innovation contribute to broader societal benefits. The Committee also 
urges greater collaboration between NSIL and academic institutions, start-ups, and 
ISRO units to leverage space-based applications for social development projects. 
Furthermore, the Committee highlights the importance of ensuring that all CSR-

41 
 
implementing agencies maintain high standards of governance, transparency, and 
efficiency. The Committee recommends that third-party audits and impact assessments 
be conducted regularly to ensure CSR funds are being utilised effectively and delivering 
measurable outcomes.                                                                                               (Para 6.5) 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
The Committee observes that the Department faces a 20.48% vacancy rate, 
which may impact operational efficiency. The Committee notes that out of 19,178 
sanctioned posts in ISRO, 3,927 remain vacant, with the most significant gaps in 
administrative staff (2,008) and Scientists/Engineers (1,032). While recruitment actions 
for 1,950 posts are in progress, there is a pressing need to accelerate hiring, particularly 
for S&T roles. The Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) under DoS, such as Antrix and 
NSIL, also report a concerning vacancy rate (265 out of 323 sanctioned posts), which 
may hinder their efficiency in commercial space activities. Similarly, Autonomous 
Bodies (NARL, NESAC, PRL) and IIST also face recruitment challenges, although to a 
lesser extent.                                                                                                               (Para 7.1) 
 The Committee recommends expediting the recruitment process to ensure that 
vacant posts, particularly for Scientists/Engineers and technical staff, are filled within 
the next six months. A dedicated recruitment task force should be established to oversee 
hiring efficiency, identify process bottlenecks, and ensure compliance with recruitment 
timelines. The Committee recommends that the Department must develop a structured 
workforce planning model, forecasting staffing needs for the next decade in alignment 
with ISRO’s Vision 2047. The Committee is concerned about the high vacancy rate in 
NSIL and Antrix, as it may impact India’s growing commercial space sector. It 
recommends an industry-specific recruitment approach to attract talent from both 
public and private space technology domains, ensuring that PSEs remain competitive 
and capable of supporting ISRO’s missions.                                                          (Para 7.3) 
 The Committee supports the Department’s plan to engage S&T personnel on a 
tenure basis but recommends that flexible hiring models be expanded to include 
project-based contracts for emerging space technologies.                                     (Para 7.4) 
 The Committee notes that the backlog in hiring was caused partly due to delays 
during the COVID-19 period and recruitment policy revisions. It recommends 
increasing the frequency of centralised recruitment drives to ensure that vacancies do 
not accumulate in the future. Quarterly recruitment monitoring exercises should be 
conducted to track hiring progress and address any procedural challenges.     (Para 7.5)

9. The Chairman welcomed the Secretary, Department of Space and his team of officers 
and asked them to give a brief presentation on the Demands for Grants (2025-26). Thereafter, 
The Secretary began his presentation by providing an overview of the Department of Space, 
highlighting its major components, including the Indian Space Research Organisation 
(ISRO), the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe), and the 
New Space India Limited (NSIL). He explained that ISRO, being the primary component, is 
responsible for research and development in launch vehicles, satellite applications, planetary 
exploration, and the human spaceflight program. He then presented the major 
accomplishments of the Department of Space over the years, starting from the first sounding 
rocket launch in 1963 to the recent successful missions such as Chandrayaan-3, Aditya-L1, 
and the XPoSat satellite. He highlighted that India has launched 4,002 sounding rockets, 
accomplished 100 launch vehicle missions, and built 131 satellites, including the heaviest 
satellite, GSAT-11, weighing 6,000 kg. He also mentioned that India has launched 433 
satellites for 34 foreign countries, demonstrating its capability in the global space arena. He 
elaborated on the recent achievements of ISRO, including the successful launch of the 
XPoSat satellite on January 1, 2025; INSAT-3DS meteorological satellite and  the successful 
docking experiment conducted in January 2025, which positioned India as the fourth country 
to achieve this feat. He stated that this experiment is crucial for future missions, including the 
development of a space station and the Gaganyaan human spaceflight program. He further 
highlighted the progress in the Gaganyaan program, including the human rating of launch 
vehicles, the development of the orbital module, and the crew escape system. He mentioned 
that the first uncrewed mission is planned for 2025, followed by two more uncrewed missions 
and a crewed mission. While informing about the development of a Next-Generation Launch 
Vehicle (NGLV) capable of placing 30,000 kg into low Earth orbit, he explained that the 
NGLV would use a liquid oxygen and methane propulsion system, which is reusable and 
more cost-effective. Additionally, he highlighted the development of atomic clocks and 
Traveling Wave Tube Amplifiers (TWTAs), which are critical for navigation and 
communication satellites. He also informed about the Department’s plans for India's first 
space station, with the first module targeted for launch by 2028 and the complete space 
station by 2035. He further elaborated on the Chandrayaan-4 and Chandrayaan-5 missions, 
which aims to bring back lunar samples and conduct more advanced lunar exploration.

for space missions, role of the National Atmospheric Research Laboratory in Tirupati in

health monitoring and disaster management, underutilization of funds in previous years and

strategy and its plans to support startups in the space sector, etc.
